title: A game coin balance
summary: Give numbers names, subtract the coins spent, and show what is left.
explanation:
A program is a list of instructions the computer follows.

A value is one piece of information, such as `30` or `"coins"`. Quotes mark text, also called a string. Numbers used for calculations do not need quotes.

A variable gives a value a name. In `const savedCoins = 30;`, the name is `savedCoins` and its value is 30.

`=` assigns the value on its right to the name on its left. `const` means you cannot later assign that name a different value.

Names cannot contain spaces or start with a digit. Capital letters matter: `savedCoins` and `savedcoins` are different names. A semicolon ends this instruction.

`console.log` shows information. It is a function: a reusable action you can ask to run.

The dot selects `log` from `console`. Put what you want to show inside the parentheses.

`console.log(coinsLeft)` shows the named value. With quotes, `console.log("coinsLeft")` shows the text coinsLeft instead.

`=` assigns a value. `===` compares values and gives `true` or `false`. These yes-or-no answers are called Booleans.

For calculations, `-` subtracts, `+` adds numbers, and `*` multiplies.

In your project, use `startingCoins - spentCoins` to calculate `remainingCoins`. The supplied 20 and 7 give 13.

Store the result, then print it. If you change the spending to 5 and run again, the result should be 15.

analogy.familiar: A labeled place on a score sheet
analogy.connection: The name helps you refer to the current number.
analogy.limit: A variable is not always a separate box in computer memory. Objects can be shared through names, and const prevents reassignment of the name but does not freeze every object value.

steps: Replace the TODO value with `startingCoins - spentCoins`.
Print `remainingCoins` and check that it is 13.
Change the spending to 5, predict 15, then run again.

quiz.explanation: The minus sign subtracts 6 from 18. console.log displays the calculated balance, 12.

hints: Use the two names in the subtraction so changes to their values affect the result.

math.explanation: Subtraction finds how much remains after some coins are spent.
math.question: You start with 20 coins and spend 7. How many remain?

title: A page about your favorite place
summary: Use HTML to describe the parts of a page about a place you like.
explanation:
HTML labels the parts of a web page, such as headings, paragraphs, and pictures. A browser reads those labels to show the page. HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. Markup means labels added to content. An element is a whole piece, including its tags and content. In `

Hello!

`, `

` starts a paragraph and `

` ends it. The slash marks the closing tag.

Here is a complete small page. Save it as `index.html` and open it in a browser. ```html Mountain lookout

Mountain lookout

I like watching the clouds drift past.

``` `body` holds the page content. `h1` is the main heading and `p` is a paragraph. `head` holds page information. `title` names the browser tab. `` asks the browser to use modern HTML rules. `lang="en"` says the page is in English. `charset="utf-8"` tells the browser how the file stores letters and symbols.

An attribute adds a setting inside an opening tag. In `lang="en"`, `lang` is the name and `en` is the value. Quotes mark the value's edges. Nesting means putting one element inside another. Close the inner element first: `

Text

`. Indenting the lines helps people see what belongs inside what. HTML describes the content; CSS usually controls its colors and spacing.

An `a` element makes a link. Its `href` attribute gives the destination, and its content gives the visible link words.

Changing the words does not change the destination. Use words that tell readers what they will open, such as Read the park guide.

A link can point to a full web address or a local file. It does not create that destination.

Add these elements inside `body`, after the paragraph. ```html Read the lookout guide ``` `src` gives the picture's file or address. To see this picture, put a real file named `lookout.jpg` beside `index.html`. The web address here is a placeholder. `img` is a void element: it has no content inside it and no closing `` tag. Its settings can use separate lines.

Alt text describes the useful information in a picture. It helps when a picture cannot load and when someone uses a screen reader.

A screen reader presents page information through speech or braille. Write what matters about the picture, not just its filename.

An image used only for decoration usually has `alt=""`. This exercise needs an informative image, so give it a useful description.

Build the favorite-place page with an `h1`, a short `p`, a link, and an image. Use the exact practice address `https://example.org/trail` for the link.

Add a useful image description in `alt`. The checks can find the elements and address, but cannot tell whether your words describe the real picture well.

The example address and image filename are placeholders. Use real destinations and picture files when making your own page.

analogy.connection: Tags label the job of each page part
analogy.limit: A label does not make a link useful unless its destination is correct.

title: A two-page hobby guide
summary: Connect a home page and a supplies page with links.
explanation:
A website can have several HTML files. Each file is a separate page.

A link's `href` gives the path to another file. A path tells the browser where to look. Writing a filename in ordinary text does not make a link.

Save this example as `index.html`. ```html Paper models

Paper models

Build small houses from paper.

See the materials list ``` The link points to `materials.html` in the same folder. This is a relative path: the browser works it out from the current page's address.

Relative paths describe where to look. `materials.html` names a file in the same folder. `images/fold.jpg` looks inside the images folder. `../index.html` moves up one folder first.

Match the real filename exactly. Some servers treat capital and lowercase letters as different. A page's heading does not decide its filename.

A list groups related items. Use `ul` when the order is not a set of steps, and `ol` when the order matters.

Put each item in an `li` element. Real list markup helps browsers and screen readers recognize the group.

Save this as `materials.html` beside the first file. ```html Model materials

Materials

  • Thick paper
  • Glue stick
Back to paper models
``` `main` marks the page's main content. The `ul` contains two items. The return link points back to `index.html`. Both files must exist. Links do not create pages.

Read nesting from the outside inward. Here, `body` contains `main`, and `main` contains the heading, list, and link. The list items belong inside `ul`. Closing `` before the link places that link outside the list.

Keep the starter's Garden journal heading and paragraph. Add a link to `supplies.html` with useful words.

The supplied supplies page already has its list and return link. Download both files into one folder and follow the links in both directions.

If a link fails, compare its path with the actual file's name and location.

analogy.limit: The second file must exist in the project.

title: A clear event page
summary: Give each part of an event page a clear job.
explanation: Some HTML tags tell us what a part of the page is for. `<header>` introduces it. `<nav>` holds navigation links. `<main>` holds the main content. `<footer>` holds closing information. These names describe the parts; they do not choose their colors or sizes.

Here are the main parts of an event page. Put this inside ``. ```html

Science afternoon

Experiments

Experiments

Try making a paper helicopter.

Everyone is welcome.

``` `header` introduces the event. `nav` links to its details. `main` holds those details. `footer` finishes the page.

A landmark is a page area that tools such as screen readers can jump to. `<main>` and `<nav>` create landmarks. Use one visible main area here. `aria-label="Event sections"` gives the navigation a name for those tools; it does not show a heading on the page.

Headings show how ideas fit together. Use `<h1>` for the page’s main subject, `<h2>` for a section, and `<h3>` for a smaller part of that section. Choose the level by meaning, not by the text size you want.

This section contains a smaller section. ```html

Tickets

Group visits

Tell the organizer how many people are coming.

``` `

A link to a place on this page starts its `href` with `#`. The name after `#` must match the destination’s `id`. Each id should appear only once on the page. The visible heading alone does not create a link target.

title: A page usable without a mouse
summary: Describe a useful picture and give a button a clear name.
explanation: People use pages in different ways. Some use a mouse, some use a keyboard, and some use a screen reader that reads the page aloud. Clear HTML helps people understand the page and use its controls.

This example describes a picture and names a button. ```html ``` `src` gives the picture’s filename. `alt` gives words for someone who cannot see it. The button’s text says what it is for. The photo is a practice filename, not an included file. The button needs JavaScript later to perform its action.

`alt` is a text replacement for an image. Describe the useful information someone would miss without seeing it. For a real image, look at the image before writing the description. A purely decorative image can use `alt=""` so a screen reader can skip it.

A button’s visible words usually give it the name a screen reader announces. Use clear words such as `View repair times`. Keep `type="button"` for a button that should not submit a form. A real `<button>` already supports keyboard use.

Use a link to go somewhere and a button to do something. ```html Read workshop directions ``` The link points to another page. The button is for an action on the page. This small example names that action but does not yet add the code to do it.

Keyboard focus shows which control is ready for your next key press. Press Tab to move forward and Shift+Tab to move back. Make sure you can see the focused control. Enter activates a link. Enter or Space activates a button.

For this practice, imagine the picnic photo shows neighbors sharing food at a park table. Add an `alt` description of that scene. Name the button exactly `View picnic details` and set `type="button"`. The photo file is not included. This task checks the description and button name; it does not add the action that opens details.

title: An activity signup form
summary: Build a small signup form with clearly named fields.
explanation: A form groups information someone can enter. Put its fields inside `<form>`. Give each field a visible `<label>` so people know what to type or choose. A hint inside an empty field can help, but it should not replace the label.

This form asks for a name.

```html
<form>
  <label for="visitor">Visitor name</label>
  <input id="visitor" name="visitor" type="text" required>
  <button type="submit">Request information</button>
</form>
```

The label’s `for` matches the input’s `id`. `type="text"` makes a text field. `required` means it cannot be left blank. The submit button asks the form to send its values.

`id` and `name` have different jobs. `id` gives one field a unique label on the page, which `for` can point to. `name` is the key used for that field’s value when the form sends data. Give each field both.

`type="email"` asks the browser to check that the entry looks like an email address. `required` also stops the field being left blank. These checks do not prove the address exists. To stop requiring a field, remove `required`; writing `required="false"` still turns it on.

A `<select>` lets someone choose from `<option>` items.

```html
<form>
  <label for="session">Choose a session</label>
  <select id="session" name="session">
    <option value="music">Music</option>
    <option value="clay">Clay modeling</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Choose session</button>
</form>
```

The label points to the select’s id. `Music` is the text people see. `value="music"` is the value sent for that choice. The button submits the form.

Try an email field with three entries: nothing, an address missing `@`, and `learner@example.org`. A required email field should reject the first two. Browser checks help people correct mistakes. They do not save a signup; that needs a receiving service.

Add name, email and activity fields with the ids `name`, `email` and `activity`. Give each a matching label and a `name` attribute. Require name and email. Use `type="email"` for email and a `<select>` with options for activity. Keep a submit button.

analogy.familiar: A paper registration card with named blanks
analogy.connection: Labels tell people what each input is for
analogy.limit: Browser checks do not replace server validation.

Add a labeled activity select with options.
Keep the submit button, run the checks and try blank or malformed email entries.

title: Group related registration fields
summary: Put related form fields in named groups.
explanation: `<fieldset>` groups related fields. `<legend>` gives the group a name. A registration form can have one group for contact details and another for account details. Grouping helps people understand the form; it does not turn it into separate steps.

This group asks for contact details.

```html
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Participant details</legend>
    <label for="participant">Participant name</label>
    <input id="participant" name="participant" required>

    <label for="reply">Reply email</label>
    <input id="reply" name="reply" type="email" required>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
```

`<fieldset>` wraps the two fields. Its first child, `<legend>`, names the group. Each label points to its input’s id. The submit button stays outside the group but inside the form.

A constraint is a rule for an entry. `required` means it cannot be empty. `type="email"` checks the shape of an email address. `minlength` sets the shortest allowed text. Use `required` too if a short-text field must not be left blank.

Help text explains a field’s rule before someone types. Give the help text an id. Use that id in the field’s `aria-describedby` so a screen reader can connect the help to the field. Keep the visible label as well.

This second group belongs inside the same form, before its button.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Account details</legend>
  <label for="secret">Passphrase</label>
  <input
    id="secret"
    name="secret"
    type="password"
    minlength="10"
    required
    aria-describedby="secret-help"
  >
  <small id="secret-help">Use at least ten characters.</small>
</fieldset>
```

The legend names Account details. `minlength="10"` asks for at least ten characters in this example. `aria-describedby` points to the help note. `type="password"` hides the typed characters on screen; it does not make an account secure by itself.

Try the form by typing. First leave required fields empty. Next try an email without `@` and a short passphrase. Finally type values that meet the rules. The browser should help you find and fix invalid fields. This practice does not create an account.

Make two fieldsets: Contact details and Account details. Give each a legend. Add labeled inputs with ids `name`, `email` and `pass`, and give each a name. Require all three. Use email type for email and password type for pass. This task asks for a minimum of eight characters. Add help text for that rule and keep a submit button.

analogy.connection: Fieldsets group related controls; legends name the groups
analogy.limit: A form does not send or safely store data by itself.

Add the three labeled, required inputs and their rules.
Add passphrase help and a submit button, then run the checks.
Type missing, invalid and valid entries to try the form.

title: A profile card that fits
summary: Make a profile card fit a small space and stop growing in a large one.
explanation: Responsive means adjusting to the space available. `width: 100%` asks a card to fill its parent’s available width. `max-width` sets a limit so the card does not keep growing on a wide screen.

`box-sizing` chooses what a stated width includes. With `content-box`, padding and borders add to the content width. A 300-pixel content area, 12 pixels of padding on each side, and 2-pixel borders use 328 pixels altogether. With `border-box`, the stated 300 pixels already includes padding and borders. Margin stays outside in both cases.

A percentage means a share of another size. For this card, the reference is its parent’s available width. Half of 360 pixels is 180 pixels, so `width: 50%` asks for 180 pixels. A `max-width` can limit the result further.

Resize the preview and look at the card’s edges. Overflow means content sticks outside the available space. A card’s width limit does not stop every long word or large child from overflowing. Keep the supplied image’s shape, and check that the badge and description stay inside.

analogy.familiar: Packing a lunchbox that can expand but still fit inside a small backpack.
analogy.connection: The card can fill a narrow space yet stop growing on a wide screen.
analogy.limit: A width rule cannot guarantee every image or word fits; content still needs sensible limits.

title: A temperature checker
summary: Compare a temperature with a limit and store each yes-or-no answer.
explanation:
A type is a kind of value. Numbers are for calculations, strings are text, and Booleans are `true` or `false`.

`17` is a number. `"17"` is text. A comparison asks how values relate and gives a Boolean answer.

`<` means less than; `>` means greater than. `<=` and `>=` also include equality.

`===` asks whether two values are equal without changing their types. A single `=` stores a value instead.

In `const below = temperature < limit;`, the comparison makes an answer, then `=` stores it.

`"19" === 19` is false: text and a number have different types. `19 === 19` is true.

Changing a value to another type is called coercion. `===` does not do that. Keep the temperatures as numbers.

In the project, 24 is above 22. So `below` and `atLimit` are false, while `above` is true.

Each comparison asks its own question. It does not change the temperature.

Try a number below, at, and above the limit. Print the answers in the same order so you can tell which is which.

Store Booleans, not quoted text. `true` and `"true"` may look similar when printed, but they are different values.

analogy.connection: Comparison operators tell the program which side of the mark a number falls on.
analogy.limit: A Boolean reports true or false; it does not explain why the temperature has that value.

Parentheses hold the condition. Braces hold its action. `else` needs no condition because it handles the remaining cases.

title: A countdown display

explanation:
A loop repeats instructions. One trip through them is an iteration.

A `for` loop has a start, a condition for continuing, and an update. Its braces hold the repeated instructions, called the body.

`for (let n = 4; n >= 1; n--)` means: start at 4, continue while `n` is at least 1, then subtract 1 after each trip.

The two semicolons separate those three parts. `n--` reduces `n` by 1 before the next condition check.

When `n` is 1, the condition is true, so 1 is added. The update changes it to 0. That fails the condition, so 0 is never added.

There are four entries. Their positions, called indexes, start at 0 and end at 3. `length` tells you the number of entries.

Make sure the update moves toward stopping. Increasing a number while checking that it stays above 1 may never stop. A missing update can cause the same problem.

A loop that never stops is an infinite loop. Follow the start, a few repeats, and the stopping check before running.

Its length is 5. Positions 0 and 4 hold the first and last numbers. In the checks, `&&` means both questions must be true.

An array is an ordered list of values. Put its entries inside `[]`, with commas between them.

An index is a position in the array. Positions start at 0, so `tools[0]` reads the first item.

title: A reusable distance converter
summary: Write a function that multiplies a distance by a supplied factor and returns the answer.

A function is a set of steps you can use again. Defining it writes the steps; calling it runs them.

A parameter is an input name in the definition. An argument is the value given in a call.

In `scale(value, factor)`, the input names are `value` and `factor`. Calling `scale(4, 3)` gives them 4 and 3, in that order.

`return` gives an answer back. `console.log` shows information on screen. These are separate jobs.

title: A reaction timer
summary: Measure how much time passes between a signal and a click.
explanation:
A timestamp is a number that tells us when something happened. `Date.now()` gives the current time in milliseconds since the start of 1970 in UTC.

A millisecond is one thousandth of a second.
```javascript
const recorded = Date.now();
console.log(typeof recorded);
console.log(Number.isFinite(recorded));
```
Output:
```text
number
true
```
`typeof` checks the kind of value. `Number.isFinite` checks that it is an ordinary, finite number. The timestamp itself changes as time passes.

Our timer needs to remember two values: when it started and how much time passed. These saved values are its state.

Use `let` because the values can change. Start with `null`, meaning no time is saved yet. Do not use zero for missing time: a real result can be zero.

`startedAt !== null` checks that a start time exists. Without one, the click is ignored.

`Math.max(0, now - startedAt)` chooses the larger number. If the supplied click time is earlier than the start, it saves zero. This avoids a negative result, but cannot fix an incorrect clock.

A real button's click listener could call `clickAt(Date.now())`. The signal action could call `signal(Date.now())`.

Our exercise passes in fixed times instead. That makes the answers easy to check without waiting for a person to click.

Complete `signal`, `clickAt`, and `reset`. The starter's times, 1000 and 1240, should leave `elapsed` equal to 240.

Starting a new round clears the old result. Resetting clears both values.

A device's clock can be adjusted. For more reliable duration measurements in a browser, `performance.now()` uses a clock that does not jump when the date or time is changed.

analogy.familiar: Starting a stopwatch at a signal and stopping it when the player taps.
analogy.connection: Store the first timestamp; subtract it from the click timestamp.
analogy.limit: This small demo uses wall-clock time; production timing may use a monotonic clock to avoid system clock adjustments.

steps: When the signal appears, save the current time as the start time.

title: A data-loading card
summary: Keep track of loading, success, and failure while waiting for data.
explanation:
A Promise represents work that may finish later. It is pending while waiting, fulfilled when it succeeds, or rejected when it fails.

The Promise is not the loaded data. We must wait for its result before using that data.

An `async` function returns a Promise. Inside it, `await` waits for another Promise to finish.

Only that function pauses; the rest of the page can keep working. If the Promise succeeds, `await` gives its value. If it fails, `await` throws the error.

Put work that might fail inside `try`. If it throws an error, the matching `catch` handles it.

`error.message` reads an Error object's message. `Promise.resolve(value)` supplies a successful practice result. `Promise.reject(new Error(...))` supplies a failed one.

Give each stage its own state: `idle` before starting, `loading` while waiting, `success` with data, and `error` with a message.

A page can read this state to decide what to show. `{ status: "success", data }` saves the variable `data` in a property also named `data`.

Complete `loadCard(fetchData)`. Set `cardState` to loading before awaiting `fetchData()`.

Add `showSuccess(data)` to save `{ status: "success", data }`. Add `showError(error)` to save the error status and `error.message`. Call the right helper from the loader.

Keep `successfulLoad` as the Promise returned by the starter call. Wait for loading to finish before checking the final data or error.

analogy.connection: The Promise settles later, and the card switches from loading to success or error.
analogy.limit: This lesson uses supplied Promise scenarios; a real network request can fail, take longer, or return invalid data.

title: A route search game
summary: Find a short route by checking nearby places before farther ones.
explanation:
A graph describes places and their connections. Each place is a node, and each connection is an edge.

An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors. For example, `{ P: ["Q", "R"] }` says P connects to Q and R.

A path lists the places visited on a route. Four places in a path have three connecting edges.

Breadth-first search, or BFS, checks nearby nodes before farther ones.

A queue holds nodes waiting to be checked. `push` adds to its end, and `shift` takes from its front, so the oldest waiting node goes next.

A `Set` remembers nodes already found, so we do not add them twice.

Each queue entry holds a node and the path to it. `[node, path]` names those two parts when the entry is removed.

`visited++` counts the processed node. `graph[node] || []` reads its neighbors, or uses an empty list if none are listed.

For each unseen neighbor, mark it seen and add it to the queue. `[...path, next]` makes a new path ending at that neighbor.

When every edge counts equally, BFS finds a route with the fewest edges. If routes tie, the listed neighbor order decides which is found first.

Remembering seen nodes prevents repeated visits, including loops that lead back to earlier places.

If the queue becomes empty before finding the target, return `path: null` and the number visited.

Complete BFS in `search(start, target)` for the supplied graph. Searching A to F should return A-B-D-F, with 6 nodes processed. That path has 3 edges.

Searching A to Z should return `path: null`. Count nodes when removing them from the queue.

This count shows work on this graph only. It does not prove that one search method is always faster.

analogy.familiar: Finding rooms using a map: check all nearby rooms before going farther, or follow one hallway until it ends.
analogy.connection: BFS explores by distance layers; DFS explores one path deeply.
analogy.limit: A measured visit count depends on the graph and neighbor order; it is not a general runtime benchmark.

steps: Use the supplied graph, which lists the connections between points. Start at A and search for F.
Use breadth-first search (BFS): check nearby points before points farther away.
Keep waiting points in a queue, and check them in the order they were added.

Return the path you found and the number of points you checked.
Also search for a point that is not in the graph. Return null for its path.

quiz.explanation: A queue takes the oldest waiting entry first. R was already waiting before S was added, so R is next.

title: A responsive search tool
summary: Keep an old search answer from replacing the answer to a newer search.
explanation:
Search answers can arrive out of order. A slow old search might finish after a newer one.

Give each search an ID when it starts. Keep the newest ID so the page can tell which answer still matters.

`latestId` starts at zero. Increase it by one for each new search.

A `Set` stores canceled IDs without duplicates. `add(id)` records one, and `has(id)` checks for it. In this exercise, marking an ID canceled does not stop real network work.

The guard checks two things: the answer's ID matches `latestId`, and it is not in `cancelledIds`.

`&&` requires both checks to pass. `!` means not. Only then should `receiveResult` change `visibleResult`.

For real requests, `AbortController` can ask unfinished work to stop. Pass its `signal` to `fetch`, then call `abort()` when the request is outdated.

Keep the ID check too. Cancellation might come too late, and stopping a client request does not undo work already done by a server. Our exercise uses fixed answers instead of network requests.

Add `const cancelledIds = new Set()` to the starter. Complete `beginSearch` so it marks the previous ID canceled, increases `latestId`, and returns the new ID.

Complete `receiveResult` with the two checks. The starter must keep `new answer` visible after `old answer` arrives.

This small example keeps old IDs in the Set. A long-running app should remove records once they are no longer needed.

analogy.familiar: Two people look up answers; the later question should keep its answer even if the earlier lookup finishes last.
analogy.connection: A request number marks which result is current.
analogy.limit: Cancellation is a request to stop work, not proof that every operation stopped; stale-result checks still matter.

steps: In beginSearch, mark the previous nonzero ID canceled, increase latestId, and return it.
In receiveResult, accept only the latest, uncanceled ID.

quiz.question: What should happen when an old response arrives after a newer one?

math.question: Request 4 starts, then request 5 starts. Request 4 finishes last. Which response should remain visible?
choices: Request 5 because it is the latest request
math.feedback: The current request is 5. Finishing later does not make request 4 current; its stale result must be ignored.

title: A tested data-processing tool
summary: Check a list of numbers before adding them together.
explanation:
A reliable function makes its rules clear. Our `total` function accepts an array of numbers that are zero or greater.

Each number must be finite: it cannot be `Infinity` or `NaN`, which stands for not a number. Text such as `"4"` is not accepted.

Check the input before adding anything.

`Array.isArray(values)` checks that the input is an array. `values.some(...)` checks whether any entry breaks a rule. `Number.isFinite(v)` rejects text, infinity, and NaN.

`||` means either condition can be true. `!` means not. Together, these let us spot a bad input.

`throw` stops the normal calculation and sends an error to the caller.

`new TypeError(message)` creates an error with a message about the wrong input. The caller can handle it with `try` and `catch`.

A valid input returns a number. An invalid input throws an error instead of pretending to be a total.

A test checks what the function does with a chosen input. Check an ordinary list, an empty list, zero, negative numbers, text, infinity, and NaN.

Also check a large list. `Array(10000).fill(1)` makes ten thousand entries containing 1. Their total should be 10000.

Complete `total(values)`. Return the sum for valid input. For invalid input, throw a `TypeError` with a clear message beginning with `Expected`.

This exercise uses arrays with no empty gaps. Extremely large sums can exceed what JavaScript numbers can store accurately; deciding how to handle that is beyond this exercise.

analogy.familiar: Checking ingredients before following a recipe, including the empty-bowl case.
analogy.connection: Input checks decide whether the supplied data can safely be processed.
analogy.limit: A handful of tests cannot prove every possible input is correct, but they can reveal common boundary failures.

steps: Accept only an array of numbers that are zero or greater. Reject text, NaN, and Infinity.
Return the sum for a valid array, including an empty array.
For invalid input, throw a TypeError with a message explaining what kind of input is allowed.
Check empty, ordinary, large, negative, and text-containing cases.
solution:
function total(values) { if (!Array.isArray(values) || values.some(v => typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0)) throw new TypeError("Expected an array of finite nonnegative numbers"); return values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0); }
console.log(total([2, 3]));

checks.label: A large valid input is processed

quiz.question: What should `total([])` return when empty input is a valid list?
quiz.explanation: The sum of no nonnegative values is defined here as zero.

hints: Validate that `values` is an array.
Check every entry is a finite number and not below zero.
Use `reduce` with an initial sum of zero after validation.

math.explanation: A total adds every valid item. An empty list adds nothing, so the chosen total is zero.
math.question: If a valid list contains 2, 3, and 5, what is its total?

title: Python Basics
summary: Give a pet’s name and age to Python, then show them in a sentence.
explanation:
A program is a list of instructions the computer follows. A value is a piece of information, such as a name or an age.

Text is called a string in Python. Put matching quotes around it: `"Pepper"`. Single quotes work too. These outside quotes mark where the text starts and ends; they are not part of the text you display.

Write a number such as `5` without quotes when you want to do math with it.

A variable is a name that refers to a value. `pet_name = "Pepper"` gives the name `pet_name` the text value Pepper.

The single `=` gives a value to a name. It does not ask whether two values are equal.

A variable name cannot contain spaces or start with a digit. An underscore, `_`, can join words. Capital and small letters matter: `pet_name` and `Pet_name` are different names.

`print` is a built-in function: a ready-made instruction Python provides. Calling a function asks it to run. Put the values you give it inside parentheses, `()`.

A value given to a function is called an argument. A name without quotes uses its stored value. Quotes make it text instead.
```python
pet_age = 5
print(pet_age)
print("pet_age")
```
Output:
```text
5
pet_age
```
Writing a function's name without calling it does not run the function.

An f-string builds text that includes values. Put `f` just before the opening quote. Braces, `{}`, mark the parts Python works out and puts into the text.

In the next example, `{pet_name}` inserts Pepper and `{pet_age}` inserts 5. Words, spaces and punctuation outside the braces stay as written. The age becomes text in the sentence, but the original `pet_age` is still a number.

The f-string builds the sentence first. Then `print` displays it.

Read this program from top to bottom.
```python
pet_name = "Pepper"
pet_age = 5
print(f"{pet_name} is {pet_age} years old.")
```
The first two lines give values to names. The last line builds and displays the sentence.
```text
Pepper is 5 years old.
```
Normally, each call to `print` starts a new output line after displaying its values.

Without `f`, braces in quoted text are printed as ordinary characters. Inside an f-string, they can also hold a calculation.
```python
pet_name = "Clover"
pet_age = 2
print(f"{pet_name} is {pet_age} years old.")
print("{pet_name} is {pet_age} years old.")
print(f"Next year: {pet_age + 1}")
```
Output:
```text
Clover is 2 years old.
{pet_name} is {pet_age} years old.
Next year: 3
```
In the last line, Python adds one before putting the result into the text.

You can give a variable a new value. Later code uses that new value.

Changing the variable does not rewrite output already shown. Call `print` again to show the new value.

For your pet-profile project, give `print` the named values and connecting words as separate arguments. Python puts a space between them. The extra projects reuse these ideas with different values.

analogy.familiar: A labeled box
analogy.connection: The f-string inserts each named value inside braces.
analogy.limit: A variable can be assigned another value later.

steps: Put pet_name, "is", pet_age, and "years old." inside print(...), in that order. Separate each item with a comma.
solution:
pet_name = "Milo"
pet_age = 3
print(pet_name, "is", pet_age, "years old.")

checks.label: Message uses both values
checks.expression: __output == ["Milo is 3 years old."] and pet_name == "Milo" and type(pet_age) is int and pet_age == 3

pet_age = 3
pet_age = pet_age + 1
print(pet_age)

What does this program display, and why?
choices: 3, because a name keeps its first value.
4, because Python adds 1 to the old age and gives pet_age the new value.
pet_age, because print displays the name itself.
quiz.explanation: Python first works out 3 + 1. It then gives pet_age the value 4. That is what print shows.

title: Types & Comparisons
summary: Check whether a parcel measurement is below, equal to, or above its limit.
explanation:
A type tells Python what kind of value it has. An integer, or `int`, is a whole number.
```python
print(15)
```
A float is a type of number that can have a decimal part.
```python
print(15.5)
```
A string, or `str`, is text. Quotes make these digits text, not a number.
```python
print("15")
```
A Boolean, or `bool`, has just two possible values: `True` or `False`. These names start with capital letters and have no quotes.
```python
print(True)
```

A comparison asks a question about two values. The sign `<` asks whether the left value is smaller.
```python
print(15 < 18)
```
The answer is `True`. The sign `>` asks whether the left value is larger.
```python
print(15 > 18)
```
The answer is `False`. Two equals signs, `==`, ask whether the values are equal.
```python
print(18 == 18)
```
The answer is `True`. Remember: one `=` gives a name a value; two `==` compare values.

A comparison can use named values. Python looks up each name before comparing.
```python
measurement = 15
limit = 18
print(measurement < limit)
print(measurement == limit)
print(measurement > limit)
```
The answers are `True`, `False`, and `False`, on separate lines. The measurement is below the limit. Asking these questions does not change either value. A comparison gives a Boolean value, which you can name or pass directly to `print`.

At the exact limit, the measurement is equal to the limit. It is neither below nor above it.
```python
measurement = 18
limit = 18
print(measurement < limit, measurement == limit, measurement > limit)
```
This shows `False True False`. Commas separate the values in the code; `print` puts spaces between them. The sign `<=` means less than or equal to.
```python
print(18 <= 18)
```
This gives `True` because equal values are allowed. The sign `>=` means greater than or equal to.
```python
print(18 >= 18)
```
This also gives `True`.

Text containing digits does not equal the number written with those digits.
```python
print("18" == 18)
```
This gives `False`. Python cannot use `<` to order a string and a number this way.
```python
print("18" < 18)
```
This causes a `TypeError`: an error about the kinds of values used. Use numbers for both the measurement and the limit. An integer and a float can still have the same number value.
```python
print(18 == 18.0)
```
This gives `True`.

In your project, the measurement and limit are both `12`. Ask the below, equal, and above questions in that order.
```python
measurement = 12
limit = 12
print(measurement < limit, measurement == limit, measurement > limit)
```
The result is `False True False`. If you picture a number line, 12 is at the limit—not to its left or right.

Try changing only the measurement. Keep the limit at `12`.
```python
measurement = 11
limit = 12
print(measurement < limit, measurement == limit, measurement > limit)
```
This shows `True False False`. Now use 12, then 13, and predict the answers before running. A printed `True` is still a Boolean value. Writing `"True"` in your code would make a string instead. This program compares the numbers you give it; it does not measure a real parcel.

analogy.familiar: A ruler with a marked limit
analogy.connection: Compare below, equal, and above as separate cases.
analogy.limit: The text "12" is not the number 12; == checks equality while = assigns.

Use <, ==, and > to ask below, equal, and above, in that order.
Print the three answers on one line, with a space between them.

title: Conditional Statements
summary: Use a moisture reading to choose a reminder.
explanation: A condition is a question with a True or False answer. Indentation means spaces at the start of a line. It shows which instructions belong together. An `if` runs its indented instructions when its condition is True. `else` runs its instructions when that condition is False. This chooses one path. End the `if` line and the `else` line with a colon (`:`). Use four spaces for each indentation level. Lines at the same level need matching spaces.

A function is a named set of instructions. `def` starts a function, followed by its name and parentheses. A parameter is a name inside those parentheses that receives a value. End the `def` line with a colon and indent the instructions inside the function. To call a function means to run it. Write its name followed by parentheses containing the value it needs. `return` sends a result back to the code that called the function and ends that call. Writing `return` outside a function causes an error.

This complete function chooses a message about light.
```python
def light_reminder(brightness):
    if brightness < 40:
        return "Turn on a lamp"
    else:
        return "Enough light"

print(light_reminder(25))
print(light_reminder(40))
```
The instructions inside the function are indented once. The instructions inside `if` and `else` are indented again. The two `print` lines are outside the function.

The `<` sign means less than, so it excludes an equal value. In the light example, 40 makes `brightness < 40` False and returns "Enough light". In your project, the comparison is `moisture < 30`. A reading of 20 returns "Water the plant". Exactly 30, or any larger reading, returns "Moisture is OK".

A conditional expression is a short way to choose between two values. The next function makes the same choice as the earlier light function. In its return line, choose the first string when the condition is True. Otherwise, choose the second string. The supplied project solution uses this form.
```python
def light_reminder(brightness):
    return "Turn on a lamp" if brightness < 40 else "Enough light"

result = light_reminder(39)
print(result)
print(light_reminder(41))
```
It displays `Turn on a lamp` and then `Enough light` on separate lines.

Returning gives a result to other code. Printing displays a value. In the previous example, `result` stores the returned string before `print(result)` displays it. Your project function must return its message so checks and other code can use it. With the completed project function, a comma lets `print` display both returned messages with a space between them: `print(reminder(20), reminder(30))`. This displays `Water the plant Moisture is OK`. The quotes mark strings in code and do not appear in the displayed messages.

Use the parameter `moisture` in your comparison so the message depends on the supplied number. Try a number below 30, exactly 30, and above 30. Replace `moisture` with each number in the condition to predict the result. This practice function receives a supplied number. It does not read a real sensor or decide how every plant should be watered.

analogy.connection: The reading chooses which reminder the function returns.
analogy.limit: The function receives a number; it does not read a real sensor.

Use `else` to return "Moisture is OK" when moisture is 30 or more.

title: Loops
summary: Use a loop to print a task for each of seven days.
explanation:
A loop repeats instructions.

A collection is a group of values. A list is a collection that keeps its values in order. Write a list inside square brackets `[]`, with commas between its values. Day names are text, so put them in quotes.

A Python `for` loop visits each value in a collection, one at a time. When it visits a list, the number of visits comes from that list. Python does not assume every schedule contains seven days.

Read `for day in days:` as: take each value from `days` in order, store it in `day` for this visit, and run the indented instructions.

A loop variable is a name that holds the current value. Here, that name is `day`.

The word `in` introduces the collection to visit. The colon `:` ends the opening line of the loop.

Indentation means spaces at the start of a line. The loop body is the indented instructions that repeat. Usually, you indent these lines with four spaces.

A line back at the loop's original starting position runs after the loop.

Code breakdown — a three-day schedule:
```python
days = ["Monday", "Wednesday", "Friday"]
for day in days:
    print(f"{day}: drawing")
print("Schedule finished")
```
List: `days` contains three day names.

Loop: `day` holds each name in order.

Inside the loop: the indented `print` runs once for each day.

After the loop: the final `print` runs once.

Output:
```text
Monday: drawing
Wednesday: drawing
Friday: drawing
Schedule finished
```

An f-string is text that can include values. The `f` before the opening quote marks it as an f-string.

Breakdown of the previous example's printed text: in `f"{day}: drawing"`, `{day}` inserts the current value of `day`. It inserts Monday on the first visit, then Wednesday, then Friday.

The colon inside the quoted text is punctuation in the output. The colon at the end of `for day in days:` introduces the loop body. The same symbol can have different jobs inside text and outside it.

Changing the list changes the number of visits.

A counter is a variable used to keep a count. This example uses `count` to count the visits.

Code breakdown — count two visits:
```python
days = ["Saturday", "Sunday"]
count = 0
for day in days:
    print(f"{day}: reading")
    count = count + 1
print(count)
```
Starting count: `count = 0` sets the counter to zero before the loop.

Loop body: both indented lines run once for each day.

Updating the count: `count = count + 1` adds one to the current count and stores the result back in `count`.

After the loop: `print(count)` displays the total, which is 2.

Output:
```text
Saturday: reading
Sunday: reading
2
```

With an empty list, the loop body runs zero times.

With seven entries and one task printed per entry, the body runs seven times and prints seven tasks. The number of tasks is visits times tasks per visit: 7 × 1 = 7.

You do not need a counter just to visit each item.

Item positions can be numbered starting at 0. That numbering does not skip an item: four items still get four visits.

If the list stays unchanged, this `for` loop stops after it has visited every item.

Project setup — your seven-day schedule:
```python
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]
# TODO: print one task per day
```
Use a `for` loop to visit each day in `days`.

Inside the loop, write `print(f"{day}: practice")`. Indent it so each day gets its own line, from `Mon: practice` through `Sun: practice`.

If this print line is outside the loop, it runs only once after the loop.

Run the seven-day version and compare its seven output lines with the seven list entries.

After checking that version, try a shorter list to see that the number of visits follows the list.

analogy.connection: The loop prints a task as it reaches each day.
analogy.limit: The number of repetitions comes from the list length; Python does not assume seven days.

title: Lists
summary: Store three collectibles, add another, and print the list and its size.
explanation:
A list stores values in an order and lets you change its contents.

Write square brackets around the values and commas between them. Strings are text values and need quotes, as shown in the code breakdown below.

Giving the list a name lets later instructions use the same list.

Mutable means changeable; Python lists are mutable.

An index is a position in the list. Python starts with index 0 for the first item, then 1 for the second and 2 for the third.

`items[0]` reads the first item in a list named `items`.

A function is a named piece of code you can run to do a job. A built-in function is one Python provides.

`len(items)` is a built-in function that gives back the number of items in `items`. This count is the list's length.

A three-item list has length 3 even though its last index is 2.

Code breakdown — create, count, and read a list:
```python
items = ["leaf", "stone", "feather"]
print(items)
print(len(items))
print(items[0])
```
`items = ["leaf", "stone", "feather"]` creates a list of three strings and names it `items`.

`print(items)` displays the full list.

`print(len(items))` displays its length.

`print(items[0])` displays its first item.

The output is:
```text
['leaf', 'stone', 'feather']
3
leaf
```
Python's display of the list includes brackets and quotes to show its structure.

Printing one string by itself displays the text without surrounding quotes.

The displayed list may use single quotes even when the source used double quotes.

A method is a function that belongs to something, such as a list.

In `items.append(value)`, the dot selects the list's `append` method. Replace `value` with the item to add; the parentheses hold that value.

Append changes the existing list by adding one item at the end. It does not replace the list or remove the earlier items.

Append gives back `None`, a special Python value that means no result. Use append as a separate instruction. Do not save its result as `items`, because that would make `items` hold `None` instead of the list.

Code breakdown — add an item and read the last item:
Continue with `items` from the earlier code breakdown, which contains leaf, stone, and feather. Run this code once after that example:
```python
items.append("button")
print(items)
print(len(items))
print(items[len(items) - 1])
```
`items.append("button")` adds button at the end.

The next two lines display the changed list and its new length.

`items[len(items) - 1]` reads the last item. The length is now 4, so subtracting 1 gives index 3.

The output is:
```text
['leaf', 'stone', 'feather', 'button']
4
button
```
You can also read the final item with `items[-1]`. A negative index counts from the end: `-1` means the last item.

An empty list has length 0 and contains no items.

Reading an index that does not exist causes an `IndexError`. This is Python's error message for a missing list position. Neither `items[0]` nor `items[-1]` can read an item from an empty list.

This exercise starts with three items and has four after append.

Length answers how many items exist. An index tells where an item sits.

The same counting idea applies to seven days with one task per day: 7 × 1 = 7 tasks.

Your original collectibles are shell, badge, and coin. Append the exact string `"stamp"`, then print the full list and its new length.

All four values should remain in this order: shell, badge, coin, stamp.

The count should be the last output line and equal `4`.

In a separate practice run, try appending a different item. Predict both the full list and its length before running the code.

Adding one item increases this list's length by one.

analogy.connection: append adds the collectible at the end of this list.
analogy.limit: Length is a count; the last index is one less because indexes start at zero.

title: Functions
summary: Write a function that multiplies ingredient amounts by a scale factor.
explanation: A function is a named set of steps you can reuse. Define one with `def`, a name, input names in parentheses, and a colon. Its indented steps run when you call it. A parameter is an input name inside the function. An argument is the value you give it in a call. Separate inputs with commas. This project takes a list of amounts and a scale factor: the number each amount is multiplied by.

`return` sends a result back to the code that called the function and ends that call. `print` only displays a value. The recipe scaler must return a new list so checks and other code can use it. `*` means multiply, so `4 * 3` means four times three. Numbers with a decimal point, such as `0.5`, are called floats. They can be multiplied too.

Start with the full loop version to see each step.
```python
def scale(amounts, factor):
    scaled = []
    for amount in amounts:
        scaled.append(amount * factor)
    return scaled

original = [1, 0.5, 4]
result = scale(original, 3)
print(result)
print(original)
```
Expected output:
```text
[3, 1.5, 12]
[1, 0.5, 4]
```
The loop adds each multiplied amount to a new list. `return` comes after the loop, so every amount is handled before the result is sent back.

A list comprehension is a short way to build a new list. Read `[amount * factor for amount in amounts]` as: for each amount in `amounts`, multiply it by `factor` and put the result in the new list. Write the calculation first, followed by `for amount in amounts`, which says which values to go through. Square brackets collect the results into a list. This is still a loop, even on one line.

This complete example uses a list comprehension to do the same job.
```python
def scale(amounts, factor):
    return [amount * factor for amount in amounts]

original = [1, 0.5, 4]
print(scale(original, 3))
print(scale(original, 0))
print(scale([], 3))
print(original)
```
Expected output:
```text
[3, 1.5, 12]
[0, 0.0, 0]
[]
[1, 0.5, 4]
```
A factor of zero makes every amount zero. An empty list has no amounts to change, so the result is another empty list. The function builds a new list without adding to or replacing values in the original list.

Arguments go in order: first the amount list, then the factor. In `scale_recipe([2, 3], 2)`, the calculations are 2 times 2 and 3 times 2, giving `[4, 6]`. A factor of 2 doubles amounts. A factor of 0.5 halves them. The project inputs `[2, 1.5, 3]` doubled give `[4, 3.0, 6]`. The `3.0` is a float because it comes from multiplying the float `1.5` by two.

Write `scale_recipe(amounts, factor)` using its parameters so it works when the inputs change. Return a new list and leave the original amounts unchanged. You may still need the original recipe after making a scaled version. Check a normal call and print the original afterward. Returning one fixed list or changing values in the original list would not meet the project requirements.

analogy.familiar: A recipe multiplier
analogy.connection: The same factor is applied to each ingredient.
analogy.limit: Returning a value and printing it are different actions; a comprehension makes a new list.

steps: Use a list comprehension to go through `amounts` and build a new list.
solution:
def scale_recipe(amounts, factor):
    return [amount * factor for amount in amounts]
amounts = [2, 1.5, 3]
print(scale_recipe(amounts, 2))

title: List Operations
summary: Sort, slice, and update a reading list without losing unrelated entries.
explanation: Organizing a list can mean sorting it, choosing part of it, and replacing one entry. A list is ordered and mutable, so position matters when you change it. Python sorts text by its character order. With the consistently capitalized titles here, that looks alphabetical. A position is called an index. Indexes start at zero.

`sorted(reading)` returns a new sorted list and leaves `reading` unchanged. `reading.sort()` rearranges the existing list and returns `None`. Use `sorted` when you need to keep the original order, and save its result under a different name. With the strings here, changing the new list does not change the original list's entries.

Here is a complete sort-and-update example.
```python
reading = ["Forest", "Bridge", "River"]
organized = sorted(reading)
print(organized)
organized[0] = "A Garden"
print(organized)
print(reading)
```
Output:
```text
['Bridge', 'Forest', 'River']
['A Garden', 'Forest', 'River']
['Forest', 'Bridge', 'River']
```
Assigning to `organized[0]` replaces only its first entry. It does not insert an entry or change the list's length.

Compare `sort` with `sorted`. In this example, `list.sort()` takes no argument. It rearranges the list it is called on and returns `None`, not the sorted list.
```python
titles = ["Moon", "Atlas"]
result = titles.sort()
print(titles)
print(result)
```
Output:
```text
['Atlas', 'Moon']
None
```
The dot selects the list's `sort` method. The empty parentheses call it.

A slice chooses a range of positions. `values[start:stop]` includes the start index and stops before the stop index. The colon separates the two boundaries. For indexes 1 up to, but not including, 3, it selects indexes 1 and 2. A slice returns a new list. Because the stop is excluded, adjacent slices can meet without repeating an entry.

Trace this numeric slice example.
```python
values = [3, 6, 9, 12]
selected = values[1:3]
print(selected)
print(values[0:2])
print(values[2:4])
```
Output:
```text
[6, 9]
[3, 6]
[9, 12]
```
Index 0 holds 3, index 1 holds 6, index 2 holds 9, and index 3 holds 12. The first slice leaves out index 3. Here, the slice length is stop minus start: 3 minus 1 equals two entries.

A slice keeps the items chosen when you make it. Replacing an entry in the original list later does not replace that entry in the slice.

A slice is a shallow copy: the outside list is new, but it still uses the same items. If an item is another list, both outside lists share that inner list. These examples use strings and numbers.

Reading a missing position with an index causes an error. A slice that goes past the end simply stops at the end.

Your supplied titles sort into Atlas, Moon, Willow. Select indexes 1 and 2 to get Moon and Willow, then replace the first organized title with A New Beginning. The source `reading` list must keep its original order. Predict the list after each line to catch an incorrect sort, slice, or replacement on its own.

analogy.connection: Use a sorted copy to arrange titles without changing their source order.
analogy.limit: sort() changes a list in place; sorted() returns a new list.

title: String Operations
summary: Trim outside spaces, change case, and count words while keeping internal spacing.
explanation: Strings are immutable, which means their existing characters cannot be changed in place. Cleanup methods return new strings. A method is a function used with a dot after a value, such as `text.strip()`. Store the result if later code needs the cleaned text. The original string stays available under its earlier name.

`.strip()` removes whitespace from the beginning and end. Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and line breaks. It does not remove spaces between words. `.lower()` returns a lowercase version. `text.strip().lower()` first trims the outside, then lowercases that result. Empty parentheses mean these methods need no extra input for their usual behavior.

This complete example shows each cleanup step.
```python
text = "  Make   Art  "
trimmed = text.strip()
cleaned = trimmed.lower()
print(trimmed)
print(cleaned)
print(text == "  Make   Art  ")
```
It displays `Make   Art`, `make   art`, and True. The three spaces between the words are preserved. The equality check confirms the original still has its initial spaces and capitalization. Assignment stores returned strings instead of changing `text` in place.

`.split()` with no argument separates a string into words using whitespace. Repeated spaces act as one separation, and surrounding whitespace does not create empty words. The result is a list of strings. `len(...)` counts its entries. `.split(" ")` is different: it splits at each space inside the quotes and can produce empty strings between repeated spaces. Use the no-argument form for this word count.

Here is a reusable cleaner and counter.
```python
def clean_note(text):
    cleaned = text.strip().lower()
    words = cleaned.split()
    return cleaned, len(words)

print(clean_note("  Make   Art  "))
print(clean_note("   "))
print("sun   moon".split())
```
The outputs are `('make   art', 2)`, `('', 0)`, and `['sun', 'moon']`. The comma in the return gives back a tuple, an ordered group. Here the cleaned text comes first and the count second. The empty cleaned string has no words, so its count is zero.

This word count uses whitespace, not a language dictionary. Punctuation attached to a word stays with it. For example, red followed by several spaces and then blue has two words. The extra spaces do not add words. Count the nonempty pieces produced by `split`: one for red and one for blue.

Your required input `Read every day`, with extra spaces outside and inside, becomes lowercase text while keeping its internal spacing. Its word count is 3. Input made only of spaces becomes an empty string with count 0. Return both values so tests can inspect them. Keep the spaces between words as they are in the cleaned string you return.

analogy.connection: Clean edge spaces and normalize case before counting words.
analogy.limit: split(" ") treats a literal space differently and can create empty pieces.

title: Tuples, Dictionaries, & Sets
summary: Use a tuple for coordinates, a dictionary for details, and a set for unique tags.
explanation: Different collections fit different jobs. A tuple holds ordered values. You cannot replace a value through a tuple index. A dictionary connects keys to values, so you can look up details by name. A set keeps unique members and has no meaningful position order. Choose based on whether you need a fixed sequence, named fields, or uniqueness.

A tuple often uses parentheses, such as `(7, 2)`, with commas between values. Its first position is index 0. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(7,)`. Parentheses alone around 7 do not make a tuple. You cannot assign a new value to `point[0]`. A tuple name can still be reassigned to a different tuple. A value inside a tuple can still change if that value itself can change. The coordinate tuple here contains only numbers.

A dictionary uses braces with a colon between each key and value.
```python
point = (7, 2)
item = {"title": "Garden Log", "year": 2018}
print(point[0])
print(item["title"])
item["year"] = 2019
print(item["year"])
```
This prints 7, Garden Log, and 2019. Brackets with a number read a tuple position. Brackets with a string key read a dictionary field. Dictionary entries can be updated; changing the year does not replace the title.

A set also uses braces, but its entries do not have key/value colons. `{"nature", "art", "nature"}` keeps only one nature entry. `len(tags)` counts distinct members. Sets do not supply ordered indexes, so do not use `tags[0]`. An empty set is `set()` because empty braces `{}` create a dictionary. Choose a list when order and duplicates matter.

```python
tags = set(["nature", "art", "nature"])
print(len(tags))
print(len(set()))
```
This prints 2, then 0. `set` takes a collection of values and returns a new set of its distinct values. With no argument, it returns an empty set. The list input is not changed.

This complete example demonstrates uniqueness and shared members.
```python
tags = {"nature", "art", "nature"}
print(len(tags))
print("nature" in tags)
first = {"gold", "silver"}
second = {"silver", "copper"}
shared = first & second
print(len(shared))
print("silver" in shared)
```
It prints 2, True, 1, and True. The `in` comparison asks whether a member belongs to a collection. The ampersand `&` finds the intersection: members present in both sets. No output relies on which order a set happens to display.

The math question gives red and blue in one set and blue and green in the other. Blue is the only shared member, so the intersection size is 1. The same uniqueness idea removes a duplicate tag in your project. A tuple's ordered pair is useful for coordinates. A dictionary's keys are useful for title and year. A set's distinct membership is useful for tags.

Your supplied coordinates are (4, 9). The dictionary's title is Cloud Atlas. Repeated mystery tags should count once alongside travel. That gives two distinct tags. Read the title using its key and use `len` to check the set's size. Do not turn it into a list just to depend on a displayed order. This project needs uniqueness, not ordering.

analogy.connection: Use coordinates as a pair, named facts as keys, and tags as unique labels.
analogy.limit: Sets have no reliable display order; use a list when order matters.

title: List Comprehensions
summary: Build a new list from numbers that meet conditions using a list comprehension.
explanation: A list comprehension builds a new list by visiting input values and calculating selected results. Its general shape is `[expression for item in collection if condition]`. Read the for/in part first to find the input values. Then read the optional if part to decide which values to keep. The part before for decides what goes into the new list. Reading values from the original list does not change it.

The remainder sign `%` helps check evenness. `n % 2` gives the remainder after dividing n by 2. An even whole number has remainder zero. So `n % 2 == 0` asks whether n is even. `==` compares; `=` assigns. The second condition, `n > 5`, asks whether the number is greater than 5. `and` requires both conditions to be true.

This complete example filters the list but keeps each chosen number the same.
```python
numbers = [1, 4, 7, 10, 12]
kept = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0 and n > 5]
print(kept)
print(numbers)
```
It prints `[10, 12]` and `[1, 4, 7, 10, 12]`. Four is even but is not greater than 5. Seven is greater than 5 but is not even. Ten and twelve pass both. The first n in the comprehension puts the kept number itself into the result.

The equivalent longer loop makes the selection steps visible.
```python
numbers = [1, 4, 7, 10, 12]
kept = []
for n in numbers:
    if n % 2 == 0 and n > 5:
        kept.append(n)
print(kept)
```
This also prints `[10, 12]`. The if block is indented inside the loop. The append line is indented inside the condition. A comprehension is still a loop. It just writes these steps in a shorter way. Use a longer loop when several actions or conditions become hard to read together.

The part before `for` can transform a selected number. `[n * 3 for n in numbers if n > 5]` would multiply each qualifying number by three instead of keeping n itself. The filter checks the original n before deciding to include the result. In your exercise, you need the original qualifying numbers, so the first part should just be n.

Check both conditions separately before joining them. For 4, the even question is True and the greater-than-5 question is False. So `and` gives False. For 6, both are True. For 7, evenness is False. Five itself is left out because it is not greater than 5. The quiz tests this math skill: an entry must satisfy every stated condition, not just one of them.

The supplied list is [2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9]. Its qualifying entries are 6 and 8, producing [6, 8] in their original order. The input list should remain unchanged. Try explaining why each rejected value fails. Two and four are too small. Five is odd and not greater than 5. Nine is odd. A new filtered list is separate, so the source remains available for other uses.

analogy.familiar: A sorting tray
analogy.connection: Only values that pass both conditions enter filtered.
analogy.limit: A comprehension is still a loop; use several lines if it becomes hard to read.

Keep a value only if it is even and greater than 5.
Put the kept values in a new list without changing `numbers`.

title: Classes
summary: Make reading sessions that each keep their own title and minutes.
explanation:
A class describes a kind of object you can make. Each object made from it is called an instance.

Our class describes a reading session. Each session keeps its own title and number of minutes. Making a second session should give it its own values.

`class ReadingSession:` starts the class. Inside it, `__init__` sets up each new session. This setup method is called an initializer. A method is a function defined in a class.

Here, `self` means the session being set up. In `self.minutes = minutes`, the name on the right holds the supplied number. The part on the left saves that number on this session. Keep both underscores before and after `init`.

Watch what happens when only the first session gets more minutes.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes += amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
print(first.minutes)
print(second.minutes)
```
It prints `23`, then `25`. Only the first session changes.

`Session(...)` makes a session and runs its setup. In `first.add_minutes(8)`, Python passes `first` into `self`. The number `8` goes into `amount`.

`self.minutes += amount` reads the saved minutes, adds `amount`, and saves the new total. Here it means the same as `self.minutes = self.minutes + amount`.

The dot selects something that belongs to this session. This method changes its saved minutes, so it does not need to return a number. Read `first.minutes` to see the new total.

Now give each session some extra minutes.
```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    def add_minutes(self, amount):
        self.minutes = self.minutes + amount

first = Session("Nature", 15)
second = Session("Art", 25)
first.add_minutes(8)
second.add_minutes(4)
print(first.title, first.minutes)
print(second.title, second.minutes)
```
It prints `Nature 23`, then `Art 29`. Each call changes only the session before the dot.

Save each session's changing data on `self`. These saved values are called instance attributes, or fields.

A value set directly inside the class, outside its methods, is a class attribute. Objects can share it. If that value is a list, changing the shared list can affect other sessions too.

Keep the indentation: methods sit inside the class, and their instructions sit inside each method.

Build `ReadingSession`. Poetry starts at 20 minutes. Adding 10 makes 30. History starts at 35 and should stay at 35.

In `first.add_minutes(10)`, `self.minutes` is the first session's saved minutes.

For the separate math question, the total grows from 25 to 40. Subtract: `40 - 25 = 15` minutes were added.

analogy.familiar: A session card for each reading block
analogy.connection: Each session stores its own duration on self.
analogy.limit: A class variable is shared; instance state belongs on self.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
summary: Use one function with objects that do the same action in different ways.
explanation:
Two objects can offer the same action but do it differently. Our shared function asks an object to send a notice. A bell rings. A light flashes.

The actions code expects an object to have are called its interface. Here, the needed action is `announce()`.

Our function only needs the object to have the right method. It does not need a certain class name or a shared parent class. This is called duck typing.

Both objects have an `announce` method, but each method can return a different message. When we call the method, `self` refers to that object.

Follow the message back through the calls. `send_notice` receives an object as `notice`. The dot in `notice.announce()` selects its method, and `()` runs it.

That method returns a message. `send_notice` returns the same message, and `print` shows it.

Without `return` in `send_notice`, that function would give back `None` instead.

For your delivery project, give both `BikeDelivery` and `LockerDelivery` a `process(self)` method.

The bike method returns `"Rider takes parcel"`. The locker method returns `"Parcel goes to locker"`.

In `process_delivery(item)`, call `item.process()` and return its result. The classes do not need a shared parent. Using the same action name for different behavior is called polymorphism.

Keep each delivery's work in its own method. Let the shared function call that method. Try both objects and check their messages.

The separate math question uses an inclusive range from 0 through 10. Inclusive means both ends count, so 10 is allowed.

analogy.connection: The caller asks either delivery object to process its parcel.
analogy.limit: This is duck typing; a common parent class is not required.

title: Modules
summary: Put conversion functions in a module and import them into a separate program.
explanation: A module is a Python file whose code another file can import. The file `measurement_toolkit.py` has the module name `measurement_toolkit`. Leave `.py` out of the import statement. Imports let a program reuse functions defined elsewhere. Python must find the module on its import path: the places it searches. For this project, keep the supplied files together.

A conversion factor is a number used to change measurements from one unit to another. One kilometer equals about 0.621371 miles. Multiply kilometers by that factor to get miles. Divide miles by the same factor to get kilometers. The star `*` multiplies, and the slash `/` divides. A constant is a value meant to stay unchanged. Python programmers usually give constants uppercase names, but Python still allows their values to change.

Save this complete example file as `measurement_toolkit.py`.
```python
MILES_PER_KILOMETER = 0.621371

def km_to_miles(km):
    return km * MILES_PER_KILOMETER

def miles_to_km(miles):
    return miles / MILES_PER_KILOMETER
```
Each function receives one number and returns a converted number. This file defines reusable calculations and does not print by itself. `return` sends the number to the code that called the function. That code can decide how to display it.

Save this as a separate main program beside the module, then run the main program.
```python
from measurement_toolkit import km_to_miles, miles_to_km

print(round(km_to_miles(8), 2))
print(round(miles_to_km(2), 2))
```
Output:
```text
4.97
3.22
```
`from` names the module. `import` names the two functions to use in this file. The comma separates the names. Python runs the conversion first, then rounds the result, then prints it. This two-file example requires the previous module file.

`round(number, 2)` rounds a number to two decimal places. It returns a number, so it does not guarantee that printing it will show two digits after the decimal point. Python cannot store some decimal numbers exactly. Rounding helps display the approximate results in this lesson. It does not change the conversion factor.

Your supplied calls convert 5 kilometers and 3.1 miles. Five times 0.621371 is 3.106855, which rounds to 3.11 miles. Dividing 3.1 by 0.621371 gives about 4.989 kilometers, which rounds to 4.99. The units tell you which direction to calculate. The matching math uses a different factor: 2.5 kilometers times 1000 meters per kilometer equals 2500 meters.

You can also check the calculation in one file before practising imports:
```python

    return km * MILES_PER_KILOMETER

print(round(km_to_miles(10), 2))
print(round(miles_to_km(1), 2))
```
Output:
```text
6.21
1.61
```
These changed inputs use the same formulas as the two-file example. This one-file calculation does not demonstrate importing. Practising imports still requires the paired files shown earlier. Both approaches make the unit direction clear and round only the final returned number.

Use the imported functions instead of copying the conversion calculations into the main program. Keep both files available and spell their names exactly. Avoid giving another file in the same folder the same name as a module you need. The checks call the functions and compare the two printed rounded results. If an import fails, first check whether the file exists where Python is looking. Correct conversion math cannot fix a missing module.

title: Errors & Exceptions
summary: Handle missing input and invalid numbers with clear messages.
explanation:
Input can be missing, have the wrong form, or fall outside the allowed range. Handle each case separately so the message says what went wrong.

An exception is Python's signal that an operation failed. If code does not handle it, the error stops that part of the program. A `try/except` block can handle expected errors while leaving other bugs visible.

Check missing input first. None means no value was supplied. `""` is an empty string. `raw is None` checks the no-value marker. `raw == ""` compares text. The word or means either condition is enough. When input is present, `float(raw)` tries to turn the text into a number with decimals. Text like `"many"` cannot convert and raises ValueError.

This complete example catches invalid numeric text.
```python
def parse_number(raw):
    try:
        value = float(raw)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return "Enter a number"
    return value

print(parse_number("42.5"))
print(parse_number("many"))
```
It prints 42.5 and `Enter a number`. The parentheses in except group the two expected exception types. TypeError covers a value of an unsuitable kind. ValueError covers a value that cannot be read as the requested number. After a successful conversion, execution continues after the except block.

A number can convert successfully and still be out of range. `0 <= score <= 100` is a chained comparison: it requires both lower and upper limits. The inclusive signs allow 0 and 100 themselves. `not` reverses the true/false answer. Check the range after conversion. Do not mix up an out-of-range number with text that was never numeric.

Here is an independently runnable full-range example with different bounds.
```python
def parse_percent(raw):
    if raw is None or raw == "":
        return "Please enter a value"
    try:
        value = float(raw)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return "Enter a number"
    if not 0 <= value <= 50:
        return "Value must be from 0 to 50"
    return f"Accepted: {value:g}"

print(parse_percent(None))
print(parse_percent("many"))
print(parse_percent("50"))
print(parse_percent("51"))
```
The four outputs are `Please enter a value`, `Enter a number`, `Accepted: 50`, and `Value must be from 0 to 50`. Every branch returns a useful result.

The f-string's `{value:g}` inserts the number using general number formatting. The colon starts a format instruction. `g` avoids an unnecessary .0 for whole values such as 50. It is not a separate variable named `g`. Catch only expected conversion exceptions. Catching every possible exception could hide a misspelled name or another programming mistake that should be fixed.

Your score range is 0 through 100. Missing values return `Please enter a score`. Malformed input returns `Enter a number`. Outside values return `Score must be from 0 to 100`. A valid 100 returns `Accepted: 100`. For the math question, 75 is within the inclusive range. -1 and 101 are outside. The range check also rejects NaN (not a number) and infinities, because they do not pass both bounds.
