choices: No, it is above the maximum
No, because it is not zero
math.feedback: The stated maximum is 5, so 6 is outside the allowed range.

title: Plan trips with flexible details
summary: Let different types provide the same useful information through a shared requirement.
explanation: A protocol lists requirements a type promises to provide. A function can use those shared requirements without knowing the exact type it receives.

`var description: String { get }` requires a readable text property. A type may store that text or calculate it when read. `get` requires reading; it does not forbid the type from also allowing changes.
A type conforms to a protocol when it declares that promise and provides the required parts. `any DrawingTool` can hold a value of a type that meets DrawingTool's requirements.
A protocol does not decide whether values are copied or objects are shared. The actual type decides that. The structs in this example use value behavior, while a class would still use references.
The trip project also has an optional note. Use `?? "No extra note"` for nil, or use if let to read a present note. Empty text is present text, so it does not take the nil fallback.

Create Transport, Train, Bicycle, and Trip as requested. Build `summary` for Salem with Train and nil. Build `bikeSummary` for Eugene with Bicycle and `Pack a light`. Read the transport's description through the shared protocol.

analogy.familiar: A form with optional boxes
analogy.connection: An optional is like a form field that may be left blank, and a protocol is like a shared instruction each transport follows.
analogy.limit: A blank optional still needs a useful explanation; silently replacing every missing value can hide important information.

steps: Define Transport with a readable String description.
Make Train and Bicycle provide that description.
Create Trip with a destination and optional note.
Build both supplied summaries, handle nil safely, and run the checks.

checks.label: Changed trip and empty present note
checks.expression: { let trip = Trip(destination: "Corvallis", note: ""); let text = tripSummary(trip, by: Bicycle()); return text.contains("Corvallis") && text.contains("Bicycle") && !text.contains("No extra note") }()

quiz.question: A trip's optional note is nil. What does that mean?
choices: The note holds the word nil
An empty text value is present
quiz.explanation: nil means no value. Empty text and the word nil are both actual text values.

hints: Use `any Transport` for the shared transport input.
A computed property can return each transport's description.
Include the destination, transport description, and note or fallback.

math.explanation: Valid input ranges: State allowed inputs and check missing, boundary, and invalid values.
math.question: A valid trip length must be 1 through 30 days. Is 0 valid?
choices: No, it is below the minimum
Yes, because zero is a number
math.feedback: The valid range starts at 1, so zero is outside it.

title: Make a practice tracker screen
summary: Use local state to update a SwiftUI screen when an entry is added.
explanation: SwiftUI describes app screens using Swift. State is data the screen keeps while it is in use. @State marks data owned by this view. When that data changes, SwiftUI updates the affected parts of the screen.

Use an iOS SwiftUI app project in Xcode. The example replaces ContentView.swift; keep the generated App file that starts the app. Run it in an Apple simulator or device. The browser cannot run this SwiftUI screen.

Text shows words, TextField accepts typing, and Button runs an action when pressed. VStack arranges views vertically. NavigationStack provides a navigation area and title. body describes the view's contents. A modifier, such as .padding(), adds a requested change to a view.

A binding is a connection that can read and change a value. $draft connects the text field to the draft state. Plain draft would supply text without that writable connection. Local @State does not save entries across app launches.

Trimming removes spaces and line breaks at the ends, leaving spaces inside a sentence. Each row uses its array position as its ID, so repeated text can appear twice. Positions work for this append-only example; deleting or reordering rows needs a more lasting ID.

Complete the supplied practice tracker using draft and entries. Add valid text and check that one row appears and the field clears. Try spaces only: no row should be added. Add the same text twice: two rows should appear. The controls are inside VStack, not a separate Form view.

analogy.familiar: A whiteboard list
analogy.connection: Local state is like the list on a whiteboard: changing it changes what everyone sees on that screen.
analogy.limit: State in one view is temporary unless you add persistence or share it with another owner.

steps: Open a SwiftUI iOS app project in Xcode and keep its App file.
Complete the supplied ContentView with draft, entries, and the Add entry action.
Check valid text, spaces only, and repeated text in a simulator or device.

quiz.question: A text field changes @State name, and a Text view displays name. What happens when you type Ari?
choices: SwiftUI updates the affected text from the changed state
Only the text field can change
The name is saved across every app launch
quiz.explanation: The binding changes state, and SwiftUI updates the view. This local state is not permanent storage.

hints: Bind the text field to $draft.
Trim before checking whether text is empty.
Append valid text, then clear draft.

math.explanation: Time differences and units: Subtract two timestamps and convert the result into the displayed unit.
math.question: A session begins at 2:15 and ends at 2:45. How long is it?
math.feedback: Subtract 2:15 from 2:45 to get 30 minutes.

externalNotes: Manual Apple check: keep the Xcode app's generated entry point and run ContentView in an iOS simulator or device. Check valid, blank, and repeated input. The browser and command-line companion cannot verify this screen.

title: Load data with cancellation
summary: Keep an older load from replacing the current result.
explanation: Two loads can finish in a different order from when they started. Give each new request a larger number. Before showing its answer, check that its number still matches the current request.
async marks a function that may pause. await marks a call where that pause may happen. Other work can run while it waits, so do not assume the request is still current when it resumes.

Task represents asynchronous work. Save its handle so cancel() can ask it to stop. Cancellation is a request, not an instant stop. Task.checkCancellation() throws when cancellation is requested; Task.isCancelled lets code check the flag.

accepts(request:current:) should return request == current. After each await, check both that the task is not cancelled and that its request number still matches. A longer delay cannot replace these checks.

An actor protects its own changing data. The store accepts a replacement only when its number is at least as new as the last stored request. This prevents an older result from overwriting a newer stored result. The loader separately checks which request is current.

@MainActor protects the loader's state on the main actor, which is used for UI work. It does not prevent changes while an awaited call pauses. Check the request again after that call before changing visible data. Cancelling also advances the request number, making earlier work outdated.

Use clear messages for loading, success, failure, and cancellation. An outdated task must not replace the current message either. Handle CancellationError separately from other errors, and check the request number in each error-handling path.

Complete the supplied loader and run its driver. Slow request 1 followed by request 2 must leave session-2 visible and stored. Request 0 must show Could not load practice data. Explicit cancellation must preserve session-2 and show Load cancelled. The driver waits for the actual task handles to finish.

analogy.familiar: A deli ticket
analogy.connection: A request ID works like a ticket number: only the currently served ticket may update the display.
analogy.limit: Cancellation does not instantly erase work; the operation must reach a cancellation check or support cancellation itself.

steps: Make accepts compare the request number with the current number.
Have the store reject replacements older than its saved request.
Cancel old work and save a fresh request number when starting.
Check cancellation and the request number after each await.
Run the supplied driver and check its result and messages.

checks.label: Latest async request wins in display and actor

quiz.question: What keeps an old response from replacing the current result?
choices: Checking that its request number is still current
Storing its text in a String
quiz.explanation: The request number tells you whether this response still belongs to the current load.

hints: Capture the new request number before starting its task.
Use the returned Task handle to wait for completion.
Keep useful results when cancelling; update only the current message.

math.explanation: State transitions and event ordering: List valid transitions and reason about two possible orders of asynchronous events.
math.question: Two requests start in order: A has ID 4, B has ID 5. B completes, then A. Which value should remain visible, and why?
choices: B, because only ID 5 is current
math.feedback: Keep B. Once ID 5 is current, the late ID 4 result fails the current-request check.

externalNotes: Run with Swift 6 language mode in a compatible Swift companion or local toolchain. The browser cannot run this Swift code. The store tracks the last saved request; it is not told whenever a new request starts or is cancelled. A real Apple interface needs its own Xcode checks.

title: Save a durable practice log
summary: Save entries to a file and handle data that cannot be read.
explanation: Persistence means keeping data so it can be loaded later. A file can keep data after a program ends. A temporary file may be removed, so this exercise checks saving and loading within one run.

A model describes the data you store. ReadingEntry holds a title and minutes. Codable lets Swift convert this model into saved data and back. Equatable lets the example compare restored entries with the originals.

JSON is a text format for storing data. JSONEncoder turns the entries into Data, a collection of bytes. JSONDecoder turns those bytes back into the requested type. [ReadingEntry].self tells it to expect an array of ReadingEntry values.
Decoding can fail if the saved data is damaged or has the wrong shape. try marks the possible failure. do-catch handles it. Give a clear message and safe result; try! would crash if decoding fails.

The .atomic option writes through a temporary file before replacing the destination. This reduces the risk of exposing a partly written file. It does not combine several files into one change or protect against two writers replacing each other's work.

The exercise has two loadEntries functions with different inputs. loadEntries(_:) decodes supplied bytes. loadEntries(from:) reads a file, then uses the byte decoder. Both return entries and a message. Failed loading should not automatically overwrite the damaged file.

Make PracticeEntry Codable. Encode the supplied Swift entry with 20 minutes, save it with .atomic, and load it from its file URL. For the supplied broken bytes, return an empty list and a message containing could not be read. Keep those words so the checks can recognize the recovery message.

analogy.familiar: A labeled archive box
analogy.connection: Persistence is like putting a labeled box on a shelf and opening it the next day.
analogy.limit: A shelf can contain a damaged label or an old format, so loading still needs an error path.

steps: Make PracticeEntry Codable and encode the supplied entry.
Write it to the supplied file URL using .atomic.
Read the file and decode its entries.
Handle broken data with an empty list and a clear message.

quiz.question: Why handle decoding with do-catch?
choices: Saved data may be damaged or use the wrong format
quiz.explanation: Decoding can fail. catch lets the program respond without crashing.

hints: Return LoadResult on both success and failure.
Use the URL loader to read bytes, then reuse the byte loader.

math.explanation: Consistency invariants: Prove the conserved total for a valid update and check interrupted and concurrent cases.
math.question: A tracker has 12 saved entries. One valid operation moves 3 entries from the “planned” group to “done.” How many total entries should exist afterward, and what failure case could break the invariant?
choices: 9; deleting planned entries is always expected
12; a crash between delete and insert could break it
math.feedback: A move preserves the total at 12. If the two writes are not atomic, interruption between them can lose or duplicate entries.

externalNotes: The Swift companion removes its temporary files after each run. This exercise does not prove saving across app restarts. A real app needs a persistent storage location and a save, stop, and reopen check in Xcode. Foundation also needs a compatible Swift toolchain.

title: Check a large list fairly
summary: Count search checks to see how the work grows with the list.
explanation: A linear search checks items one by one until it finds a match or reaches the end. Count each comparison to see how much work it does. Test a first item, a last item, and a missing value.

Array positions start at zero. Position 2 holds the third item. enumerated() supplies each item's position and value in this array. Int? means the returned position may be a whole number or nil when no match exists.

Add one to comparisons before each equality check. Return as soon as a match is found. That gives one comparison for a first-item match. Empty arrays need zero comparisons, and repeated matches return the first matching position.
To compare input sizes fairly, search for the last item in both lists. Searching the first item in one list and the last in another would compare different amounts of work for another reason.

For a last-item match, a list of 100 items takes 100 comparisons. A list of 200 takes 200. Doubling the size doubles this worst-case work. A first-item match can still take only one comparison at either size.

A work count is repeatable for the same method and input. Running time can also change because of hardware, other programs, or compiler settings. Counting comparisons explains this search's work; it does not measure every cost in the app.

Complete find with an optional index and a comparison count. Save smallRun for 99 in 100 entries, largeRun for 199 in 200 entries, and missingRun for -1 in the smaller array. Expect counts of 100, 200, and 100. Finding 0 in the smaller array should take one check.

analogy.familiar: Finding a name in a roster
analogy.connection: A linear search checks one roster entry at a time until it finds the name.
analogy.limit: A comparison count explains work for this algorithm; it does not predict every source of elapsed time.

steps: Count each compared item and return the first matching position.
Return nil and the full count when no item matches.
Check both their positions and their work counts.

checks.label: First item takes one comparison
checks.expression: find(0, in: sample).index == 0 && find(0, in: sample).comparisons == 1

checks.label: Empty and repeated target
checks.expression: find(4, in: []).index == nil && find(4, in: []).comparisons == 0 && find(4, in: [4, 4]).index == 0 && find(4, in: [4, 4]).comparisons == 1

quiz.question: Why count comparisons as well as measuring time?
choices: The count is less affected by other computer activity
The count proves every part of a program is fast
quiz.explanation: The same search on the same input makes the same number of comparisons. Its running time can still vary.

hints: Use enumerated() for the array's positions and values.
Increment the count before checking for a match.
Keep the same last-item condition when comparing sizes.

math.explanation: Algorithm growth and measurement: Compare work as input size grows and distinguish theoretical growth from one timing result.
math.question: A linear scan checks n items in the worst case. If n grows from 500 to 2,000, about how many times as many comparisons should it perform?
math.feedback: The input is four times larger, so a linear scan performs about four times as many comparisons. One timing measurement can still vary.

externalNotes: This exercise compares search work at two list sizes. It does not measure a faster UI. To compare two search methods, use the same input and expected answer and include any setup work.

title: Type a score card
summary: Describe a player and turn their score into a sentence.
explanation: TypeScript adds type checking to JavaScript. A compiler is a tool that checks the code and turns it into JavaScript. `number` means a number, `string` means text, and `boolean` means true or false.
`runner: Runner` describes the input. The final `: string` describes the returned text. Backticks make a text template. Each `${...}` inserts a value into it.
Inference means working out a type from the code. TypeScript can work out that an object with name as text and laps as a number matches Runner. You do not have to write every type label yourself.
A lap count of `"9"` is text because it has quotes. It does not match the number type. TypeScript reports this before the app runs the code.
For the project, Player has a text name and a numeric score. Make scoreSummary return a sentence such as Mina has 12 points. Use the supplied player's values and include the spaces and final period.

Type descriptions disappear from the JavaScript that runs. They do not check data arriving from outside the program. Such data needs checks while the program runs; the values in this practice are already supplied.

analogy.familiar: A labeled score sheet
analogy.connection: An interface is like a score sheet with named spaces and expected kinds of entries.
analogy.limit: A typed sheet helps while writing code; an external value still needs runtime checking.

steps: Define Player with a string name and number score.
Make scoreSummary return the player's name and score in the requested sentence.
Create Mina with 12 points, store the sentence in summary, and run the checks.

quiz.question: Score must be a number. What happens if you give it "12" with quotes?
choices: It is accepted because it contains digits
It fails only if the score is negative
TypeScript reports that text does not match number
quiz.explanation: Quoted digits are text. Use 12 without quotes for a number.

hints: Keep score as a number.
Use a text template to insert values into the sentence.
Read `player.name` and `player.score` instead of writing fixed values.

math.explanation: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication: Calculate one small example by hand, then compare it with the program result.
math.question: A player earns 4 points and then 3 more. What is the total?
math.feedback: Add 4 and 3 to get 7.

externalNotes: To try a type error, temporarily pass a quoted score to scoreSummary. Run the check, read the error, then restore the number.

title: Describe activities with types
summary: Use a kind label to tell two activity shapes apart.
explanation: An interface can describe shared properties. An intersection, written `&`, requires shared and extra properties together. A union, written `|`, allows one shape or another.
A discriminated union is a union with a label that identifies each shape. Here, `kind` is that label. Checking for `"draw"` tells TypeScript that this path has pictures.
The drawing path returns early. The remaining path must be singing, so it can read songs. Reading songs on the drawing path would be a type error.
In the project, ActivityKind lists walk, read, and code. But Activity contains only the walking and reading object types. Listing the word code separately does not create a coding activity shape.
Both project activities have a title and minutes. A walking activity also has steps. A reading activity has pages. Check kind, then include the correct detail in the returned sentence.
A record labeled walk but missing steps does not match the walking type. TypeScript can catch that mistake in checked code. Data from outside the program still needs checks while it runs.

analogy.familiar: Activity badges
analogy.connection: A union is like choosing one badge from a small set, while an intersection means an item must satisfy both descriptions.
analogy.limit: A union does not mean an object can freely omit required fields; each branch still has its own shape.

steps: Keep ActivityKind limited to walk, read, or code.
Describe the shared title and minutes.
Give walking activities steps and reading activities pages.
Check kind before reading the matching detail.
Return each requested sentence and run the checks.

quiz.question: Activity is WalkActivity or ReadActivity. After checking kind is walk, which detail can you read?
choices: Both, because a union requires both shapes
quiz.explanation: The kind check identifies the walking shape, which has steps.

hints: Use the kind label to choose a path.
Read steps only on the walk path, and pages on the read path.
Include the title, minutes, and matching detail.

math.explanation: Sets and overlap: Draw or list shared, distinct, and missing members of two small collections.
math.question: Set A has {walk, read}; set B has {read, code}. What is their overlap?
math.feedback: The shared member in both sets is read.

externalNotes: To try a type error, temporarily give a walk record pages but no steps. Run the check, read the error, then restore the valid record.

title: Calculate typed practice rewards
summary: Give one point for every full ten minutes of practice.
explanation: An enum gives names to a set of values. A method is a function that belongs to an object. Here, an activity enum names the practice, and a learner method adds points to that learner's total.
Practice.Drawing and Practice.Singing identify the activities. This numeric enum gives them 0 and 1. Those numbers are labels, not bonus amounts. Both activities use the same reward rule.
The award method adds earned points to the total, then returns only this session's reward. `this.points += earned` means add earned to this object's current points.
Each new Student starts with its own zero points. Updating `this.points` changes that student's total, not another student's total.
In the project, 20 minutes earns 2 points and 15 minutes earns 1. Save those rewards as earned and secondEarned. The learner's total should then be 3.
Quoted minutes are text and cause a type error. A number type alone does not prove a duration is valid: outside input could still be negative or not finite. This practice supplies valid durations.

analogy.familiar: A punch card
analogy.connection: The class is like a learner’s punch card, and the reward function decides how many marks one session earns.
analogy.limit: The rules in this small model are practice rules, not a universal measure of learning.

steps: Define Activity.Coding and Activity.Reading, with one point per full ten minutes.
Make Learner.award add the reward to the learner's total and return that session's reward.
Save the 20-minute coding reward as earned.
Save the 15-minute reading reward as secondEarned.
Run the checks and confirm the total is 3.

quiz.question: What does Math.floor(28 / 10) return for full ten-minute groups?
quiz.explanation: 28 divided by 10 is 2.8. Rounding down gives 2 full groups.

hints: Both activity kinds use the same reward rule.
Use `Math.floor(minutes / 10)`.
Add to `this.points`, then return earned, not the total.

math.explanation: Functions and input-output relationships: Make a small input-output table and check it against the function.
math.question: The rule gives 1 point per complete 10 minutes. How many for 30 minutes?
math.feedback: There are three complete ten-minute blocks in 30 minutes.

externalNotes: To try a type error, temporarily pass quoted minutes to learner.award. Read the error, then restore the numeric value.

title: Keep collection types reusable
summary: Use one collection class while keeping each collection's item type.
explanation: A generic class can be used with different types. `T` stands for the chosen type. A Shelf<number> stores numbers; a Shelf<string> stores text. Each uses the same class code.

Private tells TypeScript that outside code should use the methods instead of accessing values directly. Void means add promises no useful result. First returns T or undefined because the array might be empty.
An empty shelf returns undefined. Check `value !== undefined` before using a possible result. This check still accepts a stored 0 or an empty string.
A number shelf's first result is number or undefined. A text shelf's first result is string or undefined. Keeping T preserves that connection; using any would lose it.

For Collection, push each new value into `this.values`. Return `this.values[0]` from first. The supplied number and text collections should give 7 and maple. Leave an empty collection's result as undefined.
Adding text to a number collection causes a type error. TypeScript private and generic types are checking rules, not protection for secrets or checks of outside data while the program runs.

analogy.familiar: A box with a label
analogy.connection: A generic collection is like a box labeled with the kind of item it accepts.
analogy.limit: The label guides checked code, but it does not inspect unknown JSON at runtime.

steps: Store items in a T array inside Collection.
Make add append an item and first read position 0.
Save the number collection's first result as firstNumber.
Save the text collection's first result as firstWord.
Check an empty collection and run the checks.

quiz.question: Words is a Collection<string>. Which item can it accept?
quiz.explanation: This collection accepts text. Quotes make "12" a text value.

hints: Use `T[]` for the stored items.
Push adds at the end without replacing earlier items.
Return the actual first item, including undefined when the list is empty.

math.explanation: Logical constraints and correctness: State the assumptions, derive valid cases, and find a counterexample to an invalid assumption.
math.question: first<T> returns the first item or undefined. What must code allow for when calling first([])?
choices: undefined because there is no first item
The final item from an earlier call
math.feedback: An empty array has no first element. The return type allows undefined, so the caller must handle absence rather than assume a number.

externalNotes: To try a type error, temporarily add text to the number collection. Read the error, then remove the invalid call.

typeAssertions.label: Element result includes the empty case

title: Connect event names to payloads
summary: Keep each event name paired with the right details.
explanation: An event describes something that happened. Its type property names the event. Its payload is the data about that event. Each name needs the right kind of payload.
The example has selected events with a text label, and counted events with a number. Keyof gets the allowed event names. A type lookup gets the details for one name.
PayloadFor uses a type parameter K for an allowed name. The conditional type chooses the matching details. Never means no value is allowed; here, K is already limited to valid names.
The mapped type builds one event shape for each key. The final `[keyof Details]` combines those shapes into a union. Each shape keeps its own name and payload together. No loop runs to do this.
Checking event.type identifies the event shape. The selected path can read label. The counted path can read count. Mixing a selected name with a count-only payload causes a type error.

The project uses opened with a title, and progress with a percent. Return Opened Notes for the supplied opened event and Progress 50% for the supplied progress event. The percent sign is ordinary text here.
Types check your code before it runs. Incoming events still need real value checks. A number type also does not limit percent to the range 0 through 100.

analogy.familiar: Mail labels and contents
analogy.connection: The event name is a label that tells the receiver what kind of message is inside.
analogy.limit: A label only helps when the payload actually follows the declared shape; validate external messages at runtime too.

steps: Keep opened paired with a text title and progress paired with a numeric percent.
Check event.type before reading its payload.
Return the requested sentence for each event.

quiz.question: Which value correctly pairs progress with its details?
quiz.explanation: A progress event needs a numeric percent. A title belongs to an opened event.

hints: The mapped type builds a shape for each key in Payloads.
Each shape pairs `type: K` with `payload: Payloads[K]`.
Read title only for opened and percent only for progress.

math.explanation: Logical constraints and correctness: State the assumptions, derive valid cases, and find a counterexample to an invalid assumption.
math.question: A `progress` event requires `{percent: number}` and an `opened` event requires `{title: string}`. Which is a valid counterexample to a system that checks only the event name?
math.feedback: The first pair has a valid name but the wrong payload, showing why the name and payload relationship matters.

externalNotes: To try a type error, temporarily pair opened with a percent-only payload. Read the error, then restore a title payload.

title: Validate data at runtime
summary: Check outside data before trusting its fields.
explanation: Runtime means when JavaScript is actually running. TypeScript's type labels are gone by then. Outside data needs real checks. Unknown prevents you from using an unchecked value freely; any skips many of those checks.
First reject non-objects and null. Then check that both properties exist. Finally, check their values. This check allows extra properties; it only requires the named fields to meet the rules.
After isReading returns true, TypeScript lets the matching branch use label as text and amount as a number. A quoted amount such as `"6"` fails the check.

Finite means an ordinary limited number. Number.isFinite rejects Infinity and NaN, which means not-a-number. The `>= 0` check rejects negatives but accepts zero and fractions. An extra upper limit of 600 would need a separate `<= 600` check.

Validate PracticeResponse with a string title and finite, nonnegative minutes. This project has no upper limit of 600. Reject missing fields and wrong values. Writing `as PracticeResponse` would tell the checker to trust you without checking anything.
Unknown does not inspect the data by itself. Your function's running code performs the checks. Reading a field directly from unknown before checking should cause a type error.

analogy.familiar: Checking a parcel
analogy.connection: Runtime validation is like checking a parcel label and contents before signing that it is yours.
analogy.limit: A shape check only proves the conditions it tests; add checks for any rule your app depends on.

steps: Describe PracticeResponse with a text title and numeric minutes.
Check for a non-null object and both required fields.
Check the field types and require finite minutes of zero or more.
Run the checks for valid, missing, wrong-type, and invalid-number cases.

checks.label: Null, invalid ranges, and non-finite values are rejected
Finite zero and fractions accepted; missing title rejected

quiz.question: Does giving outside data the type unknown prove its minutes field is valid?
choices: No, the running code must check the value
Yes, the type label inspects the data
quiz.explanation: Unknown makes you check before use. It does not perform the check itself.

hints: Reject null before checking properties.
Use `in` to check both names.
Require Number.isFinite for minutes as well as the number type and lower limit.

math.explanation: Sets of valid values and validation constraints: Define valid external values and produce counterexamples for missing validation.
math.question: A valid API value must have a string title and a finite minutes number from 0 to 600. Which value must be rejected?
math.feedback: Infinity is not a finite value and is above the maximum 600, so it must be rejected. A valid minutes value must satisfy every stated constraint.

externalNotes: To try a type error, read a property directly from an unknown value. TypeScript should reject it until the value is checked.

title: Model a cancellable workflow
summary: Let only the current request change the workflow.
explanation: A workflow can be idle, loading, successful, failed, or cancelled. A discriminated union gives each state a kind label and only the fields it needs. Success has data; error has a message.
A request ID identifies one attempt. If request 8 starts after request 7, an old reply from 7 should not replace the result for 8.
A reducer receives a current state and an action, then returns the next state. An action describes an event, such as start, resolve, reject, or cancel.
In the full project, start may begin a new request from any state. Handle start first. Other actions require a loading state with the same request ID.
Cancel changes a matching loading request to cancelled. A later result must leave it cancelled. This stops the result from changing the model; it does not stop a real network request by itself.

Resolve gives a matching request its success data. Reject gives it an error message. An old or out-of-place action returns the same state object. Check the kind before reading fields that only some states have.
Keep the supplied five-state union and actions. Start request 2, accept its matching result, and ignore request 1. Also check rejection, cancellation, and a reply arriving after cancellation.

analogy.familiar: A package tracking page
analogy.connection: A workflow state is like one current package status: it is waiting, moving, delivered, or delayed.
analogy.limit: A status page should not let an old tracking update replace a newer one.

steps: Handle start by returning a new loading state.
For other actions, require loading and a matching request ID.
Return success, error, or cancelled for a matching action.
Return the original state for old or out-of-place actions.

checks.label: Current rejection becomes error

title: Build a profile from components

title: Build an accessible disclosure

title: Build a reading dashboard

Loading means waiting. Empty means the load succeeded with no records. Error means it failed. Success with records means the list is ready. Idle means no attempt has started. Give these different situations clear displays.

title: Explore a large list efficiently
summary: Reuse an unchanged search result while keeping the matching items correct.
explanation: A full filter checks every item once. This is linear work, written `O(n)`: the work grows with the number of items. The notation describes growth, not a promised running time.
Count one examined item each time the filter tests it. Lowercase both texts for a search that ignores capital letters. `includes` checks whether the search text appears anywhere in an item.
A render caused by unrelated state may not need a new search. `useMemo` can reuse a result while its dependencies stay the same. A changed query still needs the list to be searched again.

The exercise adds up the examined counts from new calculation results. Its Effect notices a new result object, adds its count once, and remembers that object. Showing the new totals does not change the search inputs.

The supplied list has Book 0 through Book 999. Searching `Book 99` matches 11 items: Book 99 and Book 990 through Book 999. `slice(0, 10)` shows only the first ten. Compare the actual matches too; equal counts alone do not prove equal results.

Keep items and query in both dependency lists. Include repeat only in the baseline. In the supplied run, one unchanged repeat brings the baseline total to 2,000 and leaves the memoized total at 1,000. These count completed calculation results, not page-drawing time. React may discard caches or run extra development checks, so correctness must not depend on keeping a cache.

analogy.connection: A list filter is like checking each card for a matching word; skipping a repeated check can save effort when the cards did not change.
analogy.limit: Memoization uses memory and only helps when the inputs repeat; it is not automatically faster for every small list.

title: A practice-session API
summary: Handle requests that read practice entries or add a valid entry.
explanation: An API is an agreed way for programs to ask another program to do something. This one lets callers read entries or add one. Each request has a method and path, and may also include data in its body.

Accept minutes only when they are whole numbers from 1 through 180. Check before adding to the array. Invalid input must not leave a new entry behind. The saved array is held in memory and is lost when the server stops.

req describes the request; res sends the response. express.json reads JSON bodies with a 20-kilobyte limit. app.get and app.post register handlers. res.status sets the status, and res.json sends JSON. crypto.randomUUID() creates the new entry's string ID.

The local example needs Node.js 22.13 or newer and the supplied Express dependency. The downloadable practice project includes package.json, server.mjs, and test.mjs. title: A reliable report API
summary: Build a per-user report that counts missing durations correctly.
explanation: A report summarizes records. GROUP BY user_id makes one group per user. COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(minutes) counts known durations, and AVG(minutes) averages those known values. A view gives this query a name so it can be read like a table.

```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_sessions (
  user_id TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_sessions VALUES
  ('x', 12), ('x', 24), ('y', NULL), ('y', 18);
CREATE VIEW demo_report AS
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       COUNT(minutes) AS known_count,
       AVG(minutes) AS average_minutes
FROM demo_sessions
GROUP BY user_id;
SELECT * FROM demo_report ORDER BY user_id;
```
User x has 2 rows, 2 known durations, and an average of 18. User y has 2 rows, 1 known duration, and an average of 18. AS gives each result column its name.

NULL means unknown, not zero. AVG skips unknown durations when adding and counting values. If every duration in a group is NULL, the average is NULL. Include known_count so readers can see how many durations support the average.

Grouping sessions includes only users who have session rows. Including users with no sessions would need a users table and a LEFT JOIN. In that case, count a matched session field, not COUNT(*), to avoid counting an unmatched placeholder as a session.

A join can repeat a session when it matches several rows in another table. Adding those repeated durations would inflate a total. This exercise avoids that problem by grouping the sessions table directly.

Replace the placeholder report view. Keep the columns user_id, row_count, known_count, and average_minutes. User a should have 2 rows, 2 known durations, and average 30. User b should have 2 rows, 1 known duration, and average 10.

The browser runs this SQL in its own SQLite database. A real GET /report route must run the query in the local server and send its rows. Check permission before returning private reports, then compare the actual HTTP response with the expected rows.

title: A protected practice API
summary: Change a record only after identity, ownership, and input checks pass.
explanation: A protected update needs three things: a verified identity, permission to change this record, and valid new data. Passing one check does not make up for failing another.

Check the session before reading its userId. Compare that ID with the record's stored ownerId. Return immediately when a check fails, before assigning entry.minutes. A caller's ownerId claim in the request body is not proof of ownership.
Even the owner must supply whole-number minutes from 1 through 180. Invalid minutes return 400 and leave the record unchanged. A valid owner update changes minutes and returns 200 with the entry.

A real server must verify the sign-in, recognize its session token, and check expiry before supplying the identity. This helper does none of that. Its simple session objects are practice inputs, not a working authentication system.

Middleware is code that runs before the route handler. It can reject an invalid session or pass a trusted identity to the route. In Express, next() continues to later code. Return after sending a rejection so that later writing code does not run.

Complete authorizeUpdate in this order: no session gives 401, wrong owner gives 403, and invalid minutes gives 400. Only then assign minutes and return 200 with entry. Check that every rejected call preserves the original record.

analogy.familiar: A shared notebook with a named page
analogy.connection: Being allowed into the room does not mean you may change everyone else’s page. Ownership needs its own check.
analogy.limit: A submitted name is not proof of identity; the server verifies the session.

steps: Check the verified session and stored ownership.
Update only after every check passes.
Check both returned statuses and unchanged data after rejection.

Owner can change valid input but not invalid input

quiz.question: What should a protected route use to learn who the caller is?
choices: The user ID from a verified server session
quiz.explanation: The server verifies the session, then uses that trusted identity for the permission check.

hints: Return immediately after each failed check.
Never use the request body's ownerId to establish identity.
Check the record after a rejected update.

math.explanation: An update is allowed only when three conditions are true: signed in, correct owner, valid input. One failed condition is enough to deny it.
math.question: A user is signed in and input is valid, but the record belongs to another user. Is an update allowed?
math.feedback: The combined condition uses AND. True AND false AND true is false.

title: A complete private learning tracker
summary: Keep saved data consistent when a change succeeds or fails.
explanation: A full-stack app connects its screen, server, and storage. The screen asks for a change, and the server checks it before saving. Show success only when the server confirms it. After a failed save, keep the previous confirmed data.

If saving fails, show that failure and keep the prior saved state. If saving succeeds but reading the new list fails, say Saved, but reload failed. Those are different outcomes. Also handle network errors that prevent getting a reply.

The downloaded app saves entries in practice.sqlite. It writes the owner from the verified session and reads entries for that owner only. Test as Alice, then Bob. Restarting clears sign-in sessions, so sign in again before checking that saved entries remain.

Download the local project files and use Node.js 22.13 or newer. Environment variables are settings passed to a program when it starts. In PowerShell, set `$env:ALICE_PASSWORD = "your-disposable-value"` and `$env:BOB_PASSWORD = "a-different-disposable-value"`. In a macOS or Linux shell, use `export ALICE_PASSWORD="your-disposable-value"` and `export BOB_PASSWORD="a-different-disposable-value"`. Choose different throwaway values, then run npm install and npm start in that terminal.

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 on this computer. The app's simple sign-in is for local learning. Its cookie and server expiry checks do not make it ready for public use. A public app needs an established authentication system and appropriate security controls.

Two requests may read the same old data before either saves. A real database must keep the check and related writes together using a transaction or an atomic conditional update. Atomic means the change happens as one indivisible operation. This browser function alone cannot prove safe overlapping database writes.

Complete transfer with whole amounts from zero through available. A valid move subtracts from available and adds the same amount to saved. Invalid input or fail: true returns a copy with old values. Separately test the local app's save, reload, invalid input, two-user separation, and restart behavior.

analogy.familiar: Writing a score and checking the scoreboard
analogy.connection: After a successful write, the scoreboard should show the same saved value when you look again.
analogy.limit: A screen’s optimistic number is not proof the server saved it.

steps: Validate the transfer amount before calculating new values.
Return a new state that keeps the total, or an unchanged-value copy on failure.
Optionally follow the local setup and test saving, separate users, and restart persistence.
starter:
function transfer(state,amount,fail=false){return {...state};}
console.log(transfer({available:20,saved:0},7));
solution:
function transfer(state,amount,fail=false){if(fail||!Number.isInteger(amount)||amount<0||amount>state.available)return {...state};return {available:state.available-amount,saved:state.saved+amount};}
console.log(transfer({available:20,saved:0},7));

checks.label: A successful change preserves the total
Invalid or failed changes leave old state intact
Successful and failed calls preserve ordinary mutable input

quiz.question: A save request fails. What should the screen do?
choices: Show the failure and keep the previous saved state
Give the record to another user
quiz.explanation: The screen must match the confirmed server result. A failed save must not appear successful.

hints: Subtract and add the same amount.
Preserve the input object, even on failure.
A successful browser model check does not test the downloaded app.

math.explanation: A consistency invariant is something that must stay true after every allowed change. Here available + saved must stay 20.
math.question: Two requests each spend 15 from the same balance of 20 without checking one another. Why is this unsafe?
choices: The second request can use a stale balance and overspend
Two requests cannot arrive at the same time
math.feedback: Both can read the old balance 20 before either writes. A database transaction or atomic conditional update must check the current balance when applying each change.

title: Repair a broken starter
summary: Find why a program gives the wrong answer, then test a small fix.
explanation: Debugging means finding and fixing a problem in a program. Start with one input and the answer it should produce.
This is a logic error: the program runs but does the wrong thing. A syntax error means the code is not written in a valid form. A runtime error happens while valid code is running.
Change a - b to a + b. With the same inputs, combine now returns 11. Changing just the operator makes the cause of the fix clear.
Predict the answer, run the code, compare the result, and change one thing. After the fix, try a few other inputs to check the rule.
Complete total(a, b) so it adds the two numbers. Do not always return 11: total(0, 7) must return 7, and total(-2, 5) must return 3.
This exercise supplies numbers. In JavaScript, + can also join text. A function that accepts other kinds of input needs a clear rule for handling them.

title: A project with version history
summary: Save chosen versions with Git so you can inspect changes and recover a mistake.
explanation: Git keeps versions of a project. A commit is a saved version with a message. Staging chooses the changes for the next commit. A local commit stays on your computer until you share it.

With Git installed, make a new disposable history-demo folder. Add main.js that prints Hello. From the parent folder, run this example. The sample author settings apply only to this practice project.

```bash
cd history-demo
git init
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
git status
git add main.js
git commit -m "Add greeting"
```

add stages the file. commit saves that staged version. status shows what is saved, staged, or changed.
Edit main.js to print Hello, reader. Save and run it. Use git diff to inspect the change, then git add main.js and git commit -m "Improve greeting". git log --oneline -2 shows the two latest commits.

title: A reviewed AI change
summary: Treat AI-written code as a proposed change. Read it and test the behavior you asked for.
explanation: Before accepting a change, say what it must do. Our rule gives members a 10% discount and leaves other prices unchanged. Invalid prices return null.
A program can pass one example and still be wrong. Check both a member and a nonmember so a discount given to everyone is caught.
A valid price is a number at least zero, with a finite value. Number.isFinite rejects text, Infinity, and NaN. NaN means an invalid numeric result.
Multiplying by 0.9 keeps 90% of the price. isMember === true accepts only the boolean true. Text such as "false" must not earn a discount.
Test a member, a nonmember, zero, a negative number, Infinity, NaN, and text in place of a membership flag. Each case checks a different part of the rule.
Complete finalPrice using the same rule. Read every changed line and run the checks. Keep a saved working version so you can undo a bad change. An AI's confident explanation is not a test result.

analogy.familiar: Checking someone else’s homework steps
analogy.connection: A useful suggestion still needs you to follow the steps and check the result.
analogy.limit: The assistant can make mistakes even when the explanation sounds confident.

steps: Reject prices that are not finite numbers or are below zero.
Apply the discount only when isMember === true.
Run the normal and invalid-input checks.
Explain the conditions and keep a saved working version.

console.log(finalPrice(100,false));

console.log(finalPrice(100,false));

title: A tested feature
summary: A useful test checks a promised result and fails when that behavior breaks.
explanation: A test compares what a program does with what it should do. Here, clampScore must keep whole-number scores between 0 and 100. Clamping moves an outside value to the nearest limit.
Keep scores from 0 through 100 unchanged. Turn a lower whole number into 0 and a higher one into 100. Return null for anything that is not an integer, including fractions, NaN, and Infinity.

console.log(clampScore(110));

summary: Check the version people can actually reach, and whether it is ready to do its work.
explanation: Deployment makes a built version of an app available to users. Give each release an ID so a response can show which version is running.

title: A reviewed release
summary: Approve a release using real checks, with a record of what passed and what still needs work.
explanation: A release review checks whether an app meets its requirements. Record what was tested, what happened, and what was fixed. A ticked box alone does not show that a check happened.

When displaying a note as plain text, textContent keeps its characters as text. ```html Safe text demo

``` The page shows Hello exactly. It does not turn the note into a bold text or run it as code.

Test that one user cannot read or change another user's private records. Reject invalid input before saving it. Keep secrets out of browser files and logs. Review the packages actually shipped with the release.
Use the main task with the keyboard alone. Check that controls have clear names, Tab moves in a useful order, focus is visible, and errors explain what to fix.
The browser exercise uses three review results: permissionChecks, secretChecks, and keyboardChecks. canRelease returns true only when all three are the boolean true.
Compare each field with === true. A missing value or the text "true" must fail. The function expects a review object; it does not perform the reviews itself.

Use the supplied REVIEW.md on a private test project. Fill it with actual observations about permissions, secrets, input handling, dependencies, and keyboard use. Record unresolved problems before deciding to release.

analogy.limit: A checked list is not evidence unless the actual behavior was tested.

Run checks with a false field, a missing field, and text instead of a boolean.

# Private release review

For each item record evidence and unresolved limits.
- Account and record permissions: test two users.
- Secrets: inspect browser bundle, repository and logs.
- Input: normal, invalid, boundary, oversized values.
- Output: untrusted text is displayed safely.

title: A tidy name badge
summary: Remove spaces around a name and use a guest greeting when nothing remains.
explanation:
A typed name may have extra spaces at its ends. Use a string method, an action attached to text, to clean them up.

Return the cleaned greeting without changing the original input.

`trim()` removes whitespace from both ends. Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and line breaks.

It keeps spaces inside the name and leaves capital letters alone. Save its returned string; it does not edit the original string.

`""` is an empty string. After trimming, compare with `""` to see whether any text remains.

Check after cleanup so a spaces-only name does not become a blank badge.

`+` joins strings here. Keep the comma and one space in `"Hello, "`.

This function accepts text. Keep the person's letter case and spaces inside their name.

Write `badge(name)` to return the greeting for each supplied name. Empty or whitespace-only text should give `"Hello, guest"`.

The checks use returned text. Printing alone does not return the answer.

analogy.familiar: A name card with empty space around the writing
analogy.connection: Cleanup removes unwanted space around the name before adding a greeting.
analogy.limit: This does not judge whether the name is valid or change its spelling.

steps: Create badge(name), which accepts a string.
Use trim() to remove spaces and other whitespace from the ends of the name. Then check whether anything is left.
Return "Hello, guest" if the cleaned name is empty. Otherwise, return "Hello, " followed by the cleaned name.
Run the checks and try a two-word name.

checks.label: Blank input gets a useful fallback
Inside spaces and letters are preserved
checks.expression: badge("  Ana  Lee  ") === "Hello, Ana  Lee" && badge("zoë") === "Hello, zoë"

quiz.question: What does "  Pine Grove  ".trim() return?
quiz.explanation: trim removes outside whitespace and preserves the space between the two words.

Compare the cleaned string with "".
Join "Hello, " to either "guest" or the cleaned name.

title: A shared supply list
summary: Add together requests for the same supply.
explanation:
Several people may ask for the same supply. We want one total for each item.

A `Map` connects a key with a value. Here, the item name is the key and its total quantity is the value. Each input row has `item` and `quantity`.

`new Map()` makes an empty Map. `set(key, value)` saves a value, and `get(key)` reads it. A missing key gives `undefined`.

Map keeps items in the order their keys first appeared. Updating a key does not move it.

`counts.get(item) ?? 0` reads the old total, or uses zero if no total exists.

`??` uses its right-hand value only when the left is `null` or `undefined`. An existing total of zero is kept. A `for...of` loop can visit each request.

Map compares item names exactly. `"Pen"` and `"pen"` are different keys.

Names such as `"constructor"` are ordinary Map keys too. Do not change or combine names beyond what the task asks.

Create a fresh Map inside `totals`. Read each row without changing it. Add its quantity to the saved total for its item.

Return an empty Map for an empty list. A request for zero items must still create that item's entry.

analogy.familiar: A supply sheet with one line per item
analogy.connection: Each Map key identifies the line whose total you update.
analogy.limit: Names are matched exactly; the Map does not know that two different spellings might mean the same item.

steps: Create a new Map inside totals.
For each row, look up the total already saved for that item. Use zero if the item has no saved total yet.
Add the row’s quantity to that total. Save the new total in the Map using the item name as its key.
Return the Map and try an empty list.

checks.label: Repeated supplies add in first-seen order
Empty, zero and unusual names work
Input stays unchanged and case stays distinct
checks.expression: (() => { const rows = Object.freeze([Object.freeze({item:"Pen",quantity:1}),Object.freeze({item:"pen",quantity:2})]); const result = totals(rows); return result.size === 2 && rows[0].quantity === 1; })()

quiz.question: After set("pen", 2) and set("pen", 7), how many entries use the key "pen"?
quiz.explanation: set replaces the value at an existing key. You must explicitly add the old quantity to get a total.

hints: Read row.item and row.quantity without changing the row.
Use result.get(row.item) ?? 0.
set the sum, then return result after the loop.

title: A task board that keeps its old copy
summary: Change one task in a new copy while keeping the old task board.
explanation:
Keeping an old task board can help with undo or comparing changes.

Changing an existing value is called mutation. An immutable update makes new copies of the parts that change, leaving the old data alone.

`[...tasks]` makes a new array, but both arrays still point to the same task objects.

Changing a shared task would affect both views of it. To change one task while keeping the old board, copy that task object too.

`map` runs a function for every item and puts the returned values in a new array.

Return a copied object for the matching task. Return each other task unchanged. This keeps the original order and avoids copying objects you do not change.

Object spread makes a shallow copy. It copies the task's properties, but any objects stored inside it would still be shared.

Our update changes only the `done` Boolean. Keep all other properties, such as the title. Each ID is unique, so at most one task matches.

Complete `toggleTask(tasks, id)`. Always return a new array.

Check both directions: unfinished to finished, and finished to unfinished. A missing ID leaves the task objects unchanged. An empty input returns a new empty array.

After each call, the original board must still have its old values.

analogy.familiar: A revised task sheet while keeping the previous version
analogy.connection: The new array represents the revision and the copied task represents the change.
analogy.limit: Object spread is shallow, so nested data may still be shared.

steps: Use tasks.map() to make a new array without changing the original array.
When a task’s id matches, copy that task. In the copy, change done from false to true, or from true to false.
For other IDs, keep the original task objects without changing them.
Check that the original tasks stay unchanged and that the copied task keeps its title.

checks.label: The selected task toggles without losing its title
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[{id:"a",title:"Read",done:false}]; const n=toggleTask(t,"a"); return n!==t && n[0]!==t[0] && n[0].done===true && n[0].title==="Read" && t[0].done===false; })()

checks.label: Other tasks retain their identity and order
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[Object.freeze({id:"a",done:false}),Object.freeze({id:"b",done:true})]; const n=toggleTask(Object.freeze(t),"b"); return n[0]===t[0] && n[1].id==="b" && n[1].done===false; })()

checks.label: Missing IDs and empty lists return fresh arrays
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[{id:"a",done:false}]; const n=toggleTask(t,"missing"); const empty=[]; const e=toggleTask(empty,"a"); return n!==t && n[0]===t[0] && e!==empty && e.length===0; })()

quiz.question: Why is copying the array with `[...tasks]` not enough before changing a task object?
choices: It does not copy the array
Its task objects are still shared with the original
quiz.explanation: The array is new, but its entries still refer to the original objects. Copy the object you will change as well.

hints: Use task.id === id to choose the task.
Write { ...task, done: !task.done } for the changed object.
Return the result of tasks.map, including when no ID matches.

title: A note editor with reversible history
summary: Save note versions so you can undo and redo edits.
explanation:
Undo needs a record of earlier notes. Store the versions in an array of strings.

A number called `cursor` points to the version you are viewing. It must always point to an existing entry. `current()` returns that entry.

A closure is a function that remembers variables from where it was created.

`createHistory` can return functions that share its `versions` and `cursor`. Each call to `createHistory` gets separate storage. The caller uses the returned functions to change the history.

Undo moves the cursor one place back, if there is an earlier version. Redo moves it one place forward, if there is a later version.

Neither action changes the saved array. At either end, stay on the current version and return its text.

If an edit contains the same text as the current version, do nothing and return that text.

Check this before removing future versions. Otherwise, an unchanged edit could erase useful redo steps. This exercise stores strings, which cannot be edited in place.

Complete `createHistory(initial)` with `current`, `edit`, `undo`, and `redo` methods. Each must return the current note text.

Check a whole sequence: edit A to B to C, undo to B, then edit D. Redo should stay at D because the old C version was removed.

Also check an empty note, repeated undo at the start, unchanged edits, and two separate histories.

analogy.familiar: A row of saved note cards with a marker on the current one
analogy.connection: Undo moves the marker; a new edit after undo replaces the cards ahead of it.
analogy.limit: Real editors may group keystrokes and limit history size; this exercise treats each edit call as one version.

steps: Inside createHistory, keep the saved versions and a cursor that points to the current version.
Return an object with current, edit, undo, and redo methods.
Do not let undo go before the first version or redo go past the last version.
If you undo and then make a new edit, remove the later versions from the old history.
Ignore an edit if its text is the same as the current text.
Create two histories and check that changing one does not change the other.

checks.label: Undo and redo stop at the history boundaries
checks.expression: (() => {const h=createHistory(""); return h.undo()==="" && h.edit("A")==="A" && h.edit("B")==="B" && h.undo()==="A" && h.undo()==="" && h.undo()==="" && h.redo()==="A" && h.redo()==="B" && h.redo()==="B";})()

checks.label: A new branch discards old redo steps
Duplicate edits preserve redo; histories are independent

quiz.question: Your saved note versions are Plan → Draft → Final. You undo to Draft, then edit it into Revised. What should redo return now?
quiz.explanation: The new edit discards the old future version Final. Revised is now the latest version, so redo stays there.

hints: Start with [initial] and cursor 0.
Keep versions.slice(0, cursor + 1) before adding a new version.
Check equality before trimming redo history.

title: A shelf label maker
summary: Build a shelf label from an item name and a count.
explanation: A shelf label combines a name, a number, and a unit. Your function formats these values into one string. Formatting means choosing how values appear as text; it does not change the input values.

An f-string starts with `f` just before its opening quote. Braces, `{}`, mark values or calculations to put into the text. Put a parameter name inside the braces to use the current input.

Without `f`, braces are ordinary text.

This complete example inserts two values.
```python
name = "Tape"
rolls = 4
label = f"{name}: {rolls} rolls"
print(label)
```
It prints Tape: 4 rolls. Python converts the number to text in the f-string. The colon and spaces appear exactly as written.

Choose the word for one item when `count == 1`. Choose the word for more than one item for zero and every other allowed count.

This exercise accepts whole-number counts of zero or greater. It does not accept negative counts or fractions.

You can choose a word before formatting the final text.
```python
def ticket_label(count):
    word = "ticket" if count == 1 else "tickets"
    return f"{count} {word}"
print(ticket_label(1))
print(ticket_label(0))
```
The output is 1 ticket and 0 tickets. The conditional expression chooses one value. An ordinary if/else block would also work.

`return` gives the finished label back to the code that called the function. That code can choose to display it or save it.

`print` displays a value and gives back `None`. Return the string from `shelf_label` so other code can use it.

Keep the requested punctuation and spaces in the label.

Test counts of zero, one, and several items. Try a two-word name and a name with a non-English letter. The function should carry the name through unchanged. These tests check where the wording changes; one sample with three items would not reveal a mistaken singular rule.

analogy.familiar: A printed label with spaces for a name and quantity
analogy.connection: The f-string fills those spaces using the current values.
analogy.limit: Formatting text does not change inventory or validate the count.

steps: Use the word `"items"` for every other count.
Return the label with an f-string, keeping the requested spaces and punctuation.
Try counts of zero, one, and twelve.
Try an item name with two words.
starter:
def shelf_label(item, count):
    # TODO: choose item/items and return the formatted label.
    return ""

print(shelf_label("Pencil", 3))
solution:
def shelf_label(item, count):
    word = "item" if count == 1 else "items"
    return f"{item}: {count} {word}"

print(shelf_label("Pencil", 3))

checks.label: Zero and larger counts use plural labels
Names are preserved exactly
checks.expression: shelf_label("Blue pen", 2) == "Blue pen: 2 items" and shelf_label("Café", 1) == "Café: 1 item"

quiz.question: The label-building function returns text but the caller never prints the returned value. What should you expect in a normal script?
choices: The returned label need not appear on screen
The function must raise an error
quiz.explanation: Returning makes a value available to the caller. Printing is a separate effect; a script does not automatically display every returned value.

hints: Begin an f-string with f before the quote.
Place item, count, and your chosen word inside braces.
Return f"{item}: {count} {word}".

title: An inventory import report
summary: Build a CSV stock reader that adds valid quantities and counts rejected rows.
explanation: CSV means comma-separated values. It stores rows as text, often from a spreadsheet. A comma can also be part of a value, such as "Pens, blue", so splitting each line at every comma can break the data. Python's standard `csv` module handles quoted values and quote marks inside them.

`csv.DictReader` uses the first row as column names and gives you a dictionary for each following row. `io.StringIO` lets a string act like a text file, so you can read the supplied text without writing a file. Import both `csv` and `io`. This exercise supplies the `item` and `quantity` headers and correctly written CSV quoting.

Here is a complete example with a comma inside a quoted item name.
```python
import csv
import io
text = 'item,quantity\n"Pens, blue",2\nTape,1\n'
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row["item"], row["quantity"])
```
The first item is the single string `Pens, blue`. Quantities are still strings here; the CSV reader does not turn them into numbers.

Validation means checking that a row follows the project's rules before using it. Remove spaces from both ends of the item and quantity fields with `strip()`. Reject a blank item name. A quantity must be nonempty and contain only characters from `0123456789`. Reject `-2`, `2.5`, and `two`. Accept `0` and leading zeroes such as `003`, which represents 3.

A missing field can be `None`. Use `(row.get("item") or "").strip()` to replace a missing or empty value with empty text before trimming. Here, `or` returns one of the values, which is not necessarily a Boolean.

Check the text before converting it to an integer.
```python
raw = " 003 ".strip()
valid = bool(raw) and all(char in "0123456789" for char in raw)
if valid:
    amount = int(raw)
    print(amount)
```
It prints `3`. ASCII digits are the ordinary characters `0` through `9`. Checking this exact set follows the project's rules. Some broader Unicode digit checks accept characters that `int` cannot convert.

`bool(raw)` checks whether the text is nonempty: `bool("")` is `False`, while `bool("0")` is `True`. The separate character check decides whether every character is allowed.

Keep totals in a dictionary. Add each valid quantity to the total for its trimmed item name. Repeated names add to the same total. Increase `rejected` once for each invalid row, then continue to the next row.

`csv.DictReader` ignores completely blank lines. A row such as `,4` still contains fields, so reject it for having a blank item name.

`totals.get(item, 0)` returns the stored amount, or zero if the item is missing. It does not add the missing key.
```python
totals = {"Pens": 4}
print(totals.get("Pens", 0))
print(totals.get("Tape", 0))
print("Tape" in totals)
```
It prints `4`, `0`, and `False`. To save the updated amount, use `totals[item] = totals.get(item, 0) + int(raw)`.

Build `read_stock(text)` to return `{"totals": totals, "rejected": rejected}`. This lets the code that called the function see the stock totals and how many rows were rejected.

This exercise rejects individual bad rows. Broken CSV quoting and missing headers are outside its rules for supplied input. Do not count the header as a stock row. Check quoted commas, repeated names, zero stock, missing quantities, and completely blank lines. Input containing only headers should return `{"totals": {}, "rejected": 0}`.

analogy.familiar: Checking a delivery sheet before adding items to a shelf
analogy.connection: Each valid row contributes stock; rejected rows are counted for review.
analogy.limit: The importer follows the written format and cannot decide whether a plausible number was typed incorrectly.

steps: Import `csv` and `io`. Start fresh totals and a rejected-row count inside `read_stock`.
Read rows with `csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))` and trim both fields.
Reject a row once if its item is blank or its quantity is not a nonempty string of digits `0` through `9`.
Add each valid quantity to its item's total, then return `{"totals": totals, "rejected": rejected}`.
Check quoted commas, repeated names, zero and leading zeroes, invalid quantities, missing fields, and blank lines.

checks.label: Quoted commas and duplicate names total correctly
Bad quantities, missing fields and blank names are rejected
Zero, padded digits and blank lines work

quiz.question: Why use csv.DictReader instead of splitting each row on commas?
choices: It automatically fixes every invalid quantity
Quoted fields can contain commas that are part of a value
It removes the need for headers
quiz.explanation: The CSV reader understands quoting, so a comma inside a quoted item name does not split that item into two columns.

hints: Use `(row.get("quantity") or "").strip()` to handle a missing quantity.
Check that `raw` is nonempty before `all(char in "0123456789" for char in raw)`.
Use `totals.get(item, 0)` to add repeated items, and count invalid rows separately.

title: A reading log summary
summary: Write reading_summary(text) to return the distinct book count, total pages, and page totals by book from valid JSON records.
explanation: JSON means JavaScript Object Notation, but many languages use it to share data. It stores strings, numbers, arrays, objects, true, false, and null. Python's json module turns JSON text into Python values. Here, a JSON array becomes a list, and each JSON object becomes a dictionary.

Use json.loads(text) to parse a JSON string. The s in loads refers to a string; json.load reads from an open file. Parsing checks JSON syntax, but it does not prove the result has the fields you expect. This exercise supplies valid records: book is a string, and pages is a nonnegative integer.

This complete example reads two entries.
```python
import json
text = '[{"book":"River","pages":8},{"book":"River","pages":3}]'
entries = json.loads(text)
print(entries[0]["book"])
print(sum(entry["pages"] for entry in entries))
```
It prints River and 11. Index 0 selects the first list entry; the string key "book" selects a dictionary value.

A session is one record; a book may have several sessions. Counting records would count the same book more than once. Group pages by the exact book name using a dictionary. Each new name creates one key, and later sessions add to that key. Capitalization matters under this project's rules.

Here is a small grouped sum.
```python
by_book = {}
for entry in [{"book": "Hill", "pages": 4}, {"book": "Hill", "pages": 6}]:
    name = entry["book"]
    by_book[name] = by_book.get(name, 0) + entry["pages"]
print(len(by_book))
print(sum(by_book.values()))
```
It prints 1 and 10. len counts dictionary keys, while values() gives the grouped page totals.

A zero-page session still records a book name, so keep that name with a total of zero. The empty array [] has no names or pages; the sum of an empty collection is zero. Return a dictionary with exactly the three requested result fields so code that called the function can use them without reading printed text.

You can use json.dumps to turn a Python result back into JSON text when exporting, but this function must return the Python dictionary itself. Never use eval to read outside data: it runs Python expressions. Test several sessions, several books, and the empty list. Reading malformed JSON or checking arbitrary field types is a separate extension.

analogy.familiar: Combining several reading sessions under each book title
analogy.connection: Each title gets one page total, even when it appears several times.
analogy.limit: Exact titles are the identifiers here; a real library may need unique IDs for books with the same title.

steps: Use `json.loads` to turn the JSON text into Python values.
Make a dictionary that adds up pages for each exact book name.
Count the dictionary keys to find the number of different books.
Add the dictionary values to find the total pages.
Test an empty input list too.

checks.label: Repeated sessions combine while distinct books are counted
The empty list produces an empty summary
Zero sessions and exact book names are preserved

quiz.question: Three records all name the same book. How many different books are there?
choices: It depends on the page total
quiz.explanation: Each record is a session, but the same book name makes one dictionary key.

hints: A row is a dictionary; use entry["book"] and entry["pages"].
Use by_book.get(name, 0) before adding the next session.
len(by_book) counts distinct names; sum(by_book.values()) totals pages.

title: A workshop preparation planner
summary: Put workshop tasks in an order that finishes each needed task first.
explanation:
Before painting, you may need to sand. Before sanding, you may need to cut. A prerequisite is a task that must happen first.

These links form a graph. Each task is a node, and each link is an edge. A valid plan puts prerequisites before the tasks that need them.

Depth-first search follows a chain of prerequisites before finishing the current task.

Keep a result list and two sets: `visiting` for the unfinished chain, and `finished` for completed tasks. The recursive `visit` function follows each prerequisite by calling itself.

Follow the prerequisite before printing its task:
```python
tasks = {"paint": ["sand"], "sand": []}
finished = set()
def visit(name):
    if name in finished:
        return
    for before in tasks[name]:
        visit(before)
    finished.add(name)
    print(name)
visit("paint")
```
Output:
```text
sand
paint
```
This small example assumes there are no cycles or missing tasks. Your project must handle those too.

A cycle is a chain that comes back to itself: A needs B, while B needs A. Neither can go first.

Reaching a task already in `visiting` shows a cycle. A task in `finished` is safe to reuse, but add it to the result only once.

The sets track different states:
```python
visiting = {"build", "prepare"}
finished = {"collect"}
print("build" in visiting)
print("collect" in finished)
visiting.remove("prepare")
finished.add("prepare")
```
Output:
```text
True
True
```
After finishing a task's prerequisites, move its name from `visiting` to `finished`.

Check that a task exists before reading `tasks[name]`. Sort the task names and each prerequisite list before visiting them. This makes the order predictable without changing the input.

Put `visit` inside `plan`, so each plan gets fresh lists and sets. The helper can add to those outer collections without replacing their names.

If a recursive visit fails, each waiting call must pass that failure back too. Otherwise the plan could wrongly return only part of the answer.

Return `None` for any missing task or cycle. Otherwise return the completed list; an empty input gives `[]`.

This is a topological ordering: every prerequisite comes first. Apart from sorting, the search visits each task and link once. Very deep graphs can exceed Python's recursion limit and need a loop-based version.

Check a chain, shared prerequisites, a missing name, and cycles.

analogy.familiar: Preparing workshop jobs in an order that lets each job start
analogy.connection: A prerequisite must be ready before the job that uses it.
analogy.limit: This plan orders dependencies only; it does not estimate time, people or parallel work.

title: A supply category directory
summary: List each usable category once, even when many items share it.
explanation: `DISTINCT` removes repeated result rows. A category directory can use it to show each category once, even when many items have that category.
SQL compares the whole selected row. If you select only category, repeated categories become one result. If you also select different item names, those rows are different and both remain.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_supplies(category TEXT);
INSERT INTO demo_supplies VALUES
  ('paper'), ('tools'), ('paper'), (NULL), ('');
SELECT DISTINCT category
FROM demo_supplies
WHERE category IS NOT NULL AND category <> ''
ORDER BY category;
```
The result is `paper`, then `tools`, with each shown once.
`IS NOT NULL` leaves out missing values. `<> ''` leaves out empty text; `<>` means not equal. These checks do not remove spaces or change capital letters.
`ORDER BY category` asks for a sorted display. DISTINCT removes repeats but does not promise an order by itself.
A view saves a query instead of saving a separate copy of its results. Define it with `CREATE VIEW category_directory AS` followed by your SELECT. Reading the view uses the current supply rows.
