analogy.connection: DISTINCT keeps each category heading once.
analogy.limit: Distinctness follows database comparison rules; it does not know that differently spelled names might mean the same thing.

Filter out NULL and empty text.
Display its category column in order.

summary: Choose email first, phone second, or a clear fallback message.

title: An order status dashboard
summary: Count all orders and paid orders without losing customers who have none.
explanation: Conditional aggregation means choosing which values go into a summary. A CASE inside SUM can count paid orders while another column counts all orders.
Start with customers and LEFT JOIN their orders. Use COUNT(o.id) to count real orders. COUNT(*) would also count the unmatched row kept for a customer with no orders.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE demo_orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, status TEXT, cents INTEGER);
INSERT INTO demo_customers VALUES (1, 'Rin'), (2, 'Sam');
INSERT INTO demo_orders VALUES
  (10, 1, 'paid', 300), (11, 1, 'pending', 500), (12, 1, 'paid', 200);
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM demo_customers AS c
LEFT JOIN demo_orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
```
Rin has `3` total orders, `2` paid orders, and `500` paid cents. Sam has `0` for all three.
Group by customer ID and name. Two people can share a name, so grouping by name alone could wrongly combine their orders.
The CASE choices use ELSE 0. A customer with no order contributes zero to each paid total. COUNT(o.id) also gives zero because the unmatched order ID is NULL.
Do not filter the whole joined result to paid orders. That would lose unpaid orders from total_orders and could remove customers with no paid orders.

Create `customer_orders(customer_id, name, total_orders, paid_orders, paid_cents)` from customers and orders. Keep every customer. For paid_cents, use the supplied amount_cents. These small totals use whole cents. Display the view in customer_id order and keep both source tables unchanged.

analogy.familiar: One summary line for each customer on a shop report
analogy.connection: Conditional totals count different kinds of orders without losing the customer.
analogy.limit: A summary depends on the stored status; it does not verify that a real payment occurred.

Use CASE inside each paid sum.
Group by ID and name, then create the view.
solution:
CREATE VIEW customer_orders AS
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
SELECT * FROM customer_orders ORDER BY customer_id;

title: A folder path explorer
summary: Build folder paths by repeating the same step for each level.
explanation: A root folder has no parent. A folder tree starts at a root and branches into children. A recursive query repeats a step using rows it has already found, so it can follow folders through many levels.

A common table expression, or CTE, is a query given a temporary name with `WITH`. `WITH RECURSIVE` lets that query use its own earlier results. First it finds starting rows. Then it finds the next level.

```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_folders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, parent_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO demo_folders VALUES
  (1, 'Home', NULL), (2, 'Notes', 1), (3, 'Ideas', 2);
WITH RECURSIVE paths(id, path, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 FROM demo_folders WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT child.id, parent.path || '/' || child.name, parent.depth + 1
  FROM demo_folders AS child
  JOIN paths AS parent ON child.parent_id = parent.id
)
SELECT id, path, depth FROM paths ORDER BY path;
```
The paths are `Home` at depth 0, `Home/Notes` at depth 1, and `Home/Notes/Ideas` at depth 2.

The first `SELECT` is the starting part, called the anchor. It finds every root with `parent_id IS NULL`. Each root starts with its own name and depth 0. Choosing every root also handles several separate trees.

The second `SELECT` finds children of a path already found. `||` joins the parent path, a slash, and the child's name. Adding 1 gives the child's depth. `UNION ALL` includes the new rows without removing repeated values.

This exercise's folders have valid parents and no loops. Each branch ends when it has no more children. Other data may need checks for loops or a depth limit. Link folders by ID, because different folders can share a name.
Put the repeating query after `CREATE VIEW folder_paths AS`. Return `id`, `path`, and `depth`. Show the view with `ORDER BY path`. The source folders stay unchanged.

analogy.familiar: Following branches from each top-level folder
analogy.connection: Each discovered parent provides the starting path for its children.
analogy.limit: The supplied data is a tree; arbitrary cyclic relationships need additional handling.

steps: Start a recursive CTE with every root at depth 0.
Join each child to a parent path already found.
Append the child name and add 1 to the depth.
Save the query as `folder_paths`, show the paths in order, and run the checks.

summary: Ask a question and keep the typed answer as text.
explanation:
`input()` waits for you to type an answer and press Enter. The text it shows is called a prompt; here, it is a question.

The question is not part of your answer.

You can give the answer a name so your program can use it later.

title: A countdown that knows when to stop
summary: Make countdown(start) count down to 1; starting at zero gives an empty list.
explanation: A while loop repeats its body while a condition is true.
Python checks the condition before each repetition. If it is false at the start, the body runs zero times.

The number changes after each display.
```python
energy = 3
while energy > 0:
    print(energy)
    energy = energy - 1
```
The displayed values are 3, 2, and 1. After energy becomes 0, 0 > 0 is false.
Indentation puts both instructions inside the repeated body. If the update were outside it, energy would stay 3 and the loop would not stop.
The comparison sign decides whether zero is included. With `energy >= 0`, the same loop also displays 0 before stopping.

You can keep repeated results in a list instead of displaying them.
```python
steps = []
remaining = 2
while remaining > 0:
    steps.append(remaining)
    remaining = remaining - 1
print(steps)
```
This produces [2, 1]. append stores the current number before the update changes remaining.
In your function, create a fresh list for each call. Return it after the loop finishes, not during the first repetition.
Try a start of 0, then 1, then 4. These test an empty loop, one repetition, and several repetitions.

analogy.familiar: Follow a small change from its starting state to its result.
analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.
analogy.limit: Use the actual code and checks rather than relying on the comparison.

steps: Start a fresh result list inside `countdown`.
While the remaining number is above zero, save it and subtract one.
Return the list after the loop finishes.
Check that starting at 0 gives `[]` and starting at 1 gives `[1]`.
starter:
def countdown(start):
    values = []
    # TODO: collect start down to 1, then return values.
    return values

print(countdown(4))
solution:
def countdown(start):
    values = []
    remaining = start
    while remaining > 0:
        values.append(remaining)
        remaining = remaining - 1
    return values

print(countdown(4))

Calls do not keep an earlier result

quiz.explanation: The condition includes zero, so zero is displayed. The next update makes energy -1, which fails the next condition check.

hints: Check the condition before appending.
The number must move toward a false condition.
Keep return outside the loop so all repetitions can finish.
externalNotes: The input contract is a nonnegative integer. Browser runs have a timeout; stop a run if a loop does not finish. Do not intentionally remove the update while running the loop.

title: Keep subjects that meet the total
summary: Use HAVING to choose groups by their total.
explanation: `WHERE` filters individual rows before they are grouped.
`GROUP BY` puts matching group values together. SUM then adds the known numbers in each group.
`HAVING` filters groups after their totals are calculated.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE practice(subject TEXT, minutes INTEGER);
INSERT INTO practice VALUES
  ('Drawing', 8), ('Drawing', 14), ('Singing', 15);
SELECT subject, SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes
FROM practice
GROUP BY subject
HAVING SUM(minutes) >= 20
ORDER BY subject;
```
The query keeps groups totaling at least 20 minutes.
Drawing remains with `22` minutes. Its two small entries add up to enough, even though neither entry reaches 20 alone.
`WHERE minutes >= 20` would remove both Drawing rows before adding. That asks about each entry instead of the total.
`>=` includes the target itself. A total of 30 passes a minimum of 30.
SUM skips NULL values. A group with only NULL minutes has an unknown total, so it does not pass this number check.
Create `qualifying_subjects(subject, total_minutes)` as a view of sessions. Group by subject and use HAVING to keep totals of at least 30. Leave sessions unchanged.

title: Return one page of entries
summary: Return a limited slice of entries in a predictable order.
explanation: A page is part of a longer list. limit says how many items to return at most. offset says how many items to skip first.
Query settings arrive as text. In /entries?limit=2&offset=1, read and validate that text before using it as numbers.
The supplied parsePage helper converts accepted text with Number. It also uses Number.isSafeInteger to require whole numbers JavaScript can represent exactly.
Its /^\d+$/ pattern accepts one or more digits and nothing else. Arrays, objects, blank text, negative signs, and decimal points fail this text check.
Allowed limits are 1 through 20. Offsets start at 0. Missing settings use limit 5 and offset 0. A valid whole number must still meet these range rules.
If parsePage returns null, return status 400 before selecting any entries. This tells the caller to fix the page settings.
Sort by numeric ID before taking a page. Copy the array first because sort changes the array it receives. The supplied entries have distinct, finite numeric IDs.
slice(start, end) includes start and stops before end. To skip offset items and take limit items, use offset + limit for the end.
An offset beyond the list gives an empty page. It is not an error when the page settings themselves are valid. A short final page may contain fewer than limit items.

Complete pageEntries using the provided parsePage helper. Return status 200 and the sorted slice for valid settings, or status 400 for invalid settings. In Express, the route can supply req.query to this helper.

The browser checks this function, not an HTTP server. With offset paging, adding or deleting records between requests can shift page boundaries. A predictable sort helps define each page but does not freeze a changing list.

title: A useful page head
summary: Set a page's tab name and the information the browser needs.
explanation: `head` holds information about the page. `body` holds the content people use, such as headings and paragraphs.
`title` names the browser tab. `h1` is the main heading inside the page. They can have different words.

Changing one title does not change the other. ```html Recipe archive

Today’s soup

``` The tab says Recipe archive. The heading on the page says Today’s soup. These parts belong inside the page's `html` element.
`<meta charset="utf-8">` tells the browser how the file stores letters and symbols. Put it near the start of `head`.

The viewport is the area a browser uses to lay out a page. This setting lets a phone use its own width.
```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
It is a useful starting point for a phone layout. The page's CSS must also let its content fit.

A `link` element can load a separate CSS file. It does not show clickable link words.

title: Read a title from JSON
summary: Read JSON text and check that it contains a text title.
explanation:
JSON is a way to store data as text. Parsing reads that text and turns it into a JavaScript value.

After parsing, we still need to check that the value contains the information our app needs.

JSON uses double quotes for object keys and text values.
```javascript
const text = '{"city":"Oslo"}';
const place = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(place.city);
```
Output:
```text
Oslo
```
`JSON.parse` turns the text into an object. `place.city` reads its city.

Check the kind of value before reading its fields.

`typeof value === "object"` is not enough. JavaScript also reports `object` for `null` and arrays. Check for those separately.

Return the title if it is a string, including an empty string. Return `null` for broken JSON, a wrong outer value, or a missing or nontext title. Do not turn numbers into text.

`JSON.stringify` goes the other way: it turns ordinary JSON-compatible data into JSON text.
```javascript
console.log(JSON.stringify({ city: "Oslo" }));
```
Output:
```text
{"city":"Oslo"}
```
JSON cannot preserve every JavaScript value. This example uses only a plain object containing text.

title: Give a function a useful default
summary: Repeat a label twice by default, or use the number supplied.
explanation: A default argument supplies a value when the code that called the function leaves that argument out.

The default is written in the function definition.
```python

    return score + bonus

print(add_bonus(8, 1))
```
The first call returns 11 because bonus is left out. The second returns 9 because the explicit 1 replaces the default.

A keyword argument names the parameter it supplies.
```python
print(add_bonus(bonus=4, score=10))
```

Zero is a supplied value, not a missing argument. The code that called the function can ask for no repetitions.

title: Missing is different from false
summary: Use a fallback only for missing values, while keeping intentional zero, false, or empty text.
explanation: A condition treats values as truthy or falsy: as a yes or a no. That is different from asking whether a setting is missing.
Values such as `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` are falsy. Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy.

`||` uses the right value when the left one is falsy:
```javascript
console.log(0 || 10);
console.log("" || "Guest");
```
Output:
```text
10
Guest
```

`??` uses the right value only when the left one is `null` or `undefined`:
```javascript
console.log(0 ?? 10);
console.log(false ?? true);
```
Output:
```text
0
false
```
Choose the rule the setting needs. Zero volume and notifications set to false can be deliberate choices. Do not replace them just because they are falsy.
These operators choose a value; they do not check whether its type is allowed. This exercise keeps every supplied value except `null` and `undefined`.
steps: Return the supplied fallback only for null or undefined.
Check 0, false, and empty text: each should stay unchanged.
Try a different fallback to confirm it is not fixed in the function.

quiz.explanation: false is falsy but is not null or undefined. ?? preserves it, while || replaces it with the default.

hints: `false` is a supplied setting, not a missing one.
`??` matches this exercise's two missing cases.

title: Save and read browser data safely
summary: Save a draft and read it back, while handling missing or damaged data.
explanation:
`localStorage` saves text in a browser for one origin: the same address scheme, host, and port.

It can keep data after a page reload, but it is not cloud sync. Users or browser settings can clear or block it.

`setItem(key, text)` saves text under a key. `getItem(key)` reads it back, or gives `null` when the key is missing.

An empty string is saved text. It is different from a missing entry.

The practice functions receive a storage object with `getItem` and `setItem` methods.

The checks use a small in-memory stand-in. That lets us test success and failure without changing your browser's saved data.

Check loaded data before using it. An old or damaged record might have the wrong shape.

For a draft, require a non-null record with a `text` property whose type is string.

Reading, writing, or parsing can throw an error. Put these operations inside `try` and handle failures in `catch`.

Return `false` when saving fails. Return `null` when loading cannot produce a valid draft. Do not report a failed write as saved.

On a real page, read `window.localStorage` inside `try` too. Even access to that property can be blocked.

Use browser storage for suitable local preferences or drafts, not passwords or secrets.

Complete `saveDraft(storage, text)` and `loadDraft(storage)` using the key `draft`.

Save JSON containing `{text: yourText}`. Return `true` only after writing succeeds. Loading returns the saved string, or `null` for missing, broken, or wrongly shaped data.

Accept only strings when saving. Return `false` for other types before attempting a write.

An empty string is valid. Check its type rather than whether it is truthy.

Read draft, parse it, and check that its text is a string.
Return false for write failures and null for missing, damaged, or unreadable drafts.

title: What a form actually sends
summary: Choose where form values go and which names they use.
explanation: A form’s `action` is the address that receives its data. Its `method` says how to send that data.

`GET` puts the form values in the page address, after a `?`. It suits a search. `POST` usually puts the values in the request’s body instead of the address. It is often used when an action saves or changes something.
`POST` does not hide data by itself. HTTPS protects data while it travels. Keep private information out of search addresses, which can be saved in browser history.
A field’s `name` is the key sent with its value. Its `id` connects the field to a label. Changing one does not automatically change the other.

A checkbox sends its value only when it is checked.

```html
<input type="checkbox" name="images" value="yes">
```

`type` makes a checkbox. `name="images"` gives its data key. When checked, it sends `images=yes`. When unchecked, it sends no pair for that key.
A disabled field is normally left out of the sent data. So is a field with no `name`. A label helps people understand the field, but its words are not the field’s data key.

Change the form to `method="get"` and keep `action="/search"`. Give the topic field `name="q"`. Give the checkbox `name="includeNotes"` and `value="yes"`. The checks inspect the data locally. They do not send it, and this practice has no search service to return results.

Run the checks. They try the checkbox both checked and unchecked.

</form>

title: Transform and select with closures
summary: Choose the values you want, then turn each one into a label.
explanation: A closure is a function value you can pass to another function. Its braces hold the work to do. This lets an array method ask your code what to do with each item.
In `minute in minute > 0`, `minute` names the current input. `in` separates that input name from the work. The comparison returns true for a value that should stay.
`filter` keeps items whose closure returns true. It keeps their values unchanged. Zero and negative numbers fail a greater-than-zero check.

```swift
let minutes = [-2, 0, 3, 5]
let labels = minutes.filter { minute in minute > 0 }
    .map { minute in "\(minute) min" }
print(labels)
```
The output is `["3 min", "5 min"]`. Filtering keeps 3 and 5, then mapping turns each into text.
`map` collects one returned value for each input it receives. Here it receives only the positive minutes. Returning text makes a new array of text labels.
`$0` is a shorter name for the closure's first input. Use it when it stays easy to read. Named inputs can make a new idea clearer.
Neither operation changes the original array. The result keeps the order of retained items, including repeated values. A Set would remove repeats and change the task.
Complete `durationLabels`. Keep durations greater than zero, then turn each into `N min`, with a space before min. Return an empty array when no duration qualifies.

title: Throw, catch, and finish cleanup
summary: Use defer to finish cleanup when a function succeeds or throws an error.
explanation: defer schedules work for when the current block ends. It can finish cleanup when a function returns normally or stops by throwing an error.
An error describes a failure. throws says a function may fail. throw stops its normal work and sends an error to the caller. An error type must follow Swift's Error protocol.
try marks a call that may throw. A do-catch block handles that possibility: do holds the attempted work, and catch handles a thrown error.
Zero is too small, so checkedSize throws. Before the function ends, its defer prints Finished. The caller then enters catch. A valid size would also run defer before returning to the caller.
defer only takes effect after the program reaches it. Put it before the work that might fail. It runs when its block ends, not as soon as it is written. It does not turn a failure into a success.
The exercise supplies a Trace object with an events array. Appending text records what happened. The caller and function share this same trace, so both can add events.
In checkedMinutes, append started. Set up defer to append finished. Then throw the supplied error for a negative number. Return zero or a positive number unchanged.

The supplied inspectMinutes caller adds accepted: N after success or rejected after failure. finished must appear before either caller message, because the function's cleanup runs before control returns to the caller.

Throw for negative minutes; return allowed minutes unchanged.
Check that finished comes before the caller's final message.

choices: defer turns the error into success
quiz.explanation: The function runs its scheduled cleanup as it exits. The caller then handles the error.

hints: Place defer before the check that can throw.
Zero minutes is allowed.
externalNotes: defer cannot promise cleanup if the whole process is stopped. It also has no effect when execution never reaches it.

Array.find searches for a matching item. If no item matches, it returns undefined.

title: Edit a copied task without changing the original
summary: Copy the task list and its inner collections, then change only the first title.
explanation: Assigning another name to a list does not copy it. Both names can use the same list.

Changing a shared list is different from giving a local name a new list.
```python
first = ["Moon"]
second = first
second.append("Sun")
print(first)
```
The first name now sees ["Moon", "Sun"] because the shared list itself changed.
A shallow copy makes a new outside list, but it can still share the items inside. A list or dictionary stored inside another collection is called nested.

For these plain nested lists and dictionaries, deepcopy makes separate nested copies.
```python
from copy import deepcopy
first = [{"tags": ["sky"]}]
second = deepcopy(first)
second[0]["tags"].append("night")
print(first[0]["tags"])
```
The original tags stay ["sky"]. Only the copied nested list gets night.
Deep copying is not always needed or right for every kind of value. Here the data is ordinary nested lists, dictionaries, and strings.

This example orders records by age.
```python
def age_of(person):
    return person["age"]
people = [{"name":"Ari", "age":9}, {"name":"Jo", "age":6}]
print(sorted(people, key=age_of))
```
Jo comes first because 6 is smaller than 9. The key function is passed without calling it first.
reverse=True puts the largest values first. It does not change the input list in place.
Python sorting is stable: items with equal keys keep their earlier order, even with reverse=True.
sorted returns a new outer list. The dictionaries inside are not copied; this task only rearranges their order.

title: Create small task records safely
summary: Create a Task dataclass that gives each task its own empty tags list by default.
explanation: A dataclass helps you make objects that mainly hold data, called records. You list their fields, and it writes common methods for you, including the setup method.
A field annotation, such as `title: str`, describes the intended type. Ordinary Python does not automatically check that type while the program runs.

This small record gets its setup method from `@dataclass`.
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

point = Point(2, 3)
print(point.x)
```
It prints `2`, the saved value of `x`.

A decorator adds or changes a class or function's behavior. Here, `@dataclass` uses a ready-made decorator from Python's standard library to add the record methods. You do not need to write the decorator yourself.

A default list should be created separately for each instance so changes stay separate. `field(default_factory=list)` calls `list` to make a fresh list when no value is supplied. If you supply a list, that list is used.

A factory is something Python calls to make a value. `field(default_factory=list)` tells the dataclass to call `list` for each Box made without an `items` value.

Watch the first box get an item while the second stays empty.
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Box:
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)

first = Box()
second = Box()
first.items.append("Map")
print(first.items)
print(second.items)
```
It prints `['Map']` then `[]`. `append` receives one item and adds it to the first list in place. The second list stays empty.
Pass `list` itself as the factory, not `list()`. Python must be able to call the factory to make a fresh value for each instance. `list()` would create a list immediately instead.
Changing the first task’s tags should not change a second task’s tags. Test that behavior rather than only checking the displayed class name.

title: A method’s receiver
summary: Keep a method connected to the object it needs.
explanation:
In an ordinary method call such as `card.describe()`, the object before the dot is the receiver.

Inside that call, `this` means `card`. That lets the method read the card's properties.

Copying a method into a variable does not keep its connection to the object.

A plain call such as `read()` has no object before the dot. In strict mode, which uses stricter JavaScript rules, `this` is then `undefined` for an ordinary function.

`bind` makes a function with a chosen receiver.
```javascript
const card = { name: "Pine", read() { return this.name; } };
const readLater = card.read.bind(card);
console.log(readLater());
```
Output:
```text
Pine
```
`bind(card)` keeps `this` connected to `card` when `readLater()` runs.

A wrapper function can also keep the connection: `() => card.read()` makes the full method call later.

Arrow functions do not get their own `this`. Keep an ordinary method when it needs the object supplied by its caller.

```javascript
console.log(badge.color);
```

```text
teal
```
The badge has no color of its own, so the lookup finds the color on `defaults`.

An own property is stored directly on an object. An inherited property is found through its prototype.

A prototype link is not a copied snapshot.

title: Test a small text pattern
summary: Check that text follows an exact code pattern.
explanation: A regular expression describes a text pattern. Its `test` method returns `true` if the pattern matches and `false` if it does not.

A pattern can match just part of a longer string.
```javascript
console.log(/cat/.test("catalog"));
```
Output:
```text
true
```
The word catalog begins with cat, so the pattern finds a match.

`^` marks the start of the whole input. `$` marks its end.

With the `m` flag, these can also mark line boundaries. Our whole-code check uses no flags, so extra characters or a final line break do not fit.

`[0-9]` matches one digit from 0 through 9. `{3}` requires exactly three of them.
```javascript
const code = /^BOX-[0-9]{3}$/;
console.log(code.test("BOX-123"));
```
Output:
```text
true
```
The pattern requires BOX-, three digits, and nothing else.

Your project uses a shorter code: `ID-` followed by exactly two digits. Its length is five characters.

You may check that length explicitly too. The start and end markers, without the `m` flag, already require the pattern to cover the whole input.

Keep this validation pattern free of the `g` and `y` flags.

Those flags make repeated tests remember a position in `lastIndex`. Our check should give the same answer every time for the same text.

Accept only uppercase `ID-` and two digits from 0 to 9. Return a Boolean. Do not accept extra spaces, line breaks, or other digit characters.

title: How flex items share space
summary: Let two boxes share the space in a row.
explanation: A flex container arranges its child elements in a row or column. Each child can have rules for how much space it uses.

`flex-shrink` lets an item get smaller when the row is too full. The starting size also affects how much each item shrinks.
`min-width: 0` lets a box become narrower than its content would normally allow. Check that the words inside still fit or wrap.

title: Keep types connected with a generic
summary: Reuse one function with different types while keeping its types connected.
explanation: A generic function works with more than one type. It uses a type parameter: a name that stands in for a type. In repeatValue<T>, T might stand for String in one call and Int in another.

```swift
func repeatValue<T>(_ value: T) -> [T] {
    [value, value]
}
print(repeatValue("Hi"))
print(repeatValue(3))
```
This prints ["Hi", "Hi"], then [3, 3]. Each call returns two copies of its input in an array. The text stays text, and the numbers stay numbers.
Within one call, each T means the same type. The input is T, and [T] means an array of that type. A generic function keeps that connection; it does not turn every value into text.
An array's first property may have no value when the array is empty. It is optional. The ?? operator chooses a fallback when that optional is nil.

title: Create independent counters
summary: Complete make_counter(start) so each returned function increases and returns its own saved count.
explanation: A closure is a function that keeps access to names from the function that made it.
A function defined inside another function is called nested. Returning it lets other code use it after the outer function has finished.

This example remembers a fixed prefix.
```python
def make_label(prefix):
    def label(text):
        return prefix + text
    return label

star_label = make_label("Star: ")
print(star_label("Sirius"))
```
The nested label can still read prefix when it is called later.

Use `nonlocal` inside a nested function to change a name from the surrounding function.

Without `nonlocal points`, Python treats `points` as a local name inside `add_two`. Then `points + 2` tries to read that local name before it has a value. This causes `UnboundLocalError`.

This example adds two to the saved points. Each call to `make_points()` makes a separate counter.
```python
def make_points():
    points = 0
    def add_two():
        nonlocal points
        points = points + 2
        return points
    return add_two

first = make_points()
second = make_points()
print(first())
print(first())
print(second())
```
It prints `2`, `4`, then `2`. The second counter still starts from its own zero.

`make_points()` needs no input and returns a function. Calling that returned function adds two to its saved points and returns the new total.
Each call to make_points creates its own saved points. Two add_two functions from different calls do not share points.
For your counter, start at the supplied start and increase by one on each call. Return the function itself, not the result of calling it right away.
The count is kept in memory. It does not stay saved after the program restarts.

analogy.familiar: Follow a small change from its starting state to its result.
analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.
analogy.limit: Use the actual code and checks rather than relying on the comparison.

steps: Inside `increment`, use `nonlocal count`, add one, and return the new count.
Check that one counter remembers its calls and two counters keep separate counts.
Try a negative starting value too: `make_counter(-2)()` should return `-1`.
solution:
def make_counter(start):
    count = start
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count = count + 1
        return count
    return increment

choices: 4, because all counters share one count.

0, because a function cannot change a saved count.
quiz.explanation: Each outer call made its own saved count. The first counter's calls do not change the second counter's count.

hints: Keep count in the outer function, make_counter.

Return increment without parentheses.

title: Wrap a calculation without losing its identity
summary: Build a wrapper that doubles a function’s result while keeping its original name.
explanation: A function decorator receives a function and returns a replacement. In this lesson, that replacement is another function.
A wrapper adds behavior around a function while still calling it to do the main work.

This example adds one to a result.
```python
def plus_one(function):
    def wrapped(value):
        return function(value) + 1
    return wrapped

def square(value):
    return value * value

changed = plus_one(square)
print(changed(3))
```
The output is 10: square returns 9, then the wrapper adds one.

Writing `@plus_one` above the function tells Python to wrap it with `plus_one` and use the returned wrapper under that name.

Here, this setup does not run the original function with a sample number. The wrapped function runs when you call it.
functools.wraps copies useful information from the original function to its wrapper, including the original name.
This exercise uses one positional input and expects a number back. A wrapper for other kinds of functions would also need to pass along their supported inputs.
Double the returned value, not the input. Those are different for functions that do more than multiply.

title: Always release a temporary session
summary: Build a context manager that always cleans up a temporary session, even after errors.
explanation: A context manager sets something up before a `with` block and cleans it up afterward.
`contextlib.contextmanager` lets a generator function work with `with`. Add `@contextmanager` above the function. Calling that function then creates a context manager.
When the `with` block begins, the generator runs to `yield`. The name after `as` refers to the yielded value.

Put `yield` inside `try` and the cleanup inside `finally`.
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def marked(log):
    log.append("begin")
    try:
        yield "inside"
    finally:
        log.append("end")

log = []
with marked(log) as value:
    print(value)
print(log)
```
Output:
```text
inside
['begin', 'end']
```
`marked(log)` uses the supplied list to record events. Inside the block, `value` refers to `"inside"`. Setup and cleanup change `log`.
`finally` runs whether the `with` block finishes normally or raises an error. The error is then passed outward. Code with a matching `except` can catch it; otherwise the error stops that run.
A generator used with `@contextmanager` must yield exactly once for each use.
Call `session(log)` again for another `with` block. Each context manager is for one use; do not reuse it after its block ends.
For this exercise, append `"open"` before yielding `"ready"`, then append `"close"` in `finally`. Do not hide an error from the block. The code that called the function decides how to handle it.

summary: Use a request key to remember a note you already created. A matching retry gets the saved result.
explanation: A browser asks for a new note. The server creates it, but the reply gets lost. The browser may send the request again.

title: Allow only three requests per window

explanation: A rate limit controls how many requests can pass during a set time. Our rule allows three requests per window.
A window is one span of time. Store its start in windowStart and the number of accepted requests in count.
The window ends when now >= windowStart + 1000. Check this first. When it ends, start a window at now with count 0.

When a real HTTP server rejects a request for exceeding a rate limit, it can return status 429: Too Many Requests.
The supplied times use the same units and never go backward. A count only makes sense when every time uses the same clock rules.
Test the fourth request before the window ends, then another exactly at the end. The first is blocked. The second starts the new window with count 1.

extraFiles.code:
import sqlite3, tempfile
from contextlib import closing
from pathlib import Path

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    backup_path = Path(folder) / "backup.sqlite"
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(":memory:")) as source:
        source.executescript("CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,title TEXT); INSERT INTO notes VALUES(1,'Moon'),(2,'Ocean');")
        source.commit()
        with closing(sqlite3.connect(backup_path)) as saved:
            source.backup(saved)
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(backup_path)) as restored:
        assert restored.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone()[0] == "ok"
        assert restored.execute("SELECT id,title FROM notes ORDER BY id").fetchall() == [(1,"Moon"),(2,"Ocean")]
    print("Disposable backup reopened and verified")

externalNotes: The browser compares well-formed snapshots with numeric IDs; expected IDs are unique. The separate Python companion uses disposable SQLite files. Passing these checks does not verify a production backup or detect every possible problem.

title: Promise callbacks wait for the current work
summary: See why a Promise callback runs after the current work finishes.
explanation:
JavaScript finishes its current synchronous work before running queued Promise callbacks.

Synchronous means the statements being run directly, one after another. A queued callback waits for its turn.

Even an already fulfilled Promise waits before running its `then` callback.
```javascript
console.log("A");
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("B"));
console.log("C");
```
Output:
```text
A
C
B
```
A and C are direct statements. B is inside the queued callback, so it appears last.

Promise callbacks use a waiting line called the microtask queue.

After the current work finishes, JavaScript runs these microtasks before moving on to a later task, such as a timer callback.

`then` returns a Promise for the callback's result. Returning that Promise lets the caller `await` its completion.

It does not move the callback ahead of the direct statements that still need to run.

Complete `schedule(log)`. Add `start` now. Queue a `then` callback that adds `micro`. Add `end` now, then return the Promise from `then`.

The exercise checks order, not a precise delay in milliseconds.

Long direct work can delay callbacks. A long chain of microtasks can also delay other page work.

Using a Promise does not automatically make slow work quick. Here, keep each step small and check the resulting order.
steps: Save the Promise from a then callback that adds micro.
Add end, then return the saved Promise.
Check that awaiting it gives start,end,micro.

checks.label: Only synchronous entries appear before returning
Awaiting completion observes the queued entry last
The caller’s remaining synchronous work precedes the callback

quiz.question: Promise.resolve().then(() => log.push("later")); log.push("now"); Which entry is added first?
choices: later, because the Promise is already fulfilled
now, because the current synchronous work completes first
Either one based on a random delay
quiz.explanation: The now statement runs directly. The fulfilled Promise queues later for after the current work.

hints: Put only the micro entry inside then.
Return the Promise from then so the caller can await it.

title: Produce one value at a time
summary: Use a generator to give the next value only when it is requested.
explanation:
An iterator gives values one at a time. Call its `next()` method to ask for the next result.

The result has a `value` and a `done` flag. `done: true` means the sequence has finished.

A generator is a convenient way to make an iterator. Write its function with `function*`.

Calling the function creates a generator object. Its body waits until a value is requested.

The next call to `next()` resumes just after the previous `yield`.

After the function finishes, `next()` reports `done: true`. The finished generator has no more values to give.

`for...of` can request values from a generator until it finishes. Spread, such as `[...generator]`, collects them into an array.

Only collect a sequence that ends. An endless generator would never finish spreading.

Each call to the generator function makes a new sequence with its own position.

Using a finished generator again does not restart it. Call the function again for a fresh one.

Complete `positiveSteps(n)` so it yields the numbers from 1 through `n`, one at a time.

The input is a whole number that is zero or greater. For zero, yield nothing. Use a loop and `yield`, without building an array first.

Yield the current number on each pass.
Do not build or return an array.
Check zero, the final value, and two separate generators.

next advances and exhaustion stays done

choices: It produces no more values because it is exhausted
It creates a second independent generator
quiz.explanation: A generator object retains its position. Call the generator function again to obtain a fresh sequence.

hints: Use yield inside a loop with the requested boundary.

title: Avoid a closure ownership cycle
summary: Let a saved function use an object without keeping that object alive.
explanation: A reference is a way to reach a class object. A strong reference also keeps that object alive. Swift's Automatic Reference Counting, or ARC, releases an object when nothing holds it strongly.

A closure is a function value that can remember things it uses. If an object stores a closure, and that closure strongly holds the object, they can keep each other alive. This loop is called a strong reference cycle.
[weak self] lets the closure refer to its owner without keeping it alive. The weak reference becomes nil after that owner is released.
self?.text reads text only while the owner exists. The ?? operator supplies Released when it is missing. No forced unwrap is needed. The closure can still run safely after its owner is gone.

Reader in the exercise stores its own callback, a function saved to call later. Complete install with a weak self capture. Read the owner's current name while it exists, and return Released afterwards.

Read the current name through self?.
Use Released as the fallback after the owner is gone.

checks.expression: { () -> Bool in let owner = Reader(name:"Ari"); owner.install(); return owner.callback?() == "Ari" }()

checks.label: Callback does not retain released owner

quiz.explanation: Removing an outside reference does not break the strong reference cycle inside.

hints: Capturing the name alone would save old text, not read the current name.

title: Contain a render failure
summary: Use an error boundary to replace a broken panel while keeping the rest of the page usable.
explanation: An error boundary catches a rendering failure in a component below it. It can show fallback content: a useful replacement for the part that failed.

React calls `getDerivedStateFromError` when a child render fails. Returning `{failed: true}` lets the next render choose the fallback. You do not call this method yourself.
Place the boundary around the panel that may fail. Keep unrelated headings and controls outside so they can remain available.

A render boundary does not generally catch an error thrown directly by a click handler or timer. Handle those failures where they happen. In this exercise, the button changes state, and the child then fails while rendering.
Complete `PanelBoundary`. Break panel should show `Panel unavailable` while Dashboard stays visible. Reset panel fixes the input and changes the boundary key so it starts with fresh state.

Show fallback content only for that panel.
Run the checks for Break panel and Reset panel.

title: Mark a result update as non-urgent
summary: Mark a result update as less urgent so React can prioritize more immediate work.
explanation: A transition marks a screen update as less urgent. `useTransition` gives you `isPending`, which reports unfinished transition work, and `startTransition`, which marks the update.
The function passed to startTransition runs immediately. State updates made directly inside it are marked as transitions. React can prioritize other updates while preparing that screen.
A transition is not a timer. It does not promise a fixed delay or a faster calculation. It tells React which rendering work can be treated as less urgent.
Keep immediate selection feedback outside the transition. A text input's current value must also update immediately rather than through a transition.

In `choose`, update `selected` immediately. Update `filter` inside startTransition so the result list follows the latest choice. The checks verify the final screen; read your code too, because matching output alone does not prove that a transition was used.
This course uses React 18's synchronous callback pattern: make the state update directly inside the callback. Do not rely on later-version behavior for async actions.
steps: Put the filter update directly inside its callback.
Run the checks and confirm the final list matches the latest choice.

checks.label: Results settle to the latest selection

summary: An input goes into a model. An output comes out.
explanation: An input is information you give a program, such as a photo.
An output is the result the program gives back, such as a word naming what is in the photo.
An AI model uses calculations to turn inputs into outputs. A photo model might receive a bird photo and return the label bird.
A model can give a wrong label. Check the result against the photo. A wrong output is still an output.

title: AI, machine learning, and deep learning
summary: Deep learning is one kind of machine learning, which is part of AI.
explanation: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks such as recognizing pictures, planning, or writing text.
Machine learning is part of AI. It finds patterns in data: recorded examples or measurements.
A neural network is one kind of machine-learning model. It passes numbers through connected calculations.
Deep learning uses neural networks with several processing layers. A layer is a group of calculations whose results feed the next part of the network.

title: Examples, features, and labels
summary: Features describe an input. A label gives its target answer.
explanation: A dataset is a collection of examples. Supervised learning uses examples paired with target answers: the answers the model is trained to produce.
A feature is an input detail, such as a fruit's color or weight. A label is its target answer, such as pear. A target can also be a number.
Check labels for mistakes. Giving a pear the label apple supplies a wrong target. It does not change the fruit.
Unsupervised learning looks for patterns without these supplied target answers. Reinforcement learning uses rewards linked to actions and their results. These are different ways to learn from data.

title: Keep practice and evaluation separate
summary: Check a model on examples it did not learn from.
explanation: Training data helps adjust a model. Evaluation means checking its results. To test how it handles new examples, use data kept out of training.
A validation set is a separate group of examples used to choose settings or compare models during development.
A test set is kept for a later check. If you keep choosing changes from its results, it becomes part of development and is no longer a fresh test.

Data leakage happens when information that should stay outside training or model selection gets used there. Keep copies and closely related records together when splitting data. Different filenames alone do not make a fair test.

title: Learning a useful pattern, not just the examples
summary: Doing well on training examples does not prove a model handles new ones.
explanation: Generalization means using a learned pattern successfully on new examples of the intended task.
Overfitting happens when a model learns details of its training examples that do not help enough on new examples.
The bird model might have learned a background that appeared often in training. Check its mistakes and the data before deciding what went wrong.

Validation photos should match the task you care about. If this model must work at night, include suitable night photos in its evaluation. Success on daylight photos alone does not show that it can do this.

title: Weights and a starting adjustment
summary: A weight multiplies an input. A bias adds an adjustment.
explanation: An artificial neuron is a small calculation unit in a neural network. It is software, not a living nerve cell.
A weight is a number that multiplies an input. Multiplying by 2 means taking two copies of that input.
A bias is a number added to the result. It lets the calculation shift up or down.
First, 3 times 2 makes 6. Then adding the bias of 1 makes 7. Keeping input and weight fixed while adding 1 more to the bias would raise the score by 1.
Training can adjust weights and biases. That changes the network's calculations. This example uses numbers we chose; it does not learn them.

quiz.question: The input and weight stay fixed. The bias increases by 1. What happens to this score?
quiz.explanation: The bias is added, so adding 1 to the bias adds 1 to this score.

title: Layers and activation functions
summary: An activation function changes a unit's score before it passes onward.
explanation: A layer is a group of calculation units. Its results can become inputs for the next layer.
A hidden layer sits between the network's input and output. Hidden describes its position inside the network.
An activation function is a rule that changes a unit's score before it passes onward. One common rule is called ReLU.
ReLU is nonlinear: its graph has a bend instead of being one straight line. Nonlinear rules help a network learn patterns that multiplying and adding alone cannot represent.

title: How a prediction gets a learning signal
summary: Loss is a number that measures how far a prediction is from the target under a chosen rule.
explanation: A prediction is the answer a model proposes. In supervised training, the target is the answer supplied for comparison.
A loss function is a rule that gives a prediction a numerical penalty. Smaller loss means a better match under that rule.
The prediction 7 is closer to 8 than the prediction 5. Its loss is smaller under this distance rule.
Different tasks can use different loss rules. Lower loss does not prove that every answer is correct or that the model meets every real-world need.

title: A direction for changing the numbers
summary: A gradient guides a change. The learning rate controls its size.
explanation: Parameters are adjustable model numbers, such as weights and biases. Training changes them to try to reduce loss.
A gradient describes how loss changes when parameters change by small amounts near their current values. It gives a local direction, not a map of every possible setting.
Gradient descent changes parameters in the opposite direction to the gradient. The learning rate is a number that controls how large this change is.
A larger learning rate makes a larger step. Too large a step can pass a useful setting and increase loss. A helpful local direction does not guarantee the best final model.

title: Backpropagation and the optimizer do different jobs
summary: Backpropagation calculates gradients. An optimizer uses them to change parameters.
explanation: A forward pass sends inputs through a network to make a prediction. The loss rule then compares that prediction with the target.
Backpropagation works backward through the calculations to find gradients. These describe how small parameter changes affect loss.
An optimizer is the rule that uses gradients to update parameters. Finding a gradient and changing a stored weight are separate actions.
The training cycle is: make a prediction, measure loss, calculate gradients, then update parameters. Calculating gradients alone does not apply the update.

title: Batches, epochs, and repeated training

explanation: A batch is a group of training examples processed together. In a simple training loop, each batch is used for one parameter update.
An epoch is one full pass through the training examples. It can contain several batches.
A second epoch goes through the training examples again. More passes can help, but too many can increase overfitting.
Watch results on separate validation examples. Finishing more epochs does not by itself show that the model is getting better.

title: Text becomes tokens
summary: Tokens are the pieces used to represent text for a language model.
explanation: A language model learns patterns used to predict or generate text. A token is one unit used to represent that text. It may be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or other text.
A tokenizer is the tool that turns text into tokens. The split depends on the tokenizer and the exact text, including spaces and capital letters.
A token identifier is a number used to identify a token. It is not a score for how meaningful or true that token is.
A sequence is an ordered list. Token order matters when forming text. Equal word counts do not guarantee equal token counts.

title: Embeddings turn items into number lists
summary: An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers, not a complete definition.
explanation: An embedding is a list of numbers used to represent an item, such as a word. Training can shape the numbers so useful relationships are easier to compare.
A model can compare embeddings to find related items. What counts as close depends on the way the numbers are compared.
Hot and cold share a topic but have opposite meanings. Even when real embeddings are close, that does not prove the words can replace each other.
An embedding is not a full dictionary definition. Similarity can help find related material, but it does not show that a statement is true.

title: Attention uses context
summary: Attention mixes information from token positions using weights calculated for the current input.
explanation: Attention combines information from different token positions. It calculates how much each position contributes to the current result.
Self-attention draws that information from the same sequence of tokens. Nearby or earlier words can help shape how a token is represented.
Different surrounding words can change the calculated mix. The model can use the same stored parameters to handle a different context without a training update.
Attention's combination weights are calculated for the current input using learned parameters. They are not simply the same fixed numbers stored during training.
Attention is a calculation, not a person's choice about what to care about. Its weights alone do not fully explain a model's answer; other calculations matter too.

The original Transformer had an encoder and a decoder. The encoder built representations of the input. The decoder used representations to produce output.

title: Data choices, fairness, and privacy
summary: Check who is represented in the data, and protect people's private information.

Data bias can mean a pattern in what was collected or labeled that leads to skewed results. This is different from a neuron's bias: the number added in its calculation.
Privacy concerns how personal information is collected, used, shared, and protected. A useful AI answer does not give permission to expose someone's private details.
Practise with fictional information or non-sensitive data you are allowed to use. Collecting less private data reduces exposure, but it does not prove the whole system protects privacy.

title: Describe a path without touching the file
summary: Describe a filename and make a new path ending in .md.
explanation: `pathlib` is a standard Python module for file paths. `from pathlib import Path` imports `Path`, which makes path values that describe file locations.
`Path("notes/sky.txt")` makes a path description. Making it does not create a folder or a file.

For that path, `.name` is `"sky.txt"`, `.stem` is `"sky"`, and `.suffix` is `".txt"`. The suffix is the final ending. These describe only the final filename, not parent folders. A name that starts with a dot, like `.draft`, has no suffix by itself.

```python
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("drafts/sea.log")
print(p.name)
print(p.with_suffix(".md"))
```
`p.name` is `sea.log`. `p.with_suffix(".md")` makes a new path description ending in `sea.md`; the original `p` still ends in `sea.log`.
`with_suffix` replaces only the last suffix. For `archive.tar.gz`, changing the suffix to `.md` gives `archive.tar.md`. A name with no suffix gains `.md`.

`str(path)` turns a path value into text. Use the keys `name`, `stem`, `suffix`, and `markdown` in this exercise. Different systems may show path separators differently; the checks use the same `Path` rules as your function.

```python

print(str(Path("note.txt")))
```
This prints `note.txt`. `str` receives the path value and returns text; it does not create or read the file. A single filename avoids separators that can differ by system in this example.

title: Record only real title changes
summary: Record a change automatically, but skip assignments that keep the same value.
explanation: A trigger is saved database work that runs automatically when a chosen event happens. Here, updating a label can add a row to a change log.
A change log stores what a value was before and after a change. The exercise has `notes` for the current titles and `note_audit` for the change records.
Inside an update trigger, `OLD` means the row before the update. `NEW` means the row after it. `OLD.title` and `NEW.title` read those two versions of the title.
`AFTER UPDATE OF label` chooses assignments to the label column. `AFTER` runs the trigger's work after the row update. An assignment can happen even when the value stays the same.

`<>` means not equal. The `WHEN` condition allows the log entry only when old and new values differ. This comparison works for the supplied titles, which are never `NULL`. If missing values are allowed, the comparison needs to handle them too.

Name your trigger `record_title_change`. Store `NEW.id`, `OLD.title`, and `NEW.title` in `note_audit`. The supplied updates make two real title changes and one unchanged assignment, so the log needs two rows.
The trigger's writes belong to the same transaction as the update. Rolling back that transaction also undoes its log entries.

title: Set unfinished edits aside safely
summary: A stash can hold unfinished edits while you work on something else. Applying it keeps the saved stash.
explanation: The working tree is the project files you can edit. A stash temporarily saves unfinished changes to tracked files: files Git already knows.

Use a new disposable folder with Git installed and configured. Create note.txt containing first. Run git init, git add note.txt, and git commit -m "First note". Change the file to draft without committing.

Run this sequence in that practice folder.

```bash
git status
git diff
git stash push -m "practice draft"
git stash list
git stash show -p "stash@{0}"
git stash apply "stash@{0}"
git diff
git stash list
```

push saves the edits and returns the tracked file to its committed content. apply brings the edits back.
After apply, check that note.txt says draft and that stash list still shows the entry. Applying does not remove the saved stash.
pop tries to apply the edits and removes the stash after a successful apply. For this practice, use apply so you can inspect the recovered work while the saved entry remains.
An ordinary stash push does not include new untracked files by default. Check those files separately before assuming your work is saved.
Applying a stash can cause a conflict with newer edits. The stash is local to this repository; it is not a published commit or remote backup.

title: Let cards choose a fitting column count
summary: Let Grid choose how many card columns fit.
explanation: A grid track is a row or column. Grid can choose the column count from the space available.
`minmax(120px, 1fr)` gives a column a minimum width of 120 pixels. The `1fr` lets it share spare space with the other columns.
`auto-fit` creates as many columns as fit. It closes empty columns so the filled columns can use that space.
Gaps use space too. Two 120-pixel columns and a 12-pixel gap need 252 pixels.
At 180 pixels wide, these three cards use one column. At 260 pixels, they use two. At 480 pixels, they use three.
At 660 pixels, the three cards share the width. Empty columns close instead of leaving blank spaces.
A minimum width still matters. A container narrower than 120 pixels could make these columns overflow. This practice uses wider containers.

title: Show a fallback while a component loads
summary: Show fallback content while React waits for a lazy component to become ready.
explanation: `React.lazy` declares a component whose loader runs when React first tries to show it. Declare it outside App so later App renders reuse the same declaration.
A Promise represents a result that may arrive later. Pending means it is still waiting. Resolving supplies the result; rejecting reports a failure.
A lazy loader must return a Promise whose result has a `default` property containing the component. Here, the result will be `{default: Greeting}`.
React remembers the Promise and loaded component for this lazy declaration. Hiding and showing it again does not need to load the code again. Removing a component can still discard its local state.
Suspense handles waiting. If the loader rejects, use an Error Boundary for the failure. Ordinary fetching inside an Effect does not automatically make Suspense show its fallback.

`new Promise` immediately gives its callback a resolve function. This example saves a function that calls resolve later. The button controls when it becomes ready; no network request or download happens.

Wrap `` in Suspense. Use `

Loading report

` as the fallback. Toggle report shows or hides it, and Finish simulated load makes it ready.

In a bundled app, lazy can use a dynamic import to load another file. This single-file exercise already contains the component code and only imitates the wait. Reset the runner to get a fresh pending Promise.
steps: Put LazyReport inside a Suspense boundary.
Use the required Loading report status message.
Run the checks for waiting, ready, and showing it again.

System.Console.WriteLine shows a value and then starts a new line. The value inside the parentheses is called an argument. Keep the spelling and capital letters as shown.
You can write these instructions directly at the top level of a modern C# console project. The compiler creates the program's starting method for you. The first instruction runs before the second.

title: Keep and replace a value
summary: A variable gives a value a name. Assigning again replaces that value.
explanation: A variable is a named place for a value. In int score = 4;, score is the name and 4 is its starting value. int means a whole-number type.
The = sign assigns a value. It does not ask whether two things are equal. Assigning 9 to score later replaces the earlier value.
Using score without quotes reads its current value. Putting score inside quotes gives the text of that word instead.
A type says what kind of value is allowed. An int holds whole numbers within its range, not arbitrary text. Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are different names.

title: Divide whole numbers and keep the remainder
summary: Integer division counts whole groups. Remainder tells you what is left.
explanation: An expression is code that produces a value. An operator, such as /, tells C# which calculation to perform. Its input values are called operands.
When both operands are integers, / divides them and drops the fractional part toward zero. With positive numbers, the result counts how many complete groups fit.
The % operator gives the remainder after division. For positive numbers, this is the amount left after making complete groups.
Integer division by zero causes an error. Use parentheses to group calculations when needed. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction unless parentheses change the grouping.

title: Combine Boolean conditions
summary: Use && to require both conditions, checking the left one first.
explanation: A bool stores true or false. && requires both sides to be true. || requires at least one side to be true. ! changes true to false and false to true.
&& skips its right side when the left side is false. || skips its right side when the left side is true. This is called short-circuit evaluation: the answer is already known.
The condition denominator != 0 checks that the number is not zero. Putting that check before && can prevent the division on the right from running with zero.
using System brings names from the System namespace into view. A namespace groups names. Here it lets us write Console instead of System.Console; it does not run a printing instruction.
The denominator is 2, so the left check passes. The right side then divides 10 by 2. The result is 5, which is greater than 1. Both checks are true.
Order matters. The guard must run before the operation it protects. Parentheses can group combined conditions when their order would otherwise be unclear.

To run the example locally, use a new practice folder with the .NET 10 SDK. Run dotnet new console --framework net10.0, replace Program.cs with the example, then run dotnet run. The browser lesson only checks your understanding.

title: Choose numeric types
summary: Numeric types affect both the values you can store and the calculations you get.
explanation: int stores whole numbers within a limited range. It does not store a fractional part.
double can store very large or small numbers and fractions. Many fractional values are stored approximately. A number written with a decimal point is usually a double unless a suffix says otherwise.
decimal uses base ten and can represent many everyday decimal fractions exactly. It still has limits. The m suffix makes a numeric literal a decimal value.
var asks the compiler to work out a variable's type from its starting value. The chosen type stays fixed; var does not let the variable switch freely between types.
The output is normally written 2.5, though your computer's number settings may use a comma. This decimal division keeps the fractional part that integer division would drop.
Choose types for the job. decimal is often useful for decimal amounts, while double is common for approximate measurements. Converting between decimal and double must be an intentional step.

analogy.limit: Small examples isolate a rule; real applications require further testing.

title: Convert numbers deliberately
summary: A cast to int drops the fraction toward zero; it does not round to the nearest whole number.
explanation: A conversion changes a value to another type. A cast requests a conversion by putting the type in parentheses before the value, such as (int)measurement.
Converting a finite fractional number to int drops its fractional part toward zero, if the whole-number result fits. This is called truncation.
Truncation is different from rounding to the nearest whole number. If rounding is needed, choose a rounding rule explicitly.
Overflow means a result cannot fit in the destination type's range. checked makes this conversion report an error when the whole-number result cannot fit in int.
Dropping the fractional part of -3.9 gives -3, which is closer to zero. The value fits in int, so the checked conversion succeeds.

A failing checked conversion throws an exception: an error that interrupts normal execution. If an overflowing constant conversion is known while compiling, the compiler can reject it before the program runs. Handling exceptions comes later.

The question mark in string? says this text value may be null. This helps C# warn about places where missing text could cause an error.
The ?? operator chooses the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null. That right-hand value is a backup.

The ?. operator reads a member only when the value exists. Here, label?.Length gives null when label is missing. Length counts the string's UTF-16 units, the pieces C# uses to store text; some visible symbols need more than one unit.
The program prints Untitled, then 0 on the next line. Both lines use their backup because label is null.

continue skips the rest of the current turn. In this for loop, i++ still runs, so the counter keeps moving.
The program prints 0, 2, and 3 on separate lines. At 1, continue skips the print. At 4, the condition stops the loop.

title: Trace a recursive call

async allows a method to use await. It does not automatically start a new thread, a separate path of running instructions.

Execution starts in main. Its braces contain the steps. In C++, reaching the end of main without a return statement gives a success status of zero.

The program prints 3 and starts a new line. There is no separate printed value for main's success status.
After changing the source, build it again before running. If compilation fails, that attempt produces no updated executable. An older executable may still exist and still show the old behavior.

Saving the source already ran the new program.

title: Combine Boolean conditions safely
summary: Check for zero before allowing a division.
explanation: bool holds true or false. && requires both checks to be true. || requires at least one. ! reverses a true-or-false answer.
For these Boolean checks, && skips its right side when the left is false. || skips its right side when the left is true. This is short-circuit evaluation: the answer is already known.
denominator != 0 checks that the divisor is not zero. Placing it first means the division is reached only when that check succeeds.
std::boolalpha makes the output stream show true or false as words. It changes the display, not the stored Boolean value.
The program prints true. The divisor is 2, so the first check passes. Ten divided by two is five, which is greater than one.
A safety check must run before the operation it protects. Here, a zero divisor makes the left check false, so the unsafe division is never reached.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change denominator to zero. What happens?
choices: The result is false, and the division is skipped.
The program divides by zero first.
The skipped division makes the result true.
quiz.explanation: The left check is false. && already knows the full answer is false, so it skips the right side.

hints: Evaluate the left side of && first.

title: Initialize and convert numeric values
summary: Choose number types and give variables safe starting values.
explanation: int stores whole numbers within a limited range. double stores numbers that can have fractions, but many fractions are only approximate.
Initialize means give a starting value. The braces in int count{3} initialize count to three. Give ordinary local number variables a value before reading them.
Brace initialization rejects a narrowing conversion, one that could lose information. Putting 3.5 inside an int's braces is rejected before the program runs.
Division between two integers drops the fractional part. The decimal points in 5.0 and 2.0 make these operands double values, allowing a fractional result.
The program prints 3, then 2.5 on the next line. count holds a whole number, and ratio holds the result of double division.

static_cast<int> explicitly converts a numeric value to int. For an in-range fractional value, it drops the fraction toward zero. A value outside the allowed range can cause undefined behavior, meaning C++ makes no promise about the result. Signed integer overflow has that problem too.

quiz.question: Replace int count{3} with int count{3.5}. What happens?
quiz.explanation: Braces reject this conversion because the int could not keep the fractional part.

title: Distinguish characters and strings
summary: Tell a single char value apart from a string of text.
explanation: char is a type that holds one small unit of character data. The ordinary letter 'A', written in single quotes, is a char value.
A string is a sequence of character units. std::string stores and manages that sequence for you. Include <string> to use it. Double quotes mark text such as "Moon".

name.size() counts the char units stored in name. For these simple English letters, each letter uses one unit. Some other characters use several units, so this is not always a count of visible letters.
Use single quotes for the one-letter char value in this example. A double-quoted string literal is a different type; C++ does not automatically turn it into a char.
The program prints A 4. mark supplies A. The single-quoted space separates the results. name.size() supplies 4 because Moon has four char units.
A string can contain one letter, many letters, or no letters. Even when it contains just one letter, it is still a string, not a char.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change char mark{'A'} to char mark{"A"}. What happens?
choices: The two forms have the same type.
The compiler rejects the double-quoted text as a char initializer.
C++ automatically takes its first character.
quiz.explanation: Single-quoted 'A' is a char. Double-quoted "A" is a string literal, which cannot initialize this char.

hints: Look at the quotes as well as the text inside them.

title: Use const and inferred types
summary: Keep a value fixed with const and let auto work out a type.
explanation: const marks a value that cannot be changed through that name. const int limit{3} gives limit the value three and prevents a later assignment to limit.
auto asks the compiler to work out a variable's type from its starting value. In auto score = 2, the starting value makes score an int. Its type stays int afterward.
score is not const, so it can receive a new value. score = score + 1 reads the old score, adds one, and stores the answer back in score.
The program prints 3 3. score starts at two and increases to three. limit stays at three.
Use const for a value that this name should only read. Use an ordinary variable when the value must change. auto chooses a type; it does not make a value fixed.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Add limit = 4 before the output. What happens?

Both score and limit change together.
The compiler rejects the assignment to limit.
quiz.explanation: limit is const, so a later assignment through that name is not allowed.

title: Validate console input
summary: Accept input only when it is a readable number and an allowed count.
explanation: std::cin reads input from the terminal. std::cin >> count tries to read an integer into count. An if condition can test whether that read succeeded. A terminal may wait until you type something or end the input.
A readable number may still break your program's rules. count >= 0 allows zero and positive counts. It rejects negative counts.
The && operator checks the read first. Only if that succeeds does it check count >= 0. The success branch runs only when both checks pass.
Reading an integer does not check the whole line. Text after the number can remain unread. Checking a complete line needs an extra step beyond this example.
The program prints Accepted: 3. It could read the integer, and three is not negative.
This program handles one attempt and then ends. A program that asks again after a failed read must first clear the input error and remove the unwanted input.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

choices: The number is readable, but it fails the rule that counts must be zero or more.
Reading the input automatically changes -2 into zero.
quiz.explanation: Reading -2 succeeds. The separate count >= 0 check is false, so the error branch runs.

hints: Reading a number and deciding whether it is allowed are separate checks.

title: Select a switch branch
summary: Use switch to choose instructions that match a value.
explanation: switch compares a value with its case labels. In this example, each label is a whole number. case 1 marks where to start when the choice is one.
break leaves the switch. This stops the program from carrying on through the instructions in the next case.
default marks where to start if no case matches. Here it provides a help message for an unknown choice.
Fallthrough means continuing from one case into the next case's instructions. It can happen without break, even though the next label does not match. This example uses break to prevent it.
The program prints Write. choice is two, so execution starts at case 2. Its break leaves the switch before the Help message.
A case label chooses a starting point. It does not create an automatic stopping point. Read the instructions from that label until a break, return, or the end of the switch.

choices: Write, because it is the last numbered case.
Help, because no numbered case matches.
Every message, because all cases run.
quiz.explanation: No case label matches nine, so execution starts at default and prints Help.

title: Control a counted loop
summary: Use a for loop to count, skip a turn, or stop.
explanation: A for loop puts its setup, test, and update in parentheses. Here i starts at zero, i < 4 tests whether to keep going, and ++i adds one after each turn.
continue skips the rest of the current turn. In this for loop, the update still happens before the next test.
break leaves the loop immediately. No more turns of that loop run.
The order is: set up once, test, run the body, update, then test again. The body is the code between the loop's braces.
The program prints 0, 2, and 3 on separate lines. When i is one, continue skips the output. When i becomes four, the loop test is false.
continue does not keep i stuck at one. The for loop still runs ++i, making i two before the next test.

0, 2, and 3, because both words do the same thing.
Nothing, because the loop starts at 1.
