title: Grow a vector safely
summary: Store a growing list of values in a vector.
explanation: A vector stores a sequence of values and manages the space they need. std::vector<int> stores integers. Include <vector> to use it; the angle brackets name the type of each item.
push_back adds one item at the end of the vector. size() reports how many items the vector currently holds.

at reads an item at a chosen position. It checks whether that position exists. If it does not, at throws an exception: an error that interrupts the normal path. A later lesson explains how to handle one.
An index is an item's numbered position. Indexes start at zero. A vector with three items has indexes zero, one, and two.
The program prints 2 3. scores.at(0) reads the first value, two. scores.size() returns three because push_back added a third item.
size() is the number of items, not the last valid index. Square-bracket access does not provide at's bounds check. Use a position that exists before reading an item.

quiz.question: After push_back, change at(0) to at(2). Which value does it read?
choices: 3, because the size is the last value.
6, because index 2 selects the third value.
quiz.explanation: The vector holds 2, 4, and 6. Their indexes are 0, 1, and 2.

hints: Start counting positions at zero.

title: Keep a fixed-size std::array
summary: Store a fixed number of values in std::array.
explanation: std::array<int, 3> holds exactly three integers. Include <array> to use it. The item type and the number of items are both part of the array's type.
values.at(1) selects the second item because positions start at zero. Assigning to it replaces that item. It does not add another position.
The values inside the braces give the array its starting contents. std::array has no push_back operation because its size cannot grow.
at checks whether a position exists. An invalid position throws an exception instead of creating a new item. This example uses valid positions only.
The program prints 9 3. The second item changes from four to nine. The array still contains three items.
The array's size stays fixed for its whole life. Its items can still change unless the array is const.

title: Visit elements with a range-for loop
summary: Visit each item in a sequence and build a total.
explanation: A range-for loop visits each item in a sequence. In for (int score : scores), each turn copies the next value from scores into score.
A running total starts at zero and grows as values are added. total = total + score adds the current score to the previous total.
Here score holds a copy of an item. Changing this copy would not change the item stored in scores. The next lesson introduces references, which can refer to the original item.
If the sequence is empty, there are no items to visit. The loop body runs zero times.
The program prints 12. The total starts at zero, then becomes two, six, and finally twelve.
Adding to total does not remove or change the scores. The vector still holds its original three values after the loop.

An extra zero item is added to the vector.
0, because no loop turn changes total.

title: Refer to an existing variable
summary: Use a reference as another name for an existing value.
explanation: A reference is another name for an existing object. An object is a stored value in the program. int& alias = score makes alias refer to the same integer as score.
Assigning through alias changes the original integer. A reference must have a target when you create it.
Once this reference is bound to score, it keeps that target. An assignment through alias changes score; it does not attach alias to another variable.
int copy = score creates a separate integer with the same starting value. Later changes to score do not update copy.
The program prints 9 3. alias = 9 changes score to nine. copy keeps the three that was copied earlier.
The & in int& is part of the reference declaration. Removing it makes alias a separate int, so assigning to alias would leave score alone.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Replace int& alias with int alias. What happens after alias = 9?
choices: score stays 3 because alias now holds a separate copy.
score becomes 9 because every variable is a reference.
The compiler rejects all integer copies.
quiz.explanation: Without &, alias is an independent int. Changing it does not change score.

hints: Ask whether the declaration creates another name or another stored value.

title: Pass inputs by const reference
summary: Let a function read a string through a reference without changing it.
explanation: A parameter is a function's named input. const std::string& name refers to the caller's string instead of copying it. const stops the function from changing the string through name.

Borrowing means using an object without taking responsibility for its lifetime. The original string must still exist whenever the function uses the reference. This function only uses it during the call.
size() reads a string's size, so it works through a const reference. clear() would remove the string's characters; that change is not allowed through this parameter.
void means show_size returns no value. It prints the size instead. Its definition appears before main so the compiler knows how to call it.
The program prints 4, then Moon on the next line. show_size reads the string's size without changing its contents.
The reference reaches the caller's original string. const limits what this function can do through that reference; it does not create a private copy of the string.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Add name.clear() inside show_size before the output. What happens?
choices: The compiler rejects the change through the const reference.
Only a separate parameter copy is cleared.
quiz.explanation: name refers to the original string, but its const access does not allow clear() to change that string.

hints: The & avoids a parameter copy. const prevents changes through that parameter.

title: Observe an object through a pointer
summary: Use a pointer to reach an existing object.
explanation: A pointer stores an address that can identify an object in memory. int* observer declares a pointer to an int. &score gets score's address.
Dereference means use a pointer to reach its target. *observer reads the integer at that target. Only do this when the pointer refers to a suitable object that still exists.
nullptr means there is no object target. When a pointer may be null, check it before trying to reach its target.
This pointer only observes score. It does not create score or take responsibility for destroying it. Later lessons explain pointers that manage the objects they own.
The program prints 3. observer points to score, so dereferencing it reads score's value.
A non-null pointer can still be invalid if its target has already been destroyed. Here score remains alive throughout the check and the output.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Set observer to nullptr instead of &score. Which branch runs?
choices: The first branch prints 3 because score exists nearby.
The else branch prints No target; original: 3 without dereferencing observer.
quiz.explanation: The null check is false, so the program uses the else branch and reads score directly.

hints: &score gets an address; *observer reaches the target at that address.

title: Respect scope and object lifetime
summary: Keep a copied value after a local variable's block ends.
explanation: Scope is the region where you can use a name. A name declared inside a block's braces is not available outside that block.
Lifetime is the time an object exists. The ordinary local variable inner is destroyed when its block ends. Saving a pointer or reference to it would not keep it alive.
Copying inner into saved gives saved its own value. saved was created in the outer block, so it remains available after the inner block ends.
A dangling pointer or reference refers to an object that no longer exists. Returning a reference to an ordinary local variable can create this problem, even if the compiler accepts the code.
The program prints 7. saved receives its own copy of seven while inner is still alive.
After the inner block, saved still exists and inner does not. The output reads saved's value, so it does not need the destroyed object.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change the final output to inner instead of saved. What happens?
choices: The compiler rejects inner because its name is outside its scope.
It prints 7 because every local name is available everywhere.
The inner block automatically runs again.
quiz.explanation: inner's name is only available inside its block. saved holds the copy that can be used afterward.

hints: Scope tells you where a name can be used; lifetime tells you when its object exists.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Choose overloads and default arguments
summary: Let input types choose a function and supply an omitted input with a default.
explanation: Overloads are functions with the same name but different parameter lists. Here one describe accepts an int and another accepts a string. Their inputs need no names because these bodies do not read their values.
The compiler uses the call's input types to choose an overload. A different return type alone cannot distinguish two functions with identical parameter lists.
A default argument supplies an input when the caller leaves it out. In add_bonus, bonus = 1 makes the bonus one when the call gives only a score.
The compiler needs one clear choice. If several overloads fit equally well, the call is ambiguous, meaning the compiler cannot choose. Defaults can cause this if too many functions fit the same call.
The program prints number, then 5 on the next line. describe receives an int. add_bonus receives four and uses its default bonus of one.
A default is used only when that argument is missing. If the caller supplies a bonus, that value is used even when it is zero.

quiz.question: Change describe(4) to describe(std::string{"4"}). Which description is returned?
choices: number, because the text looks like a number.
text, because the argument is a std::string.
quiz.explanation: The argument's type selects the string overload. Its characters do not change its type.

title: Trace recursive calls
summary: Follow a function that calls itself with a smaller input.
explanation: Recursion means a function calls itself. Each call has its own input and can wait for another call's answer.
A base case is a case that returns without making another self-call. Here n <= 0 returns zero. It gives this chain of calls a stopping point.
For a positive n, the function calls sum_down(n - 1). That smaller input moves toward the base case. The current call then adds its own n to the returned answer.
Waiting calls use memory called the call stack. Too many calls can run out of stack space. The total must also fit in int, so this example uses a small input.
The program prints 6. The inputs go from three to two to one to zero. The returning totals are zero, one, three, and six.
Returning from the base case finishes only that call. Each waiting call resumes, adds its own n, and returns its answer to the previous caller.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: What does sum_down(2) return?
choices: 6, because the worked example fixes every answer.
quiz.explanation: The calls reach zero, then return one and finally three.

hints: Follow the smaller inputs first, then add while the calls return.

title: Name states with enums and structs
summary: Give states clear names and group related values in a struct.
explanation: An enum gives names to a set of choices. enum class State creates the choices State::Ready and State::Done. These are values of type State, not strings of text.
A struct groups related values. Each named value inside it is a member. Session contains a state and a score. Its members are public by default, so outside code can access them.
Session session{State::Ready, 2} gives the members values in their declaration order. The state starts as Ready, and the score starts at two.
The dot selects a member of an object. session.state = State::Done changes the state member. It does not change the score.
The program prints true 2. The state equals Done, and the score remains two. std::boolalpha displays true as a word.
A struct groups its members, but it does not automatically link their changes. Updating one member leaves the others alone unless your code changes them too.

true 5, because changing any member marks the state Done.

title: Encapsulate a class invariant
summary: Protect a counter's allowed range with checked operations.
explanation: An invariant is a rule an object must keep. This Counter must stay between zero and three. A class groups data and operations. Its members are private until public:, so outside code must use the public operations to reach the hidden value.

add first checks whether the amount is negative or greater than the remaining space. If so, it returns false. Otherwise, value += amount adds the amount and stores the result, then the function returns true.
get returns the stored value. The const after get() prevents this member function from changing ordinary data members through the current object.
The program prints true, false, and 2 on separate lines. Adding two succeeds. Adding two more would pass the limit, so it fails. std::boolalpha makes the success results print as words.
A rejected request returns before the assignment. The previous valid value stays in place, so the counter keeps its rule.

title: Initialize members with constructors
summary: Give an object's members their starting values with a constructor.
explanation: A constructor sets up a new object. It has the same name as its class and no return type. Creating s calls the Session constructor.
The part after the colon, minutes{n}, gives minutes its starting value. This happens before the constructor body runs. The body is empty because the initializer already does the needed setup.
explicit stops this constructor from silently converting an int into a Session. Session s{12} deliberately asks to create a Session using twelve.
The program prints 12. The constructor stores twelve in minutes, and duration() reads that value.
When a class has several members, they initialize in the order they are declared in the class. Reordering the constructor's initializer list does not change that order.

title: Release resources with RAII
summary: Tie cleanup to an object's lifetime so leaving a scope releases what it owns.
explanation: A resource is something a program uses and must release, such as memory or an open file. RAII is the C++ pattern of putting that responsibility in an object. When the owner is destroyed, it releases its resource.
A destructor runs when an object is destroyed. Its name is the class name with ~ in front, and it takes no arguments. Standard containers and smart pointers already use destructors to manage cleanup.
Trace only prints messages so you can see an object's lifetime. It does not open a file or own another resource. The constructor prints enter; the destructor prints leave.
The program prints enter, work, leave, and after on separate lines. marker is destroyed at the closing brace of the inner block, before after prints.

Returning normally from a function also destroys its ordinary local objects. They are destroyed in reverse construction order. Abruptly stopping the whole process does not give the same cleanup guarantee.

title: Understand value copying
summary: Change a copied vector without changing the original.
explanation: Copying a vector of integers creates a separate vector with copies of the integers. auto b = a creates that new vector. Later changes to b do not change a.
auto& b = a would instead make b a reference to a. Both names would then reach the same vector. The & changes whether this declaration creates a copy or another name.
The program prints 2 9. a keeps its original first value. Only the copy in b changes to nine.
A vector copy needs space and work to copy its items. Use a copy when you need an independent value. A reference can avoid that copy when sharing the original is intended.

quiz.question: Replace auto b = a with auto& b = a. What prints?

title: Transfer resources with move semantics
summary: Let a vector transfer its stored data, then give the source a known value.
explanation: Moving lets an object hand owned resources to another object. std::move, from <utility>, marks a value so the receiving operation may move from it. std::move alone does not transfer anything; the receiving operation does the work.
After this vector move, b has the original items. a still exists and can be used, but do not rely on a particular set of remaining contents unless the operation promises one.
b and a are separate vectors. Changing a afterward does not change b. Moving a simple number may just copy it, so std::move is not a guarantee of faster code.
The program prints 2 7. b keeps the original first item, two. clear() removes any items left in a, and push_back puts seven into it.
clear() gives a a known empty state before the new item is added. The output therefore does not depend on guessing a's contents immediately after the move.

The later clear and push_back give a the same new contents either way.
Both vectors share their first item.

title: Prefer the rule of zero
summary: Let standard members handle copying and cleanup for your class.
explanation: The rule of zero means relying on members that already handle their own resources. You then need zero custom functions just to repeat their copying, moving, or cleanup work.
Notebook contains a string and a vector. The compiler's generated copy copies each member. Here that gives the new Notebook its own name and its own vector of page numbers.
std::string and std::vector already release their storage when destroyed. Notebook does not need a custom destructor to repeat that cleanup.
The program prints 2 3. a keeps its two page numbers. b has its own vector, which grows to three items.

The rule of zero is a useful design choice, not a ban on custom cleanup. A class that directly owns a special resource may need its own design. Writing a destructor can also stop the compiler from generating move operations automatically.

quiz.explanation: b is now another name for a. There is one Notebook, and its vector grows to three items.

title: Own one object with unique_ptr
summary: Give one smart pointer responsibility for an object's cleanup.
explanation: std::unique_ptr owns an object and destroys it when ownership ends. std::make_unique<int>(7), from <memory>, creates an integer in separately managed storage and returns its owner. You do not need to write new and delete yourself.
A unique_ptr cannot be copied. Moving it transfers ownership to the destination. Unlike a general moved-from value, a moved-from unique_ptr is specifically guaranteed to be empty.
if (q) checks whether q has a target. *q then reaches the owned integer. Comparing p with nullptr only checks whether p is empty; it does not try to read a target.
The program prints true, then 7 on the next line. p is empty after the move. q owns the integer and can read it after the check.
Only q owns the integer after this transfer. When q is destroyed, it also destroys the owned integer. An observing raw pointer would not take on that cleanup responsibility.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

choices: Both pointers share ownership of the integer.
The compiler rejects the attempt to copy a unique_ptr.
p is copied and automatically becomes empty.
quiz.explanation: unique_ptr forbids copying. Ownership can be transferred with a move, but it cannot be duplicated this way.

title: Share ownership deliberately and observe weakly
summary: Share an object's lifetime and check it through a weak observer.
explanation: Copies of std::shared_ptr share ownership of one object. The object stays alive while an owner remains. make_shared creates the object and its first owner. reset() gives up only that pointer's ownership.
A std::weak_ptr observes without keeping the object alive. Its lock() operation tries to obtain an owning shared_ptr. If the object has already been destroyed, lock() returns an empty pointer.
The if statement creates live from lock() and checks it before reading *live. live keeps the object alive while that statement runs. Its ownership ends when the if statement ends.

The program prints 8, then true. second keeps the integer alive for the first output. After second.reset(), no owner remains. expired() then reports true, meaning the weak observer's object is no longer alive.

An ownership circle can keep objects alive forever: each object owns another that leads back to it. A weak reference on the return path can break that circle. Use unique ownership when sharing is not needed.

choices: true, because the first owner was reset.
false, because second still owns the object.
quiz.explanation: second still keeps the integer alive. The weak pointer does not own it, but it can report that an owner remains.

title: Override behavior through a base interface
summary: Call behavior chosen by the actual object behind a base reference.
explanation: Shape describes a score operation. virtual allows another type to replace its behavior. The = 0 makes this operation pure virtual: Shape has no implementation of it. Shape is abstract, so you cannot create a Shape object directly.

Square : Shape makes Square a derived type: it builds on Shape. Square supplies its own score function. override asks the compiler to check that this function really replaces a virtual function from the base type.
const Shape& lets show read the original object through a Shape reference. The reference does not turn the Square into a separate Shape value. The virtual call can therefore select Square's behavior.
The program prints 4. Although show uses a Shape reference, the actual object is a Square, so Square's score function runs.
virtual ~Shape() = default gives Shape a virtual destructor with compiler-provided cleanup. It supports correct destruction through a base pointer, which the next lesson explains.

title: Destroy polymorphic objects safely
summary: Use a virtual destructor when an owner deletes a derived object through its base type.
explanation: std::unique_ptr<Base> can own an object whose actual type is Derived. The pointer's declared type and the object's actual type do not have to be the same.

For this kind of deletion through Base, Base needs a virtual destructor. It makes cleanup start with the actual Derived object. Removing virtual here would cause undefined behavior: C++ would no longer promise a valid result.
owner.reset() destroys the object it owns, then leaves the pointer empty. The Derived destructor runs before the Base destructor.
The program prints derived, base, and done on separate lines. The object is fully destroyed before execution reaches the done output.
Resetting an already-empty unique_ptr does nothing. Destruction happens once because there is no owned object left to destroy again.

title: Write a function template
summary: Write one function pattern that can work with several types.
explanation: A function template is a pattern for making functions with different types. template<typename T> introduces T as a type placeholder. The compiler creates the needed typed function before the program runs.
Both parameters use the same T. With two int inputs, the compiler chooses int. With two double inputs, it chooses double. This template cannot work out one T from a mixture of those two input types.
The chosen type must support the operations in the function. Here its values must be comparable with < and usable as the returned value.
The program prints 5, then 2.5 on the next line. Each call returns the larger of its two values.
The function returns a value, not a reference to one of its local parameters. For these numbers, the caller receives a separate numeric result.

The compiler rejects the call because the inputs suggest different types for T.
quiz.explanation: The first input suggests int and the second suggests double. This call does not provide one matching type for both T parameters.

title: Define a class template
summary: Use a class template to store a chosen type of value.
explanation: A class template is a pattern for classes with different types. T is its type placeholder. Box<int> stores an int, while Box<double> stores a double. They are two distinct types made from the same pattern.
The constructor receives a T value and uses item{value} to initialize its member. get() returns a copy of that member. explicit keeps construction from silently converting an input into a Box.
The program prints 3 1.5. count is a Box<int> holding three. ratio is a Box<double> holding one and a half.
Choosing Box<int> fixes its stored type as int. Braces reject a starting value that would need a narrowing conversion, meaning a conversion that could lose information.

title: Constrain a template with a concept
summary: Limit the types a template accepts with a concept.
explanation: A concept is a named requirement checked before the program runs. It limits which types a template can accept.
<concepts> provides std::integral. It accepts integer types such as int and rejects floating-point types such as double. template<std::integral T> applies that requirement to T.
The compiler works out T from the input, then checks the requirement. A double input fails this requirement, so that call is rejected before execution.
The program prints 6. Three has type int, which meets std::integral. The function adds three to itself.
The concept checks the type, not whether every possible calculation is safe. A signed integer result must still fit its type's range. This example uses small values that fit.

title: Capture inputs in a lambda
summary: Let a small function keep a copy of a nearby value.
explanation: A lambda is a function object written where you need it. Here auto add stores that object. Parentheses describe its input, and braces contain its work.
A capture lets a lambda use a nearby local value. [offset] stores a copy of offset when the lambda is created. Later changes to the original do not change that copy.
The parameter value receives a fresh input each time add is called. The captured offset is already stored in the lambda. The body adds these two values.
The program prints 5. The lambda kept a copy of two. Changing the original offset to five does not change that copy, so add(3) returns three plus two.
[&offset] would capture a reference instead. It would read the original's current value, but the original must still exist when the lambda uses it.

quiz.explanation: The reference reads the current offset, five. Adding the input three gives eight, and offset is still alive during the call.

title: Store a callable with std::function
summary: Store and replace a function-like operation with std::function.
explanation: A callable is something you can call like a function. std::function, from <functional>, can hold different compatible callables over time. Its stored callable must be copyable.
std::function<int(int)> accepts one int and returns an int. Both lambdas here match that shape. Their empty [] means they capture no nearby local variables.
if (operation) checks whether an operation is stored. Calling an empty std::function would throw an exception, so check when an empty value is possible.
The program prints 4, then 6 on the next line. The first operation adds one. The replacement multiplies by two.

Use auto when one lambda's own type is enough. std::function adds flexibility but can add extra work or storage. It also does not keep objects alive merely because a stored lambda captures references to them.

title: Read iterator ranges
summary: Use an iterator to walk through a sequence without reading past its end.
explanation: An iterator identifies a position in a sequence. begin() marks the first item when one exists. end() marks a position just after the last item, so end itself is not an item to read.
*it reaches the item at the iterator's current position. ++it advances this iterator to the next position. The loop uses these operations to visit the vector's values.
The condition it != values.end() runs before the body. It keeps the loop from reading the past-the-end position.
The program prints 6. The loop reads two and then four, adding both to the total. It stops when the iterator reaches end().
For an empty vector, begin() already equals end(). The first test is false, so there is no item access and the total stays at its starting value.

The program reads an invalid item.
An unknown integer because total has no starting value.
quiz.explanation: total starts at zero. begin() equals end(), so the loop body never runs.

title: Find a value with an algorithm
summary: Find the first matching value and check whether it exists.
explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps for a task. std::find, from <algorithm>, searches from the first position up to, but not including, the end position. It stops at the first equal value.
find returns an iterator, not true or false. A match gives the matching item's position. No match gives the end position. Check that result before reading *found.
The program prints 4. The search finds the first of the two fours, and the check allows that item to be read.
find does not change the vector. If there is no match, the else branch reports missing without trying to read the end position.

title: Sort with a valid ordering
summary: Sort values by answering which one should come first.
explanation: std::sort rearranges items in the given range. It works with vector iterators because they can jump directly between positions. The vector itself changes.
A comparator is a function that answers whether its first input should come before its second. Here the lambda returns a > b, so larger numbers come first.

The rule must stay consistent. No value can come before itself. If one value comes before a second, and the second before a third, the first must come before the third too. Values treated as tied must form consistent groups.
The program prints 3 2 1, with a space after each number. The comparator puts larger integers before smaller ones.

These requirements are called a strict weak ordering. For ordinary integers, < and > work. Do not replace them with <= or >=: those would say a value comes before itself and break sort's requirements.

quiz.question: Replace a > b with a < b. What sequence prints?
quiz.explanation: The rule now puts smaller numbers first, so sort rearranges the vector into increasing order.

title: Transform and accumulate a sequence
summary: Transform each item, then add the results into one total.
explanation: std::transform applies a function to each input item and writes each result to an output position. Here the lambda doubles each number and writes into doubled, leaving values unchanged.
doubled(values.size()) creates as many output items as there are inputs. Reserving storage alone would not create those items. This form of transform needs valid existing output positions.
std::accumulate, from <numeric>, adds the items to a running total. Its last argument supplies the starting value and the total's type. Here zero starts an int total.
The program prints 12. Doubling produces two, four, and six. Accumulating from zero gives their sum, twelve.
The starting value is added too; it is not just a setting. Choose its type and range so the running result fits. The small int total in this example fits safely.

title: Compose lazy range views
summary: Describe a sequence of filtering and transforming steps with a view.
explanation: A view describes how to visit data. It does not immediately build a new vector of results. This is called lazy work: results are produced as the loop asks for them.
std::views::filter keeps the items that pass a test. Its test function is called a predicate. Here x > 1 keeps only source values greater than one.
std::views::transform changes each kept value as it is read. Here it multiplies by ten. The | symbols connect the filtering and transforming steps in order.
The program prints 20 30, with a space after each number. Two and three pass the filter, then become twenty and thirty. The original vector still holds one, two, and three.
This view refers to values, so that vector must stay alive while the view uses it. The view is not a saved collection of answers. Do not return this view if its local source vector will be destroyed.

title: Avoid invalidated iterators
summary: Use the fresh iterator returned after removing a vector item.
explanation: Invalidate means make something no longer valid to use in its old way. Erasing a vector item invalidates iterators and references at that position and after it. Do not keep using the old position to read an item.
erase returns a fresh iterator to the following item. If no following item exists, it returns the vector's new end position. Assign that result back to position.
The returned iterator may be end(), so compare before reading *position. This handles removing the last remaining item too.
The program prints 4. Erasing the first item removes two. The returned iterator identifies the following item, four, which is now first.

Growing a vector can move its items to new storage. When that reallocation happens, all old iterators, references, and pointers into its items become invalid. Use each operation's rules before keeping a saved position.

title: Associate ordered keys with values
summary: Store values under keys and look them up without adding missing keys.
explanation: A map stores key-value pairs. A key identifies a value, like a name identifying a score. std::map keeps one value for each distinct key and visits keys in its comparison order.
find(key) returns the matching item's position, or end() when the key is absent. It does not insert anything. contains(key) simply reports true or false without inserting either.

Square brackets behave differently. Reading a missing key through [] adds that key with a default value. For this int map, the new value is zero. Use brackets when that possible insertion is intended.
const auto& [name, score] gives names to the two parts of each existing pair. This is a structured binding. The reference avoids copying the pair, and const makes this access read-only.
The program prints 1 2, then Ada:2 and Mina:4 on separate lines. One means the missing-key check is true. The size remains two because find did not insert Zed.
The map visits Ada before Mina because its string keys are ordered by comparison. This is independent of the order in which those two pairs were written in the initializer.

The first line is 0 3, and the loop also visits Zed:0.

title: Use hashed key lookup
summary: Look up keys in a hash-based map without relying on their visit order.
explanation: std::unordered_map stores key-value pairs. A hash function turns a key into a number used to choose where to look. An equality check then identifies the matching key.
Its visit order is not promised to be sorted or to match insertion order. Rehashing means rebuilding its internal groups; that can change the order and invalidate iterators.
contains(key) checks whether a key exists without adding it. As with map, [] can insert a missing key. A missing int value starts at zero, so incrementing that bracket result makes it one.
The program prints 0 1. Zero means lake is absent. The map still has only its original forest key because contains does not insert.
Lookup usually needs about the same amount of work as the map grows. In a worst case, it may examine many items. This is a rule about work, not a promise of a particular running time.

title: Keep distinct values in a set

explanation: std::set stores distinct values in comparison order. With ordinary integers, repeated equal values count as one item. It does not keep a count of how many duplicates were supplied.
insert tries to add a value. If an equal value is already present, the set keeps its existing item and its size stays the same.
insert returns a pair of results. first is an iterator to the stored item. second is true only when a new item was added.
The program prints 0 2, then 1 3 on the next line, with a space after each listed item. The repeated three is stored once, and inserting it again adds nothing.
The stored values also determine the set's order, so you cannot change one directly through its iterator. To replace a value, erase the old one and insert the new one.

title: Store alternatives in a variant

std::get<T> reads the requested alternative or throws std::bad_variant_access if that alternative is not active. Here the successful initialization leaves either an int or a string, so the else branch can read the string.
The program prints number 7. message holds an int, so get_if returns a valid pointer and the first branch reads seven.

explanation: C++23 std::expected<T, E> holds either a successful value of type T or an error of type E. Here success is an int and an error is a string. The caller handles the result explicitly.
The function accepts amounts from zero through one hundred. Outside that range, std::unexpected returns the error text immediately. Accepted values can be doubled without exceeding int's range.
if (result) checks for success. The first branch reads the successful value with *result. The else branch reads the error with result.error().
The program prints value 8. Four passes the range check, so the function returns its doubled value, eight.

title: Handle exceptions at a boundary
summary: Catch a failure where the program knows how to handle it.
explanation: An exception signals a failure that interrupts the usual path. throw starts that interruption. A call that throws does not return its normal value, and the remaining statements on that path are skipped.
try marks the work covered by a handler. catch handles a matching exception type. const std::invalid_argument& reads this error without copying it, and what() provides its descriptive message.

Stack unwinding means leaving calls and scopes while an exception travels to a handler. Fully constructed local objects in those exited scopes are destroyed. RAII uses that cleanup to release owned resources.
The program prints reward 3, then after boundary on the next line. The score is allowed, so no exception is thrown and the handler is skipped.
If this handler catches a failure and finishes normally, execution continues after catch. It does not retry the failed call or return to the skipped output. An uncaught exception can end the program.

title: State exception guarantees honestly
summary: Prepare a change separately so a failed operation can leave the original untouched.
explanation: An exception guarantee describes what remains true after failure. The basic guarantee keeps objects valid and avoids resource leaks. The strong guarantee also leaves the protected state unchanged if the operation fails.
candidate is a copy of scores. The function adds to that copy and checks the new score. If this work fails, scores has not been changed.
swap exchanges the original and prepared contents after validation succeeds. Swapping these vectors with their default allocators does not throw, so it can safely finish the change.
The program prints rejected 1 4. The negative value triggers an exception before swap. scores still has one item, four. back() reads that last item; it requires a nonempty vector.

catch handles the failure but does not automatically reverse earlier changes. noexcept is also not an undo command: it promises that no exception escapes the function. If one does, the program terminates.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Instead, append directly to scores, then reject the negative value without undoing the append. What remains after catch?
choices: A usable vector with two items, ending in -2.
An empty vector, because exceptions clear containers.
The original vector, because catch automatically undoes changes.
quiz.explanation: The append already happened. Handling the exception does not remove the appended item, so this version loses the strong guarantee.

hints: Find the first operation that changes the original, then check whether failure can happen after it.

title: Work with filesystem paths
summary: Work with a path's spelling without creating or opening a file.
explanation: A path describes a location in a filesystem. std::filesystem::path stores and works with that description. Creating a path object does not create a file.

lexically_normal simplifies the spelling without checking the disk. A dot means the current folder; dot-dot moves back one folder in this spelling. This is a text-level simplification, not a check of where filesystem links lead.
extension() gets the final filename's extension, such as .txt here. generic_string() turns a path into text using forward slashes for separators.
The program prints saves/run.txt, then .txt on the next line. The dot is removed, and slot followed by dot-dot cancels out in the path's spelling.
The result does not prove that the folder or file exists. Opening, creating, and checking real files are separate operations that can fail. This example performs none of those disk operations.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Replace run.txt with run.dat. Is a file created, and which extension prints?
choices: A folder is created, and the extension is empty.
No file is created, and .dat prints.
A file is created, and .txt still prints.
quiz.explanation: Only the path's spelling is examined. The new filename ends in .dat, but no file is created.

hints: A description of a file location is different from an operation on the file.

title: Read and write files with streams
summary: Write a file, check for failure, and read its text back.
explanation: A file stream connects the program to a file. std::ofstream writes, and std::ifstream reads. This example creates or overwrites practice.txt in the current folder. Run it in a disposable practice folder without a file you need to keep.
Opening ofstream this way clears an existing file before writing. std::ios::app would instead append, meaning add at the end. Writing text does not add a newline unless the text includes one.

if (!out) detects stream failure. Checking after close() can catch a failed final write. RAII still closes streams during destruction, but automatic cleanup alone does not confirm that writing succeeded.
When the operations succeed, the program prints second. The second output stream clears the earlier contents before writing its own text.

std::getline(in, text) reads up to a newline or the end of the file. It removes a found newline from the input without storing it in text. The returned stream is checked before the program prints the result.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.explanation: Appending keeps first and adds second directly after it. Neither write supplies a newline.

title: Use a non-owning string_view
summary: Look at part of an existing string without owning a copy.
explanation: std::string_view remembers where text starts and how many character units it covers. It does not own or copy that text. The owning string must keep its storage alive while the view uses it.
Changing an existing character in owner changes the text the view reads. This character assignment does not move the string's storage, so the view remains valid here.
remove_prefix(1) moves the view's start forward by one character unit. It does not erase anything from owner. The count removed must not exceed the view's length.
The program prints Forest, then orest Forest on the next line. The view sees the capital F. Removing its prefix hides that first character only from the view.

Destroying the owner, or an operation that moves its storage, can invalidate the view. Also, a view need not end at a null character, the marker used to end a C-style string. Its data() pointer alone is not a promise of that ending.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Replace owner[0] = 'F' with owner[1] = 'O'. What does the final line show after remove_prefix(1)?
quiz.explanation: The second character becomes O. The view hides only the first character, while owner keeps the complete fOrest text.

hints: Track the stored text separately from the part the view covers.

title: View contiguous values with span
summary: Let a function view consecutive items without copying the collection.
explanation: std::span describes a sequence of items stored next to one another in memory. It remembers their starting position and count. It does not own them, so their storage must remain alive and valid.
Passing span<int> by value copies the small view, not the array it refers to. The function can change the original integers through that view.
empty() checks whether the span has zero items. !values.empty() makes sure index zero exists before assigning to it. C++23 span's [] access does not promise a bounds-checking exception.
The program prints 9 3. setFirst changes the original first item to nine. The array still has three items.
span<const int> makes the viewed integers read-only through the span. const span<int> instead makes the view object itself const; its int elements can still be changed. The position of const matters.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change only the parameter to std::span<const int>. What happens to values[0] = 9?
choices: It changes the original array as before.
It edits a private copy of the array.
The compiler rejects writing through the read-only element view.
quiz.explanation: The viewed element type is const int, so assigning a new value through the span is not allowed.

hints: Look at whether const applies to the viewed items or to the view itself.

title: Evaluate constants and assert at compile time
summary: Calculate a constant and check it before the program runs.
explanation: Compile time is when source code is turned into a program. A constexpr function can be evaluated then when its inputs and operations allow it. Other calls to the same function may still run later.
constexpr int size requires its starting value to be a constant expression, one the compiler can evaluate. Here twice(3) meets that requirement.
static_assert checks a constant condition during compilation. If the condition is false, the compiler rejects the program and reports the supplied message.
The program prints 6. The compiler calculates size as six, and the size == 6 assertion passes before main runs.

A runtime check happens while a program is running. static_assert happens earlier and requires a constant condition. The separate assert facility is a runtime check that some build settings can disable.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change twice(3) to twice(4), but keep static_assert(size == 6). What happens?
choices: The program prints 8 and then gives a warning.
The compiler changes size back to 6.
Compilation fails, so this changed program cannot run successfully.
quiz.explanation: size becomes the constant eight. The assertion that it equals six is false, so the compiler rejects the program.

hints: Calculate the constant first, then test the static assertion.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Separate declarations into headers
summary: Share a declaration through a header and guard against repeated inclusion.
explanation: A header is a file of code that another source file can include. A declaration introduces a name and its type. Here score.hpp defines the Score type so main.cpp can use it.
#include brings a header's text into the source before compilation. One source file with its included text forms a translation unit: the code the compiler processes together.

An include guard prevents the same header contents from being included twice in that unit. #ifndef checks whether SCORE_HPP is undefined. #define marks it as defined, so the second inclusion skips the guarded text.
The program prints 3. The guard lets Score be defined once even though main.cpp includes the header twice.
The # directives are handled before the program runs. Including a header twice does not run it twice. Without the guard, this unit would contain two definitions of Score, which is an error.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Remove the guard lines from score.hpp but keep both includes. What happens?
choices: The compiler rejects the repeated Score definition in the same translation unit.
The program prints 6 because the header runs twice.
The linker automatically combines the repeated definitions.
quiz.explanation: Both includes bring in the same struct definition. The error is a repeated definition, not repeated execution.

hints: Track whether SCORE_HPP has already been defined before processing each inclusion.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Link translation units without duplicate definitions
summary: Compile separate source files and link their function calls to one definition.
explanation: A function declaration tells the compiler the function's name, inputs, and result type. bonus.hpp declares addBonus so main.cpp can compile a call to it.
A definition supplies the function's body. bonus.cpp contains the single definition of this ordinary function. Other source files can see its declaration without repeating that body.

Linking connects compiled parts into a program. With GCC, build both source files using g++ -std=c++23 main.cpp bonus.cpp -o example. Including a header does not automatically build another source file.
The program prints 7. The call in main.cpp reaches the definition in bonus.cpp, which adds three to four.

Compiling a call can succeed with only a declaration visible. Linking still needs the actual definition. Supplying this ordinary function's body in multiple source files also breaks the required single-definition arrangement.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Build only main.cpp, with bonus.hpp present but without compiling and linking bonus.cpp. What fails?
choices: Nothing; the declaration is enough to print 7.
quiz.explanation: The declaration lets the call compile, but the missing compiled definition leaves the linker unable to complete the program.

hints: Separate knowing how to call a function from having its executable body.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Use diagnostics and sanitizers responsibly
summary: Use compiler messages and runtime checks without treating them as proof that every path is safe.
explanation: A diagnostic is a compiler message about your code. GCC's -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic options request useful warnings. They do not enable every possible warning. -Werror makes emitted warnings fail the build.

Save the example as main.cpp. With GCC installed, build it using g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.cpp -o example. After a successful build, run ./example on Linux or macOS, or .\example.exe in Windows PowerShell.

A sanitizer adds runtime checks for certain errors. On a supported GCC platform, adding -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can help detect memory errors and undefined behavior on executed paths. These options do not install the required tools.
The program prints 2 4, with a space after each number. A failed build is not a successful run, even if an older executable remains in the folder.
A clean sanitizer run only covers the paths it checked. It does not prove every possible execution is safe. A missing or unsupported sanitizer is also not a passing check.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: With GCC's -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror options, add an unused int unused = 7 inside main. How should the result be handled?
choices: Treat the warning made into an error as a failed build and fix its cause.
Assume the build succeeded because unused variables never matter.
Read outside the array to remove the warning.
quiz.explanation: GCC warns about the unused local variable. -Werror makes that warning fail the build, so the changed program has not been successfully built.

hints: Read the build result before deciding whether there is a new program to run.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Test behavior with assertions
summary: Check expected results with assertions and keep those checks enabled when testing.
explanation: An assertion checks a condition that should be true at a particular point. assert, from <cassert>, can check whether a function returned the expected answer.
With assertions enabled, a false assert reports a problem and aborts the program. Later statements do not run. Keep each expectation focused so the failed check helps locate the problem.
Defining NDEBUG before including <cassert> disables assert. The condition is then not evaluated at all. Never put work the program needs, such as an essential assignment, inside an assertion.
With assertions enabled, the program prints checks completed after all three conditions pass. The tested answers are zero, four, and negative four.
These checks cover three inputs whose results fit in int. They do not prove the function is safe for every integer. Test the boundaries your function promises to support as well.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change the middle assertion to doubleSmall(2) == 5 and define NDEBUG before <cassert>. What does the final message prove?
choices: Only that execution reached the output; the wrong assertion was not checked.
quiz.explanation: NDEBUG removes assertion evaluation. Reaching the message does not prove that the disabled conditions passed.

hints: Before trusting an assertion result, check whether assertions were enabled.

title: Measure durations with chrono
summary: Convert a time duration while keeping track of its unit.
explanation: A duration is an amount of time. std::chrono stores a count together with its unit. milliseconds{1750} means 1,750 milliseconds, not 1,750 seconds. One second contains 1,000 milliseconds.
duration_cast converts between duration types. Converting this integer duration to seconds drops the fractional part toward zero. It does not round to the nearest whole second.
count() returns the number in the duration's own unit. After conversion to seconds, its count is measured in seconds.
The program prints 1. The supplied duration is one and three-quarter seconds, but the whole-second result keeps only one.

For actual elapsed time, subtract two steady_clock::now() time points. That clock does not move backward, which helps measure intervals. This example converts a supplied duration, so its output does not depend on how fast the computer runs.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change the supplied duration to 2500 milliseconds. What whole-seconds count prints?
quiz.explanation: The duration is two and a half seconds. The integer conversion drops the fractional half, leaving two.

hints: Convert the unit first, then drop the fraction for a whole-second result.

title: Generate bounded random values
summary: Generate whole numbers inside an inclusive range.
explanation: A pseudorandom engine follows rules to produce a sequence that looks random. A distribution turns the engine's results into the kind of values you need. Here the engine is mt19937 and the distribution produces whole numbers.
uniform_int_distribution<int>{1, 6} gives each integer from one through six the same intended chance. Both endpoints are included.

A seed chooses the engine's starting state. Using 42 makes this engine repeat its sequence. Different standard-library distributions can map that sequence differently, so do not assume identical dice results across every toolchain.
The program prints 1, meaning all twenty generated values passed the range check. The test includes both one and six.

Twenty checks show the observed values stayed in range; they do not prove statistical fairness. mt19937 is also not designed to protect secrets. Security-sensitive randomness needs a suitable generator.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Set the distribution to {4, 4} and check roll == 4. What does the final check print?
choices: The values must alternate between three and five.
1, because the only possible value in that inclusive range is four.
quiz.explanation: Both endpoints are four, so every generated value is four and every check passes.

hints: List the allowed integers between the endpoints, including both endpoints.

title: Give a thread a joining lifetime
summary: Wait for a worker thread before reading the value it changes.
explanation: A thread is a path of work that can run alongside another. std::jthread starts the supplied function on a worker thread. Creating the worker does not mean its work has finished.
Joining means waiting for a thread to finish. When this jthread leaves its scope, its destructor requests a stop and joins the worker before execution continues beyond that block.

[&result] lets the worker use the original result by reference. result belongs to the outer scope, so it stays alive until after the worker finishes. This lambda takes no call arguments; its empty parameter parentheses may be omitted here.
The program prints 7. Leaving the inner block joins the worker, so its write is complete before the main thread reads result.
A stop request does not forcibly interrupt a thread. The worker must cooperate if it uses that request. This short worker simply finishes its assignment and returns normally.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change the worker's assignment to result = 12 and keep the scopes. Could the final output still be zero because the worker was slow?
choices: No. The worker is joined before the read, so the program prints 12.
Yes. Reference capture gives the worker a private copy.
Yes. jthread destruction always leaves the worker running.
quiz.explanation: The join waits for the worker to finish. The main thread then reads the same still-live variable the worker changed.

hints: Locate the join before deciding when the result can be read.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Protect shared state with a mutex
summary: Protect a shared counter so two workers do not change it at the same time.
explanation: A data race can happen when threads access the same ordinary object without suitable coordination and at least one writes. C++ gives no valid-result guarantee for that situation. The counter needs protection during competing updates.

A mutex is a lock that one thread can hold at a time. Both workers use the same mutex to protect count. The [&] capture borrows the surrounding variables they use, which remain alive until both workers finish.
lock_guard locks its mutex when created and unlocks when destroyed. Here it protects the entire ++count operation. Protecting only a separate read would not protect the whole update.
The program prints 200. Each worker safely performs one hundred increments. Leaving their block joins both workers before the final read.
The extra finalLock is harmless but unnecessary here because both writers have finished. The locks inside the workers are still needed while those workers may run together.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Remove only finalLock, keeping both worker locks and both joins. Is the final read safe?
choices: No. Every read needs a lock forever, even after all writers finish.
Yes. Both workers have finished, and count is 200.
quiz.explanation: The worker increments remain protected. Joining both workers finishes their writes before the final read.

hints: Separate the time when workers compete from the time after both have joined.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Update a simple counter atomically
summary: Update one shared counter in a single atomic operation.
explanation: Atomic means an operation is treated as one indivisible step for competing threads. std::atomic<int> supports such operations on one integer. fetch_add reads and adds in one operation, so competing increments do not overwrite each other's work.
fetch_add(amount) adds the amount but returns the old value. The returned number and the new stored number can therefore differ.

load() reads the atomic counter without changing it. This example uses the default ordering, called sequential consistency: these atomic operations fit one shared order that respects each thread's order.
The program prints 200 203. The workers contribute two hundred increments. The final fetch_add returns the old two hundred and raises the counter to two hundred and three.
Making individual variables atomic does not make a group of changes one operation. If several values must obey a rule together, a mutex may still be needed around the whole group.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change only the final fetch_add(3) to fetch_add(5). Which pair prints?
quiz.explanation: The operation returns the old value, two hundred, then leaves the counter at two hundred and five.

hints: Keep the returned old value separate from the updated stored value.
externalNotes: The browser shows C++ code and checks your understanding; it does not run C++. Optional local examples use C++23.

title: Receive an asynchronous result
summary: Get a value or exception from work running asynchronously.
explanation: Asynchronous work can run independently while the caller continues. std::async starts a function and returns a future connected to its result.

A future lets the caller retrieve that later result. std::launch::async explicitly requests asynchronous execution. Without an explicit policy, the implementation may instead delay the work until it is needed.
get() waits if necessary and retrieves the value. For this ordinary future, get consumes the result. Do not call it again as if the future were a reusable store.
The program prints 42. calculate receives false, so it returns six times seven. get waits for and retrieves that answer.

If calculate throws, the future stores the exception. get rethrows it in the caller, where the matching catch can handle it. Asynchronous work does not guarantee faster execution or a particular finishing time.

analogy.limit: The example isolates one rule; safe real software needs further testing.

quiz.question: Change the final std::async argument from false to true. Where is calculation failed handled?
choices: It automatically becomes the integer zero.
The future silently discards the exception.
At result.get(), where the stored exception is rethrown and caught.
quiz.explanation: calculate throws on the worker path. The future carries that exception to get, which rethrows it into the caller's matching handler.

hints: Follow the result through the future, whether it contains a value or an exception.

title: Build a bounded console game-state engine
summary: Turn a command and current game state into the next game state.
explanation: State means the values describing the game now: score, turns, and whether play continues. apply receives a copy of that state and returns the next state. The caller must assign the returned value to keep the change.
collect adds one point and uses one turn. The game starts with two turns. Reaching zero turns sets playing to false.
quit stops play without using a turn. Unknown commands leave the state unchanged. The first check also leaves an already-stopped game unchanged, so later commands cannot restart it.
The program prints 2 0 0. Two collects produce two points and use both turns. The third command is ignored. The last zero means playing is false.

From this starting state, only two collects can succeed, so the arithmetic stays within a small range. State loaded from elsewhere would need validation too. This function does not promise to repair arbitrary invalid starting values.

1 0 1, because quit uses a turn and restarts play.

Save this public class Main in Main.java, matching the capital M. The java launcher starts the program at the main method used by these examples.
Editing and saving Main.java does not change an older Main.class. Compile again to create a class file from the updated source.
A package groups related Java types. Names such as String and System come from java.lang, which is automatically available. Other types may need an import or their full package name.
The program prints 3 when this version has been compiled and launched.

title: Choose numeric primitives and division
summary: Choose the division type before storing its result.
explanation: int and long hold whole numbers, with long allowing a wider range. double can hold fractional values, but many fractions are approximate. Each type has limits.
A number written directly in code is a literal. A whole-number literal with an L suffix has type long. A number with a decimal point is double by default.
The values used in a calculation are its operands. When both division operands are integers, Java drops the fractional part toward zero.
The calculation happens before assignment. Storing an integer division result in a double converts that completed result; it cannot bring back the fraction already dropped.
The program prints 2.0. Integer division first produces two. Assignment then stores that answer as a double.
To use double division, make at least one operand a double before the division happens. The quiz changes an operand's spelling to do that.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the calculation to 5.0 / 2 and keep the double result variable. What prints?
choices: 2.0, because only the destination type controls division.
2.5, because a double operand changes the division.
3.0, because Java always rounds division upward.
quiz.explanation: 5.0 is a double, so this is double division and its result is two and a half.

title: Convert values and detect overflow
summary: Check whether an exact sum fits in an int.
explanation: A cast asks Java to convert a value to another type. When an ordinary, in-range double becomes an int, its fractional part is dropped toward zero.
Dropping a fraction is different from rounding to the nearest whole number. A cast also does not check every rule your task needs, such as whether an age is allowed.
Overflow means a result does not fit in its number type. Ordinary int addition wraps around when this happens; it does not report an error.
Math.addExact adds integers and checks for overflow. If the sum does not fit, it throws ArithmeticException: an error that interrupts the normal steps. Integer.MAX_VALUE is the largest int.
The program prints 5. The check does not change an answer that already fits.
The quiz adds one to the largest int. Decide whether that new total can still fit before choosing what happens.

quiz.question: Change the addition to Math.addExact(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1). What happens?

It returns the largest int unchanged.
It throws ArithmeticException because the sum does not fit.

title: Short-circuit Boolean conditions
summary: Skip a check when its answer cannot change the result.
explanation: A boolean is true or false. && means both checks must be true. || means at least one must be true. `!` reverses true and false.
Java reads && and || from left to right. With &&, a false left side skips the right side. With ||, a true left side skips the right side. This skipping is called short-circuiting.
A divisor is the number you divide by. denominator != 0 checks that it is not zero. Putting this check before && keeps the later integer division from using zero.
Printing a boolean shows true or false. A skipped check does not run; Java already has enough information to decide the combined answer.
The program prints true. The divisor is not zero, and ten divided by two is greater than one.
The quiz changes only the divisor to zero. Start again at the left check and decide whether Java reaches the division.

quiz.question: Change denominator to zero. What happens?
choices: It prints false and skips the division.
It divides by zero and throws an error.
It prints true because the division was skipped.
quiz.explanation: The left side is false. With &&, that makes the whole condition false, so Java skips the division.

title: Compare and preserve String values
summary: Compare the text in strings, or check whether they are the same object.
explanation: An object is a value with its own data and behavior. A reference points to an object. For String references, == checks whether both point to the same object. equals checks whether their text matches.
Each new String call here creates a separate object. Both objects can hold the same text. Use equals to compare String text; matching text alone does not tell you what == will return.
A String's text cannot be changed after the object is made. Text-changing methods return a result instead. Store that result if you want to use it later.
Assigning first to second copies the reference. Both variables then point to one String object. The assignment does not copy or change its text.
The program prints false, then true on the next line. The objects are separate, but their text matches.
The quiz replaces second's starting value with first. Decide how that changes which object second points to.

quiz.question: Use String second = first; instead. What do the comparisons print?
choices: false then false, because the text is erased.
true then true, because both variables point to the same String.
true then false, because equals cannot compare one object to itself.
quiz.explanation: Both variables point to one object, so == is true. That object's text also matches itself, so equals is true.

title: Distinguish char units from Unicode text
summary: Understand why one text symbol can use two char units.
explanation: UTF-16 is Java's way of storing text as numbered units. A char holds one such unit. Single quotes make a char value; double quotes make a String, which can hold many units.
Unicode gives text elements numbers called code points. Some code points need two UTF-16 units. Those two units together are called a surrogate pair.

String.length counts UTF-16 units. codePointCount counts code points between two positions: it includes the start and stops before the end. Neither always counts the symbols a reader sees, because one visible symbol can combine code points.
The example stores one smiley using two Unicode escapes. An escape writes a text unit using its number instead of showing the symbol directly. The two escapes here form one surrogate pair.
The program prints 2, then 1 on the next line. The smiley uses two UTF-16 units but is one code point.
The letter A needs only one UTF-16 unit. The quiz asks what both measurements show when it replaces the smiley.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace the symbol string with "A". What prints?
choices: 2 then 1, because all strings have those counts.
1 then 2, because code points always outnumber units.
1 then 1, because A uses one unit and one code point.
quiz.explanation: A fits in one UTF-16 unit and is one code point, so both counts are one.

hints: The two methods count different things, even when their answers match.

title: Build changing text with StringBuilder
summary: Build changing text while keeping an earlier String unchanged.
explanation: Mutable means able to change. StringBuilder holds mutable text: you can add to the same builder. A String's text stays unchanged.
append adds text to the end of a builder. toString makes a String containing the builder's text at that moment, like a snapshot.
Changing the builder later does not change a String already made from it. The builder and the saved String can now hold different text.
A thread is a running sequence of instructions. This example uses one thread. StringBuilder alone does not protect its text when several threads change it together.
The program prints A, then AB on the next line. saved keeps the earlier text; builder includes the added letter.
The quiz changes only the letter passed to append. The snapshot is still taken before that addition.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the appended text from B to C. What prints?
choices: A then AC; saved keeps the earlier text.
AC twice; saved changes with the builder.
A twice; the builder cannot change.
quiz.explanation: append changes the builder to AC. The String saved earlier still contains A.

hints: Find the snapshot line, then find the append line.

title: Handle a missing reference
summary: Check that text exists before asking for its length.
explanation: null means a reference points to no object. An empty String is different: it is a real String with no text inside.
Calling length on null throws NullPointerException, an error caused by trying to use a missing object. Check for null before calling a method when the object may be missing.
text != null checks that an object is present. With &&, Java runs the length check only when that first check is true.
The combined check asks whether text exists and has some content. Missing text fails the first check. Empty text passes the first check but fails the length check.
The program prints false. text is null, so Java skips length instead of trying to call it on a missing object.
The quiz replaces null with an empty String. Decide whether length now runs, then decide whether its answer is greater than zero.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change text to the empty String "". What happens?
choices: It throws an error because empty text is null.
It prints false after length returns zero.
It prints true because every String contains text.
quiz.explanation: An empty String is present, so length runs. Its length is zero, which is not greater than zero.

hints: Check for an object first, then check how much text it holds.

title: Choose a switch expression result
summary: Use switch to choose one result from several cases.
explanation: An expression produces a value. A switch expression compares its input with case labels and chooses a result. The arrow form, ->, uses the matching case without continuing into the next case.
default handles values that do not match a listed case. A switch expression must cover every input allowed for that switch so it can produce a result.
Here, the whole switch produces one String. Java stores that String in action, ready for the print statement.
The program prints Write. choice is two, so the second case supplies that text.
The quiz uses a number that neither listed case matches. Follow the default case to find the result.

choices: Write, because it is the last numbered case.
No value, because only the numbered cases work.
Help, because default handles the unlisted value.

title: Control a counted loop
summary: Choose whether to skip one loop turn or stop the loop.
explanation: A for loop has a start, a test, and an update. The start runs once. Before each turn, Java checks the test. After the body runs normally, the update prepares the next turn. i++ adds one.
continue skips the remaining instructions in the current turn. In this for loop, Java still runs the update and then tests whether another turn is allowed.
break leaves the loop at once. It does not run the loop's update or start another turn.
Keep track of the counter even when a print is skipped. continue skips the print here, but the counter still increases.
The program prints 0, 2, and 3 on separate lines. When i is one, continue skips the print. When i reaches four, the loop test is false.
The quiz replaces continue with break. Decide what has already printed when the loop reaches that instruction.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace continue with break. What prints?
choices: Only 0, because reaching 1 stops the loop.
0, 2, 3, because break skips just one turn.
Nothing, because the counter starts at 1.
quiz.explanation: The first turn prints zero. On the next turn, i is one and break leaves the loop.

hints: continue moves to the next turn; break stops the loop.

title: Store values in an array
summary: Replace an array item without changing the array's length.
explanation: An array stores several values of one element type. int[] holds integers. Once an array is made, its number of slots stays fixed, but the values in those slots can change.
An index is a slot's position number. The first index is zero. An array's length field gives its number of slots; it has no parentheses because it is a field, not a method call.
Assigning a value to values[1] replaces the second item. It does not add a slot or move the other items.
Valid indexes run from zero through length minus one. Using an index outside that range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, an error meaning there is no such slot.
The program prints 9, then 3 on the next line. The second item changes to nine, and the array still has three slots.
The quiz changes the assignment's index but keeps the printed index the same. Check which slot each line uses.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Use values[2] = 9; but still print values[1] and values.length. What prints?
choices: 4 then 3, because only the third item changed.
6 then 2, because indexes start at one.
quiz.explanation: Index two is the third item. The second item remains four, and the length remains three.

hints: Read the assignment index and the print index separately.
