title: Visit elements with enhanced for
summary: Add array items by visiting each one in order.
explanation: An enhanced for loop visits each item in an array. On each turn here, Java copies the next integer into the local variable value. You do not need to manage an index.
A running total keeps the sum so far. Each turn adds value to total and stores the new sum back in total. This leaves the array unchanged.
value holds a copy of an integer. Assigning a different integer to value would change only that local variable. To replace an array item, assign through the array's index.
An empty array has no items to visit. The loop body runs zero times, so the starting total stays unchanged.
The program prints 12. The running total moves from zero to two, then six, then twelve.
The quiz keeps the starting total but removes the array's items. Decide whether any instruction inside the loop can now run.

quiz.question: Use an empty int array and keep total starting at zero. What prints?
choices: 12, because Java remembers the old array.
An error, because this loop needs at least one item.
0, because the loop never changes the starting total.
quiz.explanation: There are no items to visit, so the body never runs and total stays zero.

hints: Count how many items can reach the loop body.

title: Grow an ArrayList
summary: Remove one list item and follow the positions that shift.
explanation: ArrayList stores items in order and can grow or shrink. Integer is the object form of int used in this list. Java automatically wraps the added integers as Integer objects.
The import lets this file use the short name ArrayList. <Integer> says what kind of items the list holds. The empty <> on the new list lets Java work out that same type.

add places an item at the end. get reads a position, counting from zero. Here remove receives an int position, removes that item, and shifts later items down. A different remove version accepts an object to remove by value; the argument's type matters.
size() gives the current item count. A position must name an existing item for get or remove. An invalid position causes an error; it does not add items.
The program prints 4, then 2 on the next line. Removing the first item leaves four and six, so four now occupies position zero.
The quiz removes position one instead. Track the remaining first item and the new item count separately.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change remove(0) to remove(1). What are the first value and size?
choices: 2 and 2, because the middle item was removed.
4 and 3, because remove only reads an item.
6 and 1, because the argument is a count to remove.
quiz.explanation: Position one holds four. Removing it leaves two and six: two items, with two first.

hints: The int argument to remove names a position, not the number of items to remove.

title: Associate keys in a HashMap
summary: Use a key to store and find a value in a map.
explanation: A map stores key-and-value pairs. A key identifies an entry. HashMap<String,Integer> uses String keys and Integer values, so you look up a value by text rather than by a list position.
put adds a key with its value. If that key already exists, put replaces its value. There is still just one entry for that key.
getOrDefault returns the value for a present key, or the supplied fallback when the key is absent. Returning a fallback does not add the missing key to the map.
HashMap does not promise to list its entries in the order they were added or sorted by key. This example finds values directly by key, so it needs no listing order.
The program prints 5, then 1 on the next line. The second put replaces the value for read. The map still holds one entry.
The quiz looks up write, which was never added. The fallback answers that lookup while leaving the map unchanged.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change only the lookup key to "write". What prints?
choices: 5 then 2, because the lookup adds the key.
0 then 1, because it returns the fallback without adding an entry.
0 then 0, because the lookup clears the map.
quiz.explanation: write is absent, so the lookup returns zero. The existing read entry remains, giving a size of one.

hints: A lookup reads the map; this lookup does not add an entry.

title: Keep unique members in a HashSet
summary: Keep each distinct value only once in a set.
explanation: A set is a collection that keeps each distinct member only once. In a HashSet<Integer>, adding an integer already present does not create another copy.
add returns true when it adds a new member. It returns false when that member was already in the set.
size() counts the members actually present, not the number of add calls. HashSet does not give its members fixed list positions or promise a listing order.
Use a set when you need to know which values are present without repeats. A list fits tasks where repeated items and their positions matter.
The program prints false, then 1 on the next line. Four was already present, so the second add changes nothing.
The quiz changes only the second added value. Decide whether it is already a member before predicting add's answer.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change only the second added value to 7. What changes?
choices: add still returns false because the set is not empty.
Four is removed to make room for seven.
add returns true and size becomes two.
quiz.explanation: Seven is new to this set. The set keeps both four and seven, so its size becomes two.

hints: Check whether this particular value is present, not whether the set is empty.

title: Select a method overload
summary: Choose a method version by the type of input passed to it.
explanation: Overloading means giving methods the same name but different input types or counts. Changing only the result type is not enough to create a separate overload.
Here, one describe method accepts an int and another accepts a String. Java chooses between them using the input's type. Text that looks like a number is still text.
Writing both method definitions does not run either one. A call selects a matching version and runs that method's body.
The program prints number. The unquoted input is an int, so Java calls the version that accepts an int.
The quiz adds quotes around the input. Quotes make it a String, which changes the selected method.

choices: text, because the input is a String.
number, because the text looks like a digit.
Both results, because every overload runs.

title: Accept a variable number of arguments
summary: Let one method accept zero, one, or several integer inputs.
explanation: Arguments are the inputs passed to a method. Varargs lets a method accept a changing number of arguments. `int... values` gathers supplied integers into an int array called values.
The parameter marked with `...` must be last in the method's input list. It gathers the remaining arguments after any earlier inputs.
Calling this method with no arguments gives it an empty array. The loop has no items to visit, so the starting sum remains zero.
Inside the method, values is an ordinary array. Each item has type int, and the array has a fixed length for that call.
The program prints 12. The method adds two, four, and six, then returns their sum for main to print.
The quiz supplies no arguments. Trace the method from its starting sum and count how many additions can happen.

quiz.question: Change the call to total() with no arguments. What does it return?
choices: 12, because it keeps the previous answer.
0, because the empty array adds nothing.
Nothing, because varargs requires at least one argument.
quiz.explanation: No arguments gives values an empty array. The loop never runs, so sum stays zero.

title: Understand Java pass-by-value
summary: Pass a copy of a reference while still reaching the same array.
explanation: Java passes inputs by value: a method receives a copy of each input value. An int is copied as a number. An array reference is copied as a reference, so both copies can point to the same array.
Here, scores in main and values in change point to one array. Assigning through values[0] changes that array's first item. main can see the change through scores.
Assigning a new array to values would change only the method's local reference. It would not make scores point to that new array.
A reference variable and the object it points to are different things. Copying the reference does not copy the object. Changing the shared object differs from replacing the local reference.
The program prints 9. change reaches the same array as scores and replaces its first item.
The quiz makes values point to a new array instead. Track scores separately to see which array main still reads.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Inside change, use values = new int[]{9}; instead of values[0] = 9;. What does main print?
choices: 9, because assigning values also reassigns scores.
An error, because a parameter cannot be assigned.
3, because scores still points to the unchanged original array.
quiz.explanation: Only the local reference values changes. scores still points to the original array containing three.

hints: Ask whether the line changes an array item or changes where a local reference points.

title: Trace a recursive method
summary: Let a method solve a smaller version of its own task.
explanation: Recursion means a method calls itself. Each call gets its own input. Here, a call waits for the answer from a smaller input before finishing its own addition.
A base case is the rule that stops more calls. Here, n at or below zero returns zero straight away. Each positive input moves toward that rule by subtracting one.
For the input three, the calls use three, two, one, and zero. The zero call returns first. Then each waiting call adds its own number to the returned answer.
Java stores unfinished calls on a call stack. That storage is limited, so very deep recursion can fail. A large total can also overflow int. This lesson uses a small input.
The program prints 6. The returned answers grow from zero to one, then three, then six.
The quiz starts with two instead of three. The stopping rule stays the same, but there is one fewer positive number to add.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: What does sumDown(2) return?
choices: 3, from two plus one plus zero.
2, because calls to itself are ignored.
6, because the earlier input fixes the answer.
quiz.explanation: The calls reach two, one, and zero. Their returned sum is three.

hints: Find the stopping call first, then add each waiting call's number.

title: Create independent class instances
summary: Give each new Counter its own stored count.
explanation: A class describes data fields and methods for objects. An instance is one object made from that class. Each Counter here has its own value field. Calling increment changes the counter reached through that reference.
Each new Counter() makes a separate object. Assigning a to b instead copies a reference, so both names point to one object. It does not make another Counter.

Main is the public class in Main.java. Counter has no public keyword and can share the file. Since Counter declares no constructor, Java supplies a no-input constructor to create it. Its value field is set to zero.
The program prints 0 1. Only b's counter is incremented, so a's counter stays at zero.
The quiz makes b point to a's object. Decide which count both names will read after b.increment().

title: Initialize objects with constructors
summary: Set a new object's starting data with a constructor.
explanation: A constructor runs when an object is created. It has the class's name and no return type. Here, new Session passes a minutes input to the constructor. this means the object being prepared.
The constructor's input and the object's field are both named minutes. this.minutes names the field; minutes alone names the input. The assignment copies the input into the field.

Java supplies a no-input constructor only when a class declares no constructors. Session declares a constructor that needs an int, so a creation call must provide that input unless another matching constructor is added.
The program prints 12. The constructor stored its input in session.minutes before main read that field.
The quiz removes the input from new Session. Check which constructors the class actually declares.

title: Protect an invariant with encapsulation
summary: Keep a stored level within its allowed range.
explanation: An invariant is a rule an object must keep. This Level stores only numbers from zero through three. Its value field is private, so outside caller code cannot directly assign a different number to it.
set checks a requested value before storing it. A value outside the range returns false and leaves the old value alone. A valid value is stored and returns true. get reads the current value.

Encapsulation means keeping data and its allowed operations together, with controlled access. Here, callers use methods that protect the level rule. This alone does not protect against several threads changing the object at once.
The program prints true, false, and 2 on separate lines. Two is accepted. Seven is rejected, so the stored level remains two.
The quiz changes the second request to the highest allowed value. Check whether the rejection condition is true for it.

7, because checking the range is disabled.
3, because the second request is also allowed.

title: Separate static state and final bindings
summary: Separate a shared class field from a variable that cannot be reassigned.
explanation: A static field belongs to the class, so the Ticket objects here share issued. Each constructor call increases that shared count. This example makes the tickets one at a time.
A final variable can be assigned only once. Each Ticket has its own final number, set by its constructor. Later code cannot assign a different number to that field.
For an array reference, final fixes which array the variable points to. It does not freeze the array's items. Changing scores[0] is allowed; assigning a different array to scores is not.
The first line prints 1 2 2: the two ticket numbers and the shared count. The next line prints 9 because the array item changed while its reference stayed the same.

title: Override inherited behavior
summary: Let a child class supply its own version of an inherited method.
explanation: Inheritance lets one class build on another. Cat extends Animal makes Cat a child class of Animal. A Cat is also an Animal, so an Animal reference can point to a Cat.

Overriding means supplying a new version of an inherited instance method. @Override asks Java to check that the method really does this. Its inputs must match; changing the inputs can make a separate overload instead.
For an overridden instance method, Java uses the actual object's type to choose the body when the program runs. Fields and static methods do not follow this same rule.
The program prints meow. The reference's declared type is Animal, but it points to a Cat, whose sound method runs.

meow, because Cat still exists in the file.

title: Define an abstract base type
summary: Require child classes to provide a missing method body.
explanation: An abstract method names an operation but has no body. Shape declares that its objects need an area method. Square supplies the body, making it a concrete class: a class that can be used to create objects.
An abstract class cannot be created directly with new. Its type can still name a reference to a concrete child object. An abstract class may also have fields, constructors, and methods with bodies.
The program prints 4. This Square's area method is written to return four.

title: Implement an interface contract
summary: Use an interface to describe a method a class must provide.
explanation: An interface describes behavior that different classes can provide. Reporter requires a report method that returns a String. This method declaration is public and abstract even though those words are not written.

implements Reporter means ConsoleReporter promises to provide that behavior. Its report method must be public, so callers can use the access the interface promises. @Override checks that it matches the required method.

Java checks the method's name, inputs, result type, and access rules. It cannot decide whether the returned report is useful or true. Interfaces can also contain methods with bodies, but this example needs only the required operation.
The program prints ready. The call uses the report body supplied by ConsoleReporter.

title: Model a data carrier with a record
summary: Group related data in a record and read it with generated methods.
explanation: A record is a compact class for carrying data. Its named pieces are components. Java supplies a matching constructor, methods to read the components, and equals, hashCode, and toString methods based on them.

Record fields are final, so they cannot be reassigned later. A record class also cannot have child classes. A referenced object may still change: a record holding a changeable list does not automatically freeze that list.
This record holds a String and an int. The methods topic() and minutes() read those components. Their parentheses show that these are method calls, not direct field access.

Read 10, because every record must have the same values.

title: Close a hierarchy with sealed types
summary: Limit which classes can directly implement an interface.
explanation: A sealed interface limits its direct implementations: the types that implement it without an intermediate parent. Outcome lists Success and Failure in its permits clause, so only those direct types are allowed here.

A new direct implementation must be allowed by the sealed declaration. Location rules also apply. These types share one file and the unnamed package, so they meet the location rule here.

An enum's ordinal is its position in the declaration, counting from zero. Changing the order changes that position. If saving choices for later use, choose a stable identifier instead of relying on their positions.

title: Keep equals and hashCode consistent
summary: Let a set recognize separate record objects with equal data.
explanation: For objects, == asks whether references point to the same object. equals can ask whether their data counts as equal. Key's generated record method compares its id values, so two separate Keys with the same id are equal.

A hash code is an integer used to help find objects in collections. Equal objects must have the same hash code. Different objects may also share one, so it is not a unique ID. Records generate matching equals and hashCode behavior.

HashSet uses both hash codes and equals to spot repeated members. Data used by those methods should stay unchanged while an object is stored as a key. Key's final int component keeps that data stable here.

title: Parameterize a type with generics
summary: Choose what kind of value a reusable Box can hold.
explanation: Generics let a class use a type chosen by its caller. In Box<T>, T is a type parameter: a placeholder for that choice. Box<String> chooses String, so its get method returns a String.
The field, constructor input, and result of get all use T. The empty <> in new Box<> lets the compiler work out the type from the surrounding declaration and the supplied value.

Java's generic type arguments must be reference types, such as String or Integer. A primitive type such as int cannot be used directly. Leaving the type argument out of Box loses useful checks, so keep it.
The program prints 5. get returns the stored String, and length counts its five text units.

explanation: A bound is a limit on a type parameter. T extends Number means T must be Number or a child type. That promise lets the method call doubleValue, which Number provides.

title: Use bounded wildcards safely
summary: Use wildcards to say what a method can safely read or add.
explanation: The wildcard `?` means an unknown type. In `List<? extends Number>`, each item can be read as Number. The exact item type is unknown, so adding an arbitrary non-null number is not safe: the real list may need a different Number child type.

`List<? super Integer>` means the list's item type is Integer or one of its parent types. This view allows adding an Integer. Reading gives only Object, because the list may also hold other kinds of objects.

List<Integer> is not a List<Number>: a list of integers cannot accept every kind of number. Wildcards allow just the flexibility needed. Separately, List.of makes a list that cannot be changed; new ArrayList makes a changeable list.
The program prints 5.0, then 1 on the next line. total adds the input numbers. addOne places one Integer in the output list, whose size becomes one.
The quiz tries to add inside total through its extends view. Java must reject an addition that might not fit the unknown item type, even if a supplied list could be changed.

An Integer reference can be null, but an int cannot. Trying to unbox null throws NullPointerException. Check for null before reaching the conversion.

For two Integer references, == checks whether they point to the same object. Java may reuse wrapper objects, so do not use this to compare their numbers. For a non-null wrapper, equals compares its number with another wrapper of the same type.

title: Handle checked and unchecked exceptions
summary: Handle a failed operation and continue after its catch block.
explanation: An exception reports a problem that interrupts normal steps. A checked exception, such as IOException, must be caught or listed with throws so callers know it may escape. Unchecked exceptions, including RuntimeException types, do not have that compiler requirement.

throw sends an exception toward a matching catch block. A call that throws does not also return its normal result. Here, load imitates a failed operation when fail is true; it does not read a real file.

The catch block handles IOException and uses getMessage to read its description. After this catch finishes, execution continues below it. A handler should deal with or report the failure, rather than pretend the operation succeeded.
The program prints ready, then after on the next line. load returns normally, so the catch block is skipped.
The quiz passes true. Trace where throw sends execution and which print inside try no longer receives a result.

title: Close resources with try-with-resources

AutoCloseable is the interface for resources with a close method. Its method may throw a checked Exception. Trace's version declares none, so this example needs no catch for closing it.

If several resources are opened, Java closes them in reverse order. If both the body and closing throw, the body error stays primary and closing errors are attached as suppressed errors. Memory cleanup does not replace this timely closing.
The program prints open, body, close, and after on separate lines. The resource closes before execution reaches the line after try.

isPresent checks whether a value exists. get reads it, but throws NoSuchElementException if it is absent. The if check here ensures get runs only when a value is present.
Optional.empty means an Optional with no value inside. It is different from null, which points to no object. Keep the Optional itself present so its methods can describe whether its value is missing.

A lambda captures a local variable when it uses that variable from outside its body. Such a variable must be final or effectively final, meaning it is not reassigned after its starting value. This fixes the variable's reference or value, not every change inside a referenced object.

title: Filter and map a stream
summary: Keep selected values, then transform each one into a result.
explanation: A stream describes steps for processing values from a source. stream() starts one from the list. filter keeps values that pass a true-or-false check, and map transforms those retained values. These operations do not change this source list.

Here, filter keeps even numbers using % to check the remainder after division by two. map then multiplies each kept number by ten. toList finishes the stream and collects its answers in a list that cannot be changed.
The program prints [20, 40]. Filtering keeps two and four, then mapping turns them into twenty and forty.

summary: Count how many words share each length.
explanation: A collector tells a stream how to gather its results. groupingBy puts items with the same key together. Here, String::length gets each word's length as its key, and counting counts the words in each group. collect runs that work and returns a map of lengths to counts.

The resulting map does not promise an order for listing groups. This code asks for one key directly. getOrDefault returns that group's count, or the supplied zero if the group is absent, without adding a new group.

title: Understand lazy single-use streams
summary: Finish a stream once, then create a new one for another query.
explanation: Streams are lazy: setting up their processing steps does not yet visit the source items. A terminal operation, such as toList, asks for the result. Do not rely on extra effects inside map or peek; Java may skip work that cannot change that result.

A stream is single-use. After a terminal operation, do not use that same stream again. Ask the collection for a new stream instead. Java can report detected reuse with IllegalStateException, as it does here.
The program prints [3, 5], then consumed on the next line. The first call finishes the stream. The second call throws an error that the catch block reports.
The quiz asks how to repeat the query correctly. The source list can supply a new stream even though the old stream is finished.

Make the finished stream variable final.
Create a new stream from the list and apply the same mapping.

title: Make a defensive immutable snapshot

Collections.unmodifiableList instead gives a view of the original list. That view blocks edits through itself but still shows edits made through the original reference. Neither a view nor a shallow snapshot freezes changeable data inside the item objects.

title: Organize packages and the class path
summary: Find a class by its package name and the class-path root.
explanation: A package groups named classes. Labels belongs to study, so its full name is study.Labels. Put its source in study/Labels.java. The import lets Main use the short name Labels; it does not download or copy the class.

The class path tells Java where to start looking for compiled classes. In a practice folder, compile with javac --release 25 -d classes Main.java study/Labels.java, then run java -cp classes Main. classes is the search root above the study folder.

Reflection lets running code inspect information about classes. isAnnotationPresent checks whether the requested marker is visible on a class. It does not bypass private access or module rules. Tagged is a static class nested inside Main, so it needs no enclosing Main object.

clamp keeps a number between zero and ten. Math.min first picks the smaller of ten and the input; Math.max then picks the larger of zero and that result. Each check compares clamp's answer with a stated expectation and labels any failure.

title: Join a worker before observing its result
summary: Wait for a worker thread to finish before reading its answer.
explanation: A thread runs a sequence of instructions. Thread.start starts the supplied task on another thread. The task is a Runnable: an operation with no input or result value. The lambda's empty () means no inputs. Calling run directly would stay on the calling thread.

join waits until the worker ends. When join returns successfully, later reads can see the worker's completed changes. A guessed sleep does not provide that guarantee. join can be interrupted, so main declares InterruptedException.
The program prints 7. The worker stores seven, and join finishes before main reads the array item.

title: Protect shared state with synchronization
summary: Protect a shared counter so two workers do not lose each other's changes.
explanation: count++ reads the old value, adds one, and writes it back. Those steps can overlap between workers. A synchronized instance method locks its object's monitor, a built-in lock, for the whole call. Both workers use the same Counter, so only one can run its synchronized method at a time.

Each worker adds one a thousand times. main joins both workers before reading, so both have finished and their work is visible. The synchronized get method uses the same object's lock; different objects' locks would not coordinate these updates.
The program prints 2000. Each of the two workers contributes a thousand protected additions.
The quiz reduces the number of turns in the shared task. Both workers still finish before the total is read.

An unpredictable value, even with the shared lock and both joins.

title: Update a counter atomically
summary: Use an atomic increment so a single counter update cannot be split apart.
explanation: An atomic operation acts as one indivisible step to other threads. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet safely adds one and returns the new value. It prevents lost updates for this increment. Several separate calls do not automatically become one atomic operation together.

new AtomicInteger() starts at zero; its one-int constructor sets a chosen starting value. Both workers update the same counter. After both joins finish, get reads the final value without changing it. The workers may take turns in any order.
The program prints 1000. Each worker adds one five hundred times, starting from zero.
The quiz uses new AtomicInteger(10). The workers perform the same additions on top of that starting value.

summary: Submit a calculation to managed workers and retrieve its result.
explanation: ExecutorService accepts tasks and manages threads that run them. submit returns a Future, which represents a result that may arrive later. get waits if needed and returns that result. If the task fails, get reports the failure through ExecutionException; waiting can also be interrupted.

The try-with-resources block closes this executor when leaving the block and waits for its submitted tasks to end. The fixed pool uses up to two worker threads. That number does not promise which task runs first.
The program prints 42. The worker calculates six times seven, and get retrieves that answer before it is printed.

newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor starts each task on its own virtual thread. Inside the task, Thread.currentThread returns the thread running that call, and isVirtual checks its kind. get waits for the answer; leaving try closes the executor.

completedFuture starts with an answer already available. The chained steps can use it right away; steps can also be attached before a future finishes. join gets the final answer and reports failed completion through an unchecked CompletionException.

CountDownLatch holds a count. countDown reduces it, and await waits for zero. started tells main the worker has reached setup. gate stays closed until main interrupts the worker. The catch records cancellation and restores the worker's flag; main then joins before reading the result.

Closing and memory cleanup are different jobs. A reference may still reach an object after its resource has closed. This practice Session only prints a closing message, so it shows the order without opening a real file.

explanation: Source is the text you write. A compiler translates it into machine instructions. A linker joins the compiled parts and library tools into an executable: a program you can run.
In this example, main is the starting function. `void` means it takes no inputs. Returning 0 from main reports a successful finish.
Changing main.c does not change an executable you already built. Build again to include the new instructions. Otherwise, running the old executable can still show the old message.

title: Numeric types and portable ranges
summary: A number's type sets its allowed values. Match that type when printing the number.
explanation: `int` stores whole numbers. `double` can store fractional numbers, often approximately. The exact range of int can differ between machines.
`INT_MAX`, provided by limits.h, gives the largest int on your system. Do not assume int always uses 32 bits. A bit is a single 0 or 1 used to store data.

A format mark tells printf what kind of value to expect. `%d` expects int, `%ld` expects long, and `%f` expects double. A mismatch can cause undefined behavior: C no longer promises what the program will do.
The value 3 fits every standard int range. `long` is another whole-number type with its own limits. The L in `3L` makes that number a long value.
This prints 3. The `%d` mark matches the int variable.
If you change count to long, change the format to `%ld` too. Both describe the same value type; the format is not just a label on the screen.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Which format should print the variable in `long count = 3L;`?
choices: %d, because all whole-number formats are the same.
%s, because the number appears as text.
quiz.explanation: %ld tells printf to read a long value. %d expects int and %s expects a string.

hints: Choose the printing mark that expects a long.

title: Integer and floating division
summary: The input types decide how division works. Storing the answer in double afterward cannot bring back a lost fraction.
explanation: When both inputs are integers, division drops the fractional part toward zero. `5 / 2` therefore gives 2, not 2.5.
A double input allows fractional division. `5.0 / 2` gives 2.5. But storing the result of `5 / 2` in double only changes the already-calculated 2 into 2.0.
`%.1f` tells printf to show one digit after the decimal point. It cannot change the calculation that happened earlier.

Never use zero as the divisor, the number you divide by. For signed integers, the smallest value divided by -1 may also be outside the allowed range. The small positive inputs here avoid those problems.
The division happens first and gives 2. That becomes the double value 2.0, so the program prints 2.0.
Change just 5 to 5.0 in the division. Predict the result before considering how printf will display it.

title: Overflow and checked preconditions
summary: Check that a sum will fit before calculating it. A signed integer cannot safely hold every possible answer.
explanation: Overflow means a result does not fit its type. Signed int overflow has undefined behavior: C makes no promise about the result. Do not expect the number to wrap safely.
For this check, a and b must both be nonnegative, meaning zero or greater. `a <= INT_MAX - b` asks whether there is enough room to add b. Only add after that check passes.
Unsigned integers cannot represent negative values. Their arithmetic wraps around when it passes a limit. That rule is defined, but wrapping can still give the wrong size or count.
If the check fails, this program prints rejected. That path never calculates `a + b`, so it avoids the overflow.
4 and 3 fit easily, so the check passes and the program prints 7.
Keep b at 3. Setting a to `INT_MAX - b` makes the sum just fit. Increasing a by 1 makes the check fail. Keep both inputs nonnegative and keep the check in place.

title: Boolean short-circuit conditions
summary: With &&, C checks the left side first. If it is false, C skips the right side.
explanation: In these number conditions, 0 means false and a nonzero value means true. The logical operators `&&`, `||`, and `!` give a result of 0 or 1.

`&&` means both conditions must be true. If its left side is false, C skips the right side. `||` means at least one must be true; it skips the right side when the left is true. This skipping is called short-circuiting.
The denominator is the number you divide by. Check `denominator != 0` before the division. If it is zero, the left side is false and the division is skipped.
`&` and `|` work on individual bits of integers. They do not skip the right side like `&&` and `||`. Use the double signs for this guard.
The denominator is 2, so the first check passes. 8 divided by 2 is 4, which is greater than 2. Both checks are true, so accepted prints as 1.
Set the denominator to 0. Follow the left check first and decide whether the division is reached.

accepted is 0 and the division is skipped.

title: Unsigned bit masks
summary: A bit mask lets one number hold several on-or-off flags.

A mask is a number whose set bits choose the positions you want. `flags | mask` turns those positions on. `flags & mask` keeps only positions that are on in both numbers.
Unsigned integers are useful for bit operations because they do not have a negative sign to handle. This example uses fixed masks, so no bit shifting is needed.
`flags |= 2u` turns on the bit selected by 2u and stores the result in flags. Bits that were already on stay on.
The update turns on the 2u bit. The `&` test finds that bit, and `!= 0u` turns the answer into true. printf displays 1.
Remove the update and look only for the 2u bit. Having the 1u bit on does not turn on the 2u bit.

title: Scope and initialized values
summary: A name belongs to a part of the program called its scope. A new name inside braces can hide an outer name.
explanation: Scope is the part of the code where a name is available. A variable declared inside a block of braces is available from that declaration to the end of the block.
Writing `int score = 7;` inside the inner block creates a second score. It hides the outer score while you are inside that block. This is called shadowing.
Initialize a variable by giving it a starting value. An ordinary local variable without one does not automatically start at zero. Give it a value before reading it.
This example uses the same name twice to show shadowing. In everyday code, different names can make it easier to see which value you are using.
The inner print reads the inner score, so it prints 7. After the inner block ends, the outer score is visible again and prints 3.
Remove int from the inner declaration. Then `score = 7;` updates the existing outer score instead of creating a second variable.

title: Switch branches and fallthrough
summary: A switch starts at the case that matches a value. A break tells it where to stop.
explanation: `switch` checks an integer value. It starts at the case with that value. Here, choice selects which message to print.
`break` leaves the switch. Without it, work continues into the next case, even if that case's label does not match.
`default` is the place to start when no case matches. It is optional. Here it prints other.
Continuing from one case into the next is called fallthrough. Use it only when you want both pieces of work to run. Indentation alone does not stop it.
choice is 1, so the program starts at case 1. It prints one, then break leaves the switch.
Change choice to 2 and follow the matching case until break. The code before that matching case does not run.

title: For loops and loop control
summary: continue skips the rest of one loop turn. break ends the loop.
explanation: A for loop has a start, a test, and an update. Here i starts at 0. The loop checks `i < 4` before each turn. `i++` adds 1 after the turn.
`continue` skips the rest of the current turn. In this for loop, the update still happens. Then the next test decides whether another turn can begin.
`break` leaves the loop immediately. It skips both the rest of the turn and this loop's next update.
The counter takes only small values here. When i reaches 4, the test becomes false. Always check that your loop can reach its stopping point without exceeding a number's range.
The loop prints 0, skips the print when i is 1, then prints 2 and 3. Each number appears on its own line.
Replace continue with break. Follow i from 0 and stop as soon as the break runs.

quiz.explanation: The first turn prints 0. At i = 1, break leaves the loop, so no later number prints.

title: Fixed arrays and element bounds
summary: An array holds a fixed number of items. Use an index to read or change one item.
explanation: An array stores items of one type next to each other. `int values[3]` makes room for three int items. The starting items here are 2, 4, and 6.
An index is an item's position number. C counts from zero: values[0] is first, values[1] is second, and values[2] is third.
This array has no item at index 3. Reading or writing there goes outside its bounds. It does not add a new item, and C does not promise a useful result.
Assigning to a valid index changes only that item. The array still has the same number of items afterward.
The assignment replaces the second item, 4, with 9. The print reads that same item and displays 9.
Change only the assignment's index to 2. Keep the print at index 1. Decide which item changes and which item is read.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Assign 9 to values[2] instead. What does the unchanged print of values[1] show?
choices: 4, because the second item was not changed.
quiz.explanation: The third item becomes 9. The second item stays 4, and that is the one printed.

hints: Index 2 is the third item. Index 1 is still the second item.

title: sizeof and array lengths
summary: For an actual array, divide its total size by one item's size to find how many items it holds.
explanation: `sizeof` measures storage in bytes. One C byte is the storage size of char. It is usually 8 bits, but C allows other byte sizes.
Leaving the number out of `int values[]` lets the compiler count the starting items. For this actual array, `sizeof values / sizeof values[0]` divides the total storage by one item's storage.
The result of sizeof has type `size_t`, an unsigned type for sizes. Use `%zu` to print it.

A function parameter written as an array is treated as a pointer. Measuring that pointer gives the pointer's size, not the original array's size. Pass the item count separately when the function needs it.
There are three starting items. Total array storage divided by one item's storage gives 3, which the program prints.
Add 8 after 6 in the starting list. Keep the square brackets empty so the compiler counts all the starting items again.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Add 8 as a fourth starting item and keep `values[]`. What does count become?
choices: 3, because sizeof is the same for all arrays.
4, because this array now holds four items.
quiz.explanation: The compiler makes a four-item array. Dividing its total size by one item's size gives 4.

hints: The empty brackets let the starting list decide the array length.

title: Characters and byte-oriented text
summary: Single quotes name one ordinary character value. The %c format prints it as a character.
explanation: `'A'` is a character constant: a value written with single quotes. In C, this ordinary constant has type int. Double quotes make a string instead: an array of char values ending in zero.
A char stores one byte. Text such as some accented letters or emoji can need several bytes. Do not assume one char always holds one whole visible symbol.
`%c` expects an int value and prints its character after conversion to unsigned char. It does not print the number as decimal digits.
Different systems can use different character codes. Write the character you mean in single quotes instead of guessing its number. This example names A directly.
The program stores the value for A and prints A, followed by a newline.
Replace the single-quoted A with a single-quoted B. The format stays `%c` because you still want a character.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace `'A'` with `'B'`. What changes?
choices: The program must print a number.
quiz.explanation: The stored character value changes to B. %c prints that character.

hints: %c displays the chosen character, not its decimal number.

title: Null-terminated strings
summary: A C string ends with a zero character. Its text length does not include that ending, but its storage does.
explanation: A C string is a sequence of char values ending at the first zero character, `\0`. This ending is not the printable digit `'0'`.
`char text[] = "cat";` makes an array with four spaces: c, a, t, and the ending zero. `strlen` counts the bytes before that ending, so it gives 3.
strlen does not know the size of the array. It keeps looking for the ending zero. Use it only when the string has a valid ending inside readable storage.
This array owns a writable copy of the text. A string literal, the quoted text itself, must not be changed through a pointer to it.
The output is 3 4. strlen counts the three text bytes. sizeof measures all four bytes of this array, including the ending zero.
Change the starting word to hi. Count its text bytes first, then add one space for the ending zero.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the starting text to hi. What prints?
choices: 2 3: two text bytes and three stored bytes.
3 4: every string has the same size.
quiz.explanation: strlen gives 2 for h and i. sizeof gives 3 because the array also stores the ending zero.

hints: The array needs one more space than the two letters in hi.

title: Bounded formatting with snprintf
summary: snprintf limits how much text it stores and tells you how much space the full text would need.
explanation: A buffer is storage used to hold data. Its capacity is how much it can hold. snprintf receives the buffer and its capacity. With positive capacity, it leaves room for the ending zero instead of writing past the limit.
On a successful call, snprintf returns the full text length it wanted to write. This count excludes the ending zero, even if the buffer was too small for all the text.
A negative return value means a text-conversion error. Check for that first. If you later convert needed to size_t for a size comparison, do so only after checking it is nonnegative.
Truncation means part of the text was cut off. If the nonnegative needed length is at least the buffer's capacity, the complete text did not fit. Treat that as shortened text, not a complete message.
The buffer has four spaces. It stores hel and an ending zero. The output is hel 5 because the full word hello needs five text spaces.
Increase the array to six spaces. Then the five letters and the ending zero all fit. The needed text length is still 5.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Increase the array to `char text[6]`. What prints?
quiz.explanation: Six spaces hold hello plus its ending zero. The returned text length remains 5.

hints: The returned length counts the full text, without its ending zero.

title: Validated strtol conversion
summary: strtol turns the start of text into a long integer. Check where it stopped before accepting the number.
explanation: `strtol` reads a number from text. It returns a long value. `const char *text` is a pointer to characters this code will not change through that pointer. `char *end` will point to where number reading stopped.

`&end` gives strtol the address of end so it can update that pointer. If `end == text`, no digits were read. `*end` reads the character where it stopped. This program accepts the text only if that character is the ending zero.

`errno` stores certain library error reports. Set it to 0 before calling strtol. `ERANGE` means the number is outside long's range. A returned value of zero alone does not mean failure; zero is a valid number too.
The input 10 selects decimal numbers, the usual base-ten system. Keep the answer as long here. To store it in int, you would first need to check that it fits int's smaller or equal range.
The text contains only the number 12. Digits were read, the ending was reached, and the value fits. The program prints 12.
Change the text to 12x. strtol reads 12 but stops at x. This program rejects any leftover character, including a space after the number.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the input text to 12x. What happens?
choices: 12 is accepted and x is ignored.
The program always reads past the string.
invalid prints because reading stopped at x.
quiz.explanation: strtol stops at x. The check sees that this is not the ending zero and prints invalid.

hints: Check whether end points to the ending zero or to leftover text.

title: Function declarations and prototypes
summary: A function prototype tells the compiler the input and result types. The function body tells it what work to do.
explanation: A prototype is a function declaration that lists its input types. `int twice(int value);` says twice takes an int and returns an int. It lets the compiler know those types before reading the body.
A definition supplies the instructions inside braces. Its types must agree with the declaration. A declaration by itself does not do the calculation.
In C17, `(void)` explicitly means no parameters. Empty parentheses in a declaration do not give the same information. Use clear parameter lists, as these examples do.
A call supplies an argument: the value sent into a parameter. twice multiplies that value by 2, then return sends the result back.
The call supplies 3. The body calculates 3 times 2 and returns 6. printf prints that result.
Change the call's input to 4. The function's types stay the same; its calculation uses the new input.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the call from twice(3) to twice(4). What prints?
quiz.explanation: value receives 4. The function returns 4 times 2, which is 8.

hints: The prototype names a type, not a fixed input value.

title: Pointer addresses and dereferencing
summary: A pointer refers to a place in memory. Follow it to read or change the value stored there.
explanation: Memory holds a running program's data. A pointer is a value that can refer to a location in memory. `&score` gives the address of score. `int *p` declares a pointer to int.
Dereferencing means following a pointer to the item it refers to. `*p` means the int that p points to. Assigning to `*p` changes that int.
Follow a pointer only while it refers to a live object of the right type. Live means the object's storage is still available for use. An uninitialized pointer or NULL must not be followed.
Here p points to score itself, not a copy of score. Writing through `*p` and reading through the name score reach the same value.
The pointer write changes score from 3 to 9. The final print therefore displays 9.
Change the value written through p to 5. Keep the pointer and the print unchanged.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace `*p = 9;` with `*p = 5;`. What prints?
choices: 3, because p owns a separate copy.
quiz.explanation: Writing 5 through p changes score itself. Printing score then displays 5.

hints: Draw one score value and an arrow from p to it.

title: Pass values and update through pointers
summary: A function can change your variable when you give it a pointer to that variable.
explanation: C copies each argument value into the function's parameter. Changing an ordinary int parameter changes that copy, not the caller's variable.
`set(&score)` passes the address of score. The parameter p gets a copy of that address. Both still lead to the same score, so assigning through `*p` changes score.
The void before set means the function returns no value. Its useful work is the change it makes through p. The caller must provide a valid pointer to a writable int.
Assigning a new address to p changes only the function's local pointer. That is different from assigning to `*p`, which changes the value p currently points to.
set follows p to score and stores 9 there. After the call ends, main prints the changed score: 9.
Imagine set creates a local int named other, points p at other, then writes 9 through p. The write now changes other, so score is left alone.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Inside set, p is changed to point to a local variable named other before 9 is written through p. What does main print?
choices: 9, because changing p always changes score.
An address, because the input was a pointer.
3, because the write now changes other.
quiz.explanation: p no longer points to score when the write happens. score keeps its original value, 3.

hints: Follow p's current arrow before deciding which value changes.

title: Pointer arithmetic within arrays
summary: Moving an array pointer by 1 moves it by one item, not one byte.
explanation: For an array a, `a + 1` points to the second item. Adding 1 moves by one item's size. `*p` reads the item p points to. Keep pointer movement within the array or exactly one position past its end.

Subtract two pointers only within the same array, including its one-past position. The answer counts items. Its type is `ptrdiff_t`, provided by stddef.h, and `%td` prints it. The distance must fit that type.

The program prints 7 1: the pointed-to item is 7, and it is one item after the start. Reaching main's closing brace reports success here. That rule is special to main; other functions returning values still need a valid return.
For this three-item array, `a + 3` is one position past the end. You may use it as a stopping marker. Never follow it with `*`, because no array item exists there.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If p starts at a + 2 instead, what prints?
quiz.explanation: The third item is 9. It is two items from the start, so the output is 9 2.

title: Storage duration and dangling pointers
summary: A pointer stays useful only while its target exists. A local static variable lasts for the whole program.
explanation: An ordinary local variable exists only until its block ends. Returning its address does not keep it alive. A pointer left referring to an object whose life has ended is called dangling. Do not use it to read or write.
A local variable marked static lasts for the whole program. Its starting value is set once. Every call here uses the same n. `++n` adds 1 before the function returns its address.
The first call changes n from 0 to 1. The second changes the same n to 2. first still points to that shared variable, so the print displays 2. This example has only one thread of work.
Remove the second call. The shared n is then increased only once. first still points to a live static variable.

title: Const-qualified pointer access
summary: const can prevent writes through a pointer without freezing the original variable.
explanation: In `const int *p`, const means you cannot change the int through p. You can still read it. If the original variable was not declared const, another allowed path can still change it.

In `int * const p`, const is placed after the star. That prevents changing p itself to a different address. It still allows writes to a writable target. If the actual target was declared const, never remove that protection to write to it.
n is an ordinary writable int. `n = 8` changes it through its own name. p points to that same value, so reading through p prints 8.
Replace the write to n with a write through `*p`. That tries to use a read-only path, so the compiler must report the invalid assignment.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace `n = 8;` with `*p = 8;`. What happens?
choices: The compiler reports an invalid write through p.
The pointer changes to a new address.
quiz.explanation: p points to const int, so assigning through *p is not allowed. n itself is still writable through its own name.

hints: The restriction applies to writing through p, not to reading through it.

title: Null pointers and optional outputs
summary: A function can allow NULL to mean that you do not want its optional output.
explanation: NULL is a standard way to write a null pointer value. It points to no object. You may compare a pointer with NULL, but you must not follow a null pointer to read or write.
This measure function allows NULL for its output. It checks before writing. A non-null output must point to a live, writable int. Do not assume other functions allow NULL; check their rules.
The call passes the address of n, so measure stores 6 there. It also returns 1 as its success status. The print shows 1 6: status first, output second.
Change the call to `measure(NULL)`. The function skips the output write and still returns 1. n keeps the starting value it had before the call.

quiz.question: Replace measure(&n) with measure(NULL). What prints?

hints: The returned status and the optional output are two separate results.

title: Bounded recursion
summary: Recursion means a function calls itself. Each call must move toward a stopping case.
explanation: Recursion means a function calls itself. A base case is the stopping case that makes no further call. Here, n equal to 0 returns 0. Every other call uses n minus 1, moving closer to that stop.
Each unfinished call needs some memory. This program allows n only from 0 through 10, keeping the number of calls and the sum small. C does not provide unlimited room for nested calls.
For n equal to 4, the calls reach 0, then return their answers. The waiting additions total 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0, which prints as 10.
main checks the limit before calling sum. If n is 11, it prints rejected and returns immediately. No recursive call is made.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If n is 11, what happens?
choices: main prints rejected without calling sum.
quiz.explanation: 11 is above the allowed limit. main prints rejected and ends before reaching the sum call.

title: Structures and member access
summary: A struct groups named values. Copying a struct makes a separate group with copied member values.
explanation: A struct groups named values called members. Point has x and y members. `.x = 2` names the member receiving its starting value. A dot, as in a.x, selects a member of a struct value.

Assigning a to b copies its member values into a separate struct. `p->x` follows pointer p and selects x. It means the same as `(*p).x`. If a member is itself a pointer, copying it copies only the pointer, not the data it points to.
b starts with its own copy of a's values. p points to b, so the write changes b.x to 9. a.x stays 2. The output is 2 9.
Make p point to a instead. The later write then changes a.x, while b keeps the x value copied earlier.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Make p point to a instead of b. What prints?
quiz.explanation: b copied x as 2 before the write. The write now reaches a.x and changes it to 9.

hints: First copy the values. Then follow p to see which copy changes.

title: Type aliases and tagged structures
summary: typedef gives a type a shorter name. A struct can link to another struct through a pointer.
explanation: An alias is another name for the same thing. typedef creates a type alias. `typedef struct Node Node;` lets you write Node instead of struct Node. It creates a name, not a stored node.

A node is one item in a linked group. This Node stores a value and a pointer named next. A pointer can refer to another Node without storing that whole Node inside itself. NULL marks the end of this short chain.
start.next points to end. `start.next->value` follows that pointer and reads end's value, so it prints 8. Both nodes are still alive at that point.
Change end's starting value to 12. The link still leads to the same node, so it reads that node's new starting value.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If end.value starts at 12, what prints?
quiz.explanation: start.next points to end. Reading through that link gives end.value, which is now 12.

hints: The print follows next once before reading value.
externalNotes: The browser shows C code and checks your understanding; it does not run C. Optional local examples use C17.

title: Enums and explicit states
summary: An enum gives names to integer values. Your code still decides how to move between those states.
explanation: A state describes a current condition, such as ready or done. An enum gives names to integer values. Here READY means 1 and DONE means 2, making the code easier to read.
The names alone do not make rules for changing state. finish supplies the rule: READY becomes DONE. Any other input is returned unchanged.
s starts as READY. finish returns DONE. Comparing that result with DONE is true, so the program prints 1.
If s already starts as DONE, the if condition inside finish is false. The final return sends DONE back unchanged.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If s starts as DONE, what prints?
choices: 0, because only READY can lead to DONE.
A compiler error because the work is already done.
quiz.explanation: finish returns its DONE input unchanged. The comparison with DONE is true, so it prints 1.

title: Tagged unions and active alternatives
summary: A tagged union holds one kind of value at a time, with a separate label saying which kind is stored.
explanation: A union lets different members share the same storage. It does not keep separate values for every member. Here the storage holds either a whole number or a fractional number, and the code reads the member last written.

A tag is a label describing the stored choice. kind is the tag here. C does not keep the tag and union member in step for you. Change both together. Reading the other member is not a way to convert the number.
The starting tag is WHOLE and the stored whole value is 7. The if statement selects that member, so the program prints 7.
To store 2.5, use the FRACTION tag and the fraction member together. Then the other print path reads the matching double value.

quiz.question: Set the tag to FRACTION and the fraction member to 2.5. What prints?

title: Allocate storage with malloc
summary: malloc asks for storage while the program runs. Check that it worked, fill the storage, and free it when finished.
explanation: Allocation means setting aside storage. `malloc` asks for a number of bytes. `sizeof *p` requests enough for the int p will point to; it measures the type without reading an int. In C, malloc's pointer result can be assigned to int * without a cast.

malloc returns NULL if the request fails. Check before using the pointer. New malloc storage has no starting value you can rely on. Write a value before reading it, then use free once to release the allocation.

If allocation succeeds, the program stores 12 and prints 12 before freeing the storage. If allocation fails, it returns status 1 without using p. After free, the old storage must not be read or written.
Change the stored value to 19. The printed value comes from that assignment, not from malloc.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Store 19 instead of 12. What prints if allocation succeeds?
quiz.explanation: The assignment writes 19 into the new storage. The print reads it before the storage is freed.

title: Zero-initialized arrays with calloc
summary: calloc allocates an array and clears its bits. For int items, that gives a starting value of zero.
explanation: `calloc(count, item_size)` asks for storage for a number of items. It sets all the storage bits to zero. For int items, this means each item starts at 0. Check for NULL before using the returned pointer.

Zero bits do not promise the same meaning for every type, such as every possible pointer or floating-point representation. This example uses int items. With three items, only indexes 0, 1, and 2 are valid.
The three ints start at 0. The assignment changes only a[1] to 5. The print reads a[0] and a[1], producing 0 5. free then releases the array.
Change the assignment to target a[0]. That updates the first item while the second keeps its starting value.

quiz.question: Assign 5 to a[0] instead. What prints if allocation succeeds?
quiz.explanation: The first item changes to 5. The second remains at the zero value supplied by calloc.

title: Grow allocations safely with realloc
summary: realloc can resize allocated storage. Keep the old pointer until you know whether the change worked.
explanation: `realloc` asks to resize an allocation. For a positive requested size, failure returns NULL and leaves the original allocation usable. Success may move the data. After success, use the returned pointer and stop using old pointers into that allocation.

Store the result in a temporary pointer, grown. If it is NULL, this example frees the original and stops. Otherwise, copy grown into a. The old values are kept, but added space must be filled before reading. This pattern uses a positive size.
The first item starts at 4. Successful growth keeps it and adds room for a second int. The code writes 9 to the new item, so the output is 4 9. The final free releases the resized allocation.
Set the first item to 6 before resizing. Successful realloc preserves that value too.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Set a[0] to 6 before resizing. What prints after successful growth?
quiz.explanation: realloc keeps the first item's 6. The newly added second item is explicitly set to 9.

hints: Growing the storage does not reset its existing first item.

title: Ownership and freeing exactly once
summary: Choose one owner to release allocated storage. Clear that owner's pointer after releasing it.
explanation: An owner is the part of your code responsible for releasing an allocation. A borrowed pointer may use that allocation while it is alive but does not release it. These are rules your code follows; C does not enforce them.

`int **owner` is a pointer to an int pointer. Passing `&p` lets release update p itself. owner must point to a live pointer variable. release frees the allocation, then stores NULL in that variable. Other copies of the old pointer are not cleared.
After release, p is NULL, so the comparison prints 1. The allocation was freed exactly once. Any other pointer that referred to it must stop being used.
Calling release with `&p` again is safe here because p was cleared. `free(NULL)` does nothing. Passing NULL as owner itself would be invalid, because release needs to follow owner.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Call release(&p) a second time before printing. What happens?
choices: The same allocation is always freed twice.
It still prints 1; the second free receives NULL.
quiz.explanation: The first call clears p. The second call passes that NULL value to free, which does nothing.

hints: After the first call, inspect p before deciding what the second call frees.

title: Guard allocation-size multiplication
summary: Check that an allocation's byte count will fit before multiplying the item count by the item size.
explanation: size_t is an unsigned type for sizes. A product that is too large can wrap into a small number. SIZE_MAX is the largest size_t value. For a nonzero width, `count > SIZE_MAX / width` checks for a product that would be too large without calculating it first.
This program also chooses to reject zero items. Even a byte count that fits can be too large for available memory, so the malloc result still needs a NULL check.
The count is 3 and the width is one int's size. The checks pass. If allocation succeeds, the program stores 7 in the first item, prints it, and frees the allocation.
Set count to 0. The first check rejects it before multiplication, allocation, or any array access.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If count is zero, what happens?
choices: It allocates one int and prints 7.
quiz.explanation: The zero-count check is true, so the program prints rejected and returns before calling malloc.

hints: Read the first part of the if condition before reaching malloc.

title: Dynamic arrays with size and capacity
summary: A growing array needs two counts: items in use and spaces available.
explanation: A dynamic array can ask for more storage. data points to its storage. length counts the items already filled. capacity counts the spaces available. Keep length at or below capacity, and read only items below length.

Appending means adding an item at the end. If this array is full, append first tries to grow it. This small example stops at two spaces. Failure returns 0 without increasing length. On success, `length++` uses the old length as the write position, then adds 1.

The first append fills position 0 with 3. The second grows the storage and fills position 1 with 7. The print shows length 2 and the second item, giving 2 7. Every failure path in main releases the storage before stopping.
Capacity growth alone does not add an item. Only a successful append increases length. A third append is rejected here because the two-space limit is reached.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Append 9 instead of 7 on the second call. What prints if both calls succeed?
quiz.explanation: Two appends make length 2. The second stored value is now 9, at index 1.

hints: Count successful appends separately from allocated spaces.

title: Linked nodes and cleanup
summary: When freeing linked nodes, save the next link before releasing the current node.
explanation: A linked chain stores a pointer to the next node in each node. The head is its first node. NULL marks the end. Unlike array items, linked nodes do not need to sit next to each other in memory.
To clear the chain, first save the current node's next pointer. Then free the current node and move to the saved pointer. You must not read next from a node after freeing it.
The compound literal `(struct Node){...}` makes a whole struct value for the assignment. a links to b, whose value is 8. The print follows that link before either node is freed, so it displays 8.
clear saves b's address, frees a, then moves to b. It saves NULL, frees b, and stops. If allocating b had failed, main would have freed a before returning.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If b's value starts at 11, what prints before cleanup?
quiz.explanation: a's next pointer leads to b. The print reads b's value, now 11, before cleanup starts.

hints: The print follows a's next link to b while both nodes are still alive.
externalNotes: The browser shows C code and checks your understanding; it does not run C. Optional local examples use C17.

title: Function pointers and callbacks
summary: A callback is a function you give to another function so it can call it.
explanation: A function pointer identifies a function you can call. `int (*operation)(int)` means operation points to a function that takes an int and returns an int. The parentheses keep the star attached to the pointer name.
A callback is a function passed to another function to be called. apply receives one and runs `operation(value)`. The callback's input and result types must match the function-pointer type.
main passes 4 and double_value to apply. apply calls double_value with 4. It returns 8, which printf displays. Both available callbacks take and return int.
Change only the callback to plus_one. The input remains 4, but the selected function now adds 1 instead of multiplying by 2. Keep inputs small enough for these calculations to fit int.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Pass plus_one instead of double_value, keeping the input 4. What prints?
quiz.explanation: apply calls plus_one with 4. That function returns 4 + 1, so the print displays 5.

hints: Follow the function name supplied to apply.

title: Sorting with safe comparators
summary: A comparator tells a sorting function which of two items should come first.
explanation: qsort reorders an array. Give it the array, item count, item size, and a comparator: a function that compares two items. Its const void * inputs are general pointers. Because this array holds ints, the comparator reads them through const int pointers.

Return a negative number when the left item comes first, zero when equal, or a positive number when the right comes first. `(*a > *b) - (*a < *b)` subtracts only 0-or-1 answers, avoiding overflow from subtracting the int values themselves.
The rule puts smaller values first. qsort rearranges the array, so the print shows 1 2 3. Use a consistent comparison rule. Equal items are not promised to keep their original order.
Reverse the two comparisons in the return expression. Larger values will then come first.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Use `(*a < *b) - (*a > *b)` instead. What prints?
quiz.explanation: The reversed comparison places larger numbers first, so the sorted order is 3 2 1.

hints: A negative comparison result means the left item should come first.

title: Separate headers and source files
summary: Put a shared declaration in a header and its function body in a source file. The build needs both.
explanation: A header is a file included by other source files. score.h declares the function's types. Its include guard uses `#ifndef`, `#define`, and `#endif` to include that declaration section only once per compilation, even if the header is included twice.
A translation unit is one .c file together with the headers it includes. Save each labeled part below in its own named file. Build main.c and score.c together so the linker can find score's body.
With GCC, build using `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.c score.c -o app`. Run `./app` on Linux or macOS, or `.\app.exe` in Windows PowerShell. The linked program prints 12.
If you leave score.c out of a fresh build, the caller still knows score's types from the header. But the linker cannot find its body, so the build fails.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Leave score.c out of this fresh build. What happens?
choices: Linking fails because score's body is missing.
The header creates the missing body.
quiz.explanation: The declaration lets the compiler check the call. The linker still needs the function definition from score.c.

hints: The header describes the function. score.c supplies the instructions.

title: Linkage and file-private helpers
summary: A static function at file scope keeps its name local to that compiled source file.
explanation: File scope means outside any function. A function declared static there has internal linkage: another separately compiled source file cannot link to that function by its name. Static here does not mean the function runs only once.
value.h declares public_value for callers. In value.c, public_value can call its local helper. main uses the public function and does not need to know how that helper works.
Build main.c and value.c together. main calls public_value, which calls helper and returns 9. The program prints 9.
Declaring helper again in main.c does not expose value.c's static helper. The files may each have their own static helper without sharing that name.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If main declares and calls helper directly, can it link to value.c's static helper?
choices: Yes, every function is shared by name.
Yes, if the return types match.
No, that helper's name stays local to value.c's compilation.
quiz.explanation: helper has internal linkage. main must use the public function instead of trying to link to that helper.

hints: A declaration in a different file does not remove static from the original helper.

title: Preprocessor macros and evaluation
summary: A macro substitutes code before compilation. Parentheses keep a substituted expression grouped correctly.
explanation: A macro is a rule for replacing code before the compiler reads it. In `SQUARE(x)`, the supplied expression replaces each x. Parentheses around each x and the whole result keep the intended calculation together.

This macro uses its input twice. An input that changes a variable, such as `i++`, would try to change it twice without a required order here. That has undefined behavior. Use a real function when an input must be evaluated once.
The parentheses keep each `2 + 1` grouped, so the multiplication is 3 times 3. The program prints 9.
Without the parentheses, substitution produces `2 + 1 * 2 + 1`. Multiplication happens before addition, so this changed expression gives 5.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change the macro body to `x * x`. What prints for SQUARE(2 + 1)?
choices: There is no defined result just because parentheses are missing.
9, because macros always keep inputs grouped.
quiz.explanation: The input is substituted twice without grouping. The multiplication gives 2, then the additions give 5.

hints: Substitute the input text first, then follow the usual calculation order.

title: Conditional compilation and portability
summary: Conditional compilation chooses which code is included before the program is built.
explanation: Preprocessing is the step that handles directives such as `#if` before C compilation. `#ifndef VERBOSE` means use the following default only if VERBOSE is not already defined. `#if VERBOSE` then chooses one branch using its integer value.

Conditional compilation can also handle optional features. Use a compiler's documented feature checks instead of assuming every operating system offers the same tools. This example only chooses a message; the course uses C17 rules.
With no build setting, VERBOSE becomes 0. The selected MESSAGE is brief, so the program prints brief. The other branch does not run later; it was left out before compilation.

With GCC, add `-DVERBOSE=1` to the build command. For example, use `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -DVERBOSE=1 main.c -o app`. The default guard preserves this setting, and the new program prints details.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If the build defines VERBOSE as 1, which text prints?
quiz.explanation: The default does not replace an existing VERBOSE setting. The true #if branch defines MESSAGE as details.

hints: The build setting is present before the #ifndef default is checked.
