title: Java platform types and null boundaries
summary: Treat a possibly missing Java result as nullable before using it in Kotlin.
explanation: Java code may not tell Kotlin clearly whether a result can be null. Kotlin calls such a type a platform type. Tools may show it as `String!`, but that is not syntax to write in Kotlin source. Assuming it is non-null can fail while the program runs.

A JVM system property is a named setting for the running Java program. GetProperty can return null if it is absent. This example clears its own practice key, then stores the result as `String?` so the missing case is handled explicitly.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin


fun main() {
    val key = "codequest.lesson.optional.topic"
    System.clearProperty(key)
    val topic: String? = System.getProperty(key)
    println(topic?.length ?: -1)
}
```
The screen shows `-1`. The property is missing, so the safe call gives null and the Elvis operator supplies the fallback.

The practice setting belongs to this short-lived JVM process; it is not an operating-system environment variable. At an uncertain Java boundary, allow and handle null instead of using `!!` to demand a value that may be absent.

A constant is a value that does not change. A number written without a fixed type can fit different number types, as long as its value is allowed.
When both numbers in this division are integers, Go keeps only the whole-number answer. It drops the fraction rather than rounding up.

title: Boolean conditions and short-circuiting
summary: Stop checking once a true-or-false answer is known.
explanation: A Boolean value is true or false. Go needs this kind of value for an if condition. A number or a string alone is not a Boolean condition.
`&&` means both checks must be true. It skips the right check if the left is false. `||` means either check can be true. It skips the right check if the left is true.
The denominator is the number we divide by. `denominator != 0` asks whether it is not zero. Putting that check first can stop division by zero.

title: Strings bytes and runes
summary: Count stored bytes separately from text code points.
explanation: A byte is a small unit of stored data. A Go string stores bytes, and `len(text)` counts them. UTF-8 is a way to store text that can use several bytes for one character.
Unicode gives text symbols numbers called code points. Go calls a code-point value a rune. `[]rune(text)` reads UTF-8 text into a list of runes. Taking that list's length counts code points.
Reading a string at one numbered position gives a byte. A range loop over a string reads runes instead. byte is another name for uint8; rune is another name for int32.
The written `é` in this example uses two UTF-8 bytes and one code point. A displayed character can sometimes use several code points, so a rune count is not always a visible-character count.

`\n` means start a new line. Printf needs it when you want a line ending. Println adds its own line ending.
Formatting changes how a value is displayed. It does not change the value stored in the variable.

title: Scope and short declarations
summary: Tell a new inner variable apart from an outer one.
explanation: Scope is the part of the code where a name is available. Braces create a block with its own scope. Inside a function, `:=` declares names; at least one must be new in that block, excluding the discard name `_`.
An inner block can declare its own score. This hides the outer score inside that block, but the two variables remain separate.
`=` assigns a value to an existing variable. It does not create a new variable.
To find which score a line uses, look at its surrounding braces. Then check whether the line declares a new name or updates an existing one.
The screen shows `7`, then `3`. The first line reads the inner score. After the inner block ends, the second line reads the outer score.
Replace the inner `:=` with `=`. There is then no new inner score; the assignment changes the outer variable.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace the inner := with =. What appears?
choices: 7 then 3, because every block creates a variable.
7 then 7, because the outer variable changes.
3 then 7, because the display order reverses.
quiz.explanation: The assignment updates the existing score to 7. Both display lines read that same variable.

hints: An assignment alone does not create another score.

title: Switch expressions and cases
summary: Choose a matching case from several choices.
explanation: `switch` checks a value against choices called cases. In this example, it looks for the case matching choice.
After the chosen case finishes, the switch ends. Go only continues into the next case body if you explicitly use `fallthrough`.
`default` handles a value that matches no listed case. It is the fallback choice.
Checking a case does not change the value of choice. It only chooses which instructions run.
The screen shows `read`. choice is 1, so case 1 runs.
Change choice to 2 and find its matching case. The other cases still do not run.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If choice is 2, what appears?
quiz.explanation: case 2 runs and displays rest. The switch then ends.

hints: A normal case does not continue into the next case.

title: Loop control
summary: Skip one loop turn or stop the loop.
explanation: The loop starts i at 0, checks `i < 4`, runs its body, then adds 1 with `i++`. It repeats that check before each new turn.
`continue` skips the rest of the current turn. In this loop, i++ still runs before the next check.
`break` leaves this loop completely. It does not move to another turn.
This loop stops because i increases until the check is false. When writing a loop, check how it will reach its stopping point.
The screen shows `0`, `2`, and `3` on separate lines. continue skips the display instruction when i is 1.
Replace continue with break in the same example. Now reaching 1 ends the loop.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: After replacing continue with break, what appears?
choices: Only 0, because the loop stops at 1.
quiz.explanation: The loop displays 0. On the next turn, break stops it before 1 is displayed.

hints: break stops the loop before any later turns.

title: Array values and copying
summary: Copy an array so its number values can change separately.
explanation: An array holds a fixed number of items of one type. `[3]int` means exactly three integers. A different length makes a different array type.
Assigning an array to another variable copies its value. In this integer array, changing a copied item leaves the original item unchanged.
An index is an item's numbered position. Index 0 means the first item. A position outside the array is an error; it does not make the array grow.
This copying rule describes arrays. Other types, such as slices, can share the same stored items. The next lesson shows that difference.
The screen shows `2 9`. The original first item stays 2; the copied first item becomes 9.
Change only the assigned value from 9 to 7. Follow which array receives that change.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change copy[0] = 9 to copy[0] = 7. What appears?
choices: 7 7, because both arrays share their items.
2 7, because the array value was copied.
quiz.explanation: The original first item remains 2. Only the copy's first item becomes 7.

hints: The assignment writes to copy, not original.

title: Slice views and shared arrays
summary: Use a slice to view items stored in an array.
explanation: A slice describes part of an array: where it starts, its length, and its capacity. Copying a slice copies that description, so the slices can still share their stored items.
`values[1:3]` starts at index 1 and stops before index 3. The new view's index 0 points to values[1]. Its index 1 points to values[2].
`len(view)` counts the items you can use in the slice. Here it is 2. Capacity describes how far the slice can extend within the same array; the next lesson explains it.
Changing an item through one slice changes the shared item. Another view of that same item can see the change.
The screen shows `9`. Changing view[0] changes the same stored item that values[1] reads.
Change the assignment to view[1]. That index points to values[2], while the display line still reads values[1].

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change view[0] = 9 to view[1] = 9. What does the same display line show?
choices: 9, because every view index means the same item.
6, because the end boundary is included.
quiz.explanation: view[1] points to values[2]. values[1] keeps its original value, 4.

hints: The view starts at original index 1.

title: Append length and capacity
summary: Check whether adding an item keeps or replaces shared storage.
explanation: `append` adds items and returns an updated slice. Save that result, because the slice's length or storage may change.
Length is the number of available items. Capacity is how many fit from the slice's start in its array. `make([]int, 1, 1)` starts with length 1 and capacity 1. Adding a second item needs a new array.
The old slice still points to the original array. Once values uses a new array, changing values[0] no longer changes old[0].
Go decides how much extra space to reserve when growing. Do not rely on an exact growth amount. Check whether the existing capacity is enough.

Follow which array each slice uses after append.
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	values := make([]int, 1, 1)
	values[0] = 3
	old := values
	values = append(values, 7)
	values[0] = 9
	fmt.Println(old[0], values[0])
}

```
The screen shows `3 9`. old still reads the original array; values reads the newly grown array.
Change the starting capacity to 2 but keep the length at 1. The extra item now fits in the existing array.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Start with make([]int, 1, 2). After the same append and update, what appears?
choices: 9 9, because both slices still share the first item.
3 9, because append always creates a new array.
quiz.explanation: Capacity 2 leaves enough room. append reuses the array, so both slices see the first item change to 9.

hints: Ask whether the second item fits without a new array.

title: Copy into independent slice storage
summary: Copy slice items into separate storage.
explanation: `copy(target, source)` copies items into target and returns how many it copied. It stops at the shorter slice's length. It does not grow target.
`make([]int, len(source))` creates separate storage with room for the source's items.
After making target, copy the items into it. Using only `target := source` would instead make both slices share the same array.
Here, each item is an integer, so copying gives separate number values. Items that point to other data can still share that data after copying.
The screen shows `2 9`. Updating target's first item does not change source's first item.
Replace both the make line and the copy line with `target := source`. That changes the example from copying items to sharing them.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace make and copy with target := source. After target[0] = 9, what appears?
choices: 9 9, because both slices share the array.
quiz.explanation: Both slices point to the same first item. Changing it through target is also visible through source.

hints: A slice assignment alone does not make a new array.

title: Maps and mutation
summary: Use a key to read or change a map entry.
explanation: A map matches keys to values. A key is the label used to find an entry. `map[string]int` uses text keys and whole-number values.
`alias := counts` gives another way to reach the same map. It does not copy the entries into a new map.
A map starts at nil if no storage is supplied. You can read it and check its length, but writing an entry needs an initialized map. `make` or a map value written with braces provides that storage.
Go does not promise an order when visiting map entries. Here, a direct lookup finds the known key read.
The screen shows `5`. Both names reach the same map entry.
Change the assignment through alias from 5 to 7. The lookup through counts still reads that shared entry.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change alias["read"] = 5 to alias["read"] = 7. What appears?
choices: 2, because assigning a map copies its entries.
5, because the first change is permanent.
7, because both names reach the same map.
quiz.explanation: The assignment changes the shared read entry to 7.

hints: alias and counts reach the same entries.

title: Lookup presence with comma-ok
summary: Tell a missing map entry apart from a stored zero.
explanation: Looking up a missing key in a map of integers gives 0. A stored value can also be 0, so the number alone cannot tell you whether the key exists.
`value, ok := counts[key]` gives two answers. value holds the number. ok is true if the key exists and false if it is missing.
Looking up a missing key does not add it to the map.
Check ok when missing data should be handled differently from a real zero.
The screen shows `0 true`. The read key exists, and its stored value is 0.
Look up rest instead of read. The map has no rest entry.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: What appears when the lookup uses "rest"?
choices: 0 false, because the key is missing.
0 true, because zero always means present.
quiz.explanation: The missing entry gives the int zero value, 0. ok is false because the key does not exist.

hints: Read the number and the existence check separately.

title: Range traversal
summary: Visit slice items without mistaking a copied value for the original.
explanation: `for i, value := range values` visits each slice item. i is its index. value is a copy of that item's value.
`value += 1` adds 1 to the local copy. To change the item in the slice, write to `values[i]` instead.
The name `_` discards an answer you do not need. This example keeps both the index and the copied value.
What range gives you depends on its input. For a slice, it visits items in index order. A map has no promised visiting order, and a string gives runes.
The screen shows `0 3`, then `1 5`, then `[2 4]`. The local copies changed, but the slice's items stayed the same.
Replace `value += 1` with `values[i] += 1`. This writes to the slice. The local value remains the copy taken before that write.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace value += 1 with values[i] += 1. What is the final displayed slice?
choices: [2 4], because indexed assignment changes only a copy.
[3 5], because the assignments change the slice items.
quiz.explanation: The indexed assignments add 1 to each stored slice item.

hints: Look at the name on the left of +=.

title: Multiple return values
summary: Return a result and a success check together.
explanation: A function can return more than one value. `(int, bool)` says this function returns a whole number and a true-or-false answer.
divide returns the division result and a success flag. A flag is a value that signals a condition. Here, true means the division was allowed.
When the flag is false, the returned 0 is only a placeholder. It does not mean the division succeeded with an answer of zero.
The function checks b before dividing. If b is 0, it returns immediately, so the division never runs.
The screen shows `4 true`. 8 divided by 2 gives 4, and the success flag is true.
Change the call to `divide(8, 0)`. Follow the early return and read both values it sends back.

quiz.question: What appears for divide(8, 0)?
choices: 0 true, because any zero answer is valid.
0 false, because the function rejects division by zero.
quiz.explanation: The check returns 0 and false before division. The false flag tells you not to use 0 as a calculated result.

hints: Read the first return statement.

title: Variadic functions
summary: Let one function accept any number of integer inputs.
explanation: A variadic function can take zero or more inputs of a chosen type. `values ...int` collects the supplied integers into a slice inside the function.
At the call, `values...` passes the slice's items to the variadic input. The three dots do not repeat the function.
A call with no inputs gives the loop no items to visit. The starting sum stays 0.
The number of inputs can vary, but each still needs to be an int. If changing the call leaves a local variable unused, remove that declaration; Go rejects unused local variables.
The screen shows `6`. The function adds 2 and 4.
Replace the call with `total()` and remove the now-unused values declaration in main. The function's sum still starts at 0.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Call total() and remove the unused values declaration. What appears?
choices: 0, because there are no values to add.
6, because total saves its first answer.
A compile error, because at least one input is required.
quiz.explanation: Zero inputs are allowed. The loop adds nothing, so total returns 0.

title: Closures and captured variables
summary: Let a function use a variable from the code around it.
explanation: A function can itself be a value. Here, transform holds a function we can call later.
A closure is a function that keeps access to variables around it. This function uses the outer variable factor. It does not freeze factor at its first value.
The function body runs when `transform(3)` is called. By then, factor has already changed.
This example runs in order, one step at a time. If several tasks change the same captured variable at once, they need coordination. Capturing a variable does not provide that by itself.
The screen shows `12`. The function multiplies 3 by the current factor, 4.
Change the assignment before the call to `factor = 5`. The same function will read this new value when it runs.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Set factor = 5 before transform(3). What appears?
choices: 6, because the function froze the first value, 2.
15, because the function reads the current factor.
5, because the function ignores its input.
quiz.explanation: The call multiplies its input, 3, by the current factor, 5.

hints: Follow the assignment that happens just before the call.

title: Structures and fields
summary: Group named values in a struct.
explanation: A struct groups values with names called fields. Point has X and Y fields. `Point{X: 2, Y: 5}` sets them by name. Fields you leave out start at their zero values. A dot reads a field, as in `a.X`.
`b := a` copies the struct's field values. Here the fields are integers, so changing b.X does not change a.X.
The screen shows `2 9`. a.X stays 2 while b.X becomes 9.
Copying a struct copies each field's value. If a field is a slice or a map, its copy can still share the data it points to.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Set b.X to 7 instead of 9. What appears?
quiz.explanation: Only b.X changes to 7. a.X is still 2.

hints: Read a.X first and b.X second.
externalNotes: The browser shows Go code and checks your understanding; it does not run Go. Optional local examples use Go 1.27.

title: Methods and value receivers
summary: Use a method that works on a copy of its receiver.
explanation: A method is a function called on a value. The receiver is the value the method works with. In `func (c Counter) Next()`, c is the receiver. `c.Next()` calls the method.
This receiver is a copy of the Counter. Changing its integer field changes only the copy. A slice or map field could still share data after copying.
The screen shows `5 4`. Next adds 1 to its copy and returns 5. The original c.N stays 4.
A returned answer does not automatically replace the original field. You can keep the answer in a separate variable.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: If c.N starts at 8, what appears?
quiz.explanation: Next returns 9 from its copy. The original field is still 8.

hints: Separate the returned number from the original field.
externalNotes: The browser shows Go code and checks your understanding; it does not run Go. Optional local examples use Go 1.27.

title: Pointer receivers and mutation
summary: Use a pointer receiver to change the original value.
explanation: A pointer holds the address of a value. `*Counter` means a pointer to a Counter; `&c` takes c's address. `*p` follows a pointer named p to its value. A nil pointer points to nothing, so do not follow it.
Add receives a copy of the pointer, but the copy still points to the original counter. `c.N++` adds 1 to the field in that counter. Go lets a struct pointer use the dot directly.
The screen shows `5`. Add changed the original field from 4 to 5.
For this variable, `c.Add()` is a shorter way to call `(&c).Add()`. Go can take its address here. A Counter and a pointer to a Counter still do not have exactly the same set of methods.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Call c.Add() twice before displaying c.N. What appears?
quiz.explanation: Both calls update the same field. Starting at 4, it becomes 5 and then 6.

hints: Each call adds 1 to the original counter.

title: Embedding and composition
summary: Include one struct inside another and use its fields.
explanation: A Person can contain an Address. Writing just `Address` inside Person embeds it: the field uses its type name as its name.
`p.City` is a shorter way to read `p.Address.City` here. Person contains an Address; it is not itself an Address. When creating the Person, set the Address field explicitly.
The screen shows `Rome`. The shorter path reads the City field inside p.Address.
Both paths read the same field. The shorter path works because Go makes an unambiguous embedded field or method available through the outer value.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.explanation: The display line reads City from the embedded Address, now Oslo.

title: Implicit interface satisfaction
summary: Use an interface to require a particular method.
explanation: An interface describes the methods a value must provide. Reader requires `Read() int`. A type with the required methods fits automatically; it does not need to say it implements Reader.
A type's method set is the list of methods it provides. A value-receiver method belongs to both Counter and *Counter. A pointer-receiver method like this Read belongs to *Counter, not Counter.
The screen shows `7`. show receives a *Counter that fits Reader, then calls its Read method.

Go can shorten a direct call on an addressable variable, such as `c.Read()`. Passing c into an interface does not automatically turn it into a pointer. Pass `&c` when the pointer is the type that fits.

Go rejects Counter because Read requires a pointer receiver.

title: Nil interfaces and typed nil
summary: Tell an empty interface apart from an interface holding a nil pointer.
explanation: An interface value keeps track of the type it holds and the value of that type. A nil interface holds neither. `any` is an interface that can hold a value of any type.

p is a nil pointer of type *Counter. Putting it in value keeps that type. The pointer still points to nothing, but the interface is no longer nil. This example only compares the pointer; it never follows it.
The screen shows `true false`. p is nil. value contains a *Counter, so value is not nil.
Set value itself to nil instead of storing p. Now value has no stored type or value. p remains unchanged.

title: Type assertions and type switches
summary: Check the actual type held inside an interface.
explanation: A type assertion asks whether an interface holds a chosen type. `text, ok := value.(string)` asks for a string. On a mismatch, ok is false and text is empty. The two-result form avoids a panic, which would interrupt the program.
A type switch chooses among several types. `switch v := value.(type)` can have string and int cases. In a case naming just one type, v has that type. A default case handles other types.
The screen shows `true 4`. The value holds the string maps, and that string uses four bytes.
Change the held value to the number 7. The assertion checks its type; it does not convert the number to text.

title: Errors as returned values
summary: Check the returned error before using an answer.
explanation: An error value describes what went wrong. Its `Error()` method returns a text message. `errors.New` creates an error with a message. A function can return an answer and an error together; a nil error usually means success.
minutes rejects negative inputs by returning 0 and an error. The caller checks err first. On failure, that 0 is not a valid minute count.
The screen shows `5`. The input is allowed, so minutes returns 5 and a nil error.
With a negative input, the caller shows the error message and returns early. The numeric result is never used.

title: Wrapping errors with context
summary: Add an error message while keeping the original cause.
explanation: Wrapping an error adds information about what was happening. In `fmt.Errorf`, `%w` keeps a link to the original error. `%v` includes its message as text but does not keep that link.
`errors.Is(err, missing)` asks whether err matches missing, including through a wrapped cause. Checking the cause is more reliable than comparing message text.
The screen shows `true`. The new error still links to missing.
Change %w to %v. The message can still contain the word missing, but the new error no longer wraps the original one.

title: Deferred cleanup order
summary: Set a call aside to run when its function ends.
explanation: `defer` schedules a call for the end of the surrounding function. Its arguments are worked out when defer is reached. The call waits, but its input values are already chosen.

Deferred calls run in reverse order: the last one scheduled runs first. A defer in a loop still waits for the function to end. Deferred cleanup can also run during a panic, but you may still need to check for cleanup errors.

Follow when each value is chosen and when each call runs.
```go
package main
import ("fmt")
func main() {
 n := 1
 defer fmt.Println("first", n)
 n = 2
 defer fmt.Println("second", n)
 fmt.Println("body", n)
}
```
The screen shows `body 2`, then `second 2`, then `first 1`. The first defer saved 1 before n changed.
A deferred call with n as an argument saves n's value now. A deferred closure whose body reads n can read its later value instead.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Change n = 2 to n = 3. Which lines appear in order?
quiz.explanation: The body shows 3 first. The second defer saved 3 and runs next. The first defer saved 1 and runs last.

hints: Check when each defer received its argument.

title: Panic recovery boundaries
summary: Recover from a panic at a chosen boundary.
explanation: A panic interrupts normal instructions in the current goroutine, a running path of Go work. As the calls unwind, their deferred calls run. Use returned errors for expected problems instead.

`recover()` can stop an active panic when called directly inside a deferred function in the same goroutine. The interrupted function does not restart at the panic line. After its deferred work finishes, it returns to its caller.
The screen shows `recovered`, then `after`. The deferred function recovers, guarded returns, and main continues.
Without an active panic, recover returns nil. The deferred function then has nothing to report.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Replace panic("broken") with fmt.Println("normal"). What appears?
quiz.explanation: The normal display runs. recover finds no panic, so only main's after message follows.

hints: Check whether a panic is active when recover runs.

title: Generic functions
summary: Use one function with different element types.
explanation: A generic function uses a type parameter: a name that stands for a type. In `First[T any]`, T can be any type. Go can work out T from the slice passed to First.
The function must still check whether the slice is empty. `var zero T` gives the zero value for the chosen type. Returning zero and false avoids reading a missing first item.
The screen shows `7 true`. T is int, and the first integer exists.
With an empty integer slice, zero is 0. With an empty string slice, zero is empty text. The false flag says no first item existed.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

choices: A panic from reading beyond the slice
quiz.explanation: The length check returns int's zero value and false before trying to read an item.

title: Type sets and constraints
summary: Limit a generic function to types that support its work.
explanation: A constraint is a rule for which types a function accepts. `~int | ~int64` allows types based on int or int64. The `|` means either group is allowed. The `~` includes distinct named types based on that type.

`type Count int` creates a new type based on int, so Count fits this rule. Every allowed type supports `+`, so Add can add its inputs. This constraint is a rule for type parameters, not a type for ordinary variables.
The screen shows `5`. Both Count inputs fit the constraint, and 2 plus 3 is 5.
float64 is outside this set. A constraint checks allowed types; it does not convert them or check whether a large sum overflows its type.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

quiz.question: Call Add with two float64 values. What happens?
choices: It silently changes both values to integers.

title: Context and cancellation
summary: Tell work to stop by sending a cancellation signal.

```go
package main

import (
"fmt"
"context"
)


func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    cancel()
    <-ctx.Done()
    fmt.Println(ctx.Err() == context.Canceled)
}
```
The screen shows `true`. The context was canceled, the wait finished, and Err reports the expected reason.

`sorted` takes a sequence and a key function. The key function receives one item and returns a key. `sorted` returns a new list ordered by those keys without changing the sequence.

```python
names = ["Moon", "Io", "Earth"]

print(ordered)
print(names)
```

title: Loop else and normal exhaustion
summary: Use a loop's else part to report that no matching number was found.
explanation: A loop's `else` part runs when the loop finishes normally, even when there are no items to visit. It does not run if `break` leaves the loop. A `return` or an error that leaves the loop also skips this part.

This `else` belongs to the loop. It does not belong to an `if` inside that loop.

A search can use `break` when it finds a match. Then `else` can handle the case where no match was found.

`continue` skips the rest of one repeat. The loop can still finish normally and run its `else` part.

`contains_even` reads whole numbers from something you can loop over, such as a list. It checks whether any number is even and leaves the input unchanged.

If it finds an even number, `break` ends the loop. If the loop finishes without a match, `else` returns `False`.

Code:
```python
def contains_even(values):
    for value in values:
        if value % 2 == 0:
            break
    else:
        return False
    return True

print(contains_even([1, 4, 7]))
print(contains_even([1, 3]))
```
This prints:
```text
True
False
```

title: Structural pattern matching
summary: Choose a response by matching the shape of a command.
explanation:
`match command` checks a value against the shapes listed after `case`.

The pattern `["greet", name]` needs two items. The first must be `"greet"`. The second is saved as `name`.

A name written on its own in a pattern saves a value. It does not compare against an older value of that name.

A guard is an extra `if` check after a pattern. Here, `if isinstance(name, str)` asks whether `name` is a string. It runs only after the two-item shape matches.

Only the first matching case with a passing guard runs. `_` matches anything without saving a name, so put that catch-all case last.

```python
def route(command):
    match command:
        case ["greet", name] if isinstance(name, str):
            return f"Hello {name}"
        case ["pause"]:
            return "Paused"
        case _:
            return "Unknown"

print(route(["greet", "Ada"]))
print(route(["pause"]))
print(route(["greet", 7]))
```
It prints `Hello Ada`, `Paused`, and `Unknown`. `route` reads a command and returns a message without changing the command.

These patterns can match lists or tuples. They do not split strings or bytes into items.

The greeting pattern needs exactly two items. `route(["greet", "Ada", "extra"])` has three, so it returns `"Unknown"`.

If a guard fails, Python can still try the later cases.

Build `route` with the same three cases. Keep a string name exactly as given, including spaces and non-English letters.

For extra practice, add a `["resume"]` case before `_`. Explain why it must come before the catch-all case.

title: Unicode text and UTF-8 bytes
summary: Turn text into UTF-8 bytes, count them, and turn them back into text.
explanation:
A string (`str`) holds text. A `bytes` value holds small whole numbers from 0 to 255.

Unicode gives letters, marks, and symbols numbers called code points. `len(text)` counts these code points. One visible character can use more than one.

`len(encoded)` counts bytes instead. In UTF-8, one code point can need several bytes.

`text.encode("utf-8")` turns the text into new bytes. `encoded.decode("utf-8")` turns those bytes back into text.

Neither call changes the original value. The dot selects the method, and the text inside `()` chooses the encoding.

```python
text = "é"
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")
print(len(text))
print(len(encoded))
print(encoded.decode("utf-8"))
```
It prints 1, then 2, then é. Encoding changes how the text is represented, not its meaning.

By default, decoding stops with an error if the bytes do not fit the chosen encoding.

`b"\xff"` holds one byte. `\xff` is a way to write the number 255 in hexadecimal, or base 16. That byte alone is not valid UTF-8. This example handles the error:
```python
try:
    b"\xff".decode("utf-8")
except UnicodeDecodeError:
    print("Invalid UTF-8")
```
It prints Invalid UTF-8. Ignoring malformed bytes would lose information. Use replacement text only when the application allows it.

```python
def utf8_summary(text):
    encoded = text.encode("utf-8")
    return len(encoded), encoded.decode("utf-8")
print(utf8_summary("Café"))
```
It returns and prints (5, 'Café'): the byte count and exact decoded text. The project accepts ordinary Unicode strings that UTF-8 can encode, but not isolated surrogate code points—special code values that cannot stand alone as UTF-8 text. Empty text returns (0, ""). Optional check: compare "é" with "e\u0301"; they can look alike but have different code-point sequences.

title: Floating-point closeness
summary: Check whether two numbers are close enough for your chosen rules.
explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 are not stored as exact decimal fractions in an ordinary float. Their sum can differ slightly from 0.3. This does not make every equality test wrong. Choose exact or approximate comparison to match the rules.

A tolerance is a gap you agree to allow. `math.isclose` returns `True` when two numbers fit the chosen tolerance, and `False` otherwise.

Relative tolerance (`rel_tol`) grows with the larger input's distance from zero. Absolute tolerance (`abs_tol`) allows a fixed gap, which helps near zero.

The gap must fit the larger of those two allowances. Use nonnegative tolerances, and keep relative tolerance below 1 so it allows only a small difference.

Code breakdown:
```python
import math
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=0.0))
print(math.isclose(1e-12, 0.0, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
```
Output:
```text
False
True
True
```
The outputs are False, True, True. `import math` makes the standard module available, and the dot selects `isclose`. `1e-9` means one billionth. Named arguments show each tolerance clearly.

When one input is zero and relative tolerance is below 1, relative tolerance alone cannot make a nonzero input close to zero. Changing the last `abs_tol` to 0.0 therefore gives False. Allowing a gap does not prove a measurement is accurate. It also does not make different units match.

```python
import math

def close_readings(a, b):
    return math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-6, abs_tol=1e-9)
print(close_readings(100.0, 100.00005))
print(close_readings(0.0, 1e-10))
print(close_readings(1.0, 1.01))
```
These calls return True, True, False. The project accepts finite real numbers. Deciding what NaN or infinity means is outside the project rules. If you use different units, consider how the absolute tolerance would need to change.

title: Inheritance and super
summary: Reuse a class's method, then add your own finishing touch.
explanation:
A class can reuse another class's methods. This is called inheritance.

In `class FramedLabel(Label):`, `Label` is the base class we build on. `FramedLabel` reuses its setup method and gives `render` a new version. This replacement is called overriding.

`FramedLabel("Map")` still saves `"Map"` as the new object's `self.text`.

Inside `FramedLabel.render`, `super().render()` looks for the next `render` method after `FramedLabel` in Python's class order. Here it finds `Label.render`.

Both methods work on the same object. `super()` does not create another `Label`, and it does not call every parent class.

Using `self.render()` here would call `FramedLabel.render` again. That method would keep calling itself. With no stopping rule, Python eventually raises `RecursionError`.

Use `super().render()` to reach the next method instead.

summary: Use class and static methods to create sessions and check their minutes.

@staticmethod receives only the arguments you pass. Here, valid_minutes receives minutes and returns whether it is zero or more. Python does not add self or cls. This method checks a number. It does not change existing sessions or automatically check their minutes.

title: Generator functions and resumption
summary: Write a countdown generator that yields numbers one at a time and can resume.
explanation: A generator function can pause and continue later. It uses yield. Calling countdown(start) returns a generator, but its body has not run yet. Each next resumes it until yield supplies one value. Its local variables and where it paused are kept. Returning or reaching the end finishes the stream instead of yielding another item.

countdown should supply integers from start down to 1 without building a full list. Input: a nonnegative integer. Result: a single-use generator. It advances only when used. If start is 0, it yields nothing. The subtraction after yield happens when the generator resumes, not before the yielded value is received.

next(stream) asks for one value. If nothing remains, it raises StopIteration, the error that means no more items. next(stream, "done") returns the supplied default when nothing remains. list(stream) uses up all remaining values into a new list, so use it only for bounded streams. It does not restart a partly used generator.

Calling countdown again creates a new generator with its own state. This lesson does not need send, throw, or yield from. Keep yield inside the loop. Returning the first value would finish instead of pausing. The worked example calls the generator, advances it once, then uses up the rest.

Worked call:
```python
def countdown(start):
    remaining = start
    while remaining > 0:
        yield remaining
        remaining -= 1

stream = countdown(3)
print(next(stream))
print(list(stream))
print(next(stream, "done"))
print(list(countdown(0)))
```
Expected stdout:
```text
3
[2, 1]
done
[]
```

summary: Make a countdown that gives one number at a time, then stops.
explanation:
An iterable is something you can ask for items. An iterator keeps track of which item comes next.

`__iter__` gives you the iterator. `__next__` gives the next item or raises `StopIteration` when none remain. Here, Countdown does both jobs.

`Countdown(start)` saves the starting number in `self.remaining`. Use a whole number of 0 or more.

Creating the countdown does not use a number yet. Calling `iter(counter)` gives the same counter; it does not restart it.

Each `next(counter)` calls `__next__`. It saves the current number, subtracts 1, then returns the saved number.

At 0, it raises `StopIteration`. Returning `None` would give another item, not stop the countdown.

`list(counter)` collects the remaining numbers until `StopIteration`. Once they are used up, another `list(counter)` gives `[]`.

Make a new `Countdown(start)` to start again. Keep `__iter__` returning `self` without resetting the count.

Follow this countdown:
```python
class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.remaining = start
    def __iter__(self):
        return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.remaining <= 0:
            raise StopIteration
        value = self.remaining
        self.remaining -= 1
        return value

counter = Countdown(2)
print(iter(counter) is counter)
print(next(counter))
print(list(counter))
print(list(counter))
```
Output:
```text
True
2
[1]
[]
```
Optional local practice: Explain how a reusable collection could make a new iterator each time instead of resetting this one.

analogy.limit: Use the actual code and explicit contract as evidence.

steps: Keep Countdown.__init__ storing start in self.remaining.
In __next__, raise StopIteration when self.remaining is 0 or less.
Otherwise save self.remaining as value, subtract 1, and return value.
Keep __iter__ returning self without resetting progress.
Check that Countdown(3) gives [3, 2, 1], a partly used Countdown(2) gives [1] when listed, and Countdown(0) gives [].

checks.expression: (lambda c: next(c)==2 and iter(c) is c and list(c)==[1])(Countdown(2))

checks.label: Stays exhausted
checks.expression: (lambda c: list(c)==[1] and list(c)==[] and next(c,"done")=="done")(Countdown(1))

quiz.question: If the first list(counter) becomes list(Countdown(2)), what does the final list(counter) return?
choices: [1], because a different object was consumed.
quiz.explanation: The earlier next(counter) used 2 from the original, leaving 1. Listing a new Countdown(2) does not change the original, so the final list(counter) returns [1].

hints: In __next__, stop when self.remaining is 0 or less.
Save the value before subtracting 1.
Keep __iter__ from resetting a partly used Countdown.

title: Custom exceptions and chaining
summary: Report a clear error when text cannot become a number of minutes from 1 to 60.
explanation:
`MinuteError` is a special kind of `ValueError`. Catch `MinuteError` for this specific problem, or `ValueError` for the wider group.

`pass` leaves the class body empty. `raise MinuteError(message)` creates the error with a message and reports it.

`int(text)` turns whole-number text into an integer. It raises `ValueError` if it cannot do that.

First try that conversion. Then check that the number is from 1 to 60, including both ends. Report an error for either problem instead of quietly using a default.

`raise MinuteError("whole minutes required") from error` reports your clearer message and keeps the original error as its cause. You can find that cause in `__cause__`.

A number outside 1 to 60 gets a separate error. It has no original conversion error to attach. Keep private details out of error messages and logs.

`str(error)` gives the error message. `type(error.__cause__).__name__` gives the name of the cause's class.

The supplied `__failure_details` helper reads those two details for the exercise checks. Leave that helper as supplied.

Follow a good input and a bad input:
```python
class MinuteError(ValueError):
    pass

def parse_minutes(text):
    try:
        value = int(text)
    except ValueError as error:
        raise MinuteError("whole minutes required") from error
    if not 1 <= value <= 60:
        raise MinuteError("minutes outside 1..60")
    return value

print(parse_minutes("15"))
try:
    parse_minutes("bad")
except MinuteError as error:
    print(str(error))
    print(type(error.__cause__).__name__)
```
Output:
```text
15
whole minutes required
ValueError
```
Optional local practice: Explain why a broad `except Exception` around an entire application can hide unrelated bugs.

analogy.limit: Use the actual code and explicit contract as evidence.

steps: In `parse_minutes`, put `value = int(text)` inside a `try` block.
Catch `ValueError as error` and raise `MinuteError("whole minutes required") from error`.
After conversion, raise `MinuteError("minutes outside 1..60")` when `not 1 <= value <= 60`.
Return `value` when conversion succeeds and the range is valid.
Check valid and boundary calls: `parse_minutes("15") == 15`, `parse_minutes("1") == 1`, and `parse_minutes("60") == 60`.
Use `__failure_details` to confirm `"bad"` and `"1.5"` give `("whole minutes required", "ValueError")`, while `"0"` gives `("minutes outside 1..60", "NoneType")`.

quiz.question: If "bad" changes to "0", what message and cause class are printed?
choices: No exception; successful parsing guarantees a valid range.
quiz.explanation: `int("0")` succeeds, so the range check raises `MinuteError("minutes outside 1..60")`. It has no explicit cause, so the cause class is `NoneType`.

hints: `int("bad")` and `int("1.5")` fail conversion, so use `from error` on that path.
`int("0")` works, so the 1..60 check must then raise a separate `MinuteError` without `from`.
`str(error)` shows the message, and `type(error.__cause__).__name__` shows the cause class.

title: Writing and appending text files
summary: Save text in a note, replacing the old text or adding to its end.
explanation:
Mode `"w"` creates a file, or clears an existing file as soon as it opens. Mode `"a"` adds text at the end, creating the file if needed.

In this exercise, you work with practice files inside the app. These are not files elsewhere on your device, and writing them does not create a lasting download.

`save_note(path, text, append=False)` writes the supplied text using UTF-8. `path` names the practice file. `append` chooses whether to add to its end.

`handle.write(text)` returns the number of text characters accepted, not the number of bytes. It adds no line break unless you include one.

The `with` block closes the file even after a return or error. A write can still fail partway through; the count is not a promise that the file will survive a crash.

`open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8")` opens the file or raises an error. In read mode, `handle.read()` gets its remaining text.

`repr(text)` shows a string with marks such as `\n` for a line break. The example below writes a note, adds another line, then reads the result.

Use the supplied practice paths. Replacing a file clears its old contents, and this function does not check whether a path is safe or hide file errors.

Leave the supplied `__read_note` helper as it is; it reads the test notes. The app's practice files do not show how permissions work on your own computer.

Worked call:
```python
def save_note(path, text, append=False):
    mode = "a" if append else "w"
    with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        return handle.write(text)

print(save_note("demo-note.txt", "Sky\n"))
print(save_note("demo-note.txt", "Moon\n", append=True))
with open("demo-note.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    print(repr(handle.read()))
```
Output:
```text
4
5
'Sky\nMoon\n'
```
For extra practice, try writing empty text to another practice file. Compare replacing its contents with adding to its end.

analogy.limit: Use the actual code and explicit contract as evidence.

steps: Choose `"a"` when `append` is true; otherwise choose `"w"`.
Open the practice path with UTF-8 inside a `with` block.
Write the supplied text and return the count from `write`.
Check replacement, appending, and empty text using the practice files.

quiz.question: If the second call uses append=False, what remains?
choices: Only "Moon\n"; replacement discards the earlier note.
quiz.explanation: The second call opens mode "w", which clears earlier text before writing Moon and its newline.

hints: `write` does not add a line break for you.
Opening with `"w"` clears the old file even when the new text is empty.

title: Command-line argument parsing
summary: Read a minutes option, use a default when it is missing, and reject invalid choices.
explanation:
A command-line argument is text you give a program when starting it. A parser reads that text and checks its rules.

Here, `parse_minutes(arguments)` gets a list of strings. The browser uses that list for practice; it does not open a terminal or run a shell command.

`ArgumentParser` makes the reader. `prog="study"` sets the name shown in messages. `add_help=False` leaves out the help option in this small exercise. `allow_abbrev=False` requires the full option name.

`add_argument` adds `--minutes`. Use `type=int` for a whole number, `default=10` when omitted, and `choices=range(1, 61)` for 1 through 60.

`parse_args(arguments)` reads the list and returns a `Namespace`: an object that holds the chosen options. Read the number with `options.minutes`.

Bad numbers, values outside the range, and unknown options print an error and raise `SystemExit` with code 2. They do not use the default. The supplied helper catches this error for the checks, but the printed message remains visible.

To try this in a real terminal, save the function in `study.py`. Import `sys`, then call `parse_minutes(sys.argv[1:])` inside the main guard. The slice skips the script's name.

Run `python study.py --minutes 4` in the terminal. This reads options; any further action needs its own code.

Read the supplied options:
```python
import argparse

def parse_minutes(arguments):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="study", add_help=False, allow_abbrev=False)
    parser.add_argument("--minutes", type=int, default=10, choices=range(1, 61))
    options = parser.parse_args(arguments)
    return options.minutes

print(parse_minutes(["--minutes", "4"]))
print(parse_minutes([]))
```
Output:
```text
4
10
```
Optional practice on your computer: try no option, a valid number, and a number outside 1 to 60. Compare the output and exit code. Exit code 2 means an argument was rejected.

analogy.limit: Use the actual code and explicit contract as evidence.

steps: Add `--minutes` as an integer from 1 through 60, with default 10.
Read the supplied list and return `options.minutes`.
Check a missing option, both limits, a bad number, and the shortened name `--min`.

quiz.question: If the input is `["--minutes", "61"]`, does the parser return its default of 10?
choices: It accepts 61 because integer conversion succeeded.
No; 61 is outside the choices and raises SystemExit with code 2.
Yes; every invalid supplied value is replaced by 10.
quiz.explanation: 61 is a whole number, but it is outside the allowed range. The default is used only when the option is missing.

hints: Use `range(1, 61)` to include 60.
A default fills in a missing option; it does not repair an invalid one.

title: Discovering and running unit tests
summary: Run a group of tests and report both how many ran and whether they passed.
explanation:
A test class inherits from `unittest.TestCase`. Its methods starting with `test_` are chosen as tests.

`self.assertEqual(actual, expected)` compares the two values and records a failure if they differ. Here, `test_total` checks that 2 + 3 equals 5.

A suite is a group of tests. `TestLoader().loadTestsFromTestCase(case_class)` builds a suite from the supplied class.

Make a fresh suite each time `run_case` is called. This browser exercise reads the supplied class, not files on your computer.

`io.StringIO()` holds text in memory. Give it to `TextTestRunner` to collect the test report.

`runner.run(suite)` runs the tests and returns their results. Read the count with `result.testsRun` and success with `result.wasSuccessful()`.

Check both: a suite with no tests can report success even though nothing was tested.

Optional practice on your computer: save this in a new practice folder as `test_sample.py`:
```python
import unittest

class AdditionTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_total(self):
        self.assertEqual(2 + 3, 5)
```
From that folder, run `python -m unittest discover -s . -p "test_*.py" -v`.

`-s` chooses the folder. `-p` chooses filename patterns. `-v` shows the test names. Discovery imports the matching files, so use code you trust.

A file whose name does not match is skipped. Check the test count and the command's exit code. A command that finds no tests can report a different outcome from an empty in-memory suite.

The app runs these tests inside its browser Python. It does not search your computer's files.

A failed check or an unexpected error makes `wasSuccessful()` return `False`. Leave the four supplied test classes unchanged; use them to check your runner.

Run one named test:
```python
import io
import unittest

def run_case(case_class):
    suite = unittest.TestLoader().loadTestsFromTestCase(case_class)
    output = io.StringIO()
    runner = unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=output, verbosity=0)
    result = runner.run(suite)
    return (result.testsRun, result.wasSuccessful())

class AdditionTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_total(self):
        self.assertEqual(2 + 3, 5)

print(run_case(AdditionTest))
```
Output:
```text
(1, True)
```
Optional practice: rename a test file in your practice folder so it no longer matches `test_*.py`. Run discovery again and compare the count. Rename it back afterward.

analogy.limit: Use the actual code and explicit contract as evidence.

steps: Make a `StringIO` buffer and give it to `TextTestRunner`.
Run the suite and return `(result.testsRun, result.wasSuccessful())`.
Check a passing class, a failing class, an empty class, and a repeated call.

choices: No test was selected. No failures were recorded, but the check did not run.
Every method runs twice after renaming.
The renamed check ran and passed.
quiz.explanation: The loader looks for names starting with `test_`. The count of 0 shows that the renamed check was skipped.

hints: Return the real result instead of always returning `(0, True)`.
A zero count means no selected test ran.

title: Arithmetic operators and grouping
summary: Divide an amount into full groups with //.
explanation:
Arithmetic operators are symbols that do math. `+` adds, `-` subtracts, and `*` multiplies. `**` means a power: `2 ** 3` means 2 × 2 × 2.

`/` divides. With whole-number inputs, its result is a float, a number that can have a decimal part.

`//` divides and rounds down to a whole-number result. Down means toward smaller numbers. For example, `-7 // 3` is `-3`, not `-2`.

`%` gives the remainder from division. Let `a` be the starting number and `b` be the number you divide by. The result of `//` and the remainder fit together like this: `a == (a // b) * b + (a % b)`.

When `b` is positive, the remainder is zero or greater, even if `a` is negative. You cannot divide by zero: Python reports `ZeroDivisionError`.

Parentheses tell Python which calculation to do first. Without them, multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. So `2 + 3 * 4` gives 14, but `(2 + 3) * 4` gives 20.

Powers are calculated before multiplication. Use parentheses when they make your intended order easier to see.

Code breakdown — choose a line to compare its calculation with the output.
```python
print(7 / 3)
print(7 // 3)
print(7 % 3)
print(-7 // 3)
print(-7 % 3)
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)
print(2 ** 3)
```
This prints:
```text
2.3333333333333335
2
1
-3
2
14
20
8
```

Complete `full_groups(amount, size)` by returning `amount // size`. The amount is an integer, a whole number, and the size is a positive integer.

For a negative amount, round down toward smaller numbers. Do not round to the nearest whole number or simply remove the decimal part.

analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.
analogy.limit: Use the actual code and checks rather than relying on the comparison.

Return the result and run the checks.

    return 0

def full_groups(amount, size):
    return amount // size

quiz.explanation: Floor division gives -3. The remainder is 1 because (-3)*3 + 1 equals -8.

hints: For a negative answer, // rounds toward smaller numbers. For example, -7 // 3 gives -3.

title: Stepped ranges and slices
summary: Complete select_steps to return a stepped slice without changing the original list.
explanation:
`range(start, stop, step)` describes whole numbers. `start` is the first number. `step` is how much to add each time. Stop before reaching `stop`.

If you leave out `start`, Python uses zero. If you leave out `step`, it uses one. A negative step moves toward smaller numbers.
`range` does not build a list of all its numbers. A loop can read them one at a time. The step must move toward the stopping point; otherwise there are no numbers to visit.

A slice values[start:stop:step] selects items using their positions. It uses the same step idea and leaves out stop. With a negative step, start and stop must describe the downward path you want. Leaving out both bounds in values[::-1] makes a new list in reverse order. The list itself is new, but it refers to the same items; the items are not copied. The original list stays unchanged.
Leave the supplied test helper unchanged. Complete `select_steps`, keeping the original list unchanged.
Use integers for the range's start, stop, and step. Integers are whole numbers. A step of zero is not allowed.
`list(range(...))` collects those numbers into a new list, in the same order.

```python
positions = list(range(1, 7, 2))
values = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]
print(positions)
print(values[1:7:2])
print(list(range(6, 0, -2)))
print(values[::-1])
```
This prints:
```text
[1, 3, 5]
['B', 'D', 'F']
[6, 4, 2]
['G', 'F', 'E', 'D', 'C', 'B', 'A']
```

Complete select_steps(values, start, stop, step): return the list slice values[start:stop:step]. Inputs are a list and integer bounds with a nonzero step. Leave the original list unchanged; the returned outer list is new. Empty input returns an empty list. A step pointing away from stop also returns an empty list.

analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.

quiz.explanation: Start at 2 and add 3 each time. 8 is included; the next value, 11, is past stop. 9 is left out.

hints: Use start, stop, and step in the slice you return.
The slice leaves out stop.
With a negative step, move downward toward stop.

title: Bounded exhaustive search
summary: Find a square's side length by trying allowed whole numbers.
explanation:
A bounded exhaustive search tries every possible answer within a fixed limit. Here, try every whole number from 0 through `limit`, including both ends.

`target` and `limit` are whole numbers of zero or greater. If no number matches, you only know there is no answer inside this range. An answer could exist beyond the limit.

A candidate is a possible answer. `find_square(target, limit)` returns the first candidate whose square equals `target`. To square a number, multiply it by itself.

`range(limit + 1)` gives the whole numbers from 0 through the limit. The extra 1 is needed because `range` leaves out its stopping number.

The multiplication does not change `target`. A `return` inside the loop ends the search when a match is found. The final `return None` is outside the loop, so it runs after all candidates have failed.

Imagine choosing a square garden whose area must match a requested number of tiles. A maximum side length limits the work. For target 16 and limit 3, the function must report None instead of searching beyond the allowed space.

Complete `find_square` for a target and limit that are whole numbers of zero or greater. Include both zero and the limit in your search.

Return the matching number, or `None` if none match. Do not return the last number you tried just because the loop ended.

analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.
analogy.limit: Use the actual code and checks rather than relying on the comparison.

Multiply each tried number by itself and compare it with `target`.
Return the number as soon as its square matches.

    return None

title: Bisection and a shrinking bracket
summary: Use bisection to estimate a square root by repeatedly halving a range that contains the answer.
explanation: Bisection repeatedly halves a range that contains the answer. This range is called a bracket. This lesson supports finite values from 0 through 1,000,000. Finite means a number with a limited size, excluding infinity and special “not a number” values. Use a positive finite width and a whole-number max_steps budget of 0 or more. The square root lies between 0 and max(1.0, value). Using 1 as the smallest upper bound matters when value is below 1.

Find the midpoint between low and high. If middle * middle is below value, the square root is above middle, so set low = middle. Otherwise, set high = middle. The range still contains the root. max(1.0, value) returns the larger number; it does not change either number.

Return the midpoint when high - low is at most width. Without rounding, its distance from the true root is at most half the range's width. Floating-point rounding can still affect the result. The max_steps budget limits the work when the requested width is too small to reach. Check the width again after the last allowed update. If the range is still too wide, return None. Raise ValueError for a negative value, a width of 0 or less, or a negative budget.

abs(number) gives the number's distance from 0. abs(answer - expected) measures how far apart two numbers are. This function gives an estimate, with no promise of an exact square root. It makes no accuracy promise for values outside the supported range or for numbers that are not finite.

Code breakdown:
```python
def bisect_sqrt(value, width=0.001, max_steps=100):
    if value < 0 or width <= 0 or max_steps < 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid bounds")
    low = 0.0
    high = max(1.0, value)
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        if high - low <= width:
            return (low + high) / 2
        middle = (low + high) / 2
        if middle * middle < value:
            low = middle
        else:
            high = middle
    if high - low <= width:
        return (low + high) / 2
    return None
answer = bisect_sqrt(0.25)
print(abs(answer - 0.5) <= 0.001)
print(bisect_sqrt(9, max_steps=0))
```
Output:
```text
True
None
```
The first answer is close enough to 0.5, so its check prints True. The second call allows no updates, and its starting range is too wide, so it returns None.

Complete bisect_sqrt using the shown starting range, width rule, and step budget. Support finite values from 0 through 1,000,000, a positive finite width, and a whole-number budget of 0 or more. Reject a negative value, a width of 0 or less, or a negative budget with ValueError. Return a midpoint only when the width rule is met. Leave __invalid_bounds_rejected unchanged. This supplied helper checks that three invalid inputs raise ValueError; your task is bisect_sqrt.

Otherwise, calculate middle = (low + high) / 2. Set low = middle if middle * middle < value; otherwise set high = middle.

title: Choosing tests from a specification
summary: Choose tests from the rule, especially values right at its boundary.
explanation:
The rule says people aged 18 or older may enter. Test one age below 18, age 18 itself, and one age above 18.

These three groups help you check where the answer changes.

At age 19, both `age > 18` and `age >= 18` give `True`. At age 18, they disagree.

Running a line of code is not enough. Your test must check whether it follows the rule.

`first_disagreement` tries a supplied function with three ages. It returns the first age where the answer is wrong. It returns `None` if all three answers match.

Each pair gives an age and its expected answer. Passing these tests does not prove the function works for every possible input.

```python
def entry_allowed(age):
    return age >= 18

def first_disagreement(candidate):
    for age, expected in [(17, False), (18, True), (19, True)]:
        if candidate(age) != expected:
            return age
    return None
def wrong_rule(age):
    return age > 18

print(first_disagreement(wrong_rule))
print(first_disagreement(entry_allowed))
print(entry_allowed(18))
```
Output:
```text
18
None
True
```
The test catches the missing equals sign at age 18.

Fix `entry_allowed` to include age 18. In `first_disagreement`, try the ages 17, 18, and 19 in that order.

Use the answers stated by the rule: `False`, `True`, `True`. Do not copy answers from the function you are testing.

analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.

Loop over the three supplied age-and-answer pairs.
Return the first age whose result differs from its expected answer.

title: Recursive calls and returning results
summary: Add list values with a function that calls itself.
explanation: Recursion means a function calls itself. This example sums a short list. The empty list is the stopping case, called the base case: it returns 0 without another call. Each nonempty call passes a shorter slice, so it moves toward that base case.

For [2, 5], the outer call remembers first = 2 while it waits for recursive_total([5]). That inner call remembers first = 5 while it waits for recursive_total([]). These local names belong to different calls. The inner first does not overwrite the outer first.

The empty call returns 0. The [5] call returns 5 + 0, which is 5. The [2, 5] call then returns 2 + 5, which is 7. If you call the function without using its returned value, you lose the partial result.

values[1:] makes a shorter list copy. This makes the trace clear, but it adds copying work and memory. Python also limits how deep recursive calls can go. Use this function for small lists in the exercise. Do not use it as a replacement for a loop or sum on large data.

```python
def recursive_total(values):
    if not values:
        return 0
    first = values[0]
    rest_total = recursive_total(values[1:])
    return first + rest_total
print(recursive_total([2, 5]))
print(recursive_total([]))
```
The outputs are 7 and 0; the empty case ends the chain.

summary: Let two Tag objects compare equal when their text matches.

Two separate `Tag` objects can hold matching text. We can make `==` use `__eq__` to compare that text.

`is` still asks whether the objects are the very same one. Changing the rule for `==` does not change this identity check.

`__eq__(self, other)` receives the other value to compare. `isinstance(other, Tag)` checks whether it is a `Tag`.

For other kinds of values, return `NotImplemented`. This tells Python to try the other value's comparison rule.

`NotImplemented` is a special value to return. It is different from raising the error `NotImplementedError`.

If neither value knows how to compare with the other, `==` checks whether they are the same object.

Dictionary keys also need a hash: a number Python uses to help find a key. The next lesson explains this. Do not add a made-up hash just to hide an error.

class Tag:
    def __init__(self, text):

    def __eq__(self, other):

        return self.text == other.text

right = Tag("music")

title: Growth rates and logarithmic halving
summary: Count four kinds of work and see how they grow when the input gets bigger.
explanation:
Here, `n` is the input size. We count simple loop actions and treat each small-integer operation as one unit of work.

Big O gives an upper growth limit. `O(n)` means that, for large inputs, the work is at most a fixed number times `n`. It does not give an exact step count or running time.

Theta (`Θ`) describes a matching growth rate. `Θ(n)` means the work grows roughly in proportion to `n` for large inputs. Fixed starting costs and smaller terms do not decide these growth labels.

A loop that visits n items counts n events. Put a full n-item loop inside another and they count n*n ordered pairs, including pairs where the two indices are equal. Doubling n doubles the first count but makes the pair count four times larger. This differs from a nested loop where the inner loop's limit changes with the outer index.

Repeatedly dividing a whole number by 2 reaches 1 in about `log2(n)` steps. `log2(n)` asks which power of 2 gives `n`. For 8, the answer is 3 because `2 × 2 × 2 = 8`.

Our loop takes the whole-number part of that answer: 7 takes 2 halvings, and 8 takes 3. Doubling a positive power of two adds one halving.

`remaining //= 2` divides by 2 and keeps the floor-divided whole number. Using `/` would give a float. Both 0 and 1 need no halvings.

growth_counts accepts a nonnegative integer n and returns (fixed, linear, pairs, halvings). range(n) gives integers from zero through n-1, so it makes n loop visits and is empty when n is zero. The fixed marker counts one chosen setup event, not every setup instruction.
```python
def growth_counts(n):
    fixed = 1
    linear = 0
    pairs = 0
    for i in range(n):
        linear += 1
        for j in range(n):
            pairs += 1
    halvings = 0
    remaining = n
    while remaining > 1:
        remaining //= 2
        halvings += 1
    return fixed, linear, pairs, halvings
print(growth_counts(4))
print(growth_counts(8))
```
The calls print (1, 4, 16, 2) and (1, 8, 64, 3). For positive n, the halving count is floor(log2(n)), meaning the whole-number part of log2(n). The loop computes it without a logarithm function.

Build the four counters for inputs from 0 through 64. Their names describe how they grow for larger inputs:

Constant work stays about the same. Linear work grows with `n`. Quadratic work grows with `n × n`. Logarithmic work grows like the halving count.

These are growth rules, not promises about seconds. Actual time also depends on Python, the computer, and the values used.

For extra practice, compare 7 and 8. Explain why reaching a power of two adds one halving.

title: Binary search in a sorted sequence
summary: Find an item by repeatedly halving a sorted list's search range.
explanation:
Binary search needs data already sorted from smallest to largest. It keeps a search range from `low` through `high`, including both ends.

If the target is present, a matching position must stay inside this range. Sorting is a separate job with its own work. `binary_find` does not sort the list or check every item to confirm the order.

mid = (low + high) // 2 picks the middle index using integer floor division. If values[mid] equals target, return it. If it is smaller, sorted order rules out every position through mid, so set low to mid + 1. Otherwise set high to mid - 1. Leaving out mid makes progress; keeping mid again can cause an infinite loop.

binary_find receives an ascending sorted integer list and an integer target. It returns (matching_index, probes), or (None, probes). A probe is one look at a middle position. It is not the same as one comparison: the code may use both `==` and `<` on that item. len(values) gives the item count, and high is the last valid index.
```python
def binary_find(values, target):
    low = 0
    high = len(values) - 1
    probes = 0
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        probes += 1
        if values[mid] == target:
            return mid, probes
        if values[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return None, probes
print(binary_find([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], 8))
print(binary_find([], 8))
```
Expected output:
```text
(3, 2)
(None, 0)
```
For the first call, index 2 contains 6; the remaining interval is indices 3..4, whose middle is 3. The empty list starts with high = -1 and never indexes it.

With duplicates, any matching index is acceptable; this is not a first-match search. Each unsuccessful probe removes at least about half the candidate positions, so worst-case probes grow slowly as the interval halves. The function uses indices instead of copying slices. Unsorted input breaks the reasoning, even if one particular search accidentally succeeds.

title: Insertion sort and a sorted prefix
summary: Sort records by priority, keep ties in order, and count moves to the right.
explanation: Insertion sort keeps the positions before i sorted. Then it inserts the next item into that part of the list. Each record is a tuple: (integer priority, text label). Only the priority decides the order. The label helps us see which equal-priority record came first. result[j][0] reads the priority from the record at index j.

Save the current item. Move earlier records with larger priorities one place right, then fill the gap. Check j >= 0 before indexing because and stops early if that check is false. Use >, not >=, so an earlier record with the same priority stays first. Keeping equal-priority records in their original order is called stability.

insertion_sort takes a list of these tuples and returns (new_sorted_list, shifts). records.copy() makes a new list, so rearranging it does not reorder the source. A shift counts one assignment that moves an earlier record right. Final placement is not counted. len(result) gives the copied list's number of items. range(1, len(result)) visits index 1 through the last index. The first item alone is already in order, so start with the next one.
```python
def insertion_sort(records):
    result = records.copy()
    shifts = 0
    for i in range(1, len(result)):
        item = result[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and result[j][0] > item[0]:
            result[j + 1] = result[j]
            shifts += 1
            j -= 1
        result[j + 1] = item
    return result, shifts
source = [(2, "A"), (1, "B"), (2, "C")]
print(insertion_sort(source))
print(source)
```
It prints ([(1, 'B'), (2, 'A'), (2, 'C')], 1), then the original list. Equal-priority A and C keep their order.

An already sorted list needs zero shifts, but the algorithm still checks each next item. A reverse-sorted list with distinct priorities needs 1+2+...+(n-1) shifts. This count grows quadratically. It does not include the initial copy or all comparisons. The function uses extra storage and does not sort the source list in place.

title: Merging two sorted sequences
summary: Merge two sorted lists into one new list, keeping every repeated value.
explanation:
Merging combines two lists already sorted from smallest to largest. Compare their next unused values, add the smaller one to the result, and move forward only in that list.

Keep repeats. This method does the ordering as it goes; it does not join the lists and sort them afterward.

When the next values tie, use `<=` to choose the left one first. Each repeat uses one value, and both positions move only forward.

Once one list runs out, add all the unused values from the other list. They are already sorted, so they need no more value comparisons.

merge takes two ascending sorted integer lists and returns a new list. It changes neither input. append(value) adds one value to result and returns None. extend adds every supplied element and returns None; use it as a statement, not as a new list value. left[i:] is a slice from i through the end, and is empty if i equals len(left). len gives the bounds.
```python
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = 0
    j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result
print(merge([1, 4, 4], [2, 4, 8]))
print(merge([], [3, 5]))
```
Output:
```text
[1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 8]
[3, 5]
```
Every input item appears once in the output, including each repeated value.

If the lengths are a and b, all a+b values must be copied to the result. The comparison loop makes at most a+b-1 value comparisons when both inputs are nonempty; an empty side needs none. The whole merge grows in a straight line with a+b when comparing integers costs the same each time. The slices also copy remaining values, so do not call it a no-copy merge.
