Workshop bookings
RoomSpring
MayJune
Studio85

checks.label: Data cites all relevant headers
checks.expression: document.querySelector('tbody td').getAttribute('headers')==='studio season may' && document.querySelectorAll('tbody td')[1].getAttribute('headers')==='studio season june'

quiz.question: The value under May has headers="studio season june". Is its month label correct?
choices: Yes. Its position overrides the list.
No. The list points to June.
quiz.explanation: The headers list names the connected headings. It must match the meaning of the value, not just contain real ids.

hints: Put spaces between ids in headers; do not add # signs.
Each header id must appear only once.
The cell under May must list may, not june.

title: Choose exactly one radio option
summary: Let someone choose one visit time from a pair of radio buttons.
explanation: A radio button is a round choice control. Radio buttons with the same `name` in one form belong to one group. Choosing one turns the other off. Use them when someone should choose at most one answer.

Each radio button needs its own `id` and label, but both share a `name`. `value` says what the choice sends. `checked` chooses a starting option. `required` asks the person to choose; it does not choose for them.

This form starts with Early visit selected.

```html
<form id="visit">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Choose a visit time</legend>
    <input type="radio" id="early" name="slot" value="early" required checked><label for="early">Early visit</label>
    <input type="radio" id="late" name="slot" value="late" required><label for="late">Late visit</label>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Request time</button>
</form>
```

The fieldset and legend name the question. Both radios use `name="slot"`. The checked radio sends `slot=early`. If someone chooses Late visit, the form sends `slot=late` instead.

Build the shown form inside main. Use form id `visit`, radio ids `early` and `late`, and the shared name `slot`. Add both labels and the legend `Choose a visit time`. Require both radios and start with Early visit checked. Run the checks, then try choosing Late visit.
steps: Add a form with id visit and a named fieldset.
Add both labeled radios with the shared name slot.
Require both, check Early visit by default and run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Practice</title></head>
<body>
<form id="visit">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Choose a visit time</legend>
    <input type="radio" id="early" name="slot" value="early" required checked><label for="early">Early visit</label>
    <input type="radio" id="late" name="slot" value="late" required><label for="late">Late visit</label>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Request time</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

checks.label: Two radio controls share a submitted name
Labels and group name are present
Group requires a selection and starts early

quiz.question: You remove checked but keep required. Which radio starts selected?
choices: Neither. The person must choose one.
The first one is selected automatically.
quiz.explanation: `required` asks for a choice. Only `checked` sets a starting selection in this example.

hints: The ids differ: early and late. The name stays slot on both.
Only Early visit gets the checked attribute.
Keep the radio values early and late.

title: Write a multiline answer
summary: Make a text box that can hold several lines.
explanation: `<textarea>` is a field for several lines of text. Put its starting text between the opening and closing tags. Give it a label so the person knows what to write.

`rows="4"` asks for a box about four text lines tall. It does not limit the answer to four lines. `maxlength="80"` limits the length of a typed answer. It counts text units: ordinary English letters use one each, but some symbols, such as emoji, use more.

This field starts with a short observation.

```html
<form>
  <label for="note">Observation</label>
  <textarea id="note" name="note" rows="4" maxlength="80">Saw two moths.</textarea>
  <button type="submit">Send observation</button>
</form>
```

The label points to `id="note"`. `name="note"` names the sent value. `rows` sets the height and `maxlength` sets the text limit. `Saw two moths.` is inside the tags, so it is the starting text.

Add the shown field inside main. Use id and name `note`, four rows, and maxlength `80`. Put exactly `Saw two moths.` between its tags. Do not use a `value` attribute for the starting text. Add its label, then run the checks.
steps: Add a label and textarea with matching ids.
Set rows to 4 and maxlength to 80.
Put the starting text between the tags and run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Practice</title></head>
<body>
<form>
  <label for="note">Observation</label>
  <textarea id="note" name="note" rows="4" maxlength="80">Saw two moths.</textarea>
  <button type="submit">Send observation</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

quiz.question: You change rows from 4 to 8. Does that double the text limit?
choices: It replaces the starting text with blank lines.
Yes, the box can now store twice as much.
No. The box is taller, but maxlength stays 80.
quiz.explanation: Height and text length are separate settings.

hints: Use `<textarea>`, not a text input.
The starting sentence goes before `</textarea>`, with no extra line breaks.
Changing rows does not change maxlength.

title: Constrain a numeric answer
summary: Set the allowed range and size of each step in a number field.
explanation: `type="number"` makes a number field. You can set the smallest and largest allowed numbers. You can also choose the gap between allowed values.

`min="0"` and `max="2"` allow values from 0 to 2, including both ends. With `step="0.25"`, the allowed values start at 0 and go up by a quarter: 0, 0.25, 0.5, and so on. A number can be inside the range but still miss those steps.

This field asks for a mass in grams. ```html

Enter 0 to 2 grams in quarter-gram steps.

``` `value="0.5"` sets the starting number. `required` stops an empty answer. `aria-describedby` connects the field to the help paragraph. The help explains the same range and steps as the input settings.

Build the shown mass field with its label and help paragraph. Keep the starting value `0.5`, range 0 to 2, and step `0.25`. Run the checks. Then try an empty entry, `0`, `0.6` and `2`: empty is missing, 0.6 misses a quarter step, and 0 and 2 are allowed.
steps: Add the labeled number input with min 0, max 2 and step 0.25.
Set value 0.5 and required, then connect the mass-help paragraph.
Run the checks and try the four entries from the task.
starter: Practice
solution: Enter 0 to 2 grams in quarter-gram steps.

quiz.question: You change step to 1 and keep min at 0. Is 0.5 still an allowed step?
choices: Yes, every number between 0 and 2 is allowed.
Yes, the starting value changes the minimum.
No. The allowed steps are now 0, 1 and 2.
quiz.explanation: With a minimum of 0 and steps of 1, only whole-number steps fit. A starting value can still break that rule.

hints: Keep id and name as mass.
Use `aria-describedby="mass-help"` and `id="mass-help"` on the help paragraph.
Zero is a number; it is not an empty entry.

title: Keep a value readable without disabling its submission
summary: Learn which uneditable fields still send a value.
explanation: A text input with `readonly` can be read but not edited normally. If it has a name, its value is still sent with the form. Use this when someone needs to see a value without changing it.

`disabled` does a different job. It turns off ordinary interaction with the field and leaves its value out of the form data. To turn either setting off, remove the attribute; adding the word `false` does not turn it off.

This form has three kinds of stored value.

```html
<form id="booking">
  <label for="reference">Booking reference</label><input id="reference" name="reference" value="R17" readonly>
  <label for="estimate">Draft estimate</label><input id="estimate" name="estimate" value="12" disabled>
  <input type="hidden" name="revision" value="2">
  <button type="submit">Confirm</button>
</form>
```

The readonly reference sends `reference=R17`. The disabled estimate is left out. `type="hidden"` stores `revision=2` without a visible field. Hidden values are still readable and changeable through browser tools, so they are not a safe place for secrets.

Build the shown form with id `booking`. Keep the reference labeled, named and readonly. Keep the estimate labeled, named and disabled. Add the hidden revision with value `2`. Run the checks to see which values are included. No data is sent to a service.
steps: Add the readonly reference with value R17.
Add the disabled estimate with value 12 and the hidden revision with value 2.
Keep the visible labels and run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Practice</title></head>
<body>
<form id="booking">
  <label for="reference">Booking reference</label><input id="reference" name="reference" value="R17" readonly>
  <label for="estimate">Draft estimate</label><input id="estimate" name="estimate" value="12" disabled>
  <input type="hidden" name="revision" value="2">
  <button type="submit">Confirm</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

quiz.question: You replace readonly with disabled on the reference field. What happens to its form data?
choices: It is left out, even though the value is still visible.
It is still sent because it has a name.
quiz.explanation: A disabled field is left out. A readonly text field can still send its named value.

hints: Use readonly on reference and disabled on estimate.
The hidden input still needs `name="revision"`.
Put all three inputs inside form#booking.

title: Submit several choices under one name
summary: Let someone choose several items from one list.
explanation: Add `multiple` to a `<select>` to allow more than one choice. Each selected option sends its own value under the select’s name. The browser does not turn them into one comma-separated answer.

`<optgroup>` puts related options under a group label. The group label is not a choice. Add `selected` to each option you want chosen at the start. `size="4"` asks for four visible rows; it does not limit how many choices can be selected.

This list groups seeds into Herbs and Flowers.

```html
<form id="seeds">
  <label for="choices">Seeds to request</label>
  <select id="choices" name="seed" multiple size="4">
    <optgroup label="Herbs"><option value="basil" selected>Basil</option><option value="dill">Dill</option></optgroup>
    <optgroup label="Flowers"><option value="poppy" selected>Poppy</option></optgroup>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Request seeds</button>
</form>
```

The select has the name `seed`. Basil and Poppy start selected, so the data contains `seed=basil` and `seed=poppy`. Dill is not selected, so it is left out.

Build form `seeds` with the labeled select `choices`. Use name `seed`, `multiple` and size `4`. Add the Herbs group with Basil and Dill, then the Flowers group with Poppy. Start with Basil and Poppy selected. Run the checks and try changing the choices; selection controls can differ between keyboards and touch screens.
steps: Add the labeled multiple select inside form#seeds.
Add the Herbs and Flowers groups with their options.
Select Basil and Poppy by default, then run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Practice</title></head>
<body>
<form id="seeds">
  <label for="choices">Seeds to request</label>
  <select id="choices" name="seed" multiple size="4">
    <optgroup label="Herbs"><option value="basil" selected>Basil</option><option value="dill">Dill</option></optgroup>
    <optgroup label="Flowers"><option value="poppy" selected>Poppy</option></optgroup>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Request seeds</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

quiz.question: You remove selected from Poppy. Which seed value is chosen at the start?
choices: The group names Herbs and Flowers.
quiz.explanation: Only selected options contribute values. A group label is not an option.

hints: Put `name="seed"` on select, not on the options.
Use lowercase values basil, dill and poppy.
Only Basil and Poppy get selected.

title: Choose a local file without uploading it
summary: Add a file chooser and understand what it does before upload.
explanation: `type="file"` makes a file chooser. It lets a person pick a file from their device. In this form, choosing a file does not upload it. Uploading would happen when the form sends it to a receiving service.
`multiple` allows several files. `accept="image/png,image/jpeg"` suggests PNG and JPEG pictures in the chooser. It is a hint, not proof that the chosen files are valid pictures.

This form is set up to send chosen photos. ```html

Choose PNG or JPEG photos you intend to share. Selection alone does not upload them.

``` `name="photos"` names the file field. `method="post"` chooses how to send it. `enctype="multipart/form-data"` tells the browser to package the files and other values together. `action` names the receiving address. This practice does not include that service.

Build the shown form and labeled photos input. Keep the file optional, allow multiple files, and add the exact accept value. Connect the help paragraph with `aria-describedby`. Do not add a file path in a `value` attribute: a page cannot choose a local file that way. Run the checks; you do not need to choose or send any files.
steps: Add the form with the shown action, method and enctype.
Add the labeled photos input with accept and multiple.
Add the connected help text and run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution: Choose PNG or JPEG photos you intend to share. Selection alone does not upload them.

checks.label: File choice has a visible label

quiz.question: Does accept="image/png" prove that every received file is a valid PNG picture?
choices: No. It guides the chooser; the receiving service still needs to check files.
Yes. It checks files on the receiving service.
Yes. It turns every file into a PNG.
quiz.explanation: `accept` suggests file types. It does not inspect every received file or convert its contents.

hints: Use `accept="image/png,image/jpeg"`.
Use `enctype="multipart/form-data"` on form.
Leave out required and value on the file input.

title: Identify the button that submitted a form
summary: Give two submit buttons different jobs.
explanation: A form can have more than one submit button. The button someone uses is called the submitter. Its own name and value can tell the receiving service which action was chosen.

A submit button can sit outside a form. Give it `form="draft"` to connect it to the form with `id="draft"`. Its `formaction` and `formmethod` can choose a different destination and method for that button only.

This form offers Save draft and Preview draft.

```html
<form id="draft" action="/save" method="post">
  <label for="title">Draft title</label><input id="title" name="title" value="Pond notes">
  <button id="save" type="submit" name="intent" value="save">Save draft</button>
</form>
<button id="preview" type="submit" form="draft" name="intent" value="preview" formaction="/preview" formmethod="get">Preview draft</button>
```

Save uses the form’s POST request to `/save` and adds `intent=save`. Preview uses GET to `/preview` and adds `intent=preview`. The other button’s value is left out. The form’s own settings stay the same.

Build the shown form with its labeled title and Save button. Put Preview after `</form>`, then connect it with `form="draft"`. Add its preview settings and run the checks. The practice checks these connections without sending anything; it does not include working save or preview services.
steps: Build form#draft with its title field and Save button.
Add Preview outside the form and connect it with form="draft".
Add the two intent values and Preview’s overrides, then run the checks.
starter: Practice
solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Practice</title></head>
<body>
<form id="draft" action="/save" method="post">
  <label for="title">Draft title</label><input id="title" name="title" value="Pond notes">
  <button id="save" type="submit" name="intent" value="save">Save draft</button>
</form>
<button id="preview" type="submit" form="draft" name="intent" value="preview" formaction="/preview" formmethod="get">Preview draft</button>
</body>
</html>

checks.label: Outside button belongs to the form

quiz.question: You remove form="draft" from Preview, which is outside the form. Is it still connected to that form?
choices: No. Its name and value do not connect it.
Yes, the shared name intent connects it.
quiz.explanation: An outside button needs the form attribute to identify its form. Its name describes sent data, not that connection.

hints: Save and Preview both use `name="intent"`, but their values differ.
Keep the form’s action as /save and method as post.
Only Preview gets formaction="/preview" and formmethod="get".

title: Help a browser fill the intended field
summary: Tell the browser what an email field is for.
explanation: `autocomplete="email"` tells the browser that this field asks for an email address. The browser may offer an address the person has saved. Their settings can turn that help off.
`inputmode="email"` suggests an email-friendly keyboard, often with an easy-to-reach `@` key. It does not check the answer. `type="email"` is the setting that asks for an email-shaped value.

This field gives each setting its own job.

```html
<form>
<label for="contact">Contact email</label>
<input id="contact" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" inputmode="email">
</form>
```

The label points to `contact`. `name` names the sent value. `type` checks the shape, `autocomplete` identifies the purpose, and `inputmode` suggests a keyboard.
If you change only `type="email"` to `type="text"`, the field stops using the email type check. The autofill and keyboard hints do not replace that check.

Build the labeled contact field shown in the example. Keep `type`, `autocomplete` and `inputmode` all set to `email`. Run the checks. A browser may choose not to show saved addresses or a different keyboard.
steps: Add the Contact email label and matching input id.
Add name="email" and all three email settings.
starter: <!-- Complete the described markup here. -->
solution:
<form>
<label for="contact">Contact email</label>
<input id="contact" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" inputmode="email">
</form>

checks.label: Email type and keyboard hint remain separate

quiz.question: A field has type="text" and inputmode="email". Does the keyboard hint check email syntax?
choices: No. The keyboard and autofill hints do not check it.
quiz.explanation: The hints help with typing. The email type supplies the email-shape check.

hints: Use id="contact" and label for="contact".
The three settings are type, autocomplete and inputmode.

title: Explain and correct a validation failure
summary: Tell someone exactly how to fix an incorrect form entry.
explanation: `pattern` sets a text rule for an input. Here, `[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{2}` means two uppercase English letters followed by two digits. The whole nonempty entry must match. `required` separately stops the field being left blank.

`aria-invalid="true"` tells assistive tools that the field has an error. It does not check the value itself. `aria-describedby` connects the field to text that explains the rule and how to fix the mistake.

This example shows a field with a known mistake. ```html

Use two uppercase letters followed by two digits, such as AB12.

The entered code has lowercase letters. Change them to uppercase.

``` `ab12` has lowercase letters, so it does not match the pattern. `code-help` explains the rule. `code-error` tells the person to change the letters to uppercase. The field points to both messages.

When the person corrects the value to `AB12`, the feedback should change too. Set `aria-invalid` to false or remove it, and remove or update the old error message. HTML alone does not keep that message up to date; a later JavaScript lesson can add that behavior.

Build the shown error example. Keep the starting value `ab12`, the exact pattern, and `required`. Add the label, help and error paragraphs. Connect both paragraph ids with `aria-describedby="code-help code-error"`. Run the checks. This task deliberately starts with an incorrect entry so you can practise helpful feedback.
steps: Add the labeled required input and its exact pattern.
Keep ab12 as the starting value and mark the known error.
Add the linked help and correction messages, then run the checks.
starter: <!-- Complete the described markup here. -->
solution:
Use two uppercase letters followed by two digits, such as AB12.

The entered code has lowercase letters. Change them to uppercase.

quiz.question: You set aria-invalid to false, but the value is still ab12. Does it now match the uppercase pattern?
choices: No. The letters are still lowercase.
Yes. That setting removes the text rule.
Yes. The help message changes the letters.
quiz.explanation: The pattern checks the actual text. Error feedback must describe that text accurately.

hints: The pattern is `[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{2}`.
The error message should tell the person to use uppercase letters.
Changing aria-invalid alone does not fix the typed value.

title: Reserve image space before loading
summary: Tell the browser how much space an image needs before it loads.
explanation: An image’s `width` and `height` help the browser leave space before the picture loads. The supplied ridge picture is 640 pixels wide and 320 tall. That makes it twice as wide as it is tall.
`loading="lazy"` lets the browser wait to load a picture that is far down the page. It can save loading work. Use it for a later picture, not the main picture people need to see straight away.

This example reserves the ridge picture’s shape. ```html ``` `src` names the supplied picture. `alt` describes it. `width` and `height` give its size and shape. `loading="lazy"` requests later loading when appropriate.
Changing lazy to eager asks for normal immediate loading. It does not change width or height. When the image loads and how much space it needs are separate settings.

Add the shown ridge image as a later picture on the page. Keep its width at 640, height at 320, and the exact alt text. Set loading to lazy and run the checks. To view the downloaded picture, keep the supplied SVG file beside the HTML file.
steps: Add the description and 640 by 320 dimensions.
Request lazy loading and run the checks.
starter: <!-- Complete the described markup here. -->

quiz.question: You change lazy to eager. Does that remove the image’s width-to-height shape?
choices: Yes. Eager removes the reserved space.
No. Width and height still give the same shape.
quiz.explanation: The loading setting does not change the width and height attributes.

hints: Use plain numbers in width and height, without px.
Keep the exact description: A dark green triangular ridge.

title: Load a script at a predictable stage
summary: Wait until the page is ready before a script changes its text.
explanation: The browser reads HTML to build the page. An outside script with `defer` downloads while that happens, then runs after the HTML has been read. This lets the script find elements that appear later in the file. Deferred ordinary scripts also run in their document order.

This is `index.html`, one of the two files in this example. ```html Deferred script study

Waiting for the script.

``` `src="stage.js"` names the JavaScript file. `defer` makes it wait until the page’s HTML has been read. The paragraph’s `id="stage"` gives the script a place to find. Keep both files in the same folder.

This is the matching `stage.js` file.

```javascript
document.getElementById("stage").textContent = "The paragraph was parsed before this deferred script ran.";
```

`document.getElementById("stage")` finds the paragraph. `textContent` is its text. The `=` replaces that text with the new sentence. This is the same example’s script, not a second task. CodeQuest removes scripts from HTML previews, so try these two files in a separate browser page if you want to run them.

`async` means the script can run as soon as it is ready. If you replace defer with async, the script might run before the paragraph exists and fail to find it. It may also succeed on some loads. One successful load does not mean the timing is guaranteed.

`type="module"` marks a JavaScript module: a script that can share code through imports and exports. Modules normally wait until the HTML has been read too, but follow different loading rules. This example uses an ordinary external script, so keep defer. Defer does not delay an ordinary script written directly inside its script tag.

quiz.explanation: Async runs when ready. Defer waits until the HTML has been read.

title: Distinguish progress from a bounded measurement
summary: Show work completed separately from space used.
explanation:
`<progress>` shows how much of a task is done.

```html
<label for="done">Chapters reviewed</label>
<progress id="done" value="3" max="8">3 of 8</progress>
```

`value="3"` means three chapters are done. `max="8"` is the total. The label tells us what is being counted.
If you leave out progress’s `value`, the amount done is unknown. That is different from zero. Update any matching text to say the progress is unknown too, so it does not claim an exact amount.

`<meter>` shows a measurement within a range, rather than task completion.

```html
<label for="space">Notebook space used</label>
<meter id="space" min="0" max="100" low="20" high="80" optimum="10" value="90">90 percent</meter>
```

The range goes from 0 to 100. `value="90"` means 90 percent of the notebook space is used. The label tells us what is measured.

In this meter, low and high mark the range’s lower and upper regions. `optimum="10"` marks a preferred value near the low end: using less space is better here. The current value, 90, is above high=80. Browser colors can differ, so keep clear words as well.

title: Linear gradients
summary: Blend one background color into another in a chosen direction.
explanation: A gradient is a gradual change between colors. `linear-gradient()` makes that change along a straight line. The browser creates the picture from CSS; you do not need an image file.

Inside `linear-gradient()`, commas separate the direction and color stops. A color stop gives a color and its place along the gradient. `navy 0%` puts navy at the start. `teal 100%` puts teal at the end.
Changing `to right` to `to bottom` makes the blend run downward. The endpoint colors stay the same. Use `to right` for this project.
Treat the gradient as decoration. Keep the label’s solid backing so the words stay easy to read across the whole banner. Do not use a color change as the only way to explain important information.
Check that the banner starts navy on the left and ends teal on the right. Keep the label’s white text and black backing, then run the checks.

Blend from navy at 0% to teal at 100%, toward the right.
Keep the label’s backing and run the checks.

quiz.explanation: The direction is separate from the colors.

hints: The direction comes first inside `linear-gradient()`. A comma separates it from the first color stop.

title: Borders versus shadows
summary: See why a border takes up space but a shadow does not.
explanation: A border is part of the element’s box. A shadow is a visual effect painted around it. The shadow does not reserve extra room in the page layout.

A shadow can cover nearby content because it does not make space for itself. Add real spacing, such as margin, when nearby parts need room.

title: Collapsing block margins
summary: See why two touching block margins can become one gap.
explanation: Collapsing margins means two margins join into one gap. This can happen between ordinary blocks stacked vertically. When both margins are positive, the gap uses the larger value instead of adding them.

The first block’s bottom margin meets the second block’s top margin. They collapse because this is ordinary block layout. `flow-root` keeps the group’s layout separate from its surroundings, but does not stop these sibling margins from collapsing.
If the first margin becomes 8 pixels, the second margin is now larger. The resulting gap would be 16 pixels. In this example, compare the two positive values and take the larger one.

This lesson uses horizontal writing and ordinary block siblings. Flex and grid item margins do not collapse this way. Negative margins also need different arithmetic. Do not apply the larger-value rule to every kind of spacing.
Set the first bottom margin to 24 pixels and the second top margin to 16 pixels. Inspect the gap in the preview. It should be 24 pixels, not 40.
steps: Set the first block’s bottom margin to 24px.
Set the second block’s top margin to 16px.
Run the checks and inspect the 24-pixel gap.
starter:
.demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; }
.stack { display: flow-root; } .first, .second { height: 20px; } .first { margin-bottom: 0px; } .second { margin-top: 0px; }
solution:
.demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; }
.stack { display: flow-root; } .first, .second { height: 20px; } .first { margin-bottom: 24px; } .second { margin-top: 16px; }

quiz.question: In this same layout, a 12px bottom margin meets a 20px top margin. What is the gap?
quiz.explanation: The margins collapse. The larger positive value is 20 pixels.

hints: For these two positive, collapsing margins, the larger value sets the gap.

title: Float wrapping and flow-root
summary: Let text wrap beside a map, then start the next section below it.
explanation: A float is a box that sits to one side while nearby text wraps beside it. This can be useful for a small picture inside a story.
`display: flow-root` goes on the parent story. It creates a separate block layout area that includes its floats when the parent’s height is worked out. That helps the story box surround the map.
`clear: left` makes the next section start below earlier left floats. If the map grows taller, the cleared section moves farther down. It stays below the map.

Use a float for a picture with text flowing around it. Flex or grid is usually a clearer choice for larger page layouts. Here, `left` means the physical left side; it does not switch automatically for right-to-left writing.
Float the map left, put `flow-root` on the story, and clear the next section. Check that the first text sits beside the map and the next section begins below it.

quiz.explanation: `clear: left` moves the next section below earlier floats on the left.

hints: The float belongs on the map. `flow-root` belongs on its parent. `clear` belongs on the part that must start below it.

title: Intrinsic sizing
summary: Let a label’s content help decide its width.
explanation: An intrinsic size is a size worked out from the content. `min-content` uses the narrowest width allowed by normal wrapping. `max-content` uses the width the content needs without wrapping at ordinary spaces.
Here, `fit-content` is a keyword, so it has no parentheses. The spaces between words are places where the text can wrap. The longest unbreakable word limits how narrow the label can become.
With `max-content`, the label would request enough width for all its words on one line. In this example, that would exceed the 100-pixel wrapper.

`fit-content` does not guarantee that all content will fit. One long word with no allowed break may still need more width than the wrapper has. This lesson uses the width keyword, not the separate grid function with the same name.
Keep the wrapper 100 pixels wide and set the label’s width to `fit-content`. Keep its words unchanged. Run the checks and inspect where the words wrap.

It removes spaces from the text.
quiz.explanation: A word that cannot break may need more room than the wrapper provides.

hints: Use the keyword `fit-content` without parentheses for this width setting.

title: Fitting replaced images
summary: Fit a whole picture inside a square without stretching it.
explanation: An image has its own contents and an element box around them. `object-fit` chooses how the picture fits inside that box. `contain` shows the whole picture. `cover` fills the box but can cut off part of the picture.
The supplied picture is twice as wide as it is tall. `contain` keeps that proportion, so the picture is not stretched into a square. `object-position: center` centers the picture inside the box.
With `cover`, this wide picture would fill the square and lose parts at the sides. The element box would still be 100 by 100 pixels. The change affects how the picture fits inside it.

Use `contain` when the whole diagram or picture matters. Use `cover` when a crop is acceptable. Neither setting changes the image’s `alt` text, which gives a written replacement for its useful information.

title: Relative offsets preserve space
summary: Move a box visually while leaving its original space in the layout.
explanation: Relative positioning moves a box away from where it would normally appear. The page still keeps its original space in normal flow, the usual layout order.
With `position: relative`, a positive `top` value moves the box downward from its normal position. It is an offset, or shift. It is not a margin, so it does not push the next box down.
Changing `top` to `24px` would move the first box farther down. The second box would still stay in its original place. The overlap between them could grow.
Use relative offsets for small visual adjustments. If the next part should move too, use real layout spacing such as margin. Always check that shifted content does not cover something important.

choices: Real layout spacing, such as margin.
quiz.explanation: A relative offset moves the visible box but leaves its original layout space in place.

hints: A positive `top` offset moves a relatively positioned box down. It does not add space before the next box.

title: Flex cross-axis alignment
summary: Line up a row of items, then move one item to a different edge.
explanation: Flexbox has a main axis, the direction items are arranged, and a cross axis at a right angle to it. `align-items` lines items up on the cross axis. `align-self` changes that alignment for one item.

If the direction changes to `column`, the main axis becomes vertical here. The cross axis becomes horizontal. The same alignment settings would center the first item left to right and place the second at the right edge.
Alignment follows the axes, so `align-items` does not always mean vertical alignment. First check the flex direction and the writing direction. Then decide where the cross axis starts and ends.
