summary: Reuse an object's required fields and add another one.
explanation: An interface describes an object's shape. Extends lets one interface keep another interface's requirements and add more. It does not copy actual data or create objects.
Leaving out title still causes an error. An extending interface also cannot replace a required text title with an incompatible numeric title.
Define NamedRecord with a string title. Extend it with a numeric score in ScoredRecord. Make scoredLabel return the title, a colon and space, then the score.
steps: Return the label and run the checks.

quiz.question: Why is a TimedItem with minutes but no title rejected?
choices: The parent's title is still required
quiz.explanation: Extending adds requirements while keeping the existing ones.

hints: The extended interface requires the original field as well as its new field.

typeAssertions.label: Extended value satisfies parent
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; const s:ScoredRecord={title:"A",score:2};const n:NamedRecord=s;const title:string=n.title;const score:number=s.score;type T=Assert<IsAny<ScoredRecord["title"]> extends false?true:false>;type S=Assert<IsAny<ScoredRecord["score"]> extends false?true:false>;

title: Require both object shapes
summary: Require an object to have both sets of properties.
explanation: An intersection joins types with `&`, meaning and. The value must meet both types. This combines the requirements; it does not copy or join objects while the program runs.
If the count is 0, the same function includes 0 in its result. Leaving count out is different: the object would be missing a required property.
Make Box require a text label and a numeric items value. Make boxText return the label, a colon and space, then items. Read the object without changing it.
steps: Make boxText read the label and items.
Return the text and run the checks.

quiz.question: Stock needs Named and Counted. What happens if an object has a name but no count?
choices: TypeScript rejects it because count is missing
The intersection adds a count of zero
It is accepted because one field is enough
quiz.explanation: Both requirements must be met. The type does not invent the missing count.

hints: An intersection requires both shapes. It does not supply missing values.

title: Use the fields a function needs
summary: Accept an object that has the fields a function needs.
explanation: TypeScript usually compares objects by their structure. A named object can fit a smaller type if it has the required fields with the right types. Extra fields do not automatically make those required fields wrong.
Passing visitor does not remove visits. The function reads the name and leaves the object unchanged.

A fresh object written directly in the call gets an extra-property check. Including visits directly in a call expecting only PersonName would be rejected here. Naming an object first still does not make a wrong required value, such as name: 3, acceptable.
Make Guest require a string name. Make greet return Hello, followed by a space and that name. Leave all fields of the supplied object unchanged.
steps: Require a text name in Guest.
Return the greeting using that name.
Run the checks without changing the guest.

quiz.question: What happens to visitor.visits after nameText(visitor)?
choices: It stays on the original object
quiz.explanation: A type check compares the required structure. It does not trim the actual object.

hints: Read the name; do not remove fields to make the object look smaller.

title: Check a property before reading it
summary: Check an unknown value before reading its text property.
explanation: Unknown means the value's type is not established yet. Before reading a property, check that the value is an object and is not null. Then check that the property exists and contains text. The `in` operator can find inherited properties too.
The same function returns No place for null. It keeps an empty text value unchanged. A property existing does not prove that it contains text.
Make readLabel return label only when the input is a non-null object with a string label. Otherwise return No label. Keep an empty label as empty text.
steps: Check that the value is a non-null object.
Check that label exists and contains text.
Return the label or No label, then run the checks.

quiz.question: The place property exists, but its value is 8. Should readPlace return it?
choices: Yes, existence proves it is text
No, the text-type check rejects the number
Yes, the type label converts it to text
quiz.explanation: A property can exist and still have the wrong type. Both facts need checking.

hints: Check the object before using `in`, then check the property value with typeof.

title: Keep the input type in the result
summary: Return a value while keeping its original type.
explanation: A generic function can work with different types while keeping a connection between them. Here, `T` names the input type for one call. Using T for the result means the result keeps that type.
Each call gets its own type choice. Calling keepValue with 0 still returns the number 0, even after a call with text. T does not convert the value.
Finish preserve by returning its input directly. Keep numbers, text, true-or-false values, and objects unchanged. The starter is missing its return, so it will report an error until you add it.
steps: Keep T connected to both the input and result.
Run the checks with different input types.

quiz.question: You call keepValue("Fern"), then keepValue(0). What does the second call return?
choices: The text "0" because the first call used text
Undefined because zero is treated as missing
quiz.explanation: Each call has its own type choice. The input 0 is returned unchanged.

hints: Return value without converting or copying it.

typeAssertions.label: Number and text remain useful
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; const n=preserve(3); const s=preserve("Pine"); type N=Assert<IsAny<typeof n> extends false?true:false>;type S=Assert<IsAny<typeof s> extends false?true:false>;const numberValue:number=n;const textValue:string=s;

title: Require the property a generic uses
summary: A generic can accept different types while requiring one shared property.
explanation: A generic lets a function work with different types. A constraint is a rule that those types must follow. Here, `T extends { length: number }` means every allowed value must have a number named `length`.

An empty string has a length of `0`. An array of two items has a length of `2`. An object with `length: 7` supplies the number `7`. The function reads the supplied length; it does not count the object's properties.
Complete `itemCount`. Keep its type rule and return `value.length`. Do not change the value. A plain number is not allowed because it has no numeric `length` property.
steps: Find the property that every input must have.
Run the checks. Try an empty string and explain its result.

quiz.question: Why is an object with `length: "7"` rejected?
choices: The object's name is too short.
The function changes text into a number.
Its length is text, but the rule requires a number.
quiz.explanation: Quotes make `"7"` text. The type rule requires a number and does not convert the value.

hints: The constraint makes `value.length` safe to read.

title: Choose an actual property key
summary: Allow only property names that the object type actually has.
explanation: A key is a property's name. `keyof Address` makes a type from Address's allowed keys. Here, that means street or town. It does not create an object or an array.

The brackets in `address[field]` read the property named by field. Choosing street would read Oak Road from the same object. Keyof sets the allowed names during type checking; the bracket access reads the actual value.
Define ContactField from Contact's keys. Make contactValue read the chosen name or city property without changing the contact.
steps: Return the property chosen by field.

quiz.question: What happens if readAddress receives postcode as the field name?
choices: It accepts it and always returns empty text
TypeScript rejects it because postcode is not an Address key
quiz.explanation: Only the actual keys street and town are allowed by this type.

hints: Use brackets to read a property whose name is stored in a variable.

title: Reuse the type of one property
summary: Reuse a property's type without reading an object's value.
explanation: An indexed access type looks up a property's type using square brackets. `Reading["amount"]` means the type of Reading's amount field. Here, that type is number.
The type lookup does not create a Reading object or supply an amount. The call supplies the actual value. Giving addOne the number 0 would return 1.
Define Points using Player's points field type. Make addPoint return the numeric input plus 1.
steps: Look up the points field type from Player.

quiz.question: What does Reading["amount"] provide in a type definition?
choices: A new object whose amount is zero
quiz.explanation: It provides a type. An actual value still has to be supplied separately.

hints: Use the type lookup `Player["points"]`.

typeAssertions.label: Numeric field type is retained
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; type Safe=Assert<IsAny<Points> extends false?true:false>;const points:Points=4;const n:number=points;

typeAssertions.label: Text is not the points field type

title: Reuse a value’s inferred shape
summary: Use `typeof` in a type to reuse an existing value's shape.
explanation: TypeScript can work out a value's type. In a type definition, `typeof` reuses that type. It creates a type rule, not a copy of the value.

The new job can use a different title or number. The starting value `2` does not limit `copies` to only `2`. Here, `typeof` describes a type. In running code, `typeof` instead gives text such as `"object"`.
Use `typeof sample` to define `Settings`. Complete `settingsText` so it joins the name, `": "`, and the retries number.
steps: Join the settings fields in the requested order.
Run the checks with different names and numbers.

quiz.question: The sample starts with `copies: 2`. Can a `PrintJob` have `copies: 5`?
choices: Yes. The field accepts a number.
No. Only the original object can use that type.
quiz.explanation: The field's type is `number`. It is not limited to the starting value `2`.

hints: Write `typeof sample` after the type's equals sign.

typeAssertions.label: Different values still fit
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; type Safe=Assert<IsAny<Settings> extends false?true:false>;const s:Settings={name:"Other",retries:8};const n:number=s.retries;

title: Initialize each new instance
summary: Give each new object its own starting value.
explanation: A class describes a kind of object. An instance is one object made from that class. Its constructor runs when you use `new`. Inside it, `this` means the particular object being created.
Changing the first basket's label to Vegetables leaves the second label as Bread. These are two separate objects, and each has its own label.
Make the Crate constructor receive a string and store it in that crate's label. The constructor sets up the object; it does not return a label string.
steps: Give the constructor a string label input.
Run the checks with two separate crates.

quiz.question: The first basket's label changes to Vegetables. What happens to the second basket's Bread label?
choices: It stays Bread because it belongs to a different object
quiz.explanation: Each constructor stores a label on its own object.

hints: The label after `this.` belongs to the new crate. The other label is the constructor input.

title: Make a class meet an interface
summary: Use `implements` to check that a class provides what an interface requires.
explanation: An interface lists the parts an object must have. A class is a plan for making objects. `implements` checks that the class has the required parts. It does not write them for you.

The constructor stores the label when a badge is made. The `caption` method reads that stored label. Change `"Helper"` to `"Guide"` and it returns `Badge: Guide`. Removing the method causes a type error, even if `implements Captioned` stays.
Complete `Ticket` so it meets `Printable`. Store the label in the constructor. Add `print()` and return `"Ticket: "` followed by the stored label.
steps: Store the label and write the required method.
Run the checks with different labels.

checks.label: Separate instances keep labels
checks.expression: new Ticket("A").print()==="Ticket: A" && new Ticket("B").print()==="Ticket: B"

quiz.question: A class uses `implements Captioned` but has no `caption` method. What happens?
choices: The method appears when the object is made.
quiz.explanation: `implements` checks the class. It does not add code.

hints: `implements` checks your method; you still need to write its body.

typeAssertions.label: Instance fits promised interface
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; const ticket:Printable=new Ticket("Day");const text:string=ticket.print(); type Safe=Assert<IsAny<ReturnType<Ticket["print"]>> extends false?true:false>;

typeAssertions.label: Wrong method result cannot fit interface

title: Await the value a typed promise carries
summary: Use await to get the text from a typed promise.
explanation: A promise represents a result that may become available later. Promise<string> means its successful result is text. An async function always returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain string.
Changing the name to Sam gives Hello, Sam. No server is involved. The call still returns a promise; storing that promise does not make the work finish immediately.
Finish async makeBadge so its body returns Badge: followed by a space and the label. Callers use await to get the text. Keep empty label text as an empty ending.
steps: Keep the async function's Promise<string> result type.
Return the prefix and supplied label from its body.

quiz.question: What does makeGreeting("Nora") return when called without await?
quiz.explanation: An async call returns a promise. Await gets its successful result.

hints: An async function wraps your returned text in a promise.

typeAssertions.label: Promise carries text
typeAssertions.code: type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false; type Assert<T extends true> = T; const promise=makeBadge("Builder");type Safe=Assert<IsAny<typeof promise> extends false?true:false>;const typed:Promise<string>=promise;

typeAssertions.label: Promise is not the resolved string

title: Narrow a caught value before reading it
summary: Check a caught value before reading its error message.
explanation: `throw` stops the current work and sends a value to `catch`. That value can be an `Error` object, text, or something else. Here, its type is `unknown`, so check it before reading `.message`.
An `Error` may have an empty message. Return that empty text as it is. A plain string is not an `Error` object, even if it contains the same words. It uses the fallback message.
Complete `describeFailure`. In `catch`, return `.message` for an `Error` object. For every other value, return `"Unknown failure"`.
steps: Check the caught value with `instanceof Error`.
Return its message or the fallback text.
Run the checks, including an Error with an empty message.

checks.label: Non-Error thrown values are safe
checks.expression: describeFailure("Offline")==="Unknown failure" && describeFailure(null)==="Unknown failure" && describeFailure(7)==="Unknown failure"

quiz.question: What does `failureText` return when it catches the plain string `"Door closed"`?
choices: Door closed, because throw adds a message field.
Empty text, because the string disappears.
quiz.explanation: The string stays a string. It fails the `instanceof Error` check, so the fallback is returned.

hints: Check the object type, not whether its message has any letters.

title: Choose public call shapes with overloads
summary: Overloads list the allowed ways to call one function.
explanation: An overload is one allowed way to call a function. This function allows text alone, or text followed by a number. Each overload is written as a function declaration ending with a semicolon.
The overloads share one function body. Inside that body, `count` may be missing. The body checks for `undefined` to choose which result to return.
Complete `badge` with these two allowed calls. With no count, return the text unchanged. With a count, add a space and the number in parentheses.

Passing `undefined` as a second argument is not allowed here. The public overloads allow one argument, or two arguments with a number second. The body's wider type does not create another allowed call. Use overloads only when different call shapes are useful.
steps: Check whether the count is missing inside the body.
Run the checks for one argument and two arguments.

quiz.question: Is `badge("Map", undefined)` allowed by these overloads?
choices: Yes. The body adds a third overload.
No. The second argument must be a number.
quiz.explanation: Only the two overload declarations list allowed calls. The function body's type does not add another one.

hints: Check `count === undefined` so a count of `0` still appears.

typeAssertions.label: Both call shapes
typeAssertions.code: const __a: string = badge("A"); const __b: string = badge("A",2);

typeAssertions.label: Public result is not any
typeAssertions.code: const __notAny: 0 extends (1 & (ReturnType<typeof badge>)) ? false : true = true;

title: Turn properties into boolean flags
summary: Keep the same property names, but make their values true or false.
explanation: A mapped type builds a type from another type's property names. In `[K in keyof T]`, keyof T supplies the keys and K stands for each key in turn. Writing boolean after the colon makes every new value true or false.
Settings has theme and attempts. Flags<Settings> keeps those names but gives both boolean values. This creates a type description; you still write the actual object.
Adding another required property to Settings means the flags object needs that name too. The mapped type follows the keys in Settings.
If a setting called volume originally holds a number, its flag still needs true or false. A numeric flag value such as 8 would cause a type error.
steps: Map every key of T to a boolean value.
Return the theme flag from enabledTheme.

quiz.question: If Settings adds volume as a number, what does Flags<Settings> require for volume?
quiz.explanation: The mapped type keeps the property name but replaces its value type with boolean.

hints: Keep `keyof T` for the names and use boolean for each new value type.

title: Choose a type using a condition
summary: Choose an object shape by checking its type.
explanation: A conditional type chooses one type or another. In `T extends string ? A : B`, extends asks whether T fits the string type. If it does, choose A; otherwise, choose B. This is a type check, not a running if statement.
For Stored, a string gets a text property. Other types get a value property. The question mark begins the first choice, and the colon begins the other choice.
Boolean means true or false. It does not fit string, so Stored<boolean> needs a value property holding a boolean.
Stored describes the required shape. It does not make the object or convert its data. You supply the actual object values.
steps: Choose text for string types and value for other types.
Create words with Cloud and count with 6.

quiz.question: Which object fits Stored<boolean>?
choices: True is automatically converted into text
quiz.explanation: Boolean does not fit string, so the value-property branch is selected.

hints: Keep T as the chosen property's value type in both branches.

title: Distribute a conditional across a union
summary: Apply a type choice to each member of a union separately.
explanation: When a conditional type checks T directly, it can apply to each member of a union separately. This is called distribution. Here, string becomes string[] and number becomes number[].
EachList<string | number> becomes string[] or number[]. That means an all-text list or an all-number list. The type does not create either list for you.
`(string | number)[]` means something different: each item can be text or a number, so one list can mix both kinds.
A list containing Map and 3 does not fit EachList<string | number>. It is neither all text nor all numbers.
steps: Define EachList so its conditional checks T directly.
Create names with Oak and Elm, and counts with 2 and 7.

quiz.question: Does ["Map", 3] fit EachList<string | number>?
choices: Yes, it allows both kinds in the same list
No, it is neither all text nor all numbers
No, conditional types cannot use unions
quiz.explanation: This type produces a union of separate array types, not an array whose items can mix the two types.

hints: Use T[] for each selected union member.

title: Build a finite set of string names
summary: Build a small set of allowed text values from a shared pattern.
explanation: A template literal type describes text using backticks. `${Topic}` places each allowed topic into the pattern. With topics `"goal"` and `"note"`, the pattern allows `"goal:saved"` and `"note:saved"`.
The ending `:saved` is part of the rule. `"goal:deleted"` does not fit. This type describes allowed text; it does not build a new text value while the program runs.
Define `EventName` using `Topic` and the exact ending `:saved`. Complete `eventLabel` to add `"Received "` before the event name.

These type rules are removed before the program runs. Text from a file or the internet still needs a real check. Adding `"photo"` to `Topic` would allow `"photo:saved"`, but it would not make all photo-related text valid.
steps: Use the topics inside the backtick pattern.
Run the checks and explain which names fit.

quiz.question: If `Topic` also allows `"photo"`, which new event name fits?
choices: Every string that starts with photo.
quiz.explanation: Each topic gets the same exact ending: `:saved`.

hints: `${Topic}` stands for each allowed member of `Topic`.

title: Admit that a dictionary entry can be missing
summary: Treat a missing dictionary entry as a real possibility.
explanation: A dictionary stores values under keys. An index signature describes the values read with those keys. Here, `[key: string]: number | undefined` says a text-key lookup may give a number or no value.

ScoreOrZero reads the chosen entry and checks whether it is a number. The `? :` expression chooses between that number and zero. Checking the actual value also prevents an inherited function, such as toString, from being returned as a number.
The art entry really contains 0. It stays 0. A zero result therefore does not tell you whether the key existed or the backup was used.
An arbitrary lookup cannot be assigned straight to a number-only variable because it might be undefined. Keep absence in the type and handle it in the code.
steps: Let each Scores lookup be number or undefined.
Return the value only when it is a number; otherwise return zero.
Run the checks without changing the dictionary.

checks.label: Inherited nonnumeric value does not escape

quiz.question: Why can an arbitrary Scores lookup fail when assigned directly to a number-only variable?
quiz.explanation: The key may be missing, so the code must check the value or choose a backup.

hints: Read the entry once, then check it with typeof.

title: Omit an identifier from an edit shape
summary: Use `Omit` to leave a field out of a type.
explanation: `Omit<T, K>` makes a type like `T` without the field names in `K`. `Omit<Card, "id">` leaves out `id`. The other fields, `title` and `done`, are still required.
The edit type describes the fields an edit needs. It does not remove fields from real objects. Keep the original card's `id` by reading it from `card`, then copy only the allowed edit fields.
Complete `editCard`. Return a new object with the old `id` and the edit's `title` and `done`. Do not change either input object.

A variable may contain extra fields and still meet the edit type. If that variable also contains `id: 99`, the function must still keep the card's original `id`. Copying the chosen fields makes that rule hold while the program runs.
steps: Leave `id` out of the edit type.
Copy the old id and the two edit fields into a new object.
Run the checks and confirm both inputs stay unchanged.

quiz.question: The card's id is 7. An edit variable also has id 99. Which id does this function keep?
choices: 7, because it reads id from the original card.
Neither, because extra fields always cause an error.
99, because Omit changes the original object.
quiz.explanation: `Omit` changes the type rule. The function itself keeps the old id by copying `card.id`.

hints: Read the result's id from `card`, not from `edit`.

title: Reuse the return type of a function
summary: Use `ReturnType` to describe the value a function returns.
explanation: `ReturnType` gets the result type of a function. In `ReturnType<typeof makeReading>`, `typeof makeReading` supplies the function's type. Neither part calls the function.
`makeReading` returns a new object with a title, a page count, and a `complete` flag. A flag is a true-or-false value. Here, `complete` is true exactly when the page count is zero.
Complete `makeReading` and define `Reading` using its return type. Return a new object each time. Keep the title and page count supplied to the function.

If the function's returned fields change, `Reading` follows their types. Here, pages must be a number; text such as `"2"` does not fit. This number type alone does not rule out negative values or check data from a file.
steps: Return the title, pages, and complete flag.
Run the checks with zero pages and a nonzero count.

checks.label: Each call returns a fresh record

quiz.question: If the function is changed so its returned pages field is text, what happens to `Reading.pages`?
choices: ReturnType runs the function to find out.
It follows the returned field and becomes text.
quiz.explanation: `Reading` gets its type from the function's result type. It is not a separate handwritten copy.

hints: Use `pages === 0` for the complete flag.

title: Share a helper with subclasses
summary: Use `protected` to share a class helper with classes that extend it.
explanation: A subclass is a class that extends another class. A `protected` method can be used inside its class and subclasses. Ordinary outside code cannot call it through TypeScript's checked access.
`LabelBase` supplies a helper named `prefix`. `TopicLabel` extends that class, so it can use the helper inside `render`. Outside code calls `render`, which is public.
Keep `prefix` protected. Complete `render` so it calls `this.prefix(text)` and returns the result. Different text should keep the same `Topic: ` beginning.
An outside call such as `label.prefix("Map")` causes a type error. The `protected` word is removed from the generated JavaScript. It is a code-checking rule, not a way to hide secret data.
steps: Run the checks using the public render method.

quiz.question: Can outside TypeScript code call `new TopicLabel().prefix("Map")` normally?
choices: No, because protected encrypts the method.
No. The type checker blocks it, but protected is not runtime secrecy.
Yes. Extending a class makes every method public.
quiz.explanation: Outside code can call `render`. The protected helper is for use inside the class family.

hints: `this.prefix(text)` calls the helper on the current object.

typeAssertions.label: Public and subclass access
typeAssertions.code: const __s: string = new TopicLabel().render("A"); class __Child extends LabelBase { go(){return this.prefix("B");} }

title: Read a declaration beside real JavaScript
summary: A declaration describes code's types. The real JavaScript still has to exist.
explanation: A declaration file ends in `.d.ts`. It tells TypeScript which names and types exist, but it does not create running code. This optional example uses several files on your computer. It does not run in the app's single-file editor.

File: `labels.d.ts`
```typescript
export declare function label(text: string): string;
```
This describes `label`: it takes text and returns text. There is no function body here. A wrong description can pass type checks while the real code behaves differently.

Optional local run: put these files in a separate folder. Add `package.json` containing `{"type":"commonjs"}`. With TypeScript 5.9.3 installed, check `tsc --version`. Run `tsc --strict --target ES2015 --module commonjs --noEmitOnError main.ts`, then `node main.js`. If `labels.js` is missing, checking can pass but running fails. Restore it before running again. `--noEmitOnError` stops new output on errors; it does not delete old output files.
steps: Read the real function and its separate description.
Explain why the JavaScript file is still needed. Running locally is optional.

quiz.question: What can happen if labels.js is missing but labels.d.ts remains?
choices: Type checking passes, but Node cannot load the function.
The declaration creates the function automatically.
TypeScript must run the function before accepting it.
quiz.explanation: The declaration describes the function. Node still needs the JavaScript file that actually creates it.

hints: The declaration supplies types, not the function body.
externalNotes: This lesson uses files on your computer. The app's single-file editor does not run this module example.

title: Separate emitted syntax from available APIs
summary: Changing the generated code does not add missing features to a browser.
explanation: `target` chooses the JavaScript syntax that TypeScript writes. `lib` lists built-in features the type checker knows about. Neither setting installs missing features. This optional local example changes only the target and compares the generated code.

File: `tsconfig.es5.json`
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES5",
    "lib": ["ES2015", "DOM"],
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmitOnError": true,
    "outDir": "out-es5"
  },
  "files": ["main.ts"]
}
```
ES5 is an older JavaScript syntax level. TypeScript rewrites the arrow as a regular function. `outDir` names the folder for generated files.

File: `tsconfig.es2015.json`
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2015",
    "lib": ["ES2015", "DOM"],
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmitOnError": true,
    "outDir": "out-es2015"
  },
  "files": ["main.ts"]
}
```
This target can keep the arrow. The other settings stay the same: `module` chooses how files share code, and `strict` enables stricter type checks. Here, `DOM` supplies the description of `console`; it does not turn Node into a browser.

Optional local run: use a separate folder with Node and TypeScript 5.9.3. Add `package.json` containing `{"type":"commonjs"}`. Run `tsc -p tsconfig.es5.json`, then `tsc -p tsconfig.es2015.json`. The `-p` option selects a settings file. Run `node out-es5/main.js` and `node out-es2015/main.js`; both should print `4,10`. Compare their arrow syntax. Removing `DOM` from these settings makes the console type check fail, even though Node still has console. Failed builds can leave old output files behind.
steps: Compare the target setting in the two files.
Find the arrow in each generated file if you run the optional local example.
Explain why a type description does not install a missing feature.

quiz.question: What does adding a built-in feature to `lib` do?
choices: It makes target stop affecting the code.
It automatically installs the feature in a browser.
It gives the type checker a description of the feature.
quiz.explanation: The place running the code must still provide that feature. A type description does not create it.

hints: The app does not expose these settings. This comparison uses files on your computer.
externalNotes: This optional comparison runs on your computer. It does not change the app runner's TypeScript settings.

title: A component returns a small UI tree
summary: A component is a function that describes one part of the screen.
explanation: A React component is a function that describes part of a screen. React uses that description to show it. In this course, the app starts the component named `App` for you.
A component name starts with a capital letter. An HTML tag, such as `<h1>`, starts with a lowercase letter. Change the text inside `Welcome` to change the heading. `App` can stay the same.
Make `Welcome` return an `<h1>` with the text `Trail station`. Have `App` return `<Welcome />`. The text appears on the page, not in the console.
steps: Run the checks and read the heading on the screen.

checks.label: Welcome also renders on its own
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Welcome))); return host.querySelector("h1")?.textContent === "Trail station"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question:
Welcome now returns `

Route notes

`. App still uses ``. What appears?
choices: An h2 heading that says Route notes.
The word Welcome as plain text.
The old heading, because App stayed the same.
quiz.explanation: React uses the description returned by Welcome, including its new heading.

hints: Use a capital W for the component name in both places.

title: JSX inserts expression results
summary: Use curly braces to put a JavaScript value into JSX.
explanation: JSX is the tag-like code used to describe a React screen. Inside JSX, curly braces `{ }` let JavaScript work out a value. Text outside those braces stays as written.
Changing `level` to `6` makes the number on the page `7`. The colon and space stay the same. `className` gives the paragraph a CSS class name; it does not add any styles by itself.
Return a paragraph with `className="status"`. Use `{label}` for the name and `{stops + 2}` for the number. With the starter values, the page should read `Route: 8`.
steps: Keep the fixed colon and space outside the braces.
Put the name and calculation inside braces.
Run the checks and read the paragraph.

quiz.question:
If level is 5, what does `

level + 1: {level + 1}

` show?
quiz.explanation: Only the calculation inside braces is worked out. The other words stay as written.

hints: Words written outside braces are shown as text.

title: Props configure separate component uses
summary: Props give a component the information it needs to show.
explanation: A prop is an input passed to a component. The component receives its props in an object. Read those inputs without changing them.
`props.name` reads the name supplied to that use of `Pass`. Changing only the second name changes only the second paragraph. The component does not need a new definition.
Make `Pass` show its `name` prop. In `App`, use it for `Cedar` and `Fern`. It should also work when given a different name.
steps: Use Pass twice with the required names.
Run the checks and try another name.

checks.label: Another name works
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Pass,{name:"Meadow"}))); return host.textContent==="Meadow"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question: App uses `<Pass name="Oak" />` twice. What appears?
choices: One paragraph, because Pass is defined once.
Two paragraphs that overwrite one shared name.
quiz.explanation: Each use of Pass produces its own paragraph, even when the names match.

hints: Show the supplied prop instead of writing a fixed name inside Pass.

title: Children compose a wrapper
summary: Use children to place supplied content inside a shared wrapper.
explanation: A wrapper is a component that surrounds other content. JSX placed between its opening and closing tags arrives in a prop named `children`.
The same `Panel` can receive a button or another element instead of a paragraph. It keeps its heading and shows the new content where `{props.children}` appears.
Make `Panel` show an `<h2>` that says `Notice`, followed by its children. In `App`, put a paragraph saying `Bring a bottle.` inside `Panel`.
steps: Keep the Notice heading inside Panel.
Put the requested paragraph inside Panel and run the checks.

checks.label: A different supplied child works
checks.expression: (() => { const host=document.createElement("div"); document.body.append(host); const root=ReactDOM.createRoot(host); try { ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>root.render(React.createElement(Panel,null,React.createElement("strong",null,"Closed today")))); return host.querySelector("strong")?.textContent === "Closed today" && host.querySelector("h2")?.textContent === "Notice"; } finally { root.unmount(); host.remove(); } })()

quiz.question: Does Panel need new code to show `Closed today` as its child?
choices: No. props.children carries the supplied strong element.
No. React removes the strong element.
quiz.explanation: Panel places the content it receives below its heading.

hints: The content between `<Panel>` and `</Panel>` becomes children.

title: Pass a handler for React to call later
summary: Give a button a function to run when it is clicked.
explanation: An event is something that happens, such as a click. A handler is a function that responds to it. Give `onClick` the function itself so React can call it later.

`onClick={chooseMap}` passes the function without running it. Adding `()` would call it while React is drawing the screen. Changing this ordinary variable does not ask React to redraw, so the button text stays the same.
Keep `lastAction` as `"none"` at first. Pass `chooseMap` to the `Choose map` button. It should record the action only after a click. The next lesson shows how to update the screen too.
steps: Pass chooseMap to onClick without calling it.
Run the checks to compare before and after a click.

quiz.question: What goes wrong with `onClick={chooseMap()}` here?
choices: It runs during rendering and passes its return value.
It passes the same function as before.
quiz.explanation: `chooseMap()` calls the function immediately. The button needs the function to call later.

hints: Parentheses call a function now. Leave them out when passing this handler.

title: State requests a new render
summary: State remembers a value and lets React update the screen when it changes.
explanation: State is a value React remembers for a component on the screen. `useState` gives you that value and a setter: a function that asks React to update it.

One click changes the screen to `Tickets: 3`. Another separate click makes it `Tickets: 4`. Keep `useState` at the top of the component, outside conditions and handlers. It is a Hook: a React function that gives a component a feature such as state.
Start your counter at `3`. Add one for each separate click. Keep the button text `Add ticket`. Use the setter to update the count.
steps: Start the count at 3 with useState.
Ask for count + 1 when the button is clicked.
Run the checks and click several times.

quiz.question: The count starts at 3. What appears after three separate clicks?
choices: 4, because every click uses the starting value.
quiz.explanation: Each click adds one to the current count: 3, then 4, then 5, then 6.

hints: The first name reads the state. The second name changes it.

title: A handler reads one state snapshot
summary: A setter does not change the state value inside a handler that is already running.
explanation: A render is React calling a component to work out what to show. Each render gives its handlers the state values from that render. This is called a snapshot. A setter asks for a later update; it does not replace the value the current handler is reading.
On the next click, the new handler reads `2`. It asks for a count of `3` and a report of `Read 2`. The report is meant to show the earlier value.
Start at `2`. Each `Record` click should add one to the count and report the number read before adding. Keep the count and report in separate state values.
steps: Read count inside the click handler.
Ask for count + 1 and a report made from count.
Run the checks and compare the count with the report.

checks.label: Next event gets a new snapshot

quiz.question: Starting at 2, what report appears after two separate Record clicks?
quiz.explanation: The first click reads 2 and asks for 3. The next click reads 3 and asks for 4.

hints: Even after setCount, this handler's count still has its earlier value.

title: Queued updater functions compose
summary: Pass updater functions when several state changes must build on one another.
explanation: An updater is a function that receives the pending state and returns the next state. Pending means waiting to be applied. React works through queued updaters in order, passing each result to the next one.

Calling `setCount(count + 1)` twice would use the same old count both times. Starting at 0, both calls would ask for 1. Keep updater functions pure: return a result without changing outside data. React may call them more than once to check for mistakes.

Start at `1`. Pass `increment` to the setter twice per click. The screen should show `3` after one click and `5` after another. The checks compare these results; the quiz checks why the updater works.
steps: Write increment to return its input plus one.
Pass it to setCount twice in the handler.
Run the checks and follow both additions.

quiz.question: A handler reads count 5 and calls `setCount(count + 1)` twice. What next count is requested?
quiz.explanation: Both calculations use 5, so both ask for 6. Updater functions let the second change use the first change's result.

hints: Use `setCount(increment)`, without calling increment yourself.

title: Choose whether a panel exists
summary: Choose whether a panel is included on the screen.
explanation: Conditional rendering means choosing what React shows. `condition ? yes : no` chooses one of two results. Here, `null` means there is no panel to show.
The `open` state is either true or false. Each click changes it to the opposite value. `aria-expanded` tells assistive tools whether the panel is open. It uses that same state value.

Starting with `useState(true)` would show the panel immediately. `aria-controls="detail"` connects the button to the panel's matching ID. Keep `useState` at the top of the component so it runs in the same order each time.
Make `Details` add and remove the section. Keep `aria-expanded` correct for both states. Returning `null` removes the panel; it does not leave an empty section behind.
steps: Use open to choose the section or null.
Run the checks and open and close the panel.

checks.label: Open, then remove the panel
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const b=document.querySelector("button");if(!b||document.querySelector("#detail"))return false;b.click();if(!await until(()=>!!document.querySelector("#detail")))return false;if(b.getAttribute("aria-expanded")!=="true")return false;b.click();return await until(()=>!document.querySelector("#detail")&&b.getAttribute("aria-expanded")==="false");})()

quiz.question:
If the false branch becomes `

Closed

`, what appears while open is false?
choices: The Closed paragraph, without the section.
Both the section and the paragraph.
quiz.explanation: React shows the chosen branch. A paragraph appears; null would add nothing.

hints: Use the same open value for the panel choice and aria-expanded.

title: Let each record own its key
summary: Give each list item a stable key so its input stays with the right record.
explanation: A key tells React which item is which when a list changes. Use a stable ID from the record. Stable means it stays the same when the item moves. Its position in the list is not a stable ID.
`map` makes one component for each record. `key={card.id}` tells React the record's identity. The separate `card` prop gives `Card` its data; React does not pass key as an ordinary prop.
Two records can share a title and still need different keys. Their IDs keep them separate. `[...current]` copies the array before `reverse()` changes its order, so the original array stays unchanged.
Fix the key on each `Card`. The starter uses the item's current position, which changes after reversing. Use its record ID instead. Keep the original order of `initialCards`.
steps: Use each record's ID as its key.
Edit a note, then reverse the rows.
Run the checks and confirm the note follows its record.

checks.label: Stable record identity survives reordering
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const inputs=[...document.querySelectorAll("li input")];if(inputs.length!==2)return false;type(inputs[0],"personal");document.querySelector("button").click();if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("li")?.textContent.startsWith("Lamp")))return false;const after=[...document.querySelectorAll("li input")];return after[1]===inputs[0]&&after[1].value==="personal"&&initialCards[0].id==="map";})()

quiz.question: Two records have the same title but different stable IDs. Which key should each Card use?
quiz.explanation: The ID still identifies the same record after a move. A shared title cannot distinguish the two records.

hints: A key belongs to the record, not to its current place in the list.

title: Let state control a labeled field
summary: Use one state value for both a text field and its message.
explanation: A controlled input gets its text from React state. Its `value` prop shows the state. Its `onChange` handler saves the latest edit back into state.

The browser gives the handler an event. `event.target.value` is the text currently in the input. Pass that text to the setter right away. `htmlFor` matches the input's `id` so the label names the right field.
An empty string, `""`, is a real text value. Use it when the field is blank. Keep this state as a string instead of switching between text and `undefined`.
Make the labeled field and status message follow typing and Clear. Change the state through its setter; do not change the input's displayed text separately.
steps: Show title in the input's value.
Run the checks, then erase all text and use Clear.

checks.label: Typing and clearing use one state string
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const input=document.querySelector("#title");if(!input||document.querySelector("label")?.htmlFor!==input.id)return false;type(input,"Orbit");if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]")?.textContent==="Title: Orbit"))return false;document.querySelector("button").click();return await until(()=>input.value===""&&document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Title: ");})()

quiz.question: What happens if the field has `value={title}` but the change handler never updates title?
choices: The browser takes over the text permanently.
Typed edits do not stay as the controlled value.
React copies the text into state automatically.
quiz.explanation: The field shows the state React supplies. The handler must update that state to keep the edit.

hints: Both the input and message should read the same title state.

title: Handle saving at the form boundary
summary: Handle a form's save action in one place: onSubmit.
explanation: A submission asks a form to send or save its values. Put the save handler on the form's `onSubmit`. Avoid also saving in the button's `onClick`, which could save twice.
`draft` is the text being edited. `saved` keeps the text from the last submission. `event.preventDefault()` stops the form's usual page navigation. It does not save anything to a server.
After saving, typing more changes only the draft. The saved text stays the same until another submission. This is why the two state values have different jobs.

This preview does not enable native form submission. Use Run checks to test the handler here. Try the Save button and Enter key on a normal browser page outside this preview. Complete the handler so each submission saves once and stops page navigation.
steps: Keep all save work in the form's submit handler.
Prevent default navigation and record the draft once.
Run the checks. Test normal button and Enter submission separately outside this preview.

checks.label: One update per cancelable submission
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const form=document.querySelector("form"),input=document.querySelector("#entry");if(!form||!input)return false;ReactDOM.flushSync(()=>type(input,"Moon"));const e=new Event("submit",{bubbles:true,cancelable:true});form.dispatchEvent(e);if(!e.defaultPrevented)return false;if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Saved: Moon; count: 1"))return false;form.dispatchEvent(new Event("submit",{bubbles:true,cancelable:true}));return await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Saved: Moon; count: 2");})()

quiz.question: After saving Moon, you type Star without submitting. What should the saved message show?
quiz.explanation: Typing changes draft. Only a submission replaces saved.

hints: The button starts a submission. The form's onSubmit does the saving.

title: Replace a field without rewriting the old object
summary: To update an object in state, make a new object with the changed field.
explanation: Treat an object already in state as read-only. Make a new object for the next state. This lets you change one field without rewriting the earlier object.
`{...plan}` copies the plan's fields into a new object. Writing `minutes` after the spread replaces that copied field. Fields written later win when names match.
The name stays the same because the spread copies it. This copy is shallow: objects inside the plan would still be shared. If you change a nested field, copy that inner object too.
Complete `extend` so it returns a new plan with five more minutes. Use it in the state update. Keep every other field and leave the input object unchanged.
steps: Copy the plan's fields into a new object.
Replace minutes with its old value plus 5.
Run the checks and confirm the old plan is unchanged.

checks.label: Replacement preserves input and updates screen
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const source={name:"Probe",minutes:20};const result=extend(source);if(result===source||source.minutes!==20||result.minutes!==25||result.name!=="Probe")return false;document.querySelector("button").click();if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Survey: 15 minutes"))return false;document.querySelector("button").click();return await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Survey: 20 minutes"&&initialPlan.minutes===10);})()

quiz.question: plan.minutes is 10. What does `{minutes: 15, ...plan}` keep for minutes?
choices: Both numbers under the same field name.
quiz.explanation: The spread comes last, so it replaces 15 with the plan's old value, 10.

hints: Write the updated minutes field after `...plan`.

title: Remove a record by keeping the others
summary: Remove one record by making a new array of the records you want to keep.
explanation: `filter` makes a new array. Its test decides which items to keep. To remove a chosen ID, keep each record whose ID is different.
`task.id !== id` means the record's ID does not equal the selected ID. Each button uses its own task's ID, so a label or position change will not select the wrong record.
Two records may have the same text. Their IDs still let you remove only the chosen record. If the ID is absent, every record is kept in a new array.
Complete `without` and connect it to each remove button. Keep the old array unchanged. `filter` makes a new array but shares the kept record objects; it does not copy their contents.
steps: Use the resulting array as the next state.
Run the checks, including removing the last item.

checks.label: Removal preserves source and reaches empty state
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};const source=[{id:"x"},{id:"y"}];const result=without(source,"x");if(source.length!==2||result===source||result.length!==1||result[0]!==source[1])return false;const absent=without(source,"z");if(absent.length!==2)return false;document.querySelector("button").click();if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Remaining: 1"))return false;if(document.querySelector("li").textContent!=="CheckRemove Check")return false;document.querySelector("button").click();return await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Remaining: 0"&&document.querySelectorAll("li").length===0&&initialTasks.length===2);})()

quiz.question: What does this filter return when the selected ID is absent?
choices: A new array containing all the original items.
quiz.explanation: Every record has a different ID and is kept. filter still makes a new array.

hints: The filter test should be true for each record you want to keep.

title: Calculate a total from the current records
summary: Calculate a total from the current list instead of keeping another state value.
explanation: A derived value is worked out from data you already have. Here, the list is state and the total is calculated from it. Keeping only the list in state avoids having two values to update separately.
`reduce` combines the list's numbers into one result. It starts with `0`, then adds each number to the running total. This function calculates a result without changing state.
An empty list still produces 0 because reduce has a starting sum. Adding three after Clear makes a new list containing 3, so the total becomes 3.
Calculate the total from the current array during rendering. Keep the total out of state. The checks test the displayed results; also read your code to confirm the total is calculated directly.
steps: Add the values with a starting sum of 0.
Calculate total from minutes inside App.
Run the checks, including Add three after Clear.

checks.label: Total follows edits, empty state and reuse
checks.expression: (async()=>{const until=async(test)=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,10));}return true;};const type=(el,value)=>{Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(el,value);el.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true}));};if(totalMinutes([])!==0||totalMinutes([2,7,1])!==10)return false;const buttons=document.querySelectorAll("button");if(document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent!=="Total: 13 minutes")return false;buttons[0].click();if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Total: 16 minutes"))return false;buttons[1].click();if(!await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Total: 0 minutes"))return false;buttons[0].click();return await until(()=>document.querySelector("[role=status]").textContent==="Total: 3 minutes"&&initialMinutes.length===2);})()

quiz.question: Why does reduce receive 0 as its second argument?
choices: It starts the sum and gives an empty list a result of 0.
quiz.explanation: The sum starts at 0. If there are no numbers to add, it stays 0.

hints: The total is a calculation, so it does not need its own useState.

title: Rendering calculates; events change things
summary: Keep rendering as a calculation. Let event handlers request changes.
explanation: A pure render calculates the screen from its current props and state without changing outside data. Given the same inputs, it should give the same result. React may repeat the calculation.
`Badge` multiplies its supplied count by two. This creates a local result without changing count. Both uses of Badge receive the same input, so their numbers match.
Change background flips the separate `night` value. It does not change count, so both numbers stay the same. `data-night` records that value on the element; styling it would need a separate CSS rule.
Keep `Badge` as a calculation from its count prop. Do not increase an outside counter during rendering. Check that Add point changes both numbers and Change background leaves them alone.
steps: Calculate each badge from its count prop.
Keep state changes inside the click handlers.
Run the checks and compare both badges.

checks.label: Both cards depend only on the supplied count
checks.expression: (async()=>{const wait=async test=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(resolve=>setTimeout(resolve,10));}return true;};const buttons=[...document.querySelectorAll('button')];const add=buttons.find(b=>b.textContent==='Add point'),theme=buttons.find(b=>b.textContent==='Change background');const values=()=>[...document.querySelectorAll('[data-badge]')].map(e=>e.textContent);if(!add||!theme||values().join('|')!=='4 points|4 points')return false;theme.click();if(!await wait(()=>document.querySelector('main').getAttribute('data-night')==='true'))return false;if(values().join('|')!=='4 points|4 points')return false;add.click();return await wait(()=>values().join('|')==='6 points|6 points');})()

quiz.question: Why is increasing an outside counter during rendering a problem?
choices: Multiplying a local number always changes the prop.
React promises to call a component exactly once.
The result depends on earlier calls instead of just the current inputs.
quiz.explanation: React can render again with the same inputs. A pure calculation still gives the same result.

hints: Avoid changing an outside variable inside Badge.

title: A ref reaches the committed input
summary: Use a ref to reach an input and move keyboard focus to it.
explanation: A ref is a small holder with a `current` property. `useRef(null)` creates it. Updating a ref does not ask React to redraw the screen.

`ref={field}` asks React to put the actual input element in `field.current` after it is on the page. React clears it when the element is removed. A click handler can then use the element's `focus()` method.
`focus()` moves focus to an element. `blur()` removes focus from it. Use these actions in response to an event or after React has added the element, not during rendering.
Connect the ref to the input and call `focus()` after the button is clicked. Keep the label connected through its matching `htmlFor` and `id`. Check the visible focus as well as running the checks.
steps: Create the ref at the top of App.
Make Focus topic focus that input and run the checks.

checks.label: The button moves focus to the labeled field

quiz.question: Does changing a ref's current value by itself ask React to redraw?
choices: No, because refs cannot hold page elements.
No. Use state for values that should update the screen.
quiz.explanation: A ref keeps a value without requesting a render. It can still point to an input for an event handler to use.

hints: The actual input is in field.current after React adds it to the page.

title: An Effect synchronizes a browser value
summary: Use an Effect to keep a browser value in step with React state.
explanation: An Effect runs work that connects React to something outside its screen description. Here, it changes the preview document's title. It does not change the main CodeQuest tab's title.
The Effect reads `topic`, so `[topic]` tells React when to repeat it. These listed values are called dependencies. React runs the setup after the component has been added or updated on the page.

The returned function is cleanup: work that undoes this setup. React runs it before a changed setup and when removing the note. Here, it restores the previous title. Using `[]` would miss topic changes and leave the title out of date.

Make the title follow topic and restore the earlier title when the note is removed. Keep one TitleNote in charge of this title. Ordinary text shown in JSX can be calculated directly; it does not need an Effect.
steps: Read topic inside the Effect and include it in the dependencies.
Return cleanup that restores the captured title.
Run the checks for topic changes and removal.

checks.label: External title follows a changed dependency
checks.expression: (async()=>{const wait=async test=>{const end=Date.now()+1500;while(!test()){if(Date.now()>end)return false;await new Promise(resolve=>setTimeout(resolve,10));}return true;};if(!await wait(()=>document.title==='Study: Maps'))return false;document.querySelector('button').click();return await wait(()=>document.title==='Study: Birds');})()

checks.label: Unmount restores the prior frame title

title: A changed key starts a fresh draft
summary: Change a component's key when you deliberately want fresh local state.
explanation: Keeping a component's type and key lets React keep its state. Changing its key tells React to replace that component with a fresh one. This deliberately discards its old local state.
`useState(name)` uses name when that component instance starts. A later prop change does not automatically replace its text. `key={name}` asks for a fresh Draft when the selected name changes.

Without the changing key, the same Draft would keep its edited text after the name prop changes. A key does not save old drafts for later. To keep them, you would need to store those drafts elsewhere.

Edit the draft, then switch topics.
Run the checks and confirm the intended reset.

This example's connection is only a local counter. `open()` adds one and returns a function that subtracts one later. Return that close function from the Effect so React can use it for cleanup.

Returning nothing would leave the connection active after removal. `return close()` would close it immediately instead of giving React a cleanup function. The closed flag prevents the supplied close function from subtracting twice.

title: Quoted values and calculated columns
summary: Build a label by joining text with a calculated number.
explanation: Single quotes mark a text value. An apostrophe inside that text needs two apostrophes in the code: `'Lena''s notes'` means `Lena's notes`. Use double quotes for a table or column name when that name needs quoting.

CREATE TEMP VIEW shown AS

SELECT label
FROM shown;

title: Unknown is not false
summary: Use IS NULL to find missing information.
explanation: `NULL` means a value is missing or unknown. It is different from zero or empty text. Comparing it with `=` gives an unknown answer. Use `IS NULL` to ask whether a value is missing.
`WHERE` keeps a row only when its check is true. A false or unknown check leaves the row out. `NOT` reverses true and false, but an unknown answer stays unknown.

Run this query:
```sql
SELECT NULL = 3 AS comparison,
       NULL IS NULL AS missing,
       NOT (NULL = 3) AS negated;
```
The row is `NULL`, `1`, `NULL`. In SQLite, `1` means true and `0` means false. The missing-value check has a clear answer; the other two do not.

Sometimes a known check settles the result. True OR unknown is true, because one check already passes. False AND unknown is false, because both cannot pass. Otherwise, an unknown check may leave the combined answer unknown.
Create `unfinished(id)` from `jobs`. Include jobs whose state is `'waiting'` or is missing. Use `IS NULL` for the missing case. Keep jobs unchanged; the result should contain IDs `2` and `3`.
steps: Also check whether state IS NULL.
Join these checks with OR and save the matching IDs.
starter:
CREATE VIEW unfinished AS
SELECT id
FROM jobs
WHERE state <> 'done';
solution:
CREATE VIEW unfinished AS
SELECT id
FROM jobs
WHERE state <> 'done' OR state IS NULL;
SELECT *
FROM unfinished
ORDER BY id;

title: Membership in a small set
summary: Use IN to match any value in a short list.
explanation: `IN` asks whether a value matches anything in a list. For known colors, checking for blue or gold can be written as `colour IN ('blue', 'gold')`.
The list holds values to match. `IN` checks each source row once. Two different blue rows can both pass, but repeating blue in the list does not make extra copies of either row.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE tiles(id INTEGER, colour TEXT);
INSERT INTO tiles VALUES
  (1, 'blue'), (2, 'blue'), (3, 'gold'), (4, 'red');
SELECT id, colour
FROM tiles
WHERE colour IN ('blue', 'gold')
ORDER BY id;
```
IDs `1`, `2`, and `3` pass. Both separate blue rows remain.
Repeating `'blue'` in the list would not change this result. A match is just a yes-or-no choice for each row. Missing values need extra care, which the later NOT IN lesson covers.

title: Match text patterns literally
summary: Match an actual underscore instead of using it as a pattern symbol.
explanation: `LIKE` checks text against a pattern. In a pattern, `%` means any number of characters, including none. `_` means exactly one character.
To match the actual underscore, choose an escape character. Here, `!_` means an underscore because `ESCAPE '!'` gives `!` that special job.

Run this query:
```sql
SELECT 'note_a' LIKE 'note!_%' ESCAPE '!' AS matched,
       'noteXa' LIKE 'note!_%' ESCAPE '!' AS rejected,
       'note_' LIKE 'note!_%' ESCAPE '!' AS empty_tail;
```
The results are `1`, `0`, and `1`. The text must start with `note_`. Nothing has to follow it, because `%` can match no characters.
SQLite's usual LIKE check treats upper- and lower-case English letters alike. That rule does not cover every alphabet: `æ` and `Æ` do not match without extra support.

title: Choose a value with CASE
summary: Use CASE to choose one label from several checks.
explanation: `CASE` chooses a value. It checks each `WHEN` in order and returns the value after the first matching `THEN`. `ELSE` supplies a fallback, and `END` finishes the choice.
A score of 22 is at least 20 and at least 10. Check the higher limit first if it should win. CASE stops at the first true check; it does not look for a better match later.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_scores(score INTEGER);
INSERT INTO demo_scores VALUES (22), (12), (4), (NULL);
SELECT score,
       CASE
         WHEN score IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
         WHEN score >= 20 THEN 'high'
         WHEN score >= 10 THEN 'middle'
         ELSE 'low'
       END AS band
FROM demo_scores
ORDER BY score;
```
The labels are `unknown` for NULL, `low` for 4, `middle` for 12, and `high` for 22.
A missing score does not pass a number comparison. `IS NULL` gives it its own label. Without that branch, this example would reach ELSE and wrongly label the missing score low.
Create `bands(id, band)` from `scores`. Use `high` for at least 20, `middle` for at least 10 but below 20, `low` below 10, and `unknown` for NULL. Keep the original scores unchanged.

Check the high limit before the middle limit.
Use ELSE for low and name the result band.

title: Choose numeric division deliberately
summary: Choose division that keeps a fractional result.
explanation: In SQLite, dividing small whole-number values uses integer division. It drops the fractional part toward zero. So `7 / 2` gives `3`, while `-7 / 2` gives `-3`.
A REAL value can hold a fractional part. `CAST(value AS REAL)` asks SQLite to convert the value to that number type before doing the division.

Run this query:
```sql
SELECT 7 / 2 AS whole,
       CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2 AS fraction,
       -7 / 2 AS negative;
```
The result is `3`, `3.5`, and `-3`. Converting before dividing keeps the half.
SQLite returns NULL for division by zero. REAL values can also have small rounding differences because some fractions cannot be stored exactly.
Create `shares(id, average)` from `supplies`. Divide total by people using real-number division. A row with zero people must have a NULL average. Leave supplies unchanged.

title: Stored values and column affinity
summary: Check the kind of value SQLite actually stored.
explanation: An ordinary SQLite column has a preferred type, called its affinity. An INTEGER column tries to store suitable values as whole numbers. That declaration alone does not refuse every other kind of value.
`typeof(value)` reports the kind of value actually stored, such as `integer`, `real`, `text`, or `null`. It does not just repeat the column's declared type.

The numeric text can be converted; the word cannot. Ordinary SQLite tables allow this flexibility. Use stricter table rules when accepting text would break your program. The next lesson shows one way.

Create ordinary `readings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, value INTEGER)`. Insert quoted text `'17'` at id `1` and `'unknown'` at id `2`. Create `observed(id, kind)` using typeof to show how each value was stored.

title: Use a STRICT table
summary: Use STRICT to refuse values that do not fit a column's type.
explanation: `STRICT` after a table definition makes SQLite enforce the column types it supports. An INTEGER column can then refuse text that cannot become a whole number.
STRICT still allows a conversion that keeps the value. Text such as `'12'` can become integer `12`. It does not mean every value must arrive with exactly the right type.

The word `'cloudy'` cannot fit this INTEGER column, so an insert of it fails. NULL also fails here because of NOT NULL. SQLite STRICT tables accept a limited list of type names; use its supported names, such as INTEGER and TEXT.
Create `readings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, value INTEGER NOT NULL) STRICT`. Insert text `'14'` at id `1` and integer `9` at id `2`. Both must be stored as integers.

An error from an invalid insert is not a successful project run. Keep deliberate failures out of your submission. The project checks the table's STRICT setting and its saved values; those checks are not a test of every possible bad input.

title: Defaults are not missing-value repair
summary: A default fills an omitted value; it does not replace an explicit NULL.
explanation: `DEFAULT` supplies a starting value when an insert leaves out a column. It does not keep checking old rows or repair missing values later.
Leaving a column out is different from supplying `NULL`. An omitted column can use its default. An explicit NULL stays NULL when the column allows missing values.
The first insert leaves status out, so it uses the default. The second insert supplies a value—NULL—so the default is not used. A supplied text value would also take the place of the default.

`NOT NULL` is a separate rule that refuses missing values. The example requires a title but allows a missing status. With an ordinary INSERT, a default does not rescue an explicit NULL in a NOT NULL column.

Create `reminders` with an integer primary key `id`, a required text `title`, and a text `status` that allows NULL and defaults to `'open'`. Insert Read as id `1` without status. Insert Walk as id `2` with explicit NULL.

Insert Read while leaving status out.
Insert Walk with NULL as its status.

CREATE TABLE reminders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT DEFAULT 'open');

quiz.question: A status column allows NULL and defaults to queued. One insert omits status; another supplies NULL. What is stored?
quiz.explanation: Only the omitted value uses the default. The explicit NULL stays NULL.

title: Check a row rule
summary: Use CHECK for an allowed range and NOT NULL for a required value.
explanation: A constraint is a rule for stored data. `CHECK` tests a rule when a row is added or changed. Here, the rule asks whether seats is between 1 and 4.
In SQLite, CHECK refuses a row when its result is zero, meaning false. It accepts a nonzero result or NULL. An unknown result does not count as a failed CHECK.
The missing value passes CHECK because the test is unknown, not false. Add `NOT NULL` when seats must be present. CHECK and NOT NULL do different jobs.
Create `bookings` with id as its integer primary key. Require seats with NOT NULL and restrict it with `CHECK(seats BETWEEN 1 AND 4)`. Insert seats `1` at id `1` and seats `4` at id `2`.

An ordinary insert of seats 5 fails the range check. A missing seat value fails NOT NULL when that rule is present. Keep deliberate failing inserts out of the project submission; the normal checks expect a successful run.

Insert the two boundary values, 1 and 4.
Run the checks and explain what each rule does.

CREATE TABLE bookings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, seats INTEGER CHECK(seats BETWEEN 1 AND 4));

quiz.question: A column allows NULL and has CHECK(seats BETWEEN 1 AND 4). Which value fails that CHECK?
quiz.explanation: 5 is outside the range. 4 is inside it. NULL makes an unknown result, which CHECK accepts.

hints: BETWEEN includes both limits.
CHECK alone does not reject NULL.

title: Make a pair unique
summary: Use two columns together to identify a row.
explanation: A composite key is a key made from several columns. `PRIMARY KEY(person, day)` makes each person-and-day pair unique. The same person can have another day, and another person can use the same day.
Put NOT NULL on both columns so neither part is missing. Do not assume every ordinary SQLite primary-key declaration rejects missing values.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_slots (
  person TEXT NOT NULL,
  day TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY(person, day)
);
INSERT INTO demo_slots VALUES
  ('Lena', 'Mon'), ('Lena', 'Tue'), ('Noor', 'Mon');
SELECT person, day
FROM demo_slots
ORDER BY person, day;
```
All three pairs are different, so all three rows are accepted.

A UNIQUE rule can also forbid repeated complete pairs. But SQLite treats NULLs as different for uniqueness, so missing parts can allow rows that look repeated. Requiring both values avoids that problem here.
Adding Lena/Mon again would repeat the whole key and fail. Reusing only Lena or only Mon is allowed. Keep deliberate failures out of the normal project submission.
Create `slots` with required text columns `person` and `day`, using them together as the primary key. Store Mira/Mon, Mira/Tue, and Oren/Mon once each.

title: Avoid nullable NOT IN surprises
summary: Find unblocked IDs without letting missing values confuse the check.
explanation: `NOT IN` can give an unknown answer when its list contains NULL. If the blocked list has 2 and NULL, SQL cannot say for sure that 1 is absent. WHERE does not keep an unknown answer.
`NOT EXISTS` asks a different question: did the inner query find an equal row? A missing blocked value does not equal a candidate under ordinary `=` comparison.
NOT EXISTS alone would also keep the NULL candidate: ordinary equality finds no row equal to it. The separate IS NOT NULL check states that missing candidate IDs are not allowed.
Create `allowed` from the supplied tables. Keep only nonmissing candidate IDs with no equal ID in blocked. Leave both source tables unchanged. NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are not always interchangeable.

title: Give one table two roles
summary: Read the same table once as workers and once as their managers.
explanation: A self-join connects a table to itself. Give each use a short name so you can tell its role. One use reads the worker; the other reads the manager.
Match the worker's manager_id to the manager's id. The short names do not copy or change the stored table. They just tell the query which role a column belongs to.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE staff(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES
  (1, 'Ari', NULL), (2, 'Bo', 1), (3, 'Cy', 1), (4, 'Dee', 2);
SELECT person.name AS worker, boss.name AS manager
FROM staff AS person
LEFT JOIN staff AS boss ON boss.id = person.manager_id
ORDER BY person.id;
```
The pairs are Ari/NULL, Bo/Ari, Cy/Ari, and Dee/Bo.
LEFT JOIN keeps Ari even though no manager matches. An INNER JOIN would leave Ari out. This query finds only the immediate manager; it does not follow the whole chain of managers.
Create `report(worker, manager)` from the supplied staff table. Keep all four people, including Ari with a NULL manager. Leave staff unchanged.
steps: Give staff a worker role and a manager role.
LEFT JOIN the manager's id to the worker's manager_id.
Save the two names as worker and manager in report.
starter:
CREATE TABLE report AS SELECT name AS worker,name AS manager
FROM staff;
solution:
CREATE TABLE report AS SELECT child.name AS worker,parent.name AS manager
FROM staff AS child
LEFT JOIN staff AS parent ON parent.id=child.manager_id
ORDER BY child.id;
SELECT worker,manager
FROM report
ORDER BY worker;

checks.expression: SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 FROM report WHERE worker='Ari' AND manager IS NULL;

checks.label: Bo manager
checks.expression: SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 FROM report WHERE worker='Bo' AND manager='Ari';

checks.label: Cy manager
checks.expression: SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 FROM report WHERE worker='Cy' AND manager='Ari';

checks.label: Dee manager
checks.expression: SELECT COUNT(*) = 1 FROM report WHERE worker='Dee' AND manager='Bo';

title: Filter matches without losing parents
summary: Choose which tasks match without removing projects that have none.
explanation: In a LEFT JOIN, `ON` decides which right-side rows count as matches. Put the unfinished-task check there when every project must stay in the result.
If no task passes the ON checks, the project still appears with NULL task columns. A project with two unfinished tasks gets two result rows.
`WHERE t.done = 0` would filter the joined rows afterward. It removes finished tasks and also removes rows where done is NULL. Projects with no unfinished task would disappear.
Create `open_tasks(project_id, task_id)` from the supplied projects and tasks. Keep every project and match only unfinished tasks. Leave both source tables unchanged.

CREATE TABLE open_tasks AS SELECT p.id AS project_id,t.id AS task_id
FROM projects AS p
LEFT JOIN tasks AS t ON t.project_id=p.id AND t.done=0
ORDER BY p.id,t.id;

FROM open_tasks
ORDER BY project_id,task_id;
